records.title: Retirement: Azure Stream Analytics PowerBI output connector
records.summary: Microsoft will retire the Azure Stream Analytics Power BI output connector on October 31, 2027. Existing jobs using it will stop, and existing customers will no longer be able to create new jobs with it. New customers have been restricted since October 31, 2024. Migrate before retirement to avoid disruption. Options include Fabric Real-Time Intelligence or retaining Azure Stream Analytics with an alternative output for Power BI reporting. The supplied references do not establish a separate Power BI real-time streaming retirement deadline.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft will retire the Azure Stream Analytics Power BI output connector on October 31, 2027. Existing customers can use it without disruption until retirement; afterward, existing jobs using it stop and new jobs cannot use it. New customers have been restricted since October 31, 2024.

Microsoft recommends Fabric Real-Time Intelligence. The migration article also describes retaining Azure Stream Analytics processing with another output and continuing Power BI reporting through replacement data sources.

The sources identify Power BI real-time streaming retirement as related context but do not establish its separate deadline. They do not specify regional or version exceptions, or maintenance and security-update commitments.

Microsoft will retire the Azure Stream Analytics Power BI output connector on October 31, 2027. Existing customers can use it without disruption until retirement; afterward, existing jobs using it stop and new jobs cannot use it. New customers have been restricted since October 31, 2024.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Migrate jobs away from the Power BI output connector before October 31, 2027 to avoid job shutdown.

1. Identify your Azure Stream Analytics jobs that use Power BI as an output. The supplied sources provide no inventory method.
2. Select a replacement architecture. For Fabric Real-Time Intelligence, use Eventstream to ingest and transform events, with an Eventhouse KQL database recommended for real-time reporting; the article also lists Lakehouse as a destination. To retain Azure Stream Analytics processing, send its output to Fabric or use a listed DirectQuery-compatible alternative: SQL Server, PostgreSQL, SynapseSQL or Azure Data Explorer.
3. For the Azure Stream Analytics-to-Fabric pattern, configure an Eventstream custom endpoint, obtain its Event Hub namespace and connection details, configure an Event Hub output in Azure Stream Analytics, and add Eventhouse as the Eventstream destination.
4. Connect Power BI to the selected source. Automatic page refresh requires a DirectQuery-compatible source. Import mode is an option if you do not need automatic page refresh; for very short refresh intervals, the article suggests exploring Fabric Real-Time Dashboard.

The supplied content provides no detailed validation, export, backup, cutover or cleanup procedure, and does not establish full capability parity.

deadline.dateGuidance:
The Azure Stream Analytics Power BI output connector retires on October 31, 2027, when existing jobs using it will stop.

- October 31, 2024: New customers could no longer create jobs using this connector.

The migration article supplies no separate deadline for Power BI real-time streaming. Its publication and update dates are not retirement milestones; the Fabric documentation index establishes no retirement date.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Health Data Services will be retired on October 31, 2025 in the Qatar Central region
records.summary: Microsoft announced retirement of Azure Health Data Services in Qatar Central, but the supplied notice conflicts: its title and main text specify October 31, 2025, while another paragraph specifies October 31, 2024. The deadline remains unconfirmed; no extension is documented. The main notice warns that regional workloads will be deleted and associated application data lost. It directs customers to migrate to another available region and back up data they need to retain.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft announced retirement of Azure Health Data Services in Qatar Central, citing resource consolidation and low regional usage.

The main notice states that you could continue using the service without disruption until October 31, 2025, followed by deletion of regional workloads and loss of associated application data. A conflicting paragraph gives October 31, 2024 as the retirement date.

Other available Azure Health Data Services regions are migration destinations; the notice does not announce their retirement.
what.html:

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Azure Health Data Services workloads and application data in Qatar Central. The notice supplies no discovery procedure.
2. Ask Microsoft to clarify the conflicting dates and current regional status through Microsoft Q&A or, if you have a support plan and need technical assistance, a support request.
3. For workloads still available to migrate, select another available Azure Health Data Services region. Check destination availability and access restrictions; the regional reference notes that some regions restrict access but does not establish a suitable destination for your workloads.
4. Follow the notice's direction to migrate workloads and back up data you need to retain before retirement. Both stated dates have passed; the supplied content does not establish whether migration or backup remains possible. It also mentions removing data as an option.

No migration, backup, export, validation or cleanup procedure is supplied.

records.title: Retirement: Change Analysis (classic) API in Azure Monitor is retiring
records.summary: The notice sets Azure Monitor Change Analysis (classic) API retirement for October 31, 2025 and requires migration to Change Analysis powered by Azure Resource Graph before that date. It warns of workload deletion and associated application data loss, but does not confirm whether retirement or deletion occurred. The replacement guidance documents coverage exclusions and a 14-day change-history query window; it does not independently establish a retirement deadline.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Monitor Change Analysis (classic) API is retiring. Microsoft directs you to Change Analysis powered by Azure Resource Graph (ARG).

The notice describes the replacement as providing the same monitoring capabilities, plus real-time insights, granular filtering, grouping, change-actor identification, cross-query and alerting. However, the replacement guidance explicitly excludes data-plane changes and App Service file and configuration changes; do not assume coverage for those use cases.

The supplied content does not specify regional exceptions, classic API availability before retirement, or maintenance, support and security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your workloads and integrations that use Azure Monitor Change Analysis (classic) API. The supplied content provides no discovery method.
2. Assess Change Analysis powered by ARG against your use cases. It covers supported Azure Resource Manager control-plane changes, but excludes data-plane changes and App Service file and configuration changes. No alternative is documented for those excluded cases.
3. Migrate affected usage to ARG Change Analysis. The notice required migration before October 31, 2025. The replacement guidance documents the portal experience and the preferred POST Microsoft.ResourceGraph/resources API, plus scoped GET/LIST Microsoft.Resources/Changes and Microsoft.Resources/Snapshots APIs.
4. If you need change history beyond 14 days, the replacement guidance describes integrating a Resource Graph query with Azure Logic Apps and manually exporting results to an Azure data store such as Log Analytics. This is a retention option, not a documented migration requirement.

The supplied content does not provide a migration procedure, migration prerequisites, backup instructions, cutover, validation or cleanup steps.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
The retirement notice applies to workloads using Azure Monitor Change Analysis (classic) API. It warns that those workloads will be deleted and associated application data lost. It does not define the affected workload or data boundaries, give a separate deletion date, or confirm that deletion occurred. Your actual exposure cannot be determined from these pages.

The replacement records supported resource creation, updates and deletion through the Azure Resource Manager control plane. Supported resource types come from the resources, resourcecontainers and healthresources tables. Coverage includes supported App Services and virtual machines, but excludes data-plane changes and App Service file and configuration changes.

Change history is queryable for 14 days. The replacement portal experience requires no onboarding, and ARG Change Analysis is available at no extra cost. Costs for longer-retention export destinations are not specified. The content does not separately establish unaffected classic configurations or consequences for deployment tooling.

records.title: Retirement: Azure CDN Standard/Premium from Edgio (formerly Verizon) will be retired
records.summary: All Azure CDN Standard/Premium from Edgio customers needed to complete migration by January 14, 2025, ahead of the scheduled platform shutdown on January 15, 2025. The FAQ explicitly replaced the former November 4, 2025 retirement date; this was not an extension. Microsoft recommended Azure Front Door Standard/Premium for compatible workloads or another CDN. Best-effort automatic migration did not guarantee compatibility or continuity. The supplied sources describe the planned shutdown but do not confirm its outcome or your resources' current state. Retained-domain support follows separate deadlines and does not extend Edgio service.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure CDN Standard/Premium from Edgio, formerly Verizon, was scheduled to shut down on January 15, 2025, affecting all customers of that offering. Customers needed to migrate by January 14, 2025 to Azure Front Door Standard/Premium for compatible workloads or another CDN.

Microsoft scheduled best-effort automatic migration of eligible profiles to Azure Front Door Standard. Subscriptions with the opt-out flag and endpoints using *.vo.msecnd.net were excluded. Automatic migration could not be rolled back and did not guarantee feature parity or workload compatibility.

Existing services could continue operating during the configuration freeze, but Microsoft did not guarantee availability through shutdown. The supplied sources document no maintenance or security-update commitments and do not confirm the eventual shutdown or migration outcome.

Retained domains have separate support deadlines. The supplied comparison page's retirement dates for Front Door (classic) and Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic) concern different services, not extensions of Edgio service.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
The migration deadlines have passed. Establish your current resource and workload state rather than assuming automatic migration succeeded.

1. Review the Migrate away from Azure CDN from Edgio dashboard and Microsoft's migration-status emails. Inventory each affected profile, endpoint, origin, domain, caching and compression setting, WAF configuration and custom rule.
2. Select a compatible destination. Microsoft recommends Azure Front Door Standard/Premium for suitable workloads; alternatives include Akamai through Azure Marketplace or another CDN. Validate compatibility in a test environment. Documented gaps include geo-filtering rules requiring WAF configuration and private Azure Storage access using rule-engine SAS tokens requiring Front Door Premium with Private Link. Front Door does not accept internal-CA or self-signed certificates.
3. Follow the applicable migration guidance for every endpoint. Reproduce routes, domains and relevant settings; match origin paths to avoid 4xx errors. Endpoints using *.vo.msecnd.net required an alternative to automatic migration. Microsoft recommends a custom domain rather than continued reliance on provider-owned domains.
4. Test before cutover. The gradual Traffic Manager approach requires existing custom domains, an internet-connected VM capable of running Wget or PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, and URL monitoring. Establish HTTP-header and geographic-availability baselines. The guide's example uses Azure Blob Storage and needs adaptation for other origins.
5. For that gradual approach, test Front Door locally and remove temporary hosts-file entries. Reduce the custom-domain DNS TTL to 600 seconds, configure weighted Traffic Manager routing and shift traffic starting at 10%, increasing in 10% increments only after checking availability, performance and logs. The guide recommends testing over several days.
6. At completion, enable Front Door at weight 100, disable the Edgio Traffic Manager endpoint, point the custom-domain CNAME directly to Front Door, verify DNS propagation and restore the original TTL. Update clients referencing the old azureedge.net endpoint where applicable. Without custom domains, this gradual approach is unavailable; update clients unless using the documented temporary domain-retention option.
7. Validate certificates, DNS, routing, workload behavior and Front Door metrics and logs. Contact Microsoft Support for failed migrations or functionality, availability and performance issues; direct billing questions to support or your account team.

Historically, opting out required the subscription-level DoNotForceMigrateEdgioCDNProfiles flag before January 7, 2025; setting it before January 3, 2025 also avoided the configuration freeze. These are past prerequisites, not available deadline extensions.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are in scope if you used Azure CDN Standard/Premium from Edgio profiles or endpoints. The sources do not establish your inventory, migration status or current exposure.

- Workload continuity: Unmigrated workloads faced interruption at the scheduled January 15, 2025 shutdown. Microsoft did not guarantee availability beforehand. Best-effort automatic migration was not a continuity guarantee and excluded opted-out subscriptions and *.vo.msecnd.net endpoints.
- Compatibility: Automatic migration was irreversible and could affect features, availability and performance. A success email did not prove workload compatibility. Multiple endpoints required corresponding destination configuration and validation.
- Configuration access: Profiles without the early opt-out froze on January 3, 2025, including the ability to stop endpoints. The FAQ identifies profile deletion as an alternative and warns that stopping or disabling an Edgio endpoint removes supplemental-portal resources that restarting does not automatically restore.
- Domains and cutover: Gradual Traffic Manager migration requires existing custom domains. Retained *.azureedge.net domains on Front Door Standard/Premium have support through September 30, 2027. Support for retained *.azureedge.net and *.vo.msecnd.net domains on Akamai ended on March 31, 2025. Neither date extends Edgio service.
- Billing: Front Door uses a different model, including a per-profile base fee and request and data-transfer charges. The FAQ reports a billing bug affecting some migrated profiles without a resolution date. Your cost change cannot be estimated from these sources.
- Configuration retention: Microsoft planned to retain inactive profiles as references until March 15, 2025 and delete them afterward. The sources do not confirm deletion of any particular profile or establish broader workload-data retention rules.

No region-specific exceptions or separate console/API shutdown milestones are documented. Other classic-service retirements mentioned in the comparison page are separate from this Edgio retirement.

progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use the Migrate away from Azure CDN from Edgio dashboard to identify impacted resources. The supplied sources do not establish its current coverage or your resources' current state.

Microsoft scheduled automatic-migration success or failure emails for January 7, 2025 through January 14, 2025. Treat those messages as migration-status evidence, not proof of application compatibility.

Validate completion

- Check DNS routing and propagation using the documented DNS-checking methods.
- Compare HTTP headers and URL availability before and after cutover.
- Inspect Front Door metrics and application logs for 4xx/5xx errors, cache/byte hit ratios and origin health at each traffic increment.
- For the documented Traffic Manager approach, confirm all traffic routes to Front Door, the Edgio endpoint is disabled, the final CNAME points directly to Front Door, and global DNS propagation and workload operation are verified.

The guide recommends CatchPoint or ThousandEyes for geographic monitoring. Webpagetest covers only a few locations and might miss changes until traffic has fully shifted. Traffic Manager's Always serve traffic setting disables endpoint health checks, so it does not demonstrate workload health.

The FAQ identifies misleading certificate and DNS status fields for retained *.azureedge.net domains as a portal bug that did not affect certificates or traffic; it does not confirm the bug's eventual resolution.

records.title: Retirement: Azure AI Image Analysis 4.0 Preview APIs retiring on March 31, 2025
records.summary: Azure AI Image Analysis 4.0 Preview APIs have a stated retirement date of March 31, 2025. Microsoft states that calls to the retired versions will not work afterward. Migrate to Image Analysis 4.0 GA, Data Plane API version 2024-02-01. Model customization, background removal and product recognition are not preserved by this migration; product guidance suggests evaluating Azure AI Custom Vision for similar functionality, without guaranteeing feature parity. These features had a separate Studio removal date of January 10, 2025. The supplied content does not independently confirm completed shutdown.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring these Azure AI Image Analysis 4.0 Preview API versions:

- 2022-07-31-preview
- 2022-10-12-preview
- 2023-02-01-preview
- 2023-04-01-preview
- 2023-07-01-preview
- v4.0-preview.1

The documented replacement is Image Analysis 4.0 GA, Data Plane API version 2024-02-01. Model customization, background removal and product recognition become unavailable through the retiring APIs. Product guidance recommends evaluating Azure AI Custom Vision for similar functionality, not guaranteed feature parity.

This is not a service-wide retirement and does not announce retirement of Image Analysis 4.0 GA. The sources specify no regional exceptions or retirement-related maintenance, support or security-update commitments.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Automation will discontinue execution of PowerShell runbooks using AzureRM modules from February 1, 2025
records.summary: From February 1, 2025, Azure Automation discontinues execution of all runbooks that use AzureRM modules. Update affected runbooks to Az PowerShell and remove AzureRM modules from your Automation account. AzureRM's separate deprecation on February 29, 2024 ended module maintenance and support; it is not a conflicting execution deadline. Migration requires compatibility review and validation, not just cmdlet renaming.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
From February 1, 2025, Azure Automation discontinues execution of all runbooks using AzureRM modules. Az PowerShell is the documented replacement. The notice gives no regional exceptions or explicit commitments about execution availability before the cutoff.

AzureRM itself is no longer maintained or supported following its separate February 29, 2024 deprecation. Microsoft recommends Az for continued support and updates. AzureRM scripts do not automatically work with Az: module names, cmdlets, parameters and return values can change.

Support for Enable-AzureRmAlias, Az's compatibility-alias feature, is not deprecated with AzureRM.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify affected Automation runbooks. The migration guidance documents checking installed AzureRM versions with Get-Module -Name AzureRM -ListAvailable -All and searching scripts for *-AzureRM*. These checks cover only environments and scripts you examine; the retirement notice provides no Automation-specific discovery method.
2. Before migrating, ensure your scripts work with AzureRM 6.13.2, the latest release identified by the guidance. For older versions, consult the relevant major-version migration guides; additional changes may be necessary.
3. Select a migration approach. Microsoft recommends the AzureRM-to-Az migration toolkit, which can generate a change plan before modifying scripts or installing Az, followed by the automatic-migration quickstart. As a transition, the guidance describes Az with Enable-AzureRmAlias; aliases apply only to the current session by default, with a Scope parameter available to persist them across sessions.
4. Update affected runbooks to Az and validate them against documented breaking changes. Aliases do not resolve renamed parameters or changed return values and do not guarantee compatibility.
5. Remove AzureRM modules from your Automation account as directed by the retirement notice.

The supplied pages reference installation, uninstallation and migration resources but do not provide a detailed Automation cutover procedure.

records.title: Retirement: Resources interacting with Azure Automation using TLS 1.0/1.1 protocol will be blocked from March 1, 2025
records.summary: From March 1, 2025, Azure Automation blocks TLS 1.0 and 1.1 connections from the listed clients. Running or scheduled Hybrid Worker jobs using those protocols fail. Configure affected clients to use TLS 1.2 or higher. This is a protocol restriction, not retirement of Azure Automation. The product guidance also contains a conflicting general backward-compatibility statement; its explicit, client-specific cutoff remains the applicable date, with no documented extension.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Automation blocks TLS 1.0 and 1.1 connections from March 1, 2025 for:

- Agent-based and extension-based User Hybrid Runbook Workers.
- Webhook calls.
- Automation DSC nodes.
- Machines managed by Azure Automation Update management and Change Tracking & inventory.

Affected clients must use TLS 1.2 or higher. This change restricts connectivity; it does not retire Azure Automation itself. The supplied content identifies no regional exceptions or separate maintenance, support or security-update commitments.
what.html:
Azure Automation blocks TLS 1.0 and 1.1 connections from March 1, 2025 for:

  • Agent-based and extension-based User Hybrid Runbook Workers.
  • Webhook calls.
  • Automation DSC nodes.
  • Machines managed by Azure Automation Update management and Change Tracking & inventory.

Affected clients must use TLS 1.2 or higher. This change restricts connectivity; it does not retire Azure Automation itself. The supplied content identifies no regional exceptions or separate maintenance, support or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify listed workers, webhook callers, DSC nodes and managed machines that connect using TLS 1.0 or 1.1. The supplied content does not provide an inventory command or detailed discovery procedure.
2. Configure affected clients to use TLS 1.2 or higher, including webhook calls that trigger runbooks. For Windows Hybrid Workers, follow the referenced guidance to disable TLS 1.0/1.1 and enable TLS 1.2 or above; the supplied content does not include those configuration steps.
3. For Linux Hybrid Workers, check your distribution's OpenSSL configuration and supported version. The product guidance references a configuration script and directs restarting services that use OpenSSL; the supplied content does not reproduce the script.
4. As a team-owned validation step, confirm successful connections, webhook-triggered runbooks and Hybrid Worker job execution after updating.

Avoid pinning agents exclusively to TLS 1.2 unless necessary: the guidance warns that this can prevent automatic adoption of newer protocols. TLS 1.2 is supported but not enabled by default on Windows 7 SP1 and Windows Server 2008 R2 SP1. The guidance separately advises OS upgrades for its listed out-of-support Windows Server versions.

records.title: Retirement: All Azure Automation jobs running on Agent-based Hybrid Worker will be stopped from 1 April 2025
records.summary: Starting April 1, 2025, Azure Automation will stop jobs running on agent-based (V1) User Hybrid Runbook Workers on Windows and Linux. These workers retired on August 31, 2024 and no longer receive support or security fixes. Migrate to extension-based (V2) User Hybrid Runbook Workers to continue executing Hybrid jobs. The deployment guides document migration and coexistence but do not establish another deadline or extend V1 job execution.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Automation is stopping jobs on agent-based (V1) User Hybrid Runbook Workers on Windows and Linux starting April 1, 2025. Microsoft recommends extension-based (V2) User Hybrid Runbook Workers for continued Hybrid job execution.

V1 workers no longer receive support or security fixes following retirement on August 31, 2024. The supplied notice does not establish a separate maintenance commitment before job execution stops.

V2 deployment guidance covers Azure VMs and supported Azure Arc-enabled machines, including servers, VMware vSphere VMs and SCVMM VMs. Extension-based onboarding does not apply to System Hybrid Runbook Workers.

V1 and V2 can coexist on the same machine as separate platform entries. Installing V2 does not affect V1 installation or management, but this coexistence is not a commitment to continue V1 job execution after the stopping date.
what.html:
Azure Automation is stopping jobs on agent-based (V1) User Hybrid Runbook Workers on Windows and Linux starting April 1, 2025. Microsoft recommends extension-based (V2) User Hybrid Runbook Workers for continued Hybrid job execution.

V1 workers no longer receive support or security fixes following retirement on August 31, 2024. The supplied notice does not establish a separate maintenance commitment before job execution stops.

V2 deployment guidance covers Azure VMs and supported Azure Arc-enabled machines, including servers, VMware vSphere VMs and SCVMM VMs. Extension-based onboarding does not apply to System Hybrid Runbook Workers.

V1 and V2 can coexist on the same machine as separate platform entries. Installing V2 does not affect V1 installation or management, but this coexistence is not a commitment to continue V1 job execution after the stopping date.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your V1 User workers under Automation account > Process Automation > Hybrid worker groups > your group > Hybrid Workers. Check the Platform field for Agent based (V1). Do not apply this onboarding procedure to System workers.
2. Prepare V2 prerequisites: at least two cores and 4 GB RAM, a supported x64 OS and required packages, a system-assigned managed identity, and the Azure Connected Machine agent for non-Azure machines. V2 uses system-assigned managed identities instead of self-managed certificates and does not require the Log Analytics agent.
3. Check runtime compatibility. Windows requires Windows PowerShell 5.1 and .NET Framework 4.6.2 or later; the supplied prerequisites do not support PowerShell Core on Windows. Linux must not have Linux Hardening enabled and does not support Python 3.11 or later. Linux PowerShell runbooks require PowerShell Core 6.0.0 or later.
4. Allow outbound port 443 to the documented Azure Automation endpoints for your cloud. Use AutomationHybridServiceUrl, not RegistrationUrl. For custom Windows worker credentials, grant the documented folder permissions directly when UAC/LUA applies. Reapply Arc token-folder permissions after Connected Machine agent updates remove them.
5. In the existing worker group, select Hybrid Workers > + Add, select the existing V1 machine and add it. The guides also document Bicep, ARM templates, PowerShell, REST API and Azure CLI for migration at scale. Creating a worker registration alone does not install its extension.
6. Confirm successful extension installation under the VM's Extensions tab and an Extension based (V2) platform entry. As team-owned validation, test your required runbooks on V2 before removing V1; the guides provide no detailed acceptance or cutover test. Coexistence does not override the April 1, 2025 job-stopping date.
7. Remove the V1 worker after validating V2. Deleting its portal entry leaves a stale worker on the VM; follow the referenced agent-uninstall guidance. Do not delete the V2 entry as V1 cleanup: deleting V2 removes its extension. Empty a worker group before deleting it.

Microsoft recommends avoiding extension installation on domain controllers and enabling automatic extension upgrades. Minor-version upgrades are automatic by default; major-version upgrades require manual management. No retirement-specific backup or export procedure is supplied.

impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
This affects jobs running on agent-based (V1) User Hybrid Runbook Workers on Windows and Linux. Starting April 1, 2025, Azure Automation will stop those jobs if they remain on V1. V1 workers have received no support or security fixes since August 31, 2024.

Use each worker group's Platform field to identify affected registrations. The supplied sources do not establish that System workers follow this migration path or that existing V2 workers require another platform migration.

Important V2 constraints include:

- Virtual Machine Scale Sets are unsupported. Migration adds V2 within the existing worker group; a machine cannot join another group while it already belongs to one.
- The deployment guidance describes a 25% Linux CPU quota during worker configuration; one supplied summary states the limit without that qualification. Windows has no equivalent documented limit.
- Proxy configuration through cmdlets or API is not supported for Arc-enabled VMware vSphere VMs.
- Missing custom-credential folder permissions can suspend jobs. Arc agent updates can remove token-folder permissions, requiring you to reapply them.
- Windows Server 2012 and 2012 R2 appear in the OS list, but the guides also mark them end of support and advise upgrades. Their listing is not a renewed support commitment.

Installing V2 does not remove V1. Portal removal of V1 does not uninstall its machine-side worker. The sources do not document retirement-related console/API removal, stored-data access changes, retention or deletion policies, or cost consequences.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use the documented deployment checks to track migration; the guides provide no retirement-specific completion dashboard or certification.

1. Review each relevant worker group's Hybrid Workers Platform field. Separate V1 and V2 entries can represent the same machine, not completed V1 cleanup.
2. Check successful Hybrid Worker extension installation under the VM's Extensions tab. Registration happens before installation finishes, so a worker entry alone does not prove installation succeeded.
3. Use the documented worker/group retrieval cmdlets or REST GET operations to confirm registrations. Check installed extension versions using the documented Windows version folder or Linux extension-folder name. These checks do not validate runbook execution.
4. Keep team-owned migration evidence of V2 installation, required runbook validation and V1 agent removal. A removed V1 portal entry alone does not prove machine-side uninstallation.

VM insights can monitor processor, memory, network and disk performance for Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers; it does not establish migration completion. For deployment problems, the guides reference troubleshooting guidance for VM extension-based Hybrid Runbook Workers.

records.title: Retirement: Transition from Azure Data Studio to Visual Studio Code
services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines
records.service: Azure Cosmos DB · Azure Database for PostgreSQL · Azure SQL · Azure SQL Database · Azure SQL Edge · Azure SQL Managed Instance · SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines
records.summary: Azure Data Studio retired on February 28, 2026. Microsoft ended support, maintenance, updates and security fixes. Move SQL development to Visual Studio Code with the MSSQL extension, and use SSMS for SQL Server Agent and full administration. Existing queries, scripts and SQL database projects need no conversion, but extension workflows need review and some replacements remain pending. The supplied guidance does not establish application or database shutdown, file-access loss or data deletion.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Data Studio is retired. Microsoft recommends Visual Studio Code with the MSSQL extension for continued SQL development support. Existing queries, scripts and SQL database projects work without conversion.

Visual Studio Code runs on Windows, macOS and Linux. The MSSQL extension primarily supports SQL Server, Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance and SQL database in Fabric. Use SSMS for SQL Server Agent and full administration.

No version-specific or regional exceptions are stated. MySQL and Azure Cosmos DB Migration for MongoDB replacements remain pending. The separate SSMS 22 installation page does not establish retirement of earlier SSMS versions.

Azure Data Studio is retired. Microsoft recommends Visual Studio Code with the MSSQL extension for continued SQL development support. Existing queries, scripts and SQL database projects work without conversion.

Visual Studio Code runs on Windows, macOS and Linux. The MSSQL extension primarily supports SQL Server, Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance and SQL database in Fabric. Use SSMS for SQL Server Agent and full administration.

No version-specific or regional exceptions are stated. MySQL and Azure Cosmos DB Migration for MongoDB replacements remain pending. The separate SSMS 22 installation page does not establish retirement of earlier SSMS versions.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Azure Data Studio queries, scripts, projects and extensions, and match required workflows to replacement capabilities.
2. Install Visual Studio Code and the MSSQL extension from its Marketplace. Open existing queries, scripts and SQL database projects without conversion. Continue keeping database projects in source control; Visual Studio with SSDT is another project option.
3. Choose alternatives by use case: SSMS for SQL Server Agent and full administration; the PostgreSQL extension for PostgreSQL; Azure Databases for Visual Studio Code for Azure Cosmos DB's MongoDB API. MySQL and Azure Cosmos DB Migration for MongoDB replacements remain pending.
4. For migration assessment, use SQL Server enabled by Azure Arc. Replace the Azure SQL migration extension with dedicated tooling for your target: Azure SQL Managed Instance, SQL Server on Azure VMs or Azure SQL Database.
5. As a team-owned completion check, verify required workflows in the selected tools.

If you choose SSMS 22, check system requirements and compatibility: it supports SQL Server 2014 and later; consult Release history for older versions. Initial installation requires local administrator permissions and uses Visual Studio Installer, not a standalone MSI. Side-by-side installation is available.

The retirement guidance does not prescribe backup, cutover or uninstall procedures.

records.title: Retirement: Bing Search APIs with Your LLM on March 6, 2025

actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
The documented affected population is partners using S15, S16, S17 or S18 resources for Bing Search APIs with your LLM. Applications cannot continue using the product after decommissioning. New customer signups will also be unavailable. The notice does not establish whether other tiers are affected or unaffected.

If you evaluate the documented classic Grounding configuration, its existing constraints include normal network access without VPNs or Private Endpoints, model exclusions for gpt-4o-mini version 2024-07-18 and gpt-5 models, and no developer or end-user access to raw search results. Usage can incur charges; Bing queries, tool parameters and the resource key leave the Azure compliance boundary. These are classic-tool constraints, not retirement effects or confirmed replacement requirements.

The supplied content does not document retirement-related data retention, deletion, migration costs or separate console and deployment-tooling changes. No tenant resources have been inspected.

records.title: Retirement: GPU image (Preview) in AKS
records.summary: AKS GPU VHD Image (preview) retired on January 10, 2025: support ended and new node-pool creation using the image stopped. Image removal starting July 17, 2025 causes scaling failures for existing nodes using the image. Migrate affected workloads to supported GPU-enabled node pools. These milestones do not establish a workload shutdown date or retirement of all AKS GPU-enabled node pools.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired AKS GPU VHD Image (preview) on January 10, 2025. Existing node pools using it are unsupported, and you cannot create new pools with that image. Image removal starting July 17, 2025 adds scaling failures for existing nodes using it.

The retirement concerns this preview image, not GPU workloads or AKS GPU-enabled node pools generally. The notices do not specify regional exceptions or security-update commitments for the retired image.
what.html:
Microsoft retired AKS GPU VHD Image (preview) on January 10, 2025. Existing node pools using it are unsupported, and you cannot create new pools with that image. Image removal starting July 17, 2025 adds scaling failures for existing nodes using it.

The retirement concerns this preview image, not GPU workloads or AKS GPU-enabled node pools generally. The notices do not specify regional exceptions or security-update commitments for the retired image.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify workloads running on GPU VHD-enabled node pools. The supplied sources do not provide a retirement-specific inventory procedure.
2. Create replacement GPU-enabled node pools using a supported GPU VM SKU. The retirement notices identify two alternatives: manually install the NVIDIA device plugin, or bypass automatic driver installation and manually install the NVIDIA GPU Operator.
3. If you choose self-managed drivers, use the GPU driver field set to none rather than the retired driver-installation bypass tag. This requires Azure CLI 2.72.2 or later and, if installed, aks-preview 18.0.0b2 or later. You own driver maintenance and compatibility; the GPU Operator can install the required device plugin.
4. Migrate your workloads to the replacement pools, then validate GPU resources, scheduling and workload execution.

The replacement driver field is documented for node-pool creation, not update or upgrade commands, which preserve its original value. The setting does not change existing nodes; the product guidance describes scaling a pool to zero and back up to apply it.

Microsoft recommends AKS-managed GPU node pools for most GPU scenarios; use self-managed components when you need direct control. The supplied guidance also labels the managed option as preview in its next steps.

The supplied retirement notices do not document backup, cutover or old-pool cleanup procedures. A reported GPU/NVML issue with an alternative setup has no established resolution in the supplied content.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Tracking guidance is not available for this retirement.

The linked GPU product guidance does provide functional checks after migration:

1. Run kubectl get nodes, describe the relevant node and check its Capacity section for GPU resources.
2. Deploy the supplied sample manifests, then run kubectl get jobs samples-tf-mnist-demo --watch. A COMPLETIONS value of 1/1 indicates that the sample finished successfully.
3. Inspect the sample pod logs for GPU discovery, then remove the sample job with kubectl delete jobs samples-tf-mnist-demo.

These checks require cluster access and the relevant GPU setup. They verify GPU functionality, not migration of every affected pool or removal of every retired provisioning configuration.

For team-owned tracking, record affected pools, replacement destinations and validation results locally. Follow AKS release notes, retirement GitHub issues and Azure Updates for provider announcements; a closed issue does not prove that your migration is complete.

For help, use Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and need technical assistance, create a support request.

records.title: WebAssembly System Interface (WASI) Node Pools in AKS
records.summary: AKS blocked creation of new preview WebAssembly System Interface (WASI) node pools starting May 5, 2025. Microsoft confirmed the feature was retired on May 6, 2025; that confirmation does not extend the creation cutoff. You must migrate existing workloads to replacement node pools using the supported SpinKube approach. No existing-workload shutdown date or separate migration deadline is documented.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
AKS has retired WebAssembly System Interface (WASI) node pools (preview) and blocked new pool creation from May 5, 2025. No regional exceptions or separate retirement dates for Krustlet-based and SpinKube containerD-shim-based pools are documented.

Microsoft identifies SpinKube deployed to AKS through Azure Marketplace as the supported alternative for WebAssembly workloads. This is distinct from the retiring WASI node-pool feature: the SpinKube operator is not supported on Wasm/WASI node pools.

The sources do not establish how long existing pools remain usable or promise continued maintenance or security updates. The WASI documentation describes preview support as best-effort, with previews excluded from service-level agreements and limited warranty.
what.html:
AKS has retired WebAssembly System Interface (WASI) node pools (preview) and blocked new pool creation from May 5, 2025. No regional exceptions or separate retirement dates for Krustlet-based and SpinKube containerD-shim-based pools are documented.

Microsoft identifies SpinKube deployed to AKS through Azure Marketplace as the supported alternative for WebAssembly workloads. This is distinct from the retiring WASI node-pool feature: the SpinKube operator is not supported on Wasm/WASI node pools.

The sources do not establish how long existing pools remain usable or promise continued maintenance or security updates. The WASI documentation describes preview support as best-effort, with previews excluded from service-level agreements and limited warranty.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify affected pools using az aks nodepool show -g myResourceGroup --cluster-name myAKSCluster -n mywasipool --query workloadRuntime, substituting your resource names. A result of WasmWasi identifies an affected pool. The article requires the latest Azure CLI.
2. Select replacement node pools using the supported SpinKube approach available through Azure Marketplace. Do not install the SpinKube operator on existing WASI pools. The older Krustlet-to-shim path requires new WASI pools and conflicts with the creation restriction.
3. Prepare the replacement environment and migrate your workloads. The supplied SpinKube tutorial requires an existing Linux AKS cluster, Azure CLI 2.64.0 or later, kubectl 1.31.0 or later, Helm 3.15.4 or later, Spin 3.0.0 or later, and Node.js 21.6.2. It installs cert-manager if absent, KWasm and Spin operator components, annotates intended nodes, and deploys an application through an OCI-compatible registry and registry secret. Azure portal deployment is not supported.
4. As team-owned migration practice, validate replacement workloads before removing old resources. The tutorial provides deployment checks, not a retirement-specific migration procedure or compatibility guarantee.

No retirement-specific backup, export or cutover procedure is supplied. Tutorial cleanup covers its sample application, registry secret, tutorial-created ACR instance and installed components; it is not a blanket retirement cleanup requirement.

records.title: Retirement: Canonical Ubuntu 20.04 LTS Reaching End of Standard Support on May 31, 2025
records.summary: Ubuntu 20.04 LTS standard support ended on May 31, 2025. Existing Azure virtual machines can continue running, but Canonical's standard security, feature and maintenance updates have ended. Microsoft recommends upgrading to a supported Ubuntu LTS release or enabling Ubuntu Pro. For Ubuntu Pro 20.04, product documentation lists April 2030, while the announcement lists May 2030; use April 2030 for planning, with the discrepancy unresolved and no exact day confirmed.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Ubuntu 20.04 LTS on Azure virtual machines has reached the end of Canonical's standard support. Since May 31, 2025, Canonical no longer provides security, feature or maintenance updates under standard support. Existing virtual machines can continue running.

Standard security maintenance covers Main packages. Ubuntu Pro is an alternative providing expanded security maintenance for Main and Universe, covering critical, high and selected medium vulnerabilities. Optional support plans are separate from that maintenance coverage.
what.html:
Ubuntu 20.04 LTS on Azure virtual machines has reached the end of Canonical's standard support. Since May 31, 2025, Canonical no longer provides security, feature or maintenance updates under standard support. Existing virtual machines can continue running.

Standard security maintenance covers Main packages. Ubuntu Pro is an alternative providing expanded security maintenance for Main and Universe, covering critical, high and selected medium vulnerabilities. Optional support plans are separate from that maintenance coverage.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Azure deployments running Ubuntu 20.04 LTS and determine whether they use standard support or Ubuntu Pro. The supplied pages provide no fleet-inventory procedure.
2. Choose a supported path. For an operating-system upgrade, move from 20.04 to 22.04, then optionally to 24.04; a direct 20.04-to-24.04 upgrade is not supported. Alternatively, install 24.04 directly; Microsoft recommends it for new instances.
3. If retaining Ubuntu 20.04, consider enabling Ubuntu Pro on existing VMs or deploying new Pro VMs from Azure Marketplace. The Azure documentation says existing Ubuntu Server VMs running 16.04 LTS or later can move to Pro without redeployment or downtime. Follow the referenced Azure in-place upgrade guidance.
4. Scope and test operating-system upgrades with your workloads. The supplied Ubuntu Server upgrade-guide content is only a redirect notice, so it does not supply detailed instructions.

Microsoft recommended completing the support transition before May 31, 2025. The supplied content does not specify backup, cutover, cleanup or detailed post-migration validation steps.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Intelligent Recommendation Service to Be Retired
records.summary: Azure Intelligent Recommendations was scheduled to retire on March 31, 2026, when Microsoft would delete running workloads and the service's Machine Learning models. Existing customers could continue using the service without disruption until that date; new customer deployments stopped immediately under the notice, without a specified calendar date. Customers were required to migrate traffic, stop endpoint calls and delete service resources before shutdown. The supplied content does not confirm whether shutdown has completed.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft announced retirement of Azure Intelligent Recommendations on March 31, 2026, including deletion of running workloads and the service's Machine Learning models.

Existing customers could continue using the service without disruption until that date. New customer deployments stopped immediately under the notice. No version, region or customer exceptions are documented.
what.html:

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:

3. Migrate all traffic to your chosen alternative.
4. Stop calling the Recommendations endpoint.

The supplied content does not confirm shutdown completion or provide export, backup, migration-validation or post-shutdown recovery instructions.

For questions, contact irhelp@microsoft.com. If you have a support plan and need technical help, create a support request.

records.title: Retirement: Azure App Service Will No Longer Support Linked Databases as a Part of Custom Backups After March 31, 2028
records.summary: Starting March 31, 2028, Azure App Service custom backups will stop including linked databases, including those in existing configurations. Arrange separate database backups before that cutoff. Earlier restrictions on new custom backup configurations are scheduled for November 2025 for MySQL/PostgreSQL and April 2026 for Azure SQL/SQL Server; exact days are not supplied. App-content and configuration backups are not being retired, and the notice does not announce an app or database shutdown. Microsoft recommends native database backup and restore tools.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure App Service is retiring linked-database support in custom backups starting March 31, 2028. Existing linked-database configurations retain coverage until that cutoff; new configurations face the earlier database-specific restrictions.

The change does not retire app-content or configuration backups. Automatic backups already exclude linked databases and cannot replace database backups.

The supplied guidance lists SQL Database, Azure Database for MySQL, Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL in-app as supported linked databases; the retirement schedule also names SQL Server. No separate retirement exception is documented for MySQL in-app, and no regional exception is specified.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify apps that rely on linked-database custom backups. Review each app's Backups configuration and database selections in the Azure portal. Check Configuration connection strings: the guidance considers a database linked when a valid connection string points to it. MySQL in-app can be backed up without explicit configuration, so connection strings alone are not sufficient.
2. Arrange separate database backups before March 31, 2028. Microsoft recommends each database service's native backup and restore tools. Account for the earlier restrictions when creating new custom backup configurations.
3. For Azure Database for MySQL or PostgreSQL Flexible Server, use the respective database backup and restore guidance. App Service linked-database custom backups do not support Flexible Server; upgrading from Single Server can cause those backups to fail.
4. As a team-owned validation step, confirm that replacement backups cover each affected database and test recovery before relying on them. The supplied guidance does not provide a retirement-specific migration, cutover, cleanup or replacement-tool validation procedure.

If you need to download existing custom backups, their ZIP and XML files are available in Azure Storage. Do not modify files in the backup container; changes can make backups unrestorable.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if you rely on App Service custom backups to protect linked databases. Starting March 31, 2028, those backups will omit database data. Without a replacement strategy, you lose that backup coverage and risk data or functionality loss. The notice does not announce that running apps or databases will stop.

New configurations face linked MySQL/PostgreSQL selection restrictions from November 2025, and linked Azure SQL/SQL Server restrictions from April 2026. Existing configurations retain linked-database coverage until the final cutoff.

Existing coverage also has limits:

- Custom backups allow 10 GB total, including at most 4 GB of linked-database data; exceeding either limit causes backup failure.
- Backups configured over Azure Virtual Network cannot include linked databases.
- Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL support is limited to Single Server, not Flexible Server. TLS-enabled database backups are unsupported.
- Automatic backups exclude linked databases. App Service backup and restore requires Basic, Standard, Premium or Isolated tiers; Basic supports only the production slot.

The guidance's statement that standalone MySQL and PostgreSQL servers are unaffected concerns the separate Single Server retirement, not an exception to this cutoff. The supplied content does not specify retirement-driven backup deletion, retention changes, post-cutoff database restore availability or cost effects.

records.title: Retirement: Extended Support for Node 20 LTS Ends on April 30, 2026
records.summary: Extended support for Node 20 LTS on Azure App Service ended on April 30, 2026. Apps continue to run, but Microsoft no longer provides security updates or customer service for that version. Microsoft directed customers to upgrade to Node 22 LTS before that date. Changing runtime settings restarts your app.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft ended extended support for Node 20 LTS on Azure App Service on April 30, 2026. Existing apps continue to run, but security updates and customer service for that version have ended.

The Node.js runtime guidance covers Windows and Linux App Service. It says end-of-life versions are removed from the Runtime Stack dropdown; this selection change does not establish a shutdown of existing apps. The retirement notice specifies no regional exceptions or additional affected versions.
what.html:
Microsoft ended extended support for Node 20 LTS on Azure App Service on April 30, 2026. Existing apps continue to run, but security updates and customer service for that version have ended.

The Node.js runtime guidance covers Windows and Linux App Service. It says end-of-life versions are removed from the Runtime Stack dropdown; this selection change does not establish a shutdown of existing apps. The retirement notice specifies no regional exceptions or additional affected versions.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your App Service apps using Node 20 LTS. Check WEBSITE_NODE_DEFAULT_VERSION for Windows apps or linux-fx-version for Linux apps.
2. Upgrade affected apps to Node 22 LTS, the replacement Microsoft names in the notice. The required upgrade date was before April 30, 2026. Check platform-supported runtimes using az webapp list-runtimes --os-type windows or az webapp list-runtimes --os-type linux; these commands list runtimes, not affected apps.
3. For Windows, update the runtime app setting through the portal or Azure CLI. For Linux, use Azure CLI or select your app in the portal, then Configuration > General settings > Stack Settings > Major version, and save. Changing runtime settings restarts the app.

For Windows, Microsoft recommends tilde syntax rather than pinning an exact minor or patch version, whose availability is not guaranteed. The supplied guidance does not document Node 20-to-22 compatibility prerequisites or a post-upgrade validation procedure. As a team-owned check, record the resulting runtime configuration and validate your app's behavior after the restart.

what.announcement:

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Microsoft recommends migrating before March 31, 2026. Use the supplied guide's side-by-side examples; it assumes familiarity with the legacy library.

1. Identify applications using Microsoft.Azure.Storage.DataMovement v2. The supplied sources provide no dependency-discovery method.
2. Review upload, download, copy, progress-reporting and pause/resume usage against the v12 mappings. Check the compatibility limits before selecting replacements.

5. Review authentication and checkpoint configuration. Resume requires a provider supplying credentials for each participating storage service; local files need no provider. Checkpoints do not store credentials. Checkpointing defaults to a local temporary directory and can be configured or disabled.
6. Validate migrated transfers using completion waits, enabled progress reporting and completion, failure and skipped-item events. Review pause/resume separately because v12 uses PauseAsync and dedicated resume APIs.

The guide's authentication sections and several reference links are incomplete. It does not supply a complete cutover, backup or cleanup procedure.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are in scope if your applications use Microsoft.Azure.Storage.DataMovement v2. The migration guide covers local files, Blob Storage and file-share transfers; it does not document region-specific exceptions or unaffected customer populations.

Microsoft warns of potential service disruptions without migration, but the announcement does not establish that retirement shuts down existing workloads or removes data access on March 31, 2026.

Migration has documented compatibility limits:

- Legacy listing-concurrency limits, cache-size limits, user-agent prefixes, last-checkpoint observation and client request IDs are listed as not implemented in v12.
- Copy support is limited to service-side synchronous copy.
- Item-to-container transfers throw an exception; endpoint resource categories must match.
- Legacy post-transfer directory reports require replacement with enabled progress reporting or transfer-event handling.
- Logging configuration moves to TransferManagerOptions.Diagnostics. Not all TransferContext functionality is supported, and mapped APIs do not guarantee identical behavior.

The sources do not document retirement-related console or deployment-tooling changes, data deletion, retention changes or cost effects. They do not establish your application's exposure without reviewing its dependencies and usage.

records.title: Retirement: Kubenet Networking for Azure Kubernetes Service to Be Retired on March 31, 2028
records.summary: Microsoft will retire kubenet networking for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) on March 31, 2028. Migrate affected clusters to Azure CNI Overlay before that date to avoid the service disruptions warned of in the notice. Kubenet workloads will no longer be supported from that date; the notice does not specify a workload shutdown date. Overlay migration is irreversible, has eligibility and routing prerequisites, and reimages node pools with potential networking disruption. The supplied upgrade reference explains migration options but does not independently establish a retirement deadline.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring kubenet networking for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) on March 31, 2028. The notice directs affected customers to Azure CNI Overlay, which retains an IP address overlay architecture and adds scalability capabilities.

The notice does not specify version or regional exceptions, or maintenance and security-update commitments before retirement. From the retirement date, kubenet workloads will no longer be supported; an automatic workload shutdown is not documented.

The upgrade reference describes two separate changes:

- Azure CNI Overlay migration: An irreversible IPAM change available to eligible Kubenet and Azure CNI Node Subnet clusters. Migration back to Node Subnet is unsupported.
- Azure CNI Powered by Cilium: A separate, optional data-plane update, not a substitute for kubenet migration. Kubenet clusters must migrate to Overlay first. Existing Azure CNI clusters can adopt Cilium without changing their IPAM mode.

You cannot update IPAM and the data plane in one operation. The reference does not announce retirement of other networking configurations.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your AKS clusters using kubenet and review their Kubernetes versions, node operating systems and runtimes, network policy engines, identities, address ranges, route tables and custom IP masquerading settings. The supplied content does not provide an inventory command.
2. Confirm Overlay migration eligibility: Kubernetes 1.27 or later, no dynamic IP allocation, no enabled network policies and no Windows node pools using Docker. Uninstall the existing network policy engine if necessary. For Windows nodes, use OS build 20348.1668 or later to avoid the documented routing issue.
3. Prepare routing and identity. Kubenet migration requires a user-assigned managed identity and detachment of its associated route table; a system-assigned identity is unsupported for this operation. Any new overlay range must not overlap the node-pool virtual network address space or existing service CIDR.
4. Review custom non-SNAT ranges because Overlay pod IPs are unreachable from outside cluster nodes. Delete an unintentionally retained azure-ip-masq-agent-config ConfigMap before updating, but do not remove an intentional custom configuration without review.
5. Resolve the reference's pod CIDR ambiguity for your configuration. It says --pod-cidr is required for legacy CNI updates, but includes a Node Subnet example without it and says Kubenet retains its pod CIDR when omitted. Do not treat the parameter as universally required or optional.
6. Follow the referenced Overlay upgrade procedure and complete migration before March 31, 2028. Plan for irreversible addressing changes, simultaneous node-pool reimaging and potential networking disruption. Per-node-pool migration is unsupported.
7. As team-owned validation, check workload connectivity, routing and network policy behavior after migration. The supplied reference does not provide a post-update validation procedure or export/backup procedure.

Optional Cilium update: Perform it separately, after Overlay migration for kubenet clusters. Cilium excludes Windows node pools and requires Azure CLI 2.52.0 or later; az --version checks the CLI version. If node auto-provisioning is enabled, disable it before the update and re-enable it afterward. Review policy compatibility because Cilium replaces Azure Network Policy Manager or Calico.

records.title: Retirement: Docker Content Trust on March 31, 2028 – Replaced by the Notary Project and Azure Key Vault
records.summary: Azure Container Registry (ACR) will remove Docker Content Trust (DCT) and permanently delete its DCT signing and verification data on March 31, 2028. New DCT enablement stopped on September 30, 2025. Migrate affected signing and verification workflows to the Notary Project ecosystem, including Notation. Separately, Docker's Notary v1 endpoint at notary.docker.io shuts down on December 8, 2026; this is not an earlier ACR removal date. The supplied tutorials document replacement workflows, not additional retirement deadlines.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Container Registry will remove Docker Content Trust on March 31, 2028, ending its DCT image-signing and signature-verification functionality and deleting the associated data. Existing use is distinct from new enablement, which stopped on September 30, 2025.

Microsoft directs affected customers to the Notary Project ecosystem, including Notation. Azure Key Vault provides documented signing-key and certificate options; it is not presented as a standalone replacement for every DCT capability.

The supplied notice specifies no regional exceptions or maintenance, support or security-update commitments before removal. Docker's separate shutdown of notary.docker.io on December 8, 2026 does not establish an ACR shutdown on that date.

Azure Container Registry will remove Docker Content Trust on March 31, 2028, ending its DCT image-signing and signature-verification functionality and deleting the associated data. Existing use is distinct from new enablement, which stopped on September 30, 2025.

Microsoft directs affected customers to the Notary Project ecosystem, including Notation. Azure Key Vault provides documented signing-key and certificate options; it is not presented as a standalone replacement for every DCT capability.

The supplied notice specifies no regional exceptions or maintenance, support or security-update commitments before removal. Docker's separate shutdown of notary.docker.io on December 8, 2026 does not establish an ACR shutdown on that date.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify ACR workflows that use DCT for publishing or verifying images. Separately identify dependencies on notary.docker.io, which shuts down earlier. The ACR notice supplies no inventory method; Docker documents checking DCT configuration and using docker trust inspect, but this is not a complete dependency inventory.
2. Select a replacement workflow using Notation and the Notary Project ecosystem. Supplied guidance covers Azure Key Vault signing with self-signed or CA-issued certificates, Azure Pipelines, GitHub Actions and AKS verification. The self-signed certificate examples are for testing.
3. Prepare the required registry access, signing keys and certificates, authentication, trust stores and trust policies. Registry permissions depend on ABAC configuration. Notation v1.2.0 and later use the OCI referrers tag schema by default; the documented OCI Referrers API alternative is unsupported for registries encrypted with customer-managed keys.
4. Implement and validate signing and verification for your selected workflows before ACR removal on March 31, 2028. Address dependencies on Docker's endpoint before December 8, 2026. Use image digests rather than mutable tags in the documented signing workflows.

For AKS enforcement, test trusted, unsigned and untrusted-signer images. Deny blocks failed verification; Audit allows deployment and reports non-compliance. Do not combine the documented standalone Gatekeeper setup with the Azure Policy add-on.

Docker recommends securely backing up your DCT root key; a lost root key cannot be recovered. The supplied content does not document an ACR DCT data-export procedure, conversion of existing signatures, or a complete retirement cutover and cleanup procedure.

Implementation references contain unresolved differences in Key Vault plug-in versions, pipeline trust-policy paths and AKS timestamp trust-store instructions. Resolve those for your chosen configuration rather than treating example values as a single migration specification.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Tracking guidance is not available for this retirement.

For team-owned migration evidence, record affected signing and verification workflows, their endpoint dependencies and replacement results. The supplied references document checks you can use locally:

- Inspect signatures, certificates and trust policies, then verify the target image. Successful Notation verification returns the image's SHA256 digest.
- Review Azure Pipelines job logs or GitHub Actions run logs and confirm that the expected signature is attached in ACR.
- For configured AKS enforcement, test trusted, unsigned and untrusted-signer images; inspect Ratify logs and Azure Policy compliance results as applicable.

These checks require access to your configured resources and demonstrate only the tested workflow or policy behavior. They do not discover every dependency or establish retirement migration completion across your resources.

The supplied content identifies no retirement-specific tracker or escalation route. Notary Project Slack and community meetings are general discussion routes; Docker Hub Support is documented for lost non-root keys, not as retirement migration support.

records.title: Retirement: Prepare for the Retirement of Manually Registered Azure VPN Clients on March 31, 2028
records.summary: Microsoft will retire manually registered Azure VPN clients for Point-to-Site Microsoft Entra ID authentication on March 31, 2028 in Azure Public Cloud and March 31, 2029 in Azure Government and Microsoft Azure operated by 21Vianet. Affected clients will stop functioning after their applicable date. Update both gateways and deployed clients to the Microsoft-registered Audience value. The announcement also restricts creating connections with manually registered clients beginning December 30, 2025. Product guidance excludes custom Audience configurations and gives no retirement date for Azure Germany.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring manually registered Azure VPN clients used for Point-to-Site connections with Microsoft Entra ID authentication. The product guidance covers Windows and macOS clients.

Replace the manually registered Audience value with the Microsoft-registered value, c632b3df-fb67-4d84-bdcf-b95ad541b5c8, on both your gateway and deployed clients. Affected clients stop functioning after the applicable cloud retirement date.

The announcement separately restricts creating connections with manually registered clients beginning December 30, 2025. The sources do not specify maintenance or security-update commitments before retirement. Custom Audience configurations are outside the product article’s scope.
what.html:
Microsoft is retiring manually registered Azure VPN clients used for Point-to-Site connections with Microsoft Entra ID authentication. The product guidance covers Windows and macOS clients.

Replace the manually registered Audience value with the Microsoft-registered value, c632b3df-fb67-4d84-bdcf-b95ad541b5c8, on both your gateway and deployed clients. Affected clients stop functioning after the applicable cloud retirement date.

The announcement separately restricts creating connections with manually registered clients beginning December 30, 2025. The sources do not specify maintenance or security-update commitments before retirement. Custom Audience configurations are outside the product article’s scope.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Check the Audience values on your Point-to-Site gateway and deployed clients against the affected values listed under impact. Identify your cloud and its deadline. Do not apply this procedure to custom Audience configurations based on this article.
2. In the gateway’s Point-to-site configuration, change Audience to c632b3df-fb67-4d84-bdcf-b95ad541b5c8 and save. Leave other settings unchanged unless you changed tenants. If you update Issuer, preserve its trailing slash. Allow about five minutes for the update; documented downtime is fewer than five minutes.
3. Update every affected client. If only Audience or tenant values changed, you can manually edit existing connection profiles to match the gateway. Alternatively, generate and download a new VPN client configuration package and import it into each client. Use a generated package for new clients and when multiple gateway settings change.
4. If distributing a package, extract it and locate azurevpnconfig.xml in the AzureVPN folder. Users need valid Microsoft Entra ID credentials to connect.
5. Verify that every affected client’s Audience and any changed tenant values match the gateway before the applicable retirement date.

Removing the old Azure VPN Client from the tenant is optional good practice, not a prerequisite for connecting with the new Audience value.
