records.title: Retirement: D, Ds, Dv2, Dsv2, and Ls Series Virtual Machines to Be Retired on May 1, 2028
records.summary: Microsoft will retire Azure D, Ds, Dv2, Dsv2 and Ls series VMs on May 1, 2028. Migrate to supported sizes before that date to avoid deallocation and workload interruption. Three-year reservation purchases and renewals ended on May 1, 2025; one-year purchases and renewals ended on July 1, 2026. Existing reservations retain their original terms, but do not permit VM use after retirement.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft will retire Azure D, Ds, Dv2, Dsv2 and Ls series VMs on May 1, 2028. You must move affected workloads to supported sizes before retirement to keep them operating.

The notice does not establish an earlier end to VM use; reservation purchase and renewal restrictions are separate. After retirement, affected VMs are deallocated and lose support and SLA coverage.

The supplied guidance does not document regional exceptions for these five series or maintenance and security-update commitments before retirement. Exceptions stated for other VM series do not establish exceptions here.
what.html:
Microsoft will retire Azure D, Ds, Dv2, Dsv2 and Ls series VMs on May 1, 2028. You must move affected workloads to supported sizes before retirement to keep them operating.

The notice does not establish an earlier end to VM use; reservation purchase and renewal restrictions are separate. After retirement, affected VMs are deallocated and lose support and SLA coverage.

The supplied guidance does not document regional exceptions for these five series or maintenance and security-update commitments before retirement. Exceptions stated for other VM series do not establish exceptions here.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify workloads using D, Ds, Dv2, Dsv2 or Ls series VMs against the referenced retired-and-retiring size documentation. Review active reservations and their end dates in Azure Reservation Management. Reservation orders alone are not a complete VM inventory; reservation management requires appropriate reservation permissions.
2. Select a supported target based on CPU, memory, storage, regional and zone capacity, and workload compatibility. The guide lists Lsv3/Lasv3 and Lsv4/Lasv4 options for older storage-optimized families, but does not establish a single replacement for every affected size.
3. Check target availability, subscription quota, operating-system, disk-controller and networking requirements. If selecting v6, confirm Generation 2, NVMe support and a MANA-supported operating system. Request quota increases through the Azure portal if needed.
4. Migrate before May 1, 2028. Follow the referenced resizing guide: stop and deallocate the VM, resize to a compatible supported target, then start it. Plan for interruption and loss of in-memory and temporary-disk data. The supplied guidance does not provide detailed backup, application-cutover or cleanup procedures.
5. As team-owned validation, record the resulting size, successful restart and workload-validation results. These records are local evidence, not a documented automated completion check.

If you hold affected reservations, review their expiration dates to avoid unexpected pay-as-you-go billing. Eligible reservation exchanges or trade-ins for an Azure savings plan for compute are optional and subject to eligibility and limitations.

deadline.dateGuidance:

records.title: Retirement: Ubuntu 18.04 Node Pools in AKS
records.summary: AKS Ubuntu 18.04 node pools retired on June 17, 2025. AKS stopped producing their node images and security updates and deleted existing images, leaving affected pools unsupported and unable to scale. Migrate to a supported Ubuntu version and Kubernetes configuration. The notice names Ubuntu 22.04 as a replacement, but supplied product guidance separately ends its support on June 30, 2027. No workload shutdown date is specified.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
AKS retired Ubuntu 18.04 node pools on June 17, 2025. Affected pools no longer receive support, new node images or security updates, and image deletion prevents scaling.

The retirement notice names Ubuntu 22.04 as a supported replacement. However, the supplied product guidance separately ends Ubuntu 22.04 support on June 30, 2027 and removes its images and code on April 30, 2028. That guidance identifies Ubuntu 24.04 or later as its replacement; it does not establish a direct Ubuntu 18.04 migration path.

The notice documents no regional exceptions and does not announce retirement of all Ubuntu node pools or AKS itself.

The notice documents no regional exceptions and does not announce retirement of all Ubuntu node pools or AKS itself.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your AKS node pools running Ubuntu 18.04 and record their Kubernetes versions, OS SKUs and enabled features. The supplied content provides no Ubuntu-specific inventory procedure.
2. Select a supported target before migrating. The original notice recommends Ubuntu 22.04, but its support ends on June 30, 2027. Assess Ubuntu 24.04 or later against applicable upgrade guidance rather than assuming a direct migration path. The supplied guidance lists Ubuntu FIPS images as unsupported on Ubuntu 24.04 or later and supplies no FIPS-specific replacement path.
3. Check available Kubernetes upgrade targets with az aks get-upgrades. Follow the referenced cluster upgrade instructions, checking permissions, compute quota, deprecated APIs and version compatibility. Supported non-LTS clusters cannot skip minor versions. Unsupported-cluster recovery requires a full-cluster upgrade to an eligible supported target; if none is available, create a supported cluster and migrate workloads.
4. As team-owned validation, confirm the resulting node-pool OS and Kubernetes versions and validate your workloads. A successful Kubernetes upgrade alone does not establish that Ubuntu 18.04 has been replaced.

The required Ubuntu 18.04 transition deadline has passed. The supplied notice does not provide retirement-specific backup, cutover, rollback or cleanup procedures.

records.title: Retirement: Ubuntu 20.04 Node Pools in AKS
records.summary: AKS retires Ubuntu 20.04 node pools on March 17, 2027. Microsoft will stop producing Ubuntu 20.04 node images and security updates, delete existing node images and leave affected pools unsupported and unable to scale. No automatic workload shutdown date is documented. Migrate to a supported OS before that date. Product guidance specifies Kubernetes 1.35 or later; the announcement instead recommends 1.34 or later overall and gives a CVM-specific 1.33 threshold. These differing upgrade instructions do not change the retirement date. Check FIPS and CVM compatibility before choosing a replacement: Ubuntu 24.04 or later is listed as unsupported for Ubuntu FIPS images, while Ubuntu 22.04 has a separate support deadline of June 30, 2027.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
AKS is retiring Ubuntu 20.04 node pools on March 17, 2027, including the CVM and FIPS configurations addressed by the notice. After retirement, affected pools lose support, security updates, node images and scaling capability.

This is not a retirement of all Ubuntu images, Confidential VMs or FIPS functionality. The sources do not specify regional exceptions or pre-retirement maintenance commitments.

The announcement lists Ubuntu 22.04 and Ubuntu 24.04 as replacements, but feature compatibility and the separate Ubuntu 22.04 retirement constrain your choice.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Ubuntu 20.04 node pools, OS SKUs, Kubernetes versions and FIPS or CVM requirements. The supplied sources provide no Ubuntu-specific inventory procedure.
2. Use the applicable product guidance: upgrade affected node pools to Kubernetes 1.35 or later to migrate to a supported Ubuntu version. The announcement instead recommends 1.34 or later overall, identifies 1.33 or later as the Ubuntu 24.04 default threshold for CVM, and identifies 1.34 or later as the Ubuntu 22.04 default threshold for FIPS. These are differing upgrade instructions, not different retirement deadlines; prefer the explicit product migration guidance rather than treating a default-image threshold as proof of migration.
3. Confirm target compatibility before upgrading. Ubuntu 24.04 or later is listed as unsupported for Ubuntu FIPS images. Ubuntu 22.04 supports FIPS but loses support on June 30, 2027; the supplied guidance gives no longer-term Ubuntu FIPS migration solution. CVM supports Ubuntu 24.04, not Ubuntu 22.04, and cannot combine with FIPS, Arm64 or Trusted Launch. Resolve an unsupported target path before cutover, using technical support if you have a support plan.
4. Check available upgrade targets, deprecated APIs, permissions and compute quota. Supported non-LTS clusters cannot skip minor versions. Upgrade the control plane before node pools; a control-plane-only upgrade does not migrate node pools. Unsupported-cluster recovery requires a full-cluster upgrade to an eligible supported target, or workload migration to a new supported cluster if no target is available.
5. Complete migration before March 17, 2027. As team-owned validation, confirm the resulting node OS and Kubernetes versions and validate your workloads.

The supplied sources do not provide a complete retirement-specific backup, cutover, rollback or cleanup procedure. Automatic node image upgrades are not documented as a substitute for OS migration.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Maps Traffic APIs Version 1.0 to Be Retired on March 31, 2028
records.summary: Azure Maps Traffic APIs version 1.0 retire on March 31, 2028. Microsoft states they remain usable without disruption until that date; afterward, API calls will fail. Migrate incident details to Traffic Incident API version 2025-01-01 and traffic tiles to Get Map Tile API version 2024-04-01 before retirement. Traffic Flow Segment has no direct replacement for segment speeds or travel times. Traffic Incident Viewport is unnecessary with the newer APIs. All other Azure Maps services are unaffected by this announcement.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring these Azure Maps Traffic APIs version 1.0 on March 31, 2028:

- Get Traffic Flow Segment
- Get Traffic Flow Tile
- Get Traffic Incident Detail
- Get Traffic Incident Tile
- Get Traffic Incident Viewport

Get Traffic Incident Detail maps to Traffic Incident API version 2025-01-01. Traffic Flow Tile and Traffic Incident Tile map to Render Get Map Tile API version 2024-04-01.

Traffic Flow Segment has no direct replacement: traffic tiles visualize flow but do not provide segment speeds or travel times. Traffic Incident Viewport has no replacement and is not required by the newer APIs, which do not need its traffic model ID.

All other Azure Maps services are unaffected by this announcement. The supplied content states no regional or customer exceptions or specific maintenance and security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Review your applications for calls to the five affected Traffic v1.0 APIs. This is a team-owned review; the supplied content provides no discovery tool.
2. Replace incident-detail calls with Get Traffic Incident version 2025-01-01. Adapt bounding-box input and GeoJSON response handling, and use the response's incidentType enum for point icons.
3. Replace flow and incident tile calls with Render Get Map Tile version 2024-04-01. Select the appropriate tileset and format: documented flow tiles offer vector and raster options; the listed incident tileset is vector. Call Get Map Attribution and display the returned attribution wherever retrieved tiles are rendered, including third-party controls and custom renderers. Set the map view appropriately for users' locations and comply with applicable mapping laws.
4. Remove reliance on Traffic Incident Viewport and its traffic model ID when moving to the newer APIs.
5. Resolve dependencies on segment speeds or travel times separately. The guide provides no direct replacement; traffic visualization tiles do not supply those values.
6. Complete your transition before March 31, 2028 and stop calling version 1.0 by that date.

As optional team-owned validation, check coordinate handling, incident parsing, icons, attribution and tile rendering. The supplied content provides no cutover, backup or rollback procedure and no quantified cost comparison.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Maps Route APIs Version 1.0 to Be Retired on March 31, 2028
records.summary: Azure Maps Route APIs version 1.0 retire on March 31, 2028. Microsoft states that they remain usable without disruption through that date; afterward, they will be unavailable and unsupported, and calls will fail. Migrate to version 2025-01-01 before retirement. The migration requires request and response changes and has capability gaps, including unavailable asynchronous Directions batching and unsupported electric consumption models. All other Azure Maps services are unaffected.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring these Azure Maps Route APIs version 1.0 on March 31, 2028:

- Get Route Directions
- Get Route Directions Batch
- Post Route Directions
- Post Route Direction Batch
- Post Route Directions Batch Sync
- Get Route Matrix
- Post Route Matrix
- Post Route Matrix Sync
- Get Route Range

The replacement is version 2025-01-01. Version 1.0 remains usable without disruption through the retirement date; afterward, it becomes unavailable and unsupported. All other Azure Maps services are unaffected. The supplied content states no regional or customer-specific exceptions.

Migration is not just a version change: Directions and Range become POST-only and return GeoJSON instead of the previous JSON/XML formats. Directions batches support synchronous requests only. Matrix retains synchronous and asynchronous processing with changed operations and GeoJSON structures. Electric consumption models and the listed v1.0 beta travel profiles are unsupported in the target version.

Migration is not just a version change: Directions and Range become POST-only and return GeoJSON instead of the previous JSON/XML formats. Directions batches support synchronous requests only. Electric consumption models and the listed v1.0 beta travel profiles are unsupported in the target version.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. As team-owned preparation, identify integrations using the affected v1.0 APIs. Check dependencies on GET, XML, asynchronous Directions batches, electric consumption models and beta travel profiles. The supplied pages provide no automated inventory method.
2. Follow the migration guide to move to version 2025-01-01 before March 31, 2028. Map Directions GET/POST calls to Post Route Directions and all Directions batch variants to synchronous Post Route Directions Batch. Asynchronous Directions batching is currently unavailable.
3. Map Post Route Matrix to Post Route Matrix Async, and Post Route Matrix Sync to Post Route Matrix. Replace Get Route Matrix usage with Get Route Operations Status and Get Route Operation Result for asynchronous status and results.
4. Replace Get Route Range with Post Route Range. Update request bodies and response parsing for the target GeoJSON structures. Change Directions and Range coordinates from latitude/longitude to longitude/latitude; Matrix already uses longitude/latitude. For Directions localization, replace the language parameter with the Accept-Language request header.
5. Resolve capability gaps before switching. The guide provides no replacement for electric consumption models or the listed beta travel profiles. As team-owned validation, use the supplied examples to check request construction, response parsing and the routing features your application needs. The examples require an Azure Maps subscription key.
6. Complete the transition and stop using v1.0 before retirement to avoid failed calls afterward.

The supplied content does not prescribe backup, cutover or cleanup procedures.

records.title: Retirement: Support for Desired State Configuration Extension for Azure Virtual Machines to Be Retired on March 31, 2028
records.summary: Support for Desired State Configuration Extension for Azure Virtual Machines ends on March 31, 2028. Microsoft states that you can continue using it without disruption until that date and directs you to Azure Machine Configuration. Migration requires repackaging and testing configurations, updating deployment templates, and assessing compatibility gaps, including secrets management. The supplied sources do not establish that virtual machines or workloads will shut down.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring support for Desired State Configuration Extension for Azure Virtual Machines on March 31, 2028 and directs you to Azure Machine Configuration. The supplied sources identify no extension-version or regional exceptions and make no specific security-update commitments.

The migration guide describes a move from DSC version 1 with Windows PowerShell 5.1 to DSC version 2 with PowerShell 7.2. Machine Configuration supports native Azure Resource Manager assignments without an Automation Account, Azure Policy assignments at scale, multiple configurations per machine, remediation timing controls, and Azure Resource Graph reporting. Both Linux and Windows can consume PowerShell-based DSC resources.
what.html:
Microsoft is retiring support for Desired State Configuration Extension for Azure Virtual Machines on March 31, 2028 and directs you to Azure Machine Configuration. The supplied sources identify no extension-version or regional exceptions and make no specific security-update commitments.

The migration guide describes a move from DSC version 1 with Windows PowerShell 5.1 to DSC version 2 with PowerShell 7.2. Machine Configuration supports native Azure Resource Manager assignments without an Automation Account, Azure Policy assignments at scale, multiple configurations per machine, remediation timing controls, and Azure Resource Graph reporting. Both Linux and Windows can consume PowerShell-based DSC resources.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify affected VMs in the Azure portal: select each VM, then open Settings > Extensions + Applications and check for Desired State Configuration Extension. Alternatively, use the migration guide's Azure Resource Graph query, which covers Windows DSC extensions attached to Azure VMs.
2. Assess compatibility before migrating. Test existing resources against PowerShell 7.2. Machine Configuration has not implemented secrets management described by the guide, so assess dependencies on secrets supplied through extension privateSettings. Account for reboot management through Azure Resource Manager and the absence of execution-order orchestration between configurations.
3. Download and expand the existing DSC extension ZIP. Review and adapt the configuration, using the existing MOF as a basis. Make custom PowerShell modules available in $env:PSModulePath before packaging. Recreate, test and publish the package with Machine Configuration PowerShell cmdlets, then republish it to Azure Storage; the existing ZIP is incompatible.
4. Update deployment templates to replace the DSC extension with the Machine Configuration extension and add an assignment referencing the new package and its hash. Redeploy tested content and use Machine Configuration for future deployments by March 31, 2028. Avoid managing the same configuration through both platforms because they do not detect conflicts.
5. Review post-application reporting and drift results. For configurations assigned through Local Configuration Manager (LCM), Microsoft recommends removing the DSC extension and resetting LCM. The guide references Remove-DscConfigurationDocument for configuration removal. Removal stops management but does not undo applied settings.

Optionally split complex configurations into smaller packages, but keep sequentially dependent steps together. Adding the custom-resource Reasons property is optional.

Machine Configuration has not implemented secrets management described by the guide, so assess dependencies on secrets supplied through extension privateSettings. Account for reboot management through Azure Resource Manager and the absence of execution-order orchestration between configurations.
  3. Download and expand the existing DSC extension ZIP. Review and adapt the configuration, using the existing MOF as a basis. Make custom PowerShell modules available in $env:PSModulePath before packaging. Recreate, test and publish the package with Machine Configuration PowerShell cmdlets, then republish it to Azure Storage; the existing ZIP is incompatible.
  4. Update deployment templates to replace the DSC extension with the Machine Configuration extension and add an assignment referencing the new package and its hash. Redeploy tested content and use Machine Configuration for future deployments by March 31, 2028. Avoid managing the same configuration through both platforms because they do not detect conflicts.
  5. Review post-application reporting and drift results. For configurations assigned through Local Configuration Manager (LCM), Microsoft recommends removing the DSC extension and resetting LCM. The guide references Remove-DscConfigurationDocument for configuration removal. Removal stops management but does not undo applied settings.

Optionally split complex configurations into smaller packages, but keep sequentially dependent steps together. Adding the custom-resource Reasons property is optional.

impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
The retirement affects Azure VMs using Desired State Configuration Extension and deployment templates that deploy it. Check assigned VM extensions to establish your scope; the supplied information does not inspect your environment. The documented inventory query covers Windows DSC extensions, not all possible configurations.

Microsoft states that use can continue without disruption until March 31, 2028. Afterward, the extension is unsupported. Although the notice urges migration to avoid service disruptions, it does not specify whether or when existing configurations stop operating or workloads are interrupted.

Migration changes these behaviors:

- Compatibility: Existing ZIP packages need repackaging, and resources need testing across the PowerShell version change. The guide documents no implemented equivalent for secrets passed through extension privateSettings.
- Deployment and monitoring: Machine Configuration uses pull assignments rather than extension push deployment. It provides post-application reporting and drift visibility through Azure Resource Manager, but not real-time application status.
- Operations: Reboot management moves to Azure Resource Manager. Separate configurations have no execution-order orchestration, and the two platforms do not detect conflicting management.
- Cleanup: Removing LCM configuration leaves previously applied settings in place.

The sources do not document data-retention, deletion or cost consequences.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Spring Apps will be retired on March 31, 2028
records.summary: Azure Spring Apps retirement dates depend on your plan: Standard consumption and dedicated (preview) retired on March 31, 2025; Basic, Standard and Enterprise retire on March 31, 2028. After each applicable date, Microsoft ends support and instances become inaccessible. The structured deadline represents the earlier preview-plan retirement, not all plans. Three Enterprise Tanzu components separately lost support starting September 2025. Migrate to a suitable destination before your plan retires; guidance conflicts for customers retaining Spring commercial support or Tanzu components.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Azure Spring Apps Standard consumption and dedicated (preview), Basic, Standard and Enterprise plans. The preview plan retired on March 31, 2025; Basic, Standard and Enterprise retire on March 31, 2028. After the applicable retirement date, instances become inaccessible and Microsoft ends support.

For Basic, Standard and Enterprise, Microsoft documents continued workload support, SLA assurance, infrastructure maintenance, OSS/Tanzu management and application container-image updates through retirement, except for the Enterprise components below. Microsoft will not add features or accept feature requests.

Enterprise App Live View, App Accelerator and App Configuration Service lost support starting September 2025. Microsoft reserves the right to remove these unsupported components if a critical vulnerability is identified.

The retirement concerns Azure Spring Apps, not Java on Azure overall. The supplied content does not document regional exceptions. The Container Apps and AKS product pages do not independently establish a retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Azure Spring Apps plans, workloads and Enterprise Tanzu dependencies. Standard consumption and dedicated (preview) had a March 31, 2025 migration deadline; Basic, Standard and Enterprise have a March 31, 2028 deadline. The supplied content provides no automated inventory procedure.
2. Select a destination. Microsoft recommends Azure Container Apps for managed, serverless container hosting or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) for Kubernetes-based hosting. Current retirement guidance also lists Azure App Service as a PaaS alternative. Azure Container Apps meets most Spring hosting needs; full feature parity is not established.
3. If you need Spring commercial support or Tanzu components, resolve the conflicting destination guidance before choosing. The supplied guidance recommends both AKS with Tanzu purchased through your Broadcom sales representative and Tanzu Platform Spring Essentials on Azure Container Apps; the applicable choice remains unconfirmed.
4. Follow the referenced migration guidance and move workloads by your applicable deadline. The Azure CLI spring extension tool assists with Azure Container Apps environment setup; it is not documented as completing the entire migration. Detailed prerequisites, backup, cutover and cleanup procedures are not supplied.
5. As a team-owned validation step, check required capabilities and dependencies before cutover. The supplied content does not define migration-completion checks.

For technical migration help, open an Azure portal support ticket. Contact your Broadcom sales representative about purchasing and running Tanzu on AKS.

impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
Your plan determines the retirement impact:

- Standard consumption and dedicated (preview): retirement was March 31, 2025.
- Basic, Standard and Enterprise: retirement is March 31, 2028.

After the applicable date, Microsoft ends support and instances become inaccessible. The supplied content does not establish whether your environment contains affected resources or specify data-retention and deletion timing.

Existing Basic, Standard and Enterprise customers can continue creating, updating and deleting instances before retirement, but eligibility wording has limits. Current guidance requires an instance created before March 17, 2025 and also classifies customers without an instance in the past three months as new customers. records.title: Retirement: Announcing the 3-Year Retirement of Current Architecture for AKS on Windows Server 2019 and Windows Server 2022
records.summary: The current AKS architecture on Windows Server 2019 and Windows Server 2022 retires on March 27, 2028. Microsoft will end support, security and quality updates, and deployment, upgrade and scaling capabilities for that architecture. Replace affected clusters with AKS on Azure Local, version 23H2 or later, after deploying a supported Azure Local version. The supplied content does not state that existing workloads shut down. Azure Local 22H2 has a separate stated end-of-service date of May 31, 2025. Its documented infrastructure upgrade path has OEM, regional and workload restrictions, including required removal of AKS Arc and its settings before the OS upgrade.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring the current AKS architecture on Windows Server 2019 and Windows Server 2022 on March 27, 2028. The identified replacement is AKS on Azure Local, version 23H2 or later.

The retirement notice also directs AKS on Azure Local 22H2 customers to replace existing clusters and recommends updating Azure Local to continue receiving updates.

The supplied content does not specify pre-retirement maintenance commitments or retirement-specific regional exceptions. The supporting pricing, overview and upgrade pages do not independently announce a retirement.

Microsoft is retiring the current AKS architecture on Windows Server 2019 and Windows Server 2022 on March 27, 2028. The identified replacement is AKS on Azure Local, version 23H2 or later.

The retirement notice also directs AKS on Azure Local 22H2 customers to replace existing clusters and recommends updating Azure Local to continue receiving updates.

The supplied content does not specify pre-retirement maintenance commitments or retirement-specific regional exceptions. The supporting pricing, overview and upgrade pages do not independently announce a retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify whether you run AKS on Windows Server 2019, Windows Server 2022 or Azure Local 22H2. The supplied content provides no discovery procedure.
2. For the retiring Windows Server architecture, deploy a supported Azure Local version and replace affected clusters with AKS on Azure Local, version 23H2 or later, before March 27, 2028.
3. If upgrading Azure Local 22H2 infrastructure, first confirm OEM support and regional availability for the documented Azure Local 2311.2-or-later upgrade path. This process excludes 22H2 Supplemental Package clusters and third-party upgrade installation tools.
4. Before that OS upgrade, uninstall AKS Arc and its settings using Uninstall-Aks-Hci. If you used preview AKS Arc or preview Arc VMs on 22H2, use Uninstall-Moc to remove preview-created VM instances; preview Arc VMs cannot be upgraded.
5. Follow the documented sequence: upgrade the OS through PowerShell, perform post-OS tasks, validate solution upgrade readiness, then apply the solution upgrade. This infrastructure sequence is not a complete AKS workload migration procedure.

The supplied content does not provide detailed backup, workload restoration, cutover, cleanup or migration-completion procedures. For replacement pricing estimates, you can use the Azure pricing calculator or contact an Azure sales specialist; these are pricing resources, not migration support routes.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Machine Learning SDK v1 Will Be Retired on June 30, 2026 – Transition to Machine Learning SDK v2
records.summary: Azure Machine Learning Python SDK v1 support ended on June 30, 2026, following deprecation on March 31, 2025. Microsoft recommends migrating client code to SDK v2. This is not a service or workspace shutdown: existing v1 workflows continue after support ends, but Microsoft warns of security risks and possible breaking changes. CLI v1 has a separate support-end date of September 30, 2025. Migration requires client-code changes and checks for compatibility, networking and data-access constraints.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft has ended support for Azure Machine Learning Python SDK v1 and recommends Python SDK v2. New features are available only through v2.

This changes client tooling, not the Azure Machine Learning service or workspaces. Existing workspaces support both versions, subject to compatibility exceptions, and existing v1 workflows and model web services continue to function. Microsoft warns that product architecture changes can introduce security risks or breaking changes after support ends.

V2 aligns CLI and SDK features and terminology, but syntax can differ significantly from v1. The supplied guidance does not document regional exceptions or post-support maintenance and security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Review your Python client code, training jobs, deployments and CI/CD automation for SDK v1 use. Check CLI v1 separately if your automation uses it. The supplied pages provide no tenant-wide inventory procedure; the upgrade guidance assumes familiarity with Azure Machine Learning and Python SDK v1.
2. Select the appropriate v2 interface: Python SDK for complex scripting, CLI for CI/CD automation, or REST for minimal dependencies or languages without an SDK. Microsoft recommends migrating SDK v1 code to SDK v2; its recommended migration deadline has passed.
3. Resolve applicable constraints. For private-endpoint workspaces, consult the network-isolation guidance about the v1_legacy_mode flag, which prevents v2 API use. Export database datastores to object storage, usually Azure Blob. Replace v1 secret-management methods with direct Key Vault client-library access, using compute managed identity or your identity for training-script access.
4. Adapt your client code using the referenced v1-to-v2 mappings and reuse compatible workspaces and assets. For deployments, choose managed online endpoints for near-real-time inference, managed batch endpoints for batch scoring, or AKS/Arc Kubernetes for organization-managed clusters. Local endpoints are for testing, not production.
5. As team-owned validation, exercise migrated jobs, data access, secret access and inference before relying on v2 workflows. The supplied guidance does not provide a complete cutover, rollback or cleanup checklist.

Both versions can coexist in a workspace, but Microsoft discourages mixing their SDKs in the same code.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
Services deployed using Azure Cloud Services (extended support) are affected. You can identify resources in the Azure portal under Cloud services (extended support); this summary does not establish whether your environment contains any. The notice warns of service disruptions if you do not migrate by the deadline.

records.title: Public Preview: Enhance Performance and Security with Standard Load Balancer and Standard SKU Public IP Addresses in Azure DevTest Labs
records.summary: Azure Basic Load Balancer and Basic SKU public IP addresses retired on September 30, 2025, according to the supplied DevTest Labs blog and product guidance. New Basic deployments or creation were blocked after March 31, 2025. Existing Basic Load Balancers remain operational without support or SLA guarantees; behavior of existing Basic public IP addresses after retirement is unspecified. DevTest Labs preview enhancements move public/shared-IP VM creation to Standard resources; private-IP VMs are unaffected. The separately announced March 31, 2025 rollout target does not confirm rollout completion or automatic migration.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure DevTest Labs announced preview changes to public/shared-IP VM creation to accommodate the Basic SKU retirements on September 30, 2025:

- Public-IP VMs: Standard SKU public IP addresses with static allocation replace dynamic Basic SKU addresses, with one public IP address per VM.
- Shared-IP VMs: Standard Load Balancer replaces Basic Load Balancer for shared-IP traffic.
- Private-IP VMs: these retirements do not affect them.

The new public/shared-IP configurations require you to create and configure a Network Security Group for required inbound connections, such as RDP or SSH.

The changes roll out regionally in phases. The supplied sources do not confirm regional completion or automatic migration of existing resources.

actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your DevTest Labs public-IP and shared-IP VMs. In each VM's Azure compute view, use Network settings to open the linked public IP resource, or Load Balancing to open the linked load balancer. Inspect its SKU.
2. For affected Basic resources, consult the referenced Basic-to-Standard upgrade guidance for the relevant resource type. Standard public IP addresses serve public-IP VMs; Standard Load Balancer serves shared-IP VMs. The referenced migration procedures are not supplied.

4. Check the resulting resource overviews for Standard SKUs. As a team-owned validation step, verify required connectivity after your changes.

The supplied content does not establish migration prerequisites, capability gaps, or export, backup, cutover and cleanup procedures. Creating Standard resources does not establish that existing Basic resources have migrated.

records.title: Retirement: Upgrade Your Entra Domain Services to TLS 1.2 by August 31, 2025
records.summary: Microsoft Entra Domain Services is disabling TLS 1.0 and 1.1; affected applications need TLS 1.2. The announcement set a migration deadline of August 31, 2025. Product guidance gives June 30, 2026 as a temporary legacy-access cutoff, but also says the ability to disable TLS 1.2 Only Mode has already been removed. Temporary access remains unconfirmed, and the inputs do not explicitly establish an extension or a service-shutdown date.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is disabling TLS 1.0 and 1.1 for Microsoft Entra Domain Services through TLS 1.2 Only Mode. Applications using either legacy version need TLS 1.2 support.

Product guidance describes legacy protocols as supported but disabled by default, while conflicting on whether you can temporarily enable them. Do not rely on continued legacy access. The inputs do not announce retirement of Domain Services itself or document regional exceptions, pre-enforcement availability guarantees, or maintenance and security-update commitments.
what.html:
Microsoft is disabling TLS 1.0 and 1.1 for Microsoft Entra Domain Services through TLS 1.2 Only Mode. Applications using either legacy version need TLS 1.2 support.

Product guidance describes legacy protocols as supported but disabled by default, while conflicting on whether you can temporarily enable them. Do not rely on continued legacy access. The inputs do not announce retirement of Domain Services itself or document regional exceptions, pre-enforcement availability guarantees, or maintenance and security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify applications connecting to Microsoft Entra Domain Services with TLS 1.0 or 1.1. The supplied guidance does not provide a complete application-discovery method.
2. Update or replace those applications with TLS 1.2-capable alternatives before enabling TLS 1.2 Only Mode.
3. Obtain both the Application Administrator and Groups Administrator roles in Microsoft Entra ID.
4. In the Microsoft Entra admin center, select your Domain Services instance, open Security Settings, set TLS 1.2 Only Mode to Enable, and save. The guidance also documents PowerShell as an alternative.
5. Allow about 10 minutes for the security updates to take effect, then check application diagnostics for TLS handshake failures or unsupported-protocol errors.

Do not assume you can temporarily restore legacy access: the exception instructions conflict with the statement that disabling TLS 1.2 Only Mode has been removed.

The notice does not establish a workload shutdown date or data-retention consequences. The supplied reference pages do not change this deadline.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring HELM chart-based onboarding for the Azure Monitor Container Insights agent on October 1, 2025. The notice addresses Kubernetes clusters hosted outside Azure that use unmanaged onboarding methods such as HELM.

The replacement is Container Insights enabled through the Azure Arc Kubernetes extension. This is an onboarding-workflow retirement, not a documented retirement of Kubernetes workloads or all Container Insights onboarding methods.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use Monitored clusters in AzureMonitoringBrowseBlade to identify non-AKS candidates. This is an inventory starting point, not proof of HELM use or migration completion.

For team-owned tracking, record each affected cluster's original onboarding method, HELM removal, Azure Arc connection and extension-based Container Insights enablement. The supplied references provide these limited checks:

- For the documented HELM removal environments, run helm list before and after removal. Allow a few minutes for the configuration change. This verifies release removal only.
- For Arc onboarding, confirm all three required resource-provider namespaces are Registered; registration can take up to 10 minutes.
- Run kubectl get deployments,pods -n azure-arc and verify all Arc agent pods are Running. Cluster metadata can take up to 10 minutes to appear in the portal.

These checks do not prove that the Container Insights extension is collecting data. The supplied content provides no complete Arc Container Insights migration-completion check or automated retirement tracker. The AKS-specific monitoring checks are not documented as validation for this outside-Azure migration.

The Arc quickstart references connection-diagnosis and deployment-timeout troubleshooting guidance. The retirement notice references an FAQ, but that reference was unavailable.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Functions – Durable Functions support for Netherite will end on March 31, 2028
records.summary: Azure Functions Durable Functions support for the Netherite backend ends on March 31, 2028. Netherite-enabled apps will continue running afterward, but you will no longer be able to open support cases for them. Microsoft recommends evaluating Durable Task Scheduler. Switching storage providers requires a new app, and cross-provider state migration is not supported. No separate migration or shutdown deadline is documented.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Functions Durable Functions will end support for the Netherite backend on March 31, 2028. This does not retire Durable Functions itself, Durable Task SDKs or the other storage providers.

Microsoft recommends evaluating Durable Task Scheduler, particularly for workloads needing Netherite's higher throughput. Netherite-enabled apps remain operational after support ends, but support cases will no longer be available. The supplied material documents no Netherite maintenance or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Durable Functions apps that use Netherite. The supplied pages provide no inventory procedure.
2. Evaluate Durable Task Scheduler against your requirements. It requires Azure connectivity; check regional availability, identity and access permissions, SKU limits and payload limits. The storage-provider page lists extension-bundle support, KEDA 2.0 scaling and configurable price-performance as coming soon. The announcement recommends waiting for general availability before production use; the supplied material does not explicitly confirm that milestone.
3. Consider Azure Storage or MSSQL where they better fit your requirements. MSSQL supports disconnected environments, but does not support Durable Entities with .NET Isolated.
4. If you switch providers, create a new app configured for the selected provider. Existing backend data cannot currently be migrated between providers. The statement that Durable Task Scheduler requires no code changes does not remove these constraints.

Migration is not required to keep Netherite apps running, but continuing after support ends means losing support-case access. No detailed export, backup, state-transition, cutover, validation or cleanup procedure is supplied.

records.title: Retirement: Support for Python 3.9 ends on October 31, 2025 – upgrade your Azure Functions apps to Python 3.11
records.summary: Support for Python 3.9 in Azure Functions ends on October 31, 2025, the stated deadline to upgrade affected apps to Python 3.11. Apps continue running afterward, but Microsoft no longer provides Python 3.9 security updates, performance optimizations or customer service. Python versions cannot be changed in place on Consumption-plan apps; the supplied guidance does not provide a complete alternative migration procedure.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Functions is ending support for Python 3.9 in alignment with community end of support. After October 31, 2025, Microsoft no longer provides security updates, performance optimizations or customer service for Python 3.9. The notice directs affected customers to Python 3.11.

Apps continue running after support ends. The general language-support policy also permits creation and deployment of retired-language apps, but excludes them from new features until upgraded. The notice specifies no regional exceptions.
what.html:
Azure Functions is ending support for Python 3.9 in alignment with community end of support. After October 31, 2025, Microsoft no longer provides security updates, performance optimizations or customer service for Python 3.9. The notice directs affected customers to Python 3.11.

Apps continue running after support ends. The general language-support policy also permits creation and deployment of retired-language apps, but excludes them from new features until upgraded. The notice specifies no regional exceptions.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Azure Functions apps using Python 3.9, including their hosting plan and Functions runtime version. The supplied notice provides no Python-version inventory method. The FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME setting identifies the language, not its version.
2. Follow the notice's direction to upgrade affected apps to Python 3.11 by October 31, 2025. Check package dependencies, binding extensions, extension bundles and local tools. The update guide calls for Functions runtime 4.x; follow runtime migration guidance if you use an older runtime rather than merely changing its setting.
3. Test compatible code locally and back up app configuration. Consumption-plan apps do not support changing Python versions in place. The supplied guide does not provide a complete alternative migration procedure or required destination for those apps.
4. Where version changes are supported, publish compatible code before updating the stack configuration. Use a staging slot where available; Flex Consumption does not support slots, so test in a non-production app first.
5. Confirm the configured language version, Running status and function behavior. If using a staging slot, swap it into production after validation.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
Your Azure Functions apps using Python 3.9 are affected; no inspection of your resources is established by these sources. Without an upgrade, apps continue running after October 31, 2025 but lose the documented security updates, performance optimizations and Microsoft customer service for Python 3.9.

The general language-support policy says Microsoft may limit allocated instances for retired-language apps, including scaling to one instance in some cases. It does not establish that every Python 3.9 app will receive that limit.

For supported language updates, changing the version restarts the app. A direct production update typically causes 30–60 seconds of unavailability, terminates in-flight requests and rejects new requests until restart succeeds. The supplied content specifies no Python 3.9 retirement-related data deletion, retention change or cost change.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
The supplied guides document app-level checks, not a retirement-wide migration tracker:

1. Check the Functions runtime under Settings > Configuration > Function runtime settings. This verifies the runtime, not the Python version.
2. After a supported update, confirm the language version under General settings and confirm that Overview shows Running.
3. Test function behavior. For failures, inspect Monitoring > Log stream and review dependency compatibility.

These checks validate individual updates; they are not a complete migration procedure for Consumption-plan Python apps. Any inventory, upgrade-status record and test evidence you maintain are team-owned tracking.

The Functions team sends notification emails about upcoming language retirements affecting apps. No automated migration-completion dashboard is documented.

For questions, use Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and need technical help, open the Azure portal and select the question mark icon at the top of the page. The supplied Q&A reference is a product-tag directory, not retirement-specific tracking guidance.

records.title: Retirement: VM Insights Map and Dependency Agent are being on June 30, 2028
records.summary: VM Insights Map and the Dependency Agent retire and reach end of support on June 30, 2028. Offboard before that date and replace dependency monitoring or inventory tracking where needed. VM Insights performance monitoring is unaffected. Microsoft documents removal of the monitoring experiences at retirement, but the exact ingestion cutoff remains unconfirmed: the announcement places it after retirement, while the retirement guidance FAQ says sometime afterward. Existing data remains subject to your Log Analytics workspace retention settings.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring VM Insights Map and the Dependency Agent on June 30, 2028. They provide visibility into VM processes and network dependencies, including Windows and Linux machines in Azure or your own environment.

The retirement affects the Map tab, Connections Overview workbook, Service Map API, portal installation of the Dependency Agent and new agent-based data ingestion. Experience removal is listed at retirement; the exact ingestion cutoff is unconfirmed. Previously downloaded binaries might still install, but cannot send data once ingestion is disabled.

Existing maps are documented, but the supplied content does not establish a maintenance or security-update commitment through retirement. Do not enable the feature for new deployments.

VM Insights performance monitoring, which uses Azure Monitor Agent, is unaffected. This is not retirement of all VM Insights capabilities or Azure Monitor Agent.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify existing installations. Use Azure Advisor, the referenced Resource Graph query and the referenced Log Analytics query, accounting for the coverage limits described under progress. Include standalone and manually installed agents; portal extension checks alone miss manual installations.
2. Choose replacements by use case. For process and dependency monitoring, Microsoft recommends evaluating Azure Marketplace monitoring and diagnostics solutions. For inventory tracking, retirement guidance identifies Azure Monitor Agent with Change Tracking and Inventory. Feature parity, detailed migration prerequisites and replacement-validation criteria are not established by the supplied content.
3. Stop new deployments and update automation. Identify policy or initiative assignments that deploy the Dependency Agent and update or remove the relevant assignments. Contact your Azure administrator if you do not manage them.
4. Offboard and uninstall before June 30, 2028. Check the Log Analytics discovery query's Notes column first: a Caution value flags older Windows agents that might cause a system crash during uninstallation. Use the removal method matching the installation and version:
  - Portal extension: open the VM, then Extensions + applications > DependencyAgentWindows or DependencyAgentLinux > Uninstall.
  - Manual Windows installation: remove Microsoft Dependency Agent through Add and remove programs, or use the version-appropriate uninstaller in C:\Program Files\Microsoft Dependency Agent. For 9.7.7.4050 and later, use Uninstall_<version>.exe /S; for earlier versions, use Uninstall.exe /S. Uninstallers before 9.7.4.3150 lack a Microsoft digital signature.
  - Linux 9.10.2.9060 and later: use an account with sudo privileges and run sudo /opt/microsoft/dependency-agent/uninstall -s.
  - Earlier Linux versions: use sudo dpkg --purge dependency-agent dependency-agent-service microsoft-dependency-agent-dkms on Debian/Ubuntu, or sudo rpm -e --allmatches dependency-agent on RPM-based distributions.

The supplied content does not provide a complete migration sequence, export or backup requirements, or definitive cutover and validation checks.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if you rely on VM Insights Map, the Dependency Agent, the Connections Overview workbook or the Service Map API. Discovery methods cover different combinations of VMs, Virtual Machine Scale Sets, Azure Arc machines and standalone installations; this summary does not inspect your resources.

Without offboarding, you lose the retired portal, workbook and API experiences and eventually new Dependency Agent data ingestion. Policy and deployment tooling must also stop deploying the agent. The supplied content does not say that monitored VMs or applications shut down. VM Insights performance monitoring is unaffected.

Already ingested data in VMComputer, VMProcess, VMConnection and VMBoundPort is not deleted by retirement. Its availability follows your Log Analytics workspace retention settings; no separate retirement deletion date is documented.

Important assessment limits:

- Manually installed agents do not appear as portal extensions. Map supports IPv4, including IPv4 tunneled inside IPv6, but not native IPv6. Duplicate IP ranges or duplicate collection can make maps inaccurate.
- Existing Dependency Agent installations require Azure Monitor Agent on the same machine and connectivity to the Azure metadata endpoint. Supported operating systems and kernels remain constrained; Windows support stops at Windows Server 2022 and excludes Azure Stack HCI, Windows IoT Enterprise and Windows Server Core. Only x64 is supported.
- Linux distribution and kernel restrictions apply. With agent 9.10.15 and later, unsupported kernels can produce degraded collection: no VMConnection or VMBoundPort data and potentially only minimal VMProcess data. The supplied broad 9.10.* kernel statement and Debian Map-support statements do not resolve all support distinctions.
- Dependency Agent heartbeat data in InsightsMetrics incurs ingestion charges. No retirement-specific cost estimate is supplied.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance:
Offboard before June 30, 2028, when VM Insights Map and the Dependency Agent retire and reach end of support. Microsoft provides no Dependency Agent support after that date.

Separate milestones:

- June 30, 2025: The announcement says restrictions on support for new operating-system versions start on this date; retirement guidance says after this date and also excludes new Azure regions. Use the earlier boundary for planning; the wording differs.
- July 2, 2025: Retirement announcement.
- September 30, 2025: Product guidance says new-VM onboarding through the Azure portal is blocked from this date; other supplied wording says after it. Use the earlier boundary. Other onboarding methods remain available until support ends, but Microsoft directs you not to start new installations.
- June 30, 2028: Retirement, end of support, documentation archival and experience removal, according to retirement guidance.

The exact ingestion cutoff remains unconfirmed. The announcement groups ingestion loss with restrictions after retirement; retirement guidance describes it as a retirement impact, but its FAQ says ingestion is disabled sometime after June 30, 2028. This does not establish an extension of support. Both components are already deprecated; no separate deprecation date is supplied.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use the documented discovery methods to identify remaining installations:

- Azure Advisor: Open Recommendations > Reliability and filter Recommendation Type to Migrate from Dependency Agent and VM Insights Map. Check VMs, Virtual Machine Scale Sets and Azure Arc machines.
- Resource Graph Explorer: Use the query referenced by retirement guidance. It uses the current Azure portal scope and excludes on-premises VMs without Arc connectivity. The query text is not included in the supplied content.
- Log Analytics: Use the referenced query in the relevant workspace. It checks VMComputer records from the last seven days, so installations without recent records may be missed. Results can include standalone installations without Azure resource links. Review its Notes column for uninstall cautions. The query text is not included here.
- Portal checks: Inspect Extensions + applications for DependencyAgentWindows or DependencyAgentLinux. This does not cover manually installed agents. Map views require a solution-enabled workspace receiving VM data and are not a complete inventory; their default 30-minute view and historical windows of up to one hour do not prove migration completion.

For team-owned tracking, record identified machines, installation methods, agent versions, policy changes, replacement rollout and removal evidence. The supplied guidance provides no definitive migration-completion check or replacement-validation criteria; discovery results alone do not prove completion.

For assistance, use Microsoft Q&A with the azure-monitor tag or open a support ticket through Azure support plans.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Static Web Apps – Dedicated Pricing Plan
records.summary: Azure Static Web Apps Dedicated pricing plan, formerly in Public Preview, retired effective October 31, 2025. Microsoft’s notice stated that all existing Dedicated resources would be deleted that day; the supplied content does not confirm deletion completed. New Dedicated deployments were blocked from May 1, 2025. Microsoft directs Dedicated deployments to redeploy to a new Static Web App; the notice also names Azure Container Apps as an alternative. Free and Standard are not retiring under this notice. Compare replacement capabilities and capacity limits before migrating.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Static Web Apps Dedicated pricing plan, described in the notice as Public Preview, retired effective October 31, 2025. Microsoft stated that existing Dedicated resources would be deleted on that date.

This retirement does not apply to Free or Standard. Microsoft directs Dedicated deployments to redeploy to a new Static Web App; the retirement notice names Static Web Apps Standard and Azure Container Apps as migration alternatives.

The supplied content documents no regional exceptions or maintenance and security-update commitments before retirement.
what.html:

This retirement does not apply to Free or Standard. Microsoft directs Dedicated deployments to redeploy to a new Static Web App; the retirement notice names Static Web Apps Standard and Azure Container Apps as migration alternatives.

The supplied content documents no regional exceptions or maintenance and security-update commitments before retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify Dedicated deployments. For each Static Web Apps resource, check Settings > Hosting plan in the Azure portal. The supplied content provides no fleet-wide discovery method.
2. Select a replacement. The notice names Static Web Apps Standard and Azure Container Apps. The plans page also lists Free as available, but Free lacks listed capabilities including private endpoints, custom authentication registrations, bring-your-own Functions apps, and an SLA; Standard supports those capabilities. The supplied content does not compare Azure Container Apps capabilities.
3. Check capacity requirements. Dedicated lists 20 staging environments, a 2 GB maximum app size, and 10 custom domains. Standard lists 10, 500 MB, and 5; Free lists 3, 250 MB, and 2, respectively.
4. For a Static Web Apps replacement, follow the referenced deployment guide to redeploy to a new Static Web App. The documented in-place plan change applies only between Free and Standard, not Dedicated.

The deletion date has passed. The supplied content does not provide Dedicated-specific migration prerequisites, export or backup instructions, cutover, validation or cleanup procedures, or recovery options for deleted resources.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Disk Encryption
records.service: Virtual Machine Scale Sets · Virtual Machines
records.summary: Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) retires on September 15, 2028. Microsoft states that ADE remains usable without disruption until then. At retirement, workloads will continue running, but encrypted disks will fail to unlock after VM reboots. Migrate ADE-enabled Windows and Linux VMs, including backups and Azure Virtual Desktop session hosts, before retirement. Microsoft recommends encryption at host; Confidential VM sizes with OS disk encryption are another option for confidential computing needs. Migration requires replacement disks and VMs, with downtime; in-place conversion is not supported.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) on September 15, 2028. The migration guidance covers ADE-enabled Windows and Linux VMs, including backups, and Azure Virtual Desktop session hosts. No version, region or customer exceptions are specified.

Microsoft recommends replacing ADE's guest-level encryption with encryption at host, which covers temporary disks, caches and data flows between compute and storage. For confidential computing needs, consider Confidential VM sizes with OS disk encryption.

In-place conversion is not supported: migration requires new disks and VMs, with downtime. Linux VMs with ADE-encrypted OS disks require a new OS disk because Azure does not support disabling ADE on those disks.
what.html:
Microsoft is retiring Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) on September 15, 2028. The migration guidance covers ADE-enabled Windows and Linux VMs, including backups, and Azure Virtual Desktop session hosts. No version, region or customer exceptions are specified.

Microsoft recommends replacing ADE's guest-level encryption with encryption at host, which covers temporary disks, caches and data flows between compute and storage. For confidential computing needs, consider Confidential VM sizes with OS disk encryption.

In-place conversion is not supported: migration requires new disks and VMs, with downtime. Linux VMs with ADE-encrypted OS disks require a new OS disk because Azure does not support disabling ADE on those disks.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Migrate all ADE-enabled VMs, including backups, before September 15, 2028.

1. Identify affected VMs and backups. Record configuration, networking, extensions, attached resources and domain settings. Back up critical data; where possible, test migration on a nonproduction VM. The supplied content does not provide a tenant-wide discovery procedure.
2. Confirm target VM-size and subscription support for encryption at host, and plan downtime. For confidential computing workloads, consider Confidential VM sizes with OS disk encryption.
3. Select the migration path. For Windows and Linux data-disk-only encryption, disable ADE where supported and verify that guest-level decryption has finished; the portal changing to SSE + PMK does not prove completion. For Linux with an ADE-encrypted OS disk, create a new VM and OS disk with encryption at host, then migrate application data and configuration or use application-appropriate backup and restore. For Azure Virtual Desktop pooled and personal host pools, replace session hosts using a validated image without ADE and enable encryption at host during VM creation.
4. For disk-level migration, create fresh managed disks using Upload and copy the VHD data. Snapshots and Copy-based copies retain the ADE UDE flag, even after decryption. Account for the documented 512-byte upload-size offset and specify the Hyper-V generation for OS disks. Revoke source and target SAS access after copying.
5. Recreate VMs with encryption at host enabled. Restore configuration, correct Windows drive letters or Linux mount UUIDs, and update disk-ID references. For domain-joined VMs, remove original domain membership before deletion, join the replacement and validate domain functionality. Linux managed-domain joins require manual steps.
6. Validate encryption at host, applications and data integrity before decommissioning originals. For Azure Virtual Desktop, also validate host health, connections, profiles, applications and policies; drain old hosts and end existing sessions before removal.
7. After successful verification, delete original VMs and disks, remove temporary resources and update infrastructure documentation. Disable the Key Vault disk-encryption setting only if it is no longer needed for ADE.

Backups are included in the migration requirement, but the supplied content does not provide a separate backup-migration procedure.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if you use ADE-enabled VMs or backups, including Windows, Linux and Azure Virtual Desktop session hosts. The supplied content does not establish which of your resources are affected or document regional exclusions.

Without migration before September 15, 2028, workloads can continue running, but encrypted disks will fail to unlock after VM reboots. The documented consequence is reboot-related service disruption, not immediate shutdown or data deletion.

Migration requires downtime and replacement disks and VMs. Important constraints include:

- Linux ADE-encrypted OS disks cannot be decrypted in place; rebuild the OS environment and migrate data.
- Snapshots and Copy-based disk copies retain ADE metadata and do not replace the documented Upload-based migration.
- Replacement disks can require changes to drive letters, mount UUIDs and application disk references.
- Domain-joined replacements have a different computer SID. Domain-integrated applications, credentials and policies may need attention, and temporary domain-service disruption is possible.
- Azure Virtual Desktop requires session-host replacement and controlled draining of old hosts.

The supplied content does not document separate console/API retirement, automatic deletion, retention changes or cost estimates.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use the documented per-VM checks to verify migration. The supplied content does not provide a fleet-wide retirement tracker or a separate backup-completion check.

1. Where decryption is supported, verify it inside the guest before copying disks. On Windows, run manage-bde -status and confirm all volumes are fully decrypted. For Linux data disks, use sudo cryptsetup status /dev/mapper/<device-name> and lsblk to verify encrypted mappings are no longer active. Portal status alone is insufficient.
2. After replacement, check encryption at host with the documented command, substituting your resource names:

az vm show --resource-group "MyResourceGroup" --name "MyVM-New" --query "securityProfile.encryptionAtHost"

3. Separately verify application and service operation, disk access, data integrity, networking and domain authentication. Encryption-at-host status alone does not establish those checks.
4. For Azure Virtual Desktop, confirm replacement hosts are healthy and accepting connections, validate profiles and policies, and confirm old hosts have been drained and removed.

For team-owned tracking, record verification results, replacement resources, backup coverage and cleanup status in your infrastructure documentation. This is local migration evidence, not an automated tracking capability supplied by the page. The supplied content does not provide help or escalation routes.

records.title: Retirement: hsmPlatform 1 Keys in Azure Key Vault
records.summary: Azure Key Vault retires support for hsmPlatform 1 keys on September 15, 2028. Move affected workloads to new HSM Platform 2 keys or key versions; existing keys cannot transfer between platforms. Retain old keys while backups or protected content still need them. The notice does not establish a workload shutdown date. The reference and migration pages provide supporting guidance but no separate retirement deadline.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Key Vault is retiring support for hsmPlatform 1 keys on September 15, 2028. Existing keys remain bound to their original platform and cannot transfer directly to another platform.

The migration guide states that all new keys and key versions use HSM Platform 2. You can transition workloads by creating new keys or versions and updating their references where needed.

The supplied content does not document regional exceptions, pre-deadline availability changes, maintenance or security-update commitments, or post-deadline shutdown behavior. The Key Vault reference treats Managed HSM separately; it does not establish a Managed HSM retirement.
what.html:
Azure Key Vault is retiring support for hsmPlatform 1 keys on September 15, 2028. Existing keys remain bound to their original platform and cannot transfer directly to another platform.

The migration guide states that all new keys and key versions use HSM Platform 2. You can transition workloads by creating new keys or versions and updating their references where needed.

The supplied content does not document regional exceptions, pre-deadline availability changes, maintenance or security-update commitments, or post-deadline shutdown behavior. The Key Vault reference treats Managed HSM separately; it does not establish a Managed HSM retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. With appropriate list/get permissions, inventory relevant keys and versions, inspect their hsmPlatform attribute, and identify workloads that reference Platform 1 keys or versions.
2. Create new Platform 2 keys or key versions. A configured rotation policy creates a version at the next scheduled rotation; otherwise, create one manually. Existing keys cannot transfer between platforms, and Backup and Restore is not a platform-transfer method.
3. Update workload references where needed. Services with customer-managed-key autorotation enabled apply the new key automatically; other configurations require manual updates. If moving to another vault or managed HSM, grant the workload's managed identity the appropriate Azure RBAC or Managed HSM local RBAC role.
4. Apply workload-specific migration steps. For custom applications or client-side encryption, re-encrypt affected keys or data and verify the migrated data. For Azure Information Protection documents, remove protection and reapply it with the new tenant key. For Microsoft 365 Customer Key, roll or rotate root keys as needed and update data encryption policies.
5. Confirm operations work with the intended new key before retiring the previous key. Keep old keys and vaults while backups or protected content still require them.

General-purpose key export is not supported. The documented release-policy exception is limited to designated trusted confidential computing environments, not general migration. If identical key material is required across separate security domains, the guide describes BYOK from an HSM you control, with a distinct key URI for each destination.

impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
The retirement applies to Azure Key Vault keys with hsmPlatform 1. List keys and versions and inspect their platform attributes to identify your scope; the supplied material does not establish which resources you have.

New keys and versions already use Platform 2. Existing Platform 1 workloads need migration, but the effort depends on their configuration:

records.title: Retirement: DCsv2-series Azure Virtual Machines will be retired on June 30, 2026
records.summary: Azure DCsv2-series VMs retire on June 30, 2026, including uses through Virtual Machine Scale Sets and AKS. Microsoft states that remaining DCsv2 VM subscriptions stop working and stop incurring billing charges afterward. Capacity restrictions and a ban on new DCsv2 subscriptions begin on July 1, 2025. Migrate before retirement, checking regional capacity, quota, attestation and temporary-disk dependencies. DCdsv3, the recommended Intel SGX replacement, has a separate documented retirement on October 31, 2029; this does not extend the DCsv2 deadline.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Azure DCsv2-series VMs on June 30, 2026, including standalone VMs, Virtual Machine Scale Sets and app-enclave-aware containers on AKS that use DCsv2. Remaining DCsv2 VM subscriptions stop working afterward.

Until retirement, Microsoft provides workload support, SLA assurance, infrastructure updates and maintenance, but does not accept feature requests or develop new DCsv2 features. Capacity restrictions apply from July 1, 2025, so unrestricted availability before retirement is not promised.

Replacement choices depend on your programming model: Intel SGX enclaves, VM-based confidential computing, or containers. DCdsv3 retains Intel SGX but has its own retirement on October 31, 2029. Microsoft does not plan to deploy DCsv2, DCsv3 or DCdsv3 in new Azure regions.

The other supplied replacement reference pages do not independently establish retirements for those products.

Microsoft is retiring Azure DCsv2-series VMs on June 30, 2026, including standalone VMs, Virtual Machine Scale Sets and app-enclave-aware containers on AKS that use DCsv2. Remaining DCsv2 VM subscriptions stop working afterward.
