The other supplied replacement reference pages do not independently establish retirements for those products.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify DCsv2 workloads across standalone VMs, Virtual Machine Scale Sets and AKS. Assess Intel SGX and attestation requirements, performance, local temporary-disk dependencies and regional needs. The supplied guidance provides no fleet-wide discovery procedure.
2. Select a replacement for your use case:
  - Intel SGX enclaves: DCdsv3. Account for its separate October 31, 2029 retirement. DCdsv3 does not support Intel EPID Attestation Service (IAS); transition away from IAS if you use it.
  - VM-based workloads: DCasv5/DCadsv5/ECasv5/ECadsv5, DCasv6/ECasv6 or DC/ECesv6. The DCsv2 guidance labels the latter two groups as preview; the DCasv6/ECasv6 announcement describes gated access and gradual regional rollout. Supplied reference pages do not establish universal availability or replacement compatibility.
  - Containers: Azure Confidential Container Instances (C-ACI), or Virtual nodes on Azure Container Instances (C-VN2) for AKS orchestration. Confidential virtual nodes require a region supporting confidential ACI. ACI Windows containers and enclaves are preview; enclaves are Linux-only. Confidential ACI requires enforcement policies generated with the Azure CLI confcom extension, not manually created policies.
3. Check destination SKU availability and subscription quota. Request a quota increase through the Azure portal if necessary. Check guest OS, storage, networking and feature compatibility rather than assuming equivalent capabilities. DCadsv5, DCesv6 and ECesv6 support Generation 2 only and do not support Accelerated Networking or nested virtualization; DCesv6 and ECesv6 have no local storage.
4. For an available DCdsv3 size in your region, stop and deallocate the VM, select the target size, resize and start it. Resizing restarts the VM; Microsoft recommends off-peak hours. Consider a static IP before deallocation if you need to retain the address, because deallocation releases dynamic IPs.
5. For DCsv2 workloads in North Central US, Canada East, Australia Southeast or UK West, choose a supported destination region or another offering. The documented cross-region path requires backup, destination quota, deallocation, image capture and replication, then destination VM creation. The image-capture instructions select automatic deletion of the source VM after image creation. Choose specialized versus generalized imaging deliberately.
6. Review pricing and active DCsv2 Reserved Instances. The guide lists reservation exchange, trade-in for an Azure Savings Plan, or new reservations as options.
7. Complete migration before June 30, 2026. As a team-owned completion check, validate the migrated workload and its dependencies. Detailed validation, cutover and general cleanup procedures are not supplied.

You cannot directly resize between sizes with and without a local temporary disk. DCsv2-to-DCdsv3 resizing is supported; DCsv2-to-DCsv3 requires a separate migration workaround. Check images and scripts for temporary-disk dependencies. The guide's same-price, no-local-disk option contains inconsistent workaround direction; confirm its procedure and applicability before using it.

records.title: Retirement: skip-gpu-driver-install nodepool tag retirement om August 14, 2025
records.summary: On August 14, 2025, Azure Kubernetes Service retired the skip-gpu-driver-install node pool tag. GPU node-pool provisioning must use the gpu-driver replacement field to bypass automatic driver installation. The supplied sources do not establish that existing GPU workloads shut down because of this retirement.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
AKS retired the skip-gpu-driver-install node pool tag. To skip automatic NVIDIA driver installation when creating GPU-enabled node pools, use the generally available gpu-driver field set to none.

This preserves the option to manage drivers yourself, including configurations using custom GPU drivers or the GPU Operator. Microsoft does not support or manage maintenance and compatibility of self-managed drivers as part of node-image deployment. This is not a retirement of AKS GPU workloads generally.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Review your GPU node-pool provisioning configuration for the retired skip-gpu-driver-install tag. The sources provide no retirement-specific inventory procedure.
2. If you need to bypass automatic NVIDIA driver installation, replace the tag with the gpu-driver field set to none when creating node pools. You need Azure CLI 2.72.2 or later and, if installed, aks-preview 18.0.0b2 or later. You remain responsible for the required GPU software components.
3. For existing pools, account for the reference page’s limits: setting the field does not change existing nodes. The page describes scaling the pool to zero and back up to apply the change, without workload-continuity guarantees. Updates and upgrades preserve the setting chosen at pool creation; do not pass the field to those operations.
4. Validate node GPU capacity, GPU scheduling and a representative GPU workload using the documented checks.

The notice broadly describes the replacement as applicable to existing-pool updates, but the reference page explicitly limits how the field is applied. The sources do not provide a complete existing-pool migration or cutover procedure.

records.title: Retirement: General Purpose v1 (GPv1) and legacy blob storage accounts
records.summary: Azure Storage lists October 13, 2026 as the retirement date for GPv1 and legacy Blob storage accounts, including Files configurations on GPv1. Microsoft says it will convert remaining accounts to GPv2; retirement does not establish a workload shutdown. The date has passed, but the supplied sources do not confirm conversion completion. Review remaining accounts, deployment artifacts and costs, then upgrade customer-managed accounts and validate workloads and billing. Databricks-managed DBFS accounts require no customer migration action and have a separate conversion window extending into Q1 2027. Creation-blocking dates and parts of the conversion schedule conflict across sources.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Storage is retiring GPv1 and legacy Blob storage account types and moving remaining accounts to GPv2. The stated retirement date is October 13, 2026.

The scope includes:

- GPv1 accounts across all Azure regions and redundancy options, supporting Blobs, Tables, Queues and Files, including Files configurations hosted on GPv1.
- Legacy Blob storage accounts.

GPv2 supports GPv1 functionality and the blob features available in legacy Blob storage accounts. Microsoft documents the GPv1 upgrade as a permanent, in-place account-kind change that preserves data and endpoints without downtime. Existing GPv1 applications and tools continue working without changes; for legacy Blob accounts, the guidance says most blob-only workloads need no code changes, not every workload.

Microsoft will automatically convert remaining accounts. Databricks-managed DBFS accounts require no customer migration action and follow a separate schedule. Existing GPv2 accounts are not identified as requiring migration.

The sources do not document pre-retirement maintenance, support or security-update commitments. Retirement is not established as a workload shutdown.

The scope includes:

  • GPv1 accounts across all Azure regions and redundancy options, supporting Blobs, Tables, Queues and Files, including Files configurations hosted on GPv1.
  • Legacy Blob storage accounts.

GPv2 supports GPv1 functionality and the blob features available in legacy Blob storage accounts. Microsoft documents the GPv1 upgrade as a permanent, in-place account-kind change that preserves data and endpoints without downtime. Existing GPv1 applications and tools continue working without changes; for legacy Blob accounts, the guidance says most blob-only workloads need no code changes, not every workload.

Microsoft will automatically convert remaining accounts. Databricks-managed DBFS accounts require no customer migration action and follow a separate schedule. Existing GPv2 accounts are not identified as requiring migration.

The sources do not document pre-retirement maintenance, support or security-update commitments. Retirement is not established as a workload shutdown.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
For customer-managed accounts, upgrade remaining affected accounts rather than relying on an uncertain automatic-conversion schedule.

1. Inventory accounts. Use Azure Resource Graph, Azure CLI, Azure Inventory or the portal. In the portal, check Settings > Configuration > Account kind. Distinguish GPv1's Storage, legacy BlobStorage and GPv2's StorageV2. The supplied Resource Graph query filters specific Standard SKUs and excludes StorageV2; it is not proof of complete coverage or a precise list of affected kinds.
2. Separate Databricks-managed DBFS accounts. Confirm the managed resource group and that the account is read-only to you. A dbstorage name prefix alone is insufficient. Microsoft handles these accounts; no customer migration action is required.
3. Review compatibility and costs. Assess capacity, transactions, redundancy and access tiers using storage metrics and the Azure Pricing Calculator or supplied estimator. The estimator excludes contract-specific discounts, taxes and reservations. Check hardcoded pricing assumptions, tier-aware behavior and applicable minimum-retention or early-deletion charges.
4. Review deployment artifacts. Update infrastructure-as-code, pipelines, templates, modules, scripts and policies for GPv2 while preserving networking, security, redundancy, tier, encryption, identity, data protection and tags. Validate through your normal change-review process or outside production.
5. Upgrade managed accounts to GPv2. In the portal, select Upgrade under Account kind, enter the account name and confirm. Alternatives include the latest Azure CLI or PowerShell with the latest Az.Storage module. Documented Azure Policy automation can support in-place upgrades; verify the account kinds covered because the legacy guidance mixes terminology. The upgrade is irreversible. Choose Hot or Cool for block blobs; Hot is the default if omitted, and these tiers do not apply to other data objects.
6. Validate the result. Confirm the resulting account kind, application behavior, deployment behavior and billing; then monitor usage and costs.

The announcement also names BlockBlobStorage and FileStorage as workload-dependent alternatives, but the supplied detailed upgrade guidance targets GPv2 and does not provide equivalent migration procedures for those alternatives. No export, backup, separate cutover or cleanup requirement is documented.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if you use GPv1 accounts, including Files hosted on GPv1, or legacy Blob storage accounts. No tenant inventory or account-specific cost assessment is established by these sources.

Workload and deployment effects

Microsoft describes GPv1 conversion as in-place, without downtime, data loss or endpoint changes. Existing applications and tools continue working; most legacy blob-only workloads also need no code changes. Stale deployment artifacts can still cause validation or deployment failures or unintended configuration changes even while running workloads continue normally.

If you take no action, Microsoft treats non-migration as consent to automatic conversion. The upgrade page also warns of service disruption without explaining how that relates to conversion. The sources do not establish a retirement-related shutdown, data deletion, retention change or specific console/API outage.

Billing effects

The account upgrade itself is free, but GPv2 transaction charges can increase costs, particularly for read-, write- or list-heavy Blob workloads. Lower capacity prices do not guarantee a lower total bill. Cooler tiers increase access and transaction charges, and later tier changes can incur charges.

GPv1 pricing is expected to change shortly after retirement regardless of backend conversion completion. The legacy Blob overview lists billing changes beginning in November 2026. No account-specific estimate is supplied. The GPv1 overview says conversion does not change Azure Files or Azure Disks pricing.

Databricks-managed DBFS accounts support workspace operations and are read-only to customers. Microsoft migrates them separately; you do not need to migrate them.

The upgrade guidance warns of service disruption but does not reconcile that warning with automatic conversion. These statements do not establish a separate shutdown date.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Front Door (classic) and Azure CDN from Microsoft Classic SKU ending CNAME based domain validation and new domain/profile creations by August 15, 2025
records.service: Azure Front Door · Content Delivery Network
records.summary: From August 15, 2025, Azure Front Door (classic) and Azure CDN from Microsoft Classic SKUs stop supporting new profiles, new domain onboarding and switches from BYOC to managed certificates. The announcement assures existing managed-certificate continuity only until April 14, 2026; it does not establish a shutdown on that date. Current product guidance separately sets retirement for Azure Front Door (classic) on March 31, 2027 and Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic) on September 30, 2027. Migrate to Azure Front Door Standard or Premium before the applicable retirement, then complete endpoint cutover by March 31, 2028. Classic endpoints become unsupported and might stop functioning from April 1, 2028. The later endpoint milestone is not a retirement extension. Conflicting managed-certificate guidance remains unresolved.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Front Door (classic) and Azure CDN from Microsoft Classic SKUs lose support for new profiles, new domain onboarding and switching existing domains from BYOC to managed certificates from August 15, 2025. Current guidance also describes managed certificates as unsupported.

Microsoft separately retires Azure Front Door (classic) on March 31, 2027 and Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic) on September 30, 2027. Azure Front Door Standard and Premium are migration destinations, not services being retired by these notices. No regional exceptions are documented.

After migration, Microsoft automatically routes classic endpoint traffic to the new profile during transition. You must still replace classic endpoint dependencies before April 1, 2028, when those endpoints become unsupported and might stop functioning.

Certificate guidance is inconsistent: the announcement assures existing managed-certificate continuity until April 14, 2026, while current pages say managed certificates are unsupported and CDN migration instructions still describe preserving managed-certificate settings. The inputs do not resolve this inconsistency or document maintenance and security-update commitments through retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify affected classic profiles, endpoints, custom domains, certificate types, WAF associations and application references to classic hostnames. For Front Door (classic), open Settings > Migration > Validate. For CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic), run the migration tool's compatibility validation. Resolve reported issues before proceeding.
2. Confirm your certificate path. The announcement required existing managed-certificate domains to move to BYOC or migrate before August 15, 2025. Because later certificate guidance conflicts, confirm applicable behavior before relying on managed certificates. BYOC on classic is not a substitute for service migration.
3. Choose Azure Front Door Standard or Premium for your requirements. Premium includes managed WAF rules, bot protection and Private Link integration. Front Door profiles with managed WAF rules require Premium unless those rules are removed. CDN profiles exceeding Standard quotas migrate to Premium. You can upgrade Standard to Premium later, but cannot downgrade Premium to Standard.
4. Prepare the required configuration. All custom domains must use HTTPS. For Front Door, domains sharing a backend pool need consistent session affinity; configure compatible WAF policies. For CDN, start or delete stopped endpoints and remove associated preview WAF policies before revalidation, planning to recreate them afterward. BYOC migration requires managed identity access to the relevant Key Vaults.
5. Prepare, review and complete migration before March 31, 2027 for Front Door (classic) or September 30, 2027 for CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic). Preparation locks classic configuration changes. For Front Door, review the new profile before selecting Migrate. Do not delete the destination profile: the guide warns this irreversibly deletes the production environment. If migration is canceled, manually remove any newly created WAF policy copies.
6. After migration, update custom-domain DNS and replace directly used classic hostnames in applications, clients and integrations. For Front Door, no DNS changes are needed before or during migration. Validate traffic through the new endpoint while both endpoints work, and finish cutover by March 31, 2028. For CDN, update automation to the new APIs, PowerShell module and CLI interfaces, and recreate required WAF policies. A migrated CDN classic domain requires its CNAME to change before deletion; disassociate it before removing its default route.

For CDN, Microsoft recommends enabling diagnostic logging and certificate-name checking after migration. No general retirement backup or export procedure is supplied.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
The affected populations are Azure Front Door (classic) and Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic), including dependent custom domains, applications, clients and integrations. The supplied content does not establish whether your environment contains these resources or quantify your exposure.

- Availability: new profiles, new domain onboarding and BYOC-to-managed-certificate switches are blocked from August 15, 2025. The announcement's existing managed-certificate assurance ends on April 14, 2026 without specifying subsequent behavior. Microsoft warns of disruption if you do not migrate before the applicable service retirement; neither notice establishes an exact shutdown time.
- Endpoint dependencies: automatic forwarding after migration does not complete cutover. Dependencies on classic endpoints might stop receiving traffic from April 1, 2028.
- Management: preparation blocks configuration changes. After Front Door migration, the classic profile is disabled. After CDN migration, the classic profile disappears from the Azure portal, its resource ID remains unchanged and automation must use new interfaces.
- Configuration and monitoring: CDN diagnostic logs and metrics do not migrate, log fields change, and Core Analytics is unavailable in Standard/Premium. Built-in reports begin displaying data after migration. CDN session affinity becomes disabled but can be re-enabled; existing disabled certificate-name checking remains disabled until enabled.
- Cost: Azure Front Door Standard or Premium charges start when CDN migration completes. No cost estimate is supplied.

Standard and Premium are migration destinations, and these inputs do not establish retirement dates for other CDN offerings. No general retirement-related retention, deletion or backup policy is documented.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use the documented migration tools to track compatibility and migration stages; they do not prove that every endpoint dependency has been removed.

For Front Door (classic), open Settings > Migration. Validate can take up to two minutes; View errors provides remediation recommendations. Review the prepared destination configuration and applicable managed identity and Key Vault access. After migration, use the success message or banner to open the destination profile and confirm the classic profile is disabled.

For CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic), resolve compatibility-validation findings and follow the migration phases through committed migration. Use the new Front Door profile afterward; the classic profile is no longer visible in the portal. Built-in reports begin collecting data after migration, but historical diagnostic logs and metrics do not carry over. Microsoft recommends enabling diagnostic logging.

For team-owned completion evidence, record destination profiles, migration success, required WAF changes, automation updates, DNS changes, direct-hostname replacements and successful traffic validation through the new endpoints. Complete cutover by March 31, 2028. Neither guide supplies an automated check proving that every external application, client or integration has stopped using classic hostnames.

The HTTPS page's Enabled status checks HTTPS configuration only, not retirement migration completion. The announcement directs questions to Microsoft Q&A. Technical support requests require a support plan and appropriate subscription access, such as Owner, Contributor, Support Request Contributor or a custom role with Microsoft.Support/* permissions.

records.title: Retirement: Upgrade BlobFuse v1 to latest version of Blobfuse v2
records.summary: Support for BlobFuse v1 ends in September 2026; the notice gives no exact day and does not announce a workload shutdown. Microsoft recommends migrating to BlobFuse v2, where future enhancements will focus. The migration guide supports configuration conversion and side-by-side installation, but documents compatibility changes that you should review before switching workloads.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is ending support for BlobFuse v1 in September 2026. All future enhancements for Azure Blob Storage file system access will focus exclusively on BlobFuse v2.

The migration guide covers v1.X.X to v2.X.X. The separate blobfuse2 package allows both versions to coexist during migration without replacing the existing BlobFuse package.

The supplied content does not document regional exceptions or maintenance and security-update commitments before support ends.
what.html:
Microsoft is ending support for BlobFuse v1 in September 2026. All future enhancements for Azure Blob Storage file system access will focus exclusively on BlobFuse v2.

The migration guide covers v1.X.X to v2.X.X. The separate blobfuse2 package allows both versions to coexist during migration without replacing the existing BlobFuse package.

The supplied content does not document regional exceptions or maintenance and security-update commitments before support ends.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify whether your workloads use BlobFuse v1. Review their mount commands, configuration files and environment variables against the migration guide. Settings take precedence in this order: CLI flags, environment variables, configuration file.
2. If you use v1, follow Microsoft's recommendation to migrate to BlobFuse v2. Install blobfuse2 using the applicable distribution instructions. The guide states that packages are available only for x86 platforms. Ubuntu 20.04 and later use fuse3; Ubuntu 18.04 uses fuse; RedHat/CentOS and SUSE use fuse3. Kubernetes instructions are referenced but not supplied.
3. Convert and mount an existing configuration with the documented command:
blobfuse2 mountv1 <MOUNT_PATH> --config-file=<BLOBFUSE_V1_CONFIG_PATH> <BLOBFUSE_V1_CLI_PARAMETERS> --output-file=<OPTIONAL_DESIRED_BLOBFUSE2_CONFIG_PATH>

To convert without mounting, add:
--convert-config-only=true


4. Review changed, ignored and unavailable options before switching workloads. Existing environment variables require no changes. Store CA certificates in the standard Linux location rather than using the former CA-certificate option.
5. As a team-owned validation step, confirm that the resulting mount meets your workload's needs before cutover. The supplied guide does not provide a complete cutover, rollback, backup or cleanup procedure.

Microsoft recommends migration; the supplied notice does not establish a mandatory workload-shutdown deadline.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
If you use BlobFuse v1, support ends in September 2026. The supplied content does not establish whether your environment uses v1 or state that existing mounts or workloads will stop running.

When migrating to v2, review these compatibility limits:

- V1 CLI parameters are accepted, but parameters that no longer apply may be ignored. Existing environment variables remain supported.
- HTTPS-use and cache-on-list configuration equivalents have opposite boolean semantics. Attribute caching and streaming require their respective components in the component list.
- Attribute, entry and negative-entry timeout defaults change to zero.
- Upload-modified-only, pre-mount validation, invalidate-on-sync and content-type setting are always enabled.
- Cache-poll timeout and background download are unavailable; basic-remount-check is not applicable. Configuration mappings provide no replacement for caCertFile or dnsType.

The separate blobfuse2 package permits side-by-side migration without a package-name replacement breaking existing BlobFuse workloads. This does not establish workload compatibility after migration.

The supplied content documents no retirement-related data deletion, retention changes or cost effects.

The supplied content documents no retirement-related data deletion, retention changes or cost effects.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Dedicated HSM
records.summary: Azure Dedicated HSM retires on July 31, 2028, when Microsoft's full support commitment for existing customers ends. Complete your transition by that date; the notice separately asks you to prepare a transition plan by July 31, 2026. New customer onboarding stops immediately, but the notice supplies no effective calendar date. Azure Cloud HSM is the named successor, with alternatives depending on workload and compliance requirements. Workload shutdown timing and post-retirement data handling are not documented.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Azure Dedicated HSM and names Azure Cloud HSM as its successor. Existing customers retain full support until July 31, 2028. Microsoft is no longer accepting new Azure Dedicated HSM customers.

New customers must choose Azure Cloud HSM, Azure Managed HSM or Azure Key Vault according to their use case. No retirement-specific regional exceptions or separate version milestones are documented.

The Azure Cloud HSM overview and key-management comparison provide replacement-selection guidance, not independent retirement announcements.
what.html:
Microsoft is retiring Azure Dedicated HSM and names Azure Cloud HSM as its successor. Existing customers retain full support until July 31, 2028. Microsoft is no longer accepting new Azure Dedicated HSM customers.

New customers must choose Azure Cloud HSM, Azure Managed HSM or Azure Key Vault according to their use case. No retirement-specific regional exceptions or separate version milestones are documented.

The Azure Cloud HSM overview and key-management comparison provide replacement-selection guidance, not independent retirement announcements.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify whether you use Azure Dedicated HSM and document your application interfaces, stored object types, compliance requirements and Azure service integrations. The supplied sources provide no affected-resource discovery procedure.
2. Prepare your transition plan by July 31, 2026, as requested by the notice.
3. Select a replacement that fits your workload. The notice names Azure Cloud HSM as the successor and specifically directs existing customers to transition to it by July 31, 2028. It also identifies Azure Managed HSM as an alternative based on workload and compliance requirements.
4. Check compatibility before migrating, then complete your transition by July 31, 2028. The supplied sources do not provide retirement-specific migration, export, backup, cutover, cleanup or validation procedures.

Replacement considerations

- Azure Cloud HSM: Suitable for Azure Virtual Machine and lift-and-shift workloads using native PKCS#11, JCA/JCE or CNG/KSP. It is IaaS-only, does not integrate with Azure PaaS/SaaS services, and is not a secret store or certificate life-cycle management offering.
- Azure Key Vault Managed HSM: The guidance directs Azure PaaS/SaaS customer-managed-key scenarios here. It stores keys, not secrets or certificates, and offers limited PKCS#11 support for F5 and NGINX TLS offload. Its external key management supports wrap and unwrap only, is intended only when physical key control outside Microsoft infrastructure is mandatory, and is not covered by the Managed HSM SLA.
- Payment-specific workloads: The guidance identifies Azure Payment HSM options; the comparison explicitly labels Azure Payment HSM v2 as preview.

If you are a new customer, choose Azure Cloud HSM, Azure Managed HSM or Azure Key Vault instead of onboarding Azure Dedicated HSM.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Cache for Redis is retiring on September 30, 2028.
records.summary: Microsoft will retire Azure Cache for Redis Basic, Standard and Premium on September 30, 2028. Migrate these instances to Azure Managed Redis before that date to avoid shutdown. Enterprise and Enterprise Flash retire separately on March 31, 2027; Microsoft says remaining caches will migrate to Azure Managed Redis then. Creation restrictions vary by tier, cloud and customer eligibility.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Azure Cache for Redis and directing customers to Azure Managed Redis.

- Basic, Standard and Premium: Existing caches remain usable until retirement on September 30, 2028. Migrate before that date to avoid shutdown.
- Enterprise and Enterprise Flash: Existing caches remain usable until retirement on March 31, 2027. Microsoft says remaining caches will migrate to Azure Managed Redis then; the supplied content does not describe this as workload shutdown.

For Basic, Standard and Premium, qualifying existing public-cloud customers can continue creating caches until retirement. A tenant qualifies if any subscription in it had an Azure Cache for Redis instance before April 1, 2026. New public-cloud customers cannot create these caches from that date. Government and China have no creation block before retirement.

The supplied content does not specify maintenance, support or security-update commitments through retirement.

actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Azure Cache for Redis instances by tier and cloud. To assess public-cloud Basic, Standard and Premium creation eligibility, determine whether any subscription in your tenant had an instance before April 1, 2026. The supplied content provides no inventory procedure.
2. Migrate Basic, Standard and Premium workloads to Azure Managed Redis before September 30, 2028. Plan Enterprise and Enterprise Flash migration against March 31, 2027; Microsoft says remaining caches in those tiers will migrate on that date.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance:
Basic, Standard and Premium

Retirement and the migration deadline are September 30, 2028 across Azure public cloud, Azure Government and Azure operated by 21Vianet in China.

The announcement says unmigrated instances shut down on September 30, 2028. An older product-guidance section gives October 1, 2028 for shutdown. Use the earlier date, September 30, 2028, for planning: these shutdown dates differ by one day. Revised guidance confirms migration by September 30, 2028 but does not separately resolve the shutdown-date discrepancy.

From April 1, 2026, Azure public cloud blocks new customers from creating these caches. The July 2026 update removes planned creation blocks for existing customers in all clouds. Government and China have no creation block before retirement. This supersedes older creation-block dates of October 1, 2026 and April 1, 2027, not the retirement deadline.

Enterprise and Enterprise Flash

New-cache creation is blocked from April 1, 2026. Retirement is March 31, 2027, when Microsoft says remaining caches will migrate to Azure Managed Redis. This is a separate tier-specific milestone, not a conflicting Basic, Standard and Premium deadline.

records.title: Retirement: Microsoft Playwright Testing (Preview) will be retired on March 8, 2026
records.summary: Microsoft Playwright Testing (Preview) retires on March 8, 2026. The retirement notice states that remaining resources will stop working after that date. Migrate dependent workloads to Playwright Workspaces in Azure App Testing, updating workspace connections, packages, authentication and CI configuration as applicable. The migration guide states that reporting is available to all Playwright Workspaces users; earlier announcement comments describe reporting gaps, so do not assume complete reporting parity. Existing Azure Load Testing resources and tests remain unchanged.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Microsoft Playwright Testing (Preview) on March 8, 2026. The replacement is Playwright Workspaces in Azure App Testing. Remaining preview resources will stop working after that date; the supplied material does not specify maintenance, support or security-update commitments before retirement.

Migration covers Playwright Test Runner, Node.js manual browser connections, .NET NUnit and .NET manual connections. Resource operations move to the Azure Portal, the resource provider changes to Microsoft.LoadTestService, and workspace IDs become GUIDs without the region_ prefix.

The retirement notice describes identical execution capabilities, performance and pricing. Earlier announcement comments describe reporting gaps, while the migration guide states that reporting is available to all Playwright Workspaces users. Reporting availability does not establish full parity with the previous reporting experience.

Existing Azure Load Testing resources, tests, features, pricing and management remain unchanged. No regional exceptions are documented.

Microsoft is retiring Microsoft Playwright Testing (Preview) on March 8, 2026. The replacement is Playwright Workspaces in Azure App Testing. Remaining preview resources will stop working after that date; the supplied material does not specify maintenance, support or security-update commitments before retirement.

Migration covers Playwright Test Runner, Node.js manual browser connections, .NET NUnit and .NET manual connections. Resource operations move to the Azure Portal, the resource provider changes to Microsoft.LoadTestService, and workspace IDs become GUIDs without the region_ prefix.

The retirement notice describes identical execution capabilities, performance and pricing. Earlier announcement comments describe reporting gaps, while the migration guide states that reporting is available to all Playwright Workspaces users. Reporting availability does not establish full parity with the previous reporting experience.

Existing Azure Load Testing resources, tests, features, pricing and management remain unchanged. No regional exceptions are documented.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Migrate workloads that depend on Microsoft Playwright Testing (Preview) to Playwright Workspaces to avoid the documented post-retirement disruption.

1. Identify your scenario from package dependencies, configuration and browser-connection calls: Playwright Test Runner with the service package or custom connectOptions, Node.js manual connections, .NET NUnit with the service package, or .NET manual connections.
2. Create a Playwright Workspaces resource in the Azure Portal, configure access and update CI service connections to the new workspace. Regional-latency customization and local authentication are optional, depending on your needs.
3. Apply the scenario-specific changes below.
4. Update PLAYWRIGHT_SERVICE_URL and PLAYWRIGHT_SERVICE_ACCESS_TOKEN to the new workspace values. Where applicable, replace runId with runName and timeout with connectTimeout; useCloudHostedBrowsers has been removed.

Scenario-specific changes

- Playwright Test Runner with the service package: replace @azure/microsoft-playwright-testing with @azure/playwright, install @azure/identity and update @playwright/test to latest. Replace getServiceConfig with createAzurePlaywrightConfig, add DefaultAzureCredential and remove the old service reporter configuration.
- Custom connectOptions, Node.js manual connections and .NET manual connections: update custom connection logic to the new workspace endpoint and include API version 2025-09-01. For connectOptions, follow the referenced Playwright Workspaces Quickstart.
- .NET NUnit with the service package: replace Azure.Developer.MicrosoftPlaywrightTesting.NUnit with Azure.Developer.Playwright.NUnit, install Azure.Identity and update Microsoft.Playwright.NUnit to 1.50.0. Update namespaces, use PlaywrightServiceBrowserNUnit and add DefaultAzureCredential. Create CloudBrowserPageTest using the new base class and update test classes to inherit from it. Remove loggers referencing microsoft-playwright-testing and delete .runsettings files.

Assess your reporting requirements: the migration guide confirms reporting availability, but the supplied material does not establish full parity. It does not specify backup procedures, cutover sequencing, old-resource deletion or validation criteria. Azure Load Testing users do not need to change existing resources or tests because of this announcement.

  1. Identify your scenario from package dependencies, configuration and browser-connection calls: Playwright Test Runner with the service package or custom connectOptions, Node.js manual connections, .NET NUnit with the service package, or .NET manual connections.
  2. Create a Playwright Workspaces resource in the Azure Portal, configure access and update CI service connections to the new workspace. Regional-latency customization and local authentication are optional, depending on your needs.
  3. Apply the scenario-specific changes below.
  4. Update PLAYWRIGHT_SERVICE_URL and PLAYWRIGHT_SERVICE_ACCESS_TOKEN to the new workspace values. Where applicable, replace runId with runName and timeout with connectTimeout; useCloudHostedBrowsers has been removed.

Scenario-specific changes

  • Playwright Test Runner with the service package: replace @azure/microsoft-playwright-testing with @azure/playwright, install @azure/identity and update @playwright/test to latest. Replace getServiceConfig with createAzurePlaywrightConfig, add DefaultAzureCredential and remove the old service reporter configuration.
  • Custom connectOptions, Node.js manual connections and .NET manual connections: update custom connection logic to the new workspace endpoint and include API version 2025-09-01. For connectOptions, follow the referenced Playwright Workspaces Quickstart.
  • .NET NUnit with the service package: replace Azure.Developer.MicrosoftPlaywrightTesting.NUnit with Azure.Developer.Playwright.NUnit, install Azure.Identity and update Microsoft.Playwright.NUnit to 1.50.0. Update namespaces, use PlaywrightServiceBrowserNUnit and add DefaultAzureCredential. Create CloudBrowserPageTest using the new base class and update test classes to inherit from it. Remove loggers referencing microsoft-playwright-testing and delete .runsettings files.

Assess your reporting requirements: the migration guide confirms reporting availability, but the supplied material does not establish full parity. It does not specify backup procedures, cutover sequencing, old-resource deletion or validation criteria. Azure Load Testing users do not need to change existing resources or tests because of this announcement.

records.title: Retirement: Azure VPN Gateway support for SSTP Protocol will be retired on March 31, 2027
records.summary: Azure VPN Gateway SSTP point-to-site connections stop working at the March 31, 2027 cutoff. Migrate affected clients to IKEv2 or OpenVPN before that date. For the separate restriction on enabling SSTP, current product guidance specifies August 31, 2026, while the announcement specifies March 31, 2026. This synthesis uses the applicable product-guidance date; the supplied sources do not explicitly document an extension. Migration can affect connectivity, client profiles and address-pool allocation.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring SSTP for Azure VPN Gateway point-to-site (P2S) connections, with connectivity ending at the March 31, 2027 cutoff. Replace SSTP with IKEv2 or OpenVPN.

Before the cutoff, product guidance describes retaining existing SSTP connectivity while adding IKEv2 and migrating clients in batches. SSTP and OpenVPN cannot coexist on the same gateway; OpenVPN can coexist with IKEv2. The staged migration guidance does not override the restriction on enabling SSTP.

Basic SKU gateways support IKEv2 as of November 2025. New Basic gateways use IKEv2 by default, and existing SSTP-only Basic gateways can enable it.

The supplied sources state no regional exceptions or transition-period maintenance and security-update commitments. They do not announce retirement of Azure VPN Gateway itself.
what.html:
Microsoft is retiring SSTP for Azure VPN Gateway point-to-site (P2S) connections, with connectivity ending at the March 31, 2027 cutoff. Replace SSTP with IKEv2 or OpenVPN.

Before the cutoff, product guidance describes retaining existing SSTP connectivity while adding IKEv2 and migrating clients in batches. SSTP and OpenVPN cannot coexist on the same gateway; OpenVPN can coexist with IKEv2. The staged migration guidance does not override the restriction on enabling SSTP.

Basic SKU gateways support IKEv2 as of November 2025. New Basic gateways use IKEv2 by default, and existing SSTP-only Basic gateways can enable it.

The supplied sources state no regional exceptions or transition-period maintenance and security-update commitments. They do not announce retirement of Azure VPN Gateway itself.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. In the Azure portal, open each virtual network gateway and select Settings > Point-to-site configuration. Review its tunnel type and affected client profiles to identify SSTP use.
2. Choose a replacement path appropriate to your clients and gateway:
  - Staged IKEv2: Add IKEv2 alongside existing SSTP and migrate clients in batches without disrupting existing clients. Allow UDP ports 500 and 4500 through client firewalls. Basic SKU supports this path.
  - IKEv2 only: Switch directly, allowing for gateway downtime while the configuration applies.
  - OpenVPN: Replace SSTP, optionally retaining IKEv2 alongside OpenVPN. OpenVPN uses TCP port 443. Clients lose connectivity until replacement clients and profiles are configured; SSTP cannot remain enabled alongside OpenVPN.
3. Save the gateway configuration, download the updated VPN client configuration package and distribute the appropriate profiles to all affected P2S users. For OpenVPN, deploy compatible clients. The guidance identifies Azure VPN Client on Windows 10 or later and recommends Windows 11. It states that Windows clients require administrator rights to initiate the VPN connection.
4. Before March 31, 2027, verify that every affected client connects using its replacement protocol. Windows clients configured for both protocols try IKEv2 first but can fall back to SSTP, so connection success alone does not prove migration is complete.

The announcement describes replacement capabilities of up to 10,000 connections and 10 Gbps aggregate throughput, depending on gateway SKU; these limits are not guaranteed for every SKU.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if your Azure VPN Gateway P2S clients use SSTP. Review gateway tunnel settings and client profiles; this synthesis does not establish whether your environment uses SSTP. Clients already using IKEv2 or OpenVPN are outside the stated retirement scope.

Without migration, SSTP connectivity stops working at the March 31, 2027 cutoff. This is a connectivity change, not a documented deletion of gateways or shutdown of workloads in the virtual network.

Migration constraints include:

- Adding IKEv2 alongside existing SSTP preserves existing client connectivity. Switching directly to IKEv2 causes downtime while configuration applies.
- Replacing SSTP with OpenVPN disconnects clients until replacement clients and profiles are configured.
- With SSTP and IKEv2 enabled together, the P2S address pool is statically split between protocols. Smaller pools are halved, and SSTP remains limited to 128 concurrent connections regardless of gateway SKU. Traffic selectors might use the two subrange CIDRs rather than the original pool CIDR.
- Azure diagnostics does not support SSTP; the guidance directs you to IKEv2 or OpenVPN for diagnostics.

The supplied sources do not document retirement-related data deletion, retention changes or cost changes. The separate Q&A reference to Azure VPN Client for Linux does not establish additional SSTP retirement terms.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Track migration through the documented configuration and client checks:

1. Review each gateway's Settings > Point-to-site configuration and tunnel type.
2. Confirm that updated profiles have been downloaded and distributed and that replacement clients are configured.
3. Verify that every affected client connects using IKEv2 or OpenVPN. Account for Windows falling back to SSTP when both SSTP and IKEv2 are configured; successful connectivity alone is not proof of completion.

As team-owned migration evidence, record gateway configuration, profile distribution and client verification results. These are local planning records, not an automatic retirement tracker. records.title: Retirement: Operating System (OS) Disks on Standard HDD will be retired on 08 September 2028
records.summary: Azure retires Standard HDD OS disks for Linux and Windows VMs on September 8, 2028. Migrate affected OS disks to Standard SSD or Premium SSD before that date. Azure will automatically convert remaining affected disks to equivalent-size Standard SSDs afterward, with potential service disruption; the conversion schedule is unspecified. Standard HDD data disks, ephemeral OS disks, Standard HDD snapshots and Standard HDD OS disks created by Azure Site Recovery are unaffected.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure is retiring Standard HDD OS disks for Linux and Windows VMs on September 8, 2028. The guidance describes continued use before retirement without specifying new-customer restrictions. After retirement, Azure will automatically convert remaining affected disks to equivalent-size Standard SSDs.

The retirement does not affect:

- Standard HDD data disks or other managed disk types.
- Ephemeral OS disks.
- Snapshots stored on Standard HDD, including OS disk snapshots.
- Standard HDD OS disks created by Azure Site Recovery, which remain supported.

The supplied guidance does not document retirement-specific maintenance or security-update commitments.
what.html:
Azure is retiring Standard HDD OS disks for Linux and Windows VMs on September 8, 2028. The guidance describes continued use before retirement without specifying new-customer restrictions. After retirement, Azure will automatically convert remaining affected disks to equivalent-size Standard SSDs.

The retirement does not affect:

  • Standard HDD data disks or other managed disk types.
  • Ephemeral OS disks.
  • Snapshots stored on Standard HDD, including OS disk snapshots.
  • Standard HDD OS disks created by Azure Site Recovery, which remain supported.

The supplied guidance does not document retirement-specific maintenance or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify affected disks in Disk Storage Center. Filter Storage type to Standard HDD LRS and OS type to Linux and Windows. Use the Owner column to identify each associated VM. Account separately for Standard HDD OS disks created by Azure Site Recovery, which are exempt.
2. Stop selecting Standard HDD OS disks for new VMs. Choose Standard SSD for the documented closest price-to-performance ratio to Standard HDD, or Premium SSD for higher performance. Review billing guidance; Premium SSD requires a VM size that supports Premium storage. Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disk cannot serve as OS disks.
3. Plan conversion before September 8, 2028. The supplied conversion guidance applies to managed disks; unmanaged disks must first be converted to managed disks. Schedule a maintenance window for stopping, deallocating and restarting the VM. A disk's type can change only twice per day.
4. Follow the supplied conversion procedure: stop and deallocate the VM, resize it if required, update the selected OS disk's SKU, and restart the VM. Procedures that update all attached disks have broader scope than this retirement requires.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Network Policy Manager (NPM) for Linux nodes on AKS to Be Retired by September 30, 2028
records.summary: Microsoft will end support for Azure Network Policy Manager (NPM) on AKS Linux nodes on September 30, 2028. Migrate affected clusters to Cilium Network Policy by that date to avoid possible disruptions. Migration requires Azure CNI powered by Cilium, reimages all node pools and changes policy enforcement. The notice does not specify a workload shutdown date; the migration guide does not independently establish a retirement deadline.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is ending support for Azure NPM on AKS Linux nodes on September 30, 2028. The notice directs affected customers to Cilium Network Policy, which requires Azure CNI powered by Cilium.

Enabling the Cilium dataplane automatically uninstalls NPM and replaces it with Cilium. The migration guidance covers Azure CNI to Azure CNI with the Cilium dataplane; it does not cover bring-your-own CNIs or IPAM-mode changes. Windows nodes are not supported by this guidance, and the notice does not establish retirement milestones for other node operating systems.

The supplied content does not document pre-deadline maintenance or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify affected clusters using the migration guide's Azure Resource Graph query. It selects managed clusters with a non-Windows agent pool and a network policy value of azure; it does not assess workload policy compatibility.
2. Review and adapt policies before migration. For Cilium earlier than 1.17, replace endPort ranges with individual ports; Cilium 1.17 or later needs no such change. Replace named ports with numeric values because reusing a name for different ports can cause incorrect enforcement.
3. For Pod egress currently permitted through ipBlock, add appropriate namespace and Pod selectors before migration. Review dependencies on NPM's implicit local-node egress allowance. Node-IP access requires explicit Cilium policies using the appropriate host or remote-node entities after migration; the guide gives no pre-migration workaround for that access.
4. Review LoadBalancer and NodePort ingress rules using externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster. Explicitly allow expected sources rather than relying on NPM's enforcement exception.
5. Plan for every node pool to be reimaged simultaneously; upgrading pools separately is unsupported. Use Azure CLI 2.52.0 or later and migrate by September 30, 2028 with your cluster and resource-group values:

az aks update --name <clusterName> --resource-group <resourceGroupName> --network-dataplane cilium

6. After migration, create the required Cilium node-egress policies and validate expected allowed and denied traffic. Cilium starts enforcing policies only after all nodes are reimaged.

The supplied content does not provide rollback procedures.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are in scope if your AKS clusters use Azure NPM on Linux nodes. Azure Resource Graph can identify matching cluster configurations, but its query does not inspect workload policy compatibility. Windows nodes are not supported by the supplied Cilium migration guidance; this does not establish their retirement status.

If you remain on NPM after September 30, 2028, the affected configuration will be outside NPM support. The notice warns of possible disruptions but does not state whether or when workloads would stop running.

Migration reimages every node pool and can disrupt networking. Policy enforcement might be temporarily inconsistent during reimaging; Cilium enforcement starts only after all nodes are reimaged.

Connectivity can change:

- ipBlock no longer permits egress to Pod or Node IPs, even when its CIDR includes them.
- Local-node egress previously allowed implicitly by NPM requires explicit permission.
- Cilium enforces ingress policies for LoadBalancer and NodePort traffic using externalTrafficPolicy=Cluster, so previously reachable workloads might reject traffic.
- Named-port reuse can cause incorrect enforcement. endPort ranges require changes for Cilium earlier than 1.17, but not for 1.17 or later.

The supplied content does not document retirement-related data deletion or cost changes.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring AKS on VMware (preview), which uses Azure Arc to create and manage Kubernetes clusters on VMware vSphere. Microsoft identifies AKS on Azure Local as the supported replacement.

The overview describes the preview as available before retirement; deployment and support are unavailable after March 16, 2026. The supplied guidance states no regional exceptions, separate customer phases, maintenance commitments or security-update commitments.

3. As team-owned planning, establish migration, validation and cutover criteria before moving workloads. The supplied material does not specify retirement-specific export, backup, cutover, cleanup or completion procedures.

records.title: Retirement: NVv3-series Azure Virtual Machines will be retired on September 30 ,2026
records.summary: Azure NVv3-series VMs retired on September 30, 2026, except existing Azure UAE North users have an explicit extension through January 31, 2027. Microsoft states that remaining affected VMs will be deallocated after retirement, stopping workloads and VM billing, with no SLA or included support. Migrate workloads to a supported VM series or deallocate unneeded VMs. The current retirement guidance lists November 2, 2025 as the reserved-instance purchase cutoff, conflicting with September 30, 2025 in the announcement; this is separate from workload retirement.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired Azure NVv3-series VMs powered by NVIDIA Tesla M60 GPUs on September 30, 2026, with continued use for existing Azure UAE North users through January 31, 2027.

Affected sizes are:

- Standard_NV12s_v3
- Standard_NV12hs_v3
- Standard_NV24s_v3
- Standard_NV24ms_v3
- Standard_NV32ms_v3
- Standard_NV48s_v3

Microsoft states that remaining VMs will be deallocated after retirement and that NVv3 will no longer have SLA coverage or included support. The supplied content does not document pre-retirement maintenance or security-update commitments.

This retirement does not apply to NVadsA10_v5 or NVadsV710_v5. NVv4 has separate retirement guidance. The supplied NVadsA10_v5 reference page describes replacement capabilities, not another retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify VMs using the six affected NVv3 sizes and determine whether they qualify for the existing-user Azure UAE North extension. The supplied content provides no inventory command or automated assessment procedure.
2. Select a supported replacement for workloads you need to keep running. Microsoft recommends NVadsA10_v5. The retirement guidance lists NVadsA10_v5 or NC_RTXPRO6000BSE_v6 for graphics applications, virtual desktops, visualization and small AI workloads. It lists NCasT4_v3 for offline inference when latency is not a primary concern and smaller sizes or lower costs are priorities.
3. Check target-region availability, pricing and quota, and request quota for the target VM. If considering NVadsA10_v5, compare its CPU, memory, GPU, storage and network limits with your requirements. It does not support Live Migration, Memory Preserving Updates or Nested Virtualization.
4. Resize affected VMs to your selected supported size, or deallocate VMs you no longer need. The general deadline has passed; qualifying existing Azure UAE North users must migrate by January 31, 2027.

The supplied content does not provide detailed compatibility, backup, cutover or post-migration validation procedures. If you have a support plan and need resizing help, create a technical support request for Virtual Machine running Windows/Linux and select Assistance with resizing my VM.

records.title: Retirement: NVv4-series Azure Virtual Machines will be retired on September 30, 2026
records.summary: Microsoft Azure retired the eight listed NVv4-series VM sizes on September 30, 2026. Microsoft states that remaining affected VMs are deallocated after that date, stop working and no longer incur VM billing charges; SLA coverage and included support end. Migrate workloads you still need to NVads_V710_v5 or a suitable alternative. Current retirement guidance documents feature registration to unblock a known resize error. what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft Azure retired these AMD Radeon Instinct MI25-powered NVv4 sizes on September 30, 2026:

- Standard_NV4as_v4 and Standard_NV4ahs_v4
- Standard_NV8as_v4 and Standard_NV8ahs_v4
- Standard_NV16as_v4 and Standard_NV16ahs_v4
- Standard_NV32as_v4 and Standard_NV32ahs_v4

Remaining affected VMs are deallocated after retirement and lose SLA coverage and included support. The supplied guidance does not document regional exceptions or pre-retirement maintenance and security-update commitments.

Microsoft recommends NVads_V710_v5 or a suitable alternative. NVadsA10_v5 and NVads_V710_v5 are unaffected by this retirement; NVv3 has separate retirement guidance.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
The required pre-retirement action was to resize or deallocate affected VMs before September 30, 2026. If you still need an affected workload:

1. Identify VMs using the listed NVv4 sizes. The supplied guidance provides no inventory command or discovery procedure.
2. Select a replacement based on workload, regional availability and cost. Microsoft recommends NVads_V710_v5 overall. Documented alternatives are NVads_V710_v5 or NVadsA10_v5 for small AI workloads where optimal performance is not a priority or reducing cost is a goal; NVads_V710_v5, NVadsA10_v5 or NGads_V620 for graphics, virtual desktops and visualization; and NGads_V620 for gaming.
3. Check Azure Regions by Product and Azure Virtual Machine pricing, then request target quota. For NVads V710 v5, check workload requirements against documented resource limits: Generation 2 is supported, but Generation 1, Live Migration and Memory Preserving Updates are not. Network bandwidth upper limits are not guaranteed.
4. Before resizing to NVads_V710_v5, register your subscription for the Azure Feature Exposure Control feature VMTempDiskResizePreview and confirm registration. Current retirement guidance documents this prerequisite to unblock a known resize error; it does not confirm delivery of the announcement's planned April 2026 fix.
5. Resize to the selected supported size, or deallocate VMs you no longer need.

The retirement guidance provides no backup, cutover, cleanup or post-migration validation procedure. The separate diskless-VM FAQ describes conditional storage migration constraints, but does not establish that its snapshot-and-new-VM procedure is required for this NVv4 migration.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS
records.summary: Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS reached end of support on November 30, 2025. Migrate affected node pools to a supported Azure Linux version. Current AKS product guidance places node-image removal beginning October 31, 2026, after which affected pools cannot scale; the announcement instead gives March 31, 2026. The product-guidance date is preferred, but the supplied inputs do not explicitly document an extension. Neither source establishes a running-workload shutdown date.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS is retired. Since November 30, 2025, Microsoft no longer supports it or provides security updates; the announcement also ends new node images and creation of new Azure Linux 2.0 node pools.

Move affected pools to a supported Azure Linux version. Current AKS guidance says the Azure Linux 2.0 image is frozen at release 202512.06.0 and places image removal beginning October 31, 2026. The announcement instead lists March 31, 2026.

This retirement concerns Azure Linux 2.0, not every AKS operating system. The supplied sources identify no regional exceptions. Azure Linux 4.0 preview is limited to evaluation and testing, not production, and is not established as the required replacement.
what.html:
Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS is retired. Since November 30, 2025, Microsoft no longer supports it or provides security updates; the announcement also ends new node images and creation of new Azure Linux 2.0 node pools.

Move affected pools to a supported Azure Linux version. Current AKS guidance says the Azure Linux 2.0 image is frozen at release 202512.06.0 and places image removal beginning October 31, 2026. The announcement instead lists March 31, 2026.

This retirement concerns Azure Linux 2.0, not every AKS operating system. The supplied sources identify no regional exceptions. Azure Linux 4.0 preview is limited to evaluation and testing, not production, and is not established as the required replacement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your AKS pools' actual OS versions, OS SKUs and Kubernetes versions. The supplied sources provide no inventory command. Do not rely on the default SKU alone: its OS version depends on the Kubernetes version, and the guidance conflicts on whether the Azure Linux 2.0 default range starts at 1.26 or 1.27; both ranges end at 1.31.
2. Select a supported migration route. The announcement offers a Kubernetes upgrade to 1.32 or later, or an in-place change from --os-sku AzureLinux to --os-sku AzureLinux3 on Kubernetes 1.28 or later. Current guidance lists AzureLinux3 support specifically for 1.28–1.36, so do not treat the announcement's minimum as unlimited compatibility.
3. Check that the target image supports your Kubernetes version, VM size and FIPS configuration. Test your workloads on the target OS before production migration. Azure Linux 4.0 preview is not suitable for production.
4. Perform the applicable Kubernetes upgrade or supported OS-SKU update using the documented az aks nodepool update command. The in-place AzureLinux3 route preserves the Kubernetes version and reimages the pool to the equivalent Azure Linux 3.0 image.
5. As a team-owned completion check, confirm the resulting OS version and validate workloads and required scaling operations.

The original migration deadline was November 30, 2025. The supplied sources do not provide full migration commands, a retirement-specific validation procedure, or backup, cutover and cleanup requirements.

Do not rely on the default SKU alone: its OS version depends on the Kubernetes version, and the guidance conflicts on whether the Azure Linux 2.0 default range starts at 1.26 or 1.27; both ranges end at 1.31.
  2. Select a supported migration route. The announcement offers a Kubernetes upgrade to 1.32 or later, or an in-place change from --os-sku AzureLinux to --os-sku AzureLinux3 on Kubernetes 1.28 or later. Current guidance lists AzureLinux3 support specifically for 1.28–1.36, so do not treat the announcement's minimum as unlimited compatibility.
  3. Check that the target image supports your Kubernetes version, VM size and FIPS configuration. Test your workloads on the target OS before production migration. Azure Linux 4.0 preview is not suitable for production.
  4. Perform the applicable Kubernetes upgrade or supported OS-SKU update using the documented az aks nodepool update command. The in-place AzureLinux3 route preserves the Kubernetes version and reimages the pool to the equivalent Azure Linux 3.0 image.
  5. As a team-owned completion check, confirm the resulting OS version and validate workloads and required scaling operations.

The original migration deadline was November 30, 2025. The supplied sources do not provide full migration commands, a retirement-specific validation procedure, or backup, cutover and cleanup requirements.

records.title: Retirement: The F, Fs, Fsv2, Lsv2, G, Gs, Av2, Amv2, and B series VMs are retiring in 2028
records.summary: Azure retires F, Fs, Fsv2, Lsv2, G, Gs, Av2, Amv2 and the affected B-series VMs on November 15, 2028. Migrate before that date to avoid deallocation and service interruption. The announcement says B series; the migration guide specifies Bv1, so broader B-series scope is unconfirmed. Reservation purchase and renewal restrictions are separate, earlier milestones.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure is retiring F, Fs, Fsv2, Lsv2, G, Gs, Av2 and Amv2, plus the affected B-series VMs, on November 15, 2028. You must move affected workloads to supported sizes before retirement.

The announcement names B series, while the migration guide specifies Bv1 and recommends newer B-series alternatives. Whether additional B-series versions are included is unconfirmed; do not treat all B versions as retiring.

The supplied guidance distinguishes continued VM use before retirement from earlier reservation restrictions. It gives no regional exceptions for this retirement and no interim maintenance or security-update commitments. Exceptions documented for other retiring series do not establish exceptions here.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify deployed VM series and sizes against the affected-series reference. Review current reservation orders and expiration dates in the Azure portal. Reservation checks alone do not identify every affected workload. Confirm scope if your B-series version is unclear.
2. Select a supported replacement for your workload:
  - Av2/Amv2: evaluate the guide's B, D or E alternatives, confirming the target version.
  - Bv1: evaluate Bsv2/Basv2 or the listed D-family alternatives.
  - F/Fs/Fsv2: evaluate the listed D-family options or Falsv6.
  - G/Gs/Lsv2: evaluate the listed Lsv3/Lasv3 or v4 alternatives. The guide also identifies Lasv5 and Laosv5 as current L-series options.
3. Check CPU, memory, storage, operating-system compatibility, regional and zonal capacity, and quota. The guide states that v6 requires Generation 2, NVMe support and a MANA-supported operating system. Request additional v6 quota if needed. Bsv2, Bpsv2 and Basv2 are unavailable in sovereign clouds. Target-table specifications describe the smallest target size, not every size.
4. Plan an interruption and follow the full resizing guidance for your selected target. The guide describes stopping and deallocating the VM, resizing it, then starting it through the Azure portal, Azure CLI or PowerShell; its generic procedure specifically describes v6. Validate application operation and performance before considering migration complete.
5. Review reservation term ends and your replacement billing choice. Eligible exchanges, a trade-in for an Azure savings plan for compute, or replacement-series reservations are optional choices. Plan for pay-as-you-go billing when existing reservation benefits expire.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if you run the listed VM series. Bv1 is explicitly included in the migration guide; the announcement's broader B-series wording remains a scope uncertainty. This summary does not inspect your subscription.

Without migration, Azure deallocates affected VMs at retirement: workloads stop and lose support and SLA coverage. In-memory and temporary disk data is lost; managed disk data is preserved. The guide says you can resize to a supported size and restart to resume service.

Resizing itself requires stopping and deallocating the VM. Target compatibility, quota and capacity can constrain your migration. No separate console or API retirement is documented.

Existing reservations retain benefits through their original terms. After the applicable benefits expire, workloads move to pay-as-you-go pricing unless another applicable billing option applies. The supplied content does not quantify replacement costs. The guide says retired, deallocated VMs stop incurring VM charges; it does not establish that all associated resource charges end.

deadline.dateGuidance:

records.title: Retirement: Legacy Authentication in Azure Monitor - Container Insights will be retired on September 30, 2026.
records.summary: Azure Monitor Container insights legacy certificate-based authentication is being replaced by managed identity. The announcement requires migration before September 30, 2026; current migration guidance says Microsoft provides no support after that date for clusters still using legacy authentication. That guidance describes legacy authentication as already retired without giving a separate retirement date. Neither source documents an automatic workload shutdown or monitoring cutoff at the deadline. Identify affected AKS and Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters, migrate them, and verify both authentication and monitoring data flow.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Monitor Container insights is replacing legacy certificate-based local authentication with managed identity authentication. Managed identity is now the default and uses your cluster's managed identity to send monitoring data to Azure Monitor.

This changes monitoring configuration, not application code, workloads, or other Kubernetes resources. Syslog collection and High Scale mode require managed identity. The sources do not document pre-deadline maintenance or security-update commitments.

Documented migration scope includes AKS and Arc-enabled Kubernetes, including Arc-enabled Azure Red Hat OpenShift. AKS migration supports Azure public cloud, Microsoft Azure operated by 21Vianet, and Azure Government; AKS clusters with user-assigned identity are supported only in Azure public cloud.
what.html:

This changes monitoring configuration, not application code, workloads, or other Kubernetes resources. Syslog collection and High Scale mode require managed identity. The sources do not document pre-deadline maintenance or security-update commitments.

Documented migration scope includes AKS and Arc-enabled Kubernetes, including Arc-enabled Azure Red Hat OpenShift. AKS migration supports Azure public cloud, Microsoft Azure operated by 21Vianet, and Azure Government; AKS clusters with user-assigned identity are supported only in Azure public cloud.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify affected AKS and Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters using the migration page's queries in Azure Resource Graph Explorer. Set the Azure portal scope to include all resources you need to assess.
2. Before migrating, sign in to Azure CLI, use version 2.49.0 or later, and ensure you have Contributor access to the cluster. Follow the documented cloud and identity restrictions.
3. For AKS, record the configured Log Analytics workspace resource ID, disable the monitoring add-on, and upgrade service-principal clusters to system-assigned managed identity where applicable. Reenable monitoring with the recorded workspace ID.
4. For Arc-enabled Kubernetes, retrieve the workspace configured for the Container insights extension, then enable the extension with managed identity authentication using that workspace and the documented amalogs.useAADAuth=true setting.
5. Choose a documented migration route: the announcement offers a single-click Azure portal option and command-line options. For bulk migration, the migration page recommends its linked shell script; check cluster firewall requirements and read the script's first 30 lines before running it.
6. Complete migration before September 30, 2026. Allow a few minutes for configuration updates, rerun the applicable query, and confirm the cluster no longer appears. Also verify new logs and metrics, Container insights health, custom configurations, alerts, dashboards, and operational workflows.

records.title: Retirement: Azure CDN – Migrate to Azure Front Door on December 1, 2025
records.summary: Azure CDN in Microsoft Azure operated by 21Vianet (Azure China) stopped serving traffic on December 1, 2025, according to the supplied FAQ. Migration guidance required migration before November 15, 2025; the FAQ instead recommended before November 30, 2025, without documenting an extension. Eligible profiles were scheduled for automatic migration, but excluded configurations required customer action. Auto-migrated customers also needed to update automation and replace legacy CNAME targets before February 1, 2026. Standard Azure Front Door billing applies from October 1, 2026. The supplied material does not confirm any individual profile's migration status.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure CDN in Microsoft Azure operated by 21Vianet (Azure China) retired and stopped serving traffic on December 1, 2025, according to the FAQ. These sources do not establish retirement dates for Azure CDN outside China.

Microsoft offered Azure Front Door or an alternative CDN as replacement paths. Compatible profiles were scheduled for automatic, in-place migration; afterward, they were no longer visible as Azure CDN profiles. Incompatible and other excluded configurations required customer-led migration.

Azure Front Door is not feature-equivalent. The comparison lists two China PoPs, in China North 3 and China East 2, versus more than 600 mainland China PoPs for Azure China CDN. Features, endpoints, authentication, reporting and billing differ. The supplied material does not document interim maintenance, support or security-update commitments.
