Azure CDN in Microsoft Azure operated by 21Vianet (Azure China) retired and stopped serving traffic on December 1, 2025, according to the FAQ. These sources do not establish retirement dates for Azure CDN outside China.

Microsoft offered Azure Front Door or an alternative CDN as replacement paths. Compatible profiles were scheduled for automatic, in-place migration; afterward, they were no longer visible as Azure CDN profiles. Incompatible and other excluded configurations required customer-led migration.

Azure Front Door is not feature-equivalent. The comparison lists two China PoPs, in China North 3 and China East 2, versus more than 600 mainland China PoPs for Azure China CDN. Features, endpoints, authentication, reporting and billing differ. The supplied material does not document interim maintenance, support or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your profiles and status. Use the Azure portal eligibility assessment and View details to inspect incompatibilities. Determine whether each profile serves mainland China, overseas locations or both. Eligibility does not establish that migration completed.
2. Choose a compatible destination. Compare required features before choosing Azure Front Door. Unsupported capabilities include image processing, cache preloading, custom cache keys, allowing empty referrers, ignoring Cache-Control or Set-Cookie headers, and listed service-team authentication customizations. P95 billing is unsupported. Incompatible configurations require another CDN.
3. Resolve delivery-scope requirements. The migration guide describes China Front Door for mainland delivery, public Azure Front Door with a public Azure subscription for overseas delivery, and both deployments with Azure Traffic Manager for combined delivery. The FAQ instead directs noneligible overseas/global configurations to a third-party CDN. These sources do not establish one applicable route for every such profile; confirm compatibility before choosing. The guide directs you to Premium when Web Application Firewall and Private Link to origins are needed, otherwise Standard.
4. Check provider-led migration prerequisites. Certain service-team customizations require customer-led migration. For bring-your-own certificates, the comparison requires certificate auto-rotation but then refers to enabling “automatic migration”; that prerequisite is ambiguous in the supplied material.
5. Migrate, validate and cut over. The guide describes testing by locally binding the host IP to the relevant Front Door IP, testing both deployments for combined delivery, then changing custom-domain DNS for single-scope delivery. For combined delivery, it directs you to add both endpoints to Azure Traffic Manager but supplies no complete setup or final cutover procedure. No export or backup procedure is supplied.
6. Update integrations and clean up. Replace Azure CDN APIs/tooling in automation with Azure Front Door equivalents. Replace legacy mcchcdn.com CNAME targets, which became unusable on February 1, 2026. After validating migration to another CDN, delete the old Azure CDN profile to avoid unnecessary charges; the announcement also required post-validation deletion before November 15, 2025.

Contact support or your sales contact for migration help. The FAQ directs customers seeking automatic-migration opt-out to support.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
Your exposure depends on your Azure China CDN configuration and whether migration completed. Unmigrated profiles stopped serving traffic on December 1, 2025; continued portal visibility did not mean continued service. No customer resources have been inspected.

Documented automatic-migration exclusions and constraints include:

- Disabled profiles, active profiles without endpoints, and disabled endpoints within active profiles.
- Profiles or endpoints without active requests in the preceding three months.
- Domains not directly CNAME-mapped to an Azure CDN endpoint.
- Incompatible features, overseas/global configurations and certain service-team customizations.
- The certificate prerequisite described in the comparison, whose wording is ambiguous.

Microsoft described automatic migration as downtime-free for eligible instances, not as proof that any particular migration succeeded. After migration, Azure CDN profile views disappeared and automation needed Azure Front Door APIs or tooling. Legacy CNAME targets became unusable on February 1, 2026.

Front Door also changes feature configuration, authentication and reporting. It uses standard Azure REST API authentication and Azure Monitor diagnostics; basic request and usage metrics do not fully match CDN reporting. IPv4/IPv6 is dual-stack by default and cannot be configured separately.

Standard Front Door billing applies from October 1, 2026, with base, request and traffic-related fees rather than CDN egress-only billing. Costs may increase depending on traffic; no customer-specific estimate is supplied. The FAQ describes a customer-requested, time-bound discount through sales, not an automatic entitlement.

The FAQ documents portal visibility through January 31, 2026 for certain unmigrated profiles, but not subsequent retention or deletion behavior.

records.title: Retirement: Support for Service Connector (preview) on Azure Container Apps will end on March 30th, 2026
records.summary: Microsoft announced the end of support and retirement of Service Connector (preview) on Azure Container Apps for March 30, 2026. The update states that new connections through the preview become unavailable through every interface after that date; future connections require manual configuration. Existing Azure Portal-created connections remain active and unaffected. CLI-, SDK- or Visual Studio-created connections may require updates or migration, despite broader guidance that existing connections remain active. Later issue activity does not document an extension or confirm retirement completion.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Service Connector (preview) on Azure Container Apps, with an announced date of March 30, 2026. Future connections must be configured manually using service-specific documentation or templates.

- Existing Azure Portal-created connections remain active and unaffected.
- Existing Azure CLI-, SDK- or Visual Studio-created connections may require updates or migration. The linked guidance says existing connections remain active more generally; it does not resolve this tooling-specific caveat.

A Microsoft collaborator stated that no replacement service is planned for Container Apps. The supplied content gives no regional exceptions or maintenance and security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your connections and how you created them. In the Azure portal, select your container app and open Service Connector (preview) under Settings to review its connection list.
2. Review connection properties and use Validate to check health. Existing Portal-created connections require no action under the update. For CLI-, SDK- or Visual Studio-created connections, review whether updates or migration are necessary; the supplied guidance does not identify every configuration requiring changes.
3. For future connections, use the relevant Microsoft Learn service-specific instructions or templates to configure connections manually. Review deployment templates that depend on Service Connector.

The notice does not require recreating every existing connection. It supplies no detailed migration prerequisites, cutover, backup or cleanup procedure. A community-linked workaround is explicitly untested, not a validated replacement.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
You can review the connection list for each container app in the Azure portal and use Validate to check individual connection health.

For CLI inventory, install Azure CLI, sign in with az login, and register the resource provider if needed:

az provider register -n Microsoft.ServiceLinker
az containerapp connection list -g "<container-app-resource-group>" --name "<container-app-name>" --output table

Replace the placeholders with your resource group and container app name. Remove --output table for more detail. This lists connections for the specified container app, not an entire tenant. Post-retirement availability of these inventory interfaces is not confirmed.

Inventory and health checks do not prove that future manual deployment workflows are ready. As team-owned planning, record your connection reviews and evidence that your replacement deployment workflows work. The supplied content provides no retirement-specific completion tracker or escalation procedure.

records.title: Retirement: Migrate to dedicated VM for your compute clusters
records.summary: Azure Machine Learning support for compute clusters using low-priority VMs ends on March 31, 2026. Microsoft directs you to recreate affected clusters with dedicated VMs before that date. Afterward, low-priority clusters cannot be used, and the notice warns of automatic scale-down without specifying its exact timing. The September 30, 2025 Low-Priority VM end-of-life milestone is separate from the Azure Machine Learning support deadline.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Machine Learning is ending support for compute clusters that use low-priority VMs on March 31, 2026. Microsoft directs you to recreate those clusters with dedicated VMs.

Microsoft documents Azure Machine Learning support through that date, despite the separate Low-Priority VM end-of-life milestone on September 30, 2025. After March 31, 2026, low-priority clusters cannot be used. The notice does not announce retirement of Azure Machine Learning compute clusters generally or the v2 CLI and SDK.
what.html:
Azure Machine Learning is ending support for compute clusters that use low-priority VMs on March 31, 2026. Microsoft directs you to recreate those clusters with dedicated VMs.

Microsoft documents Azure Machine Learning support through that date, despite the separate Low-Priority VM end-of-life milestone on September 30, 2025. actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Azure Machine Learning compute clusters using low-priority VMs. The supplied guide documents finding clusters in your workspace under Compute, then Compute cluster, but provides no retirement-specific inventory procedure.
2. Recreate affected clusters with dedicated VMs before March 31, 2026. Check regional VM-size availability, core quotas and your CPU or GPU requirements. Cluster creation requires an Azure Machine Learning workspace; CLI or SDK use also requires the relevant v2 tooling and authentication.
3. As a team-owned validation step, confirm your jobs work on the replacement clusters before removing old compute. This is planning advice, not a documented retirement completion check.

The notice does not provide detailed migration, backup, export or cutover procedures. The Azure Batch recommendation to use Spot VMs applies to that service; it is not the documented replacement for this retirement.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
This retirement affects Azure Machine Learning compute clusters configured with low-priority VMs. The supplied content does not establish whether your resources use that configuration.

Without recreation using dedicated VMs before March 31, 2026, the notice warns of automatic scale-down. After that date, affected clusters cannot be used. The exact scale-down timing, retirement-related data-retention or deletion effects, and cost changes are not documented.

Replacement cluster choices depend on regional availability and quotas. The guide notes that a minimum node count above zero keeps nodes running while idle, and using a region different from your workspace or datastores can increase latency and data-transfer costs. These are configuration considerations, not quantified migration costs.

progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:

records.title: Retirement: Remove dependency on these preview features before March 31, 2026
records.summary: Seven preview features retire on March 31, 2026 and become unavailable afterward. Remove dependencies before that date. The notice also recommends removal before May 31, 2026, but this conflicts with the stated availability cutoff and does not document an extension. The notice does not name the service; the accompanying Azure Machine Learning preview-management reference does not independently establish the retirement scope or provide migration instructions.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Seven preview features retire on March 31, 2026 and become unavailable afterward:

- Group multiple pipeline steps to organize complex pipelines.
- Compare pipeline jobs to debug failures or unexpected issues.
- Import data into a data labelling project.
- Use v2 data assets, specifically uri_folder and mltable, in a data labelling project.
- Monitor data drift between training and inference.
- Add linked services.
- Monitor compute resources.

The notice does not name the service or specify regions, customer exceptions, or maintenance, support and security-update commitments. The Azure Machine Learning reference describes general preview management; it does not independently confirm which features are retiring or establish their availability before retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify dependencies on the seven listed features in your pipelines, data labelling projects, monitoring and integrations. The supplied content gives no retirement-specific inventory procedure.
2. Remove those dependencies before March 31, 2026, the stated retirement date. The conflicting May 31, 2026 recommendation does not establish a later usable migration window.
3. Consult the detailed migration guidance referenced by the notice. Its contents are not supplied, so replacement choices, prerequisites, capability gaps, export or backup requirements, cutover, cleanup and validation steps cannot be confirmed here.

The Azure Machine Learning Preview Features panel supports preview management, not a documented migration procedure. Disabling a toggle is not established as sufficient to remove dependencies.

For clarification, use Microsoft Q&A or create an Azure support request. Technical support requires a support plan and appropriate access: subscription-level Owner, Contributor, Support Request Contributor, or a custom role with Microsoft.Support/* permissions. Requests without a subscription require an Admin.

records.title: Retirement: Remove dependency on these Azure ML SDKs before June 30, 2026
records.summary: Azure Machine Learning Python SDK v1 support ends on June 30, 2026, when five companion SDKs also retire. Microsoft asks you to remove companion-SDK dependencies before that date. Continued use is permitted, but the companion SDKs will be unsupported and may stop working without notice. Product guidance recommends SDK v2; the announcement instead recommends V1 while announcing its end of life, leaving that announcement's migration instruction contradictory. Separately, SDK v1 was deprecated on March 31, 2025 and CLI v1 support ended on September 30, 2025. These milestones do not establish a service or workspace shutdown.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Machine Learning is ending support for Python SDK v1, identified by azureml-core. These companion SDKs retire on June 30, 2026:

- azureml-train-core
- azureml-pipeline
- azureml-pipeline-core
- azureml-pipeline-internal
- azureml-pipeline-steps

This is a client-tooling change, not retirement of Azure Machine Learning or a required workspace upgrade. CLI v1, the azure-cli-ml extension, separately reached end of support on September 30, 2025; Microsoft no longer provides technical support or updates for it.

Current product guidance recommends Python SDK v2 (azure-ai-ml) and CLI v2 (ml). The announcement's recommendation to migrate to V1 contradicts its own V1 end-of-life statement; it does not establish a supported companion-package migration mapping.

Existing workspaces can support v1 and v2 clients, subject to compatibility and networking constraints. New service features are available only through v2. The supplied content specifies no regional exceptions or post-support maintenance or security-update commitment.

  • azureml-train-core
  • azureml-pipeline
  • azureml-pipeline-core
  • azureml-pipeline-internal
  • azureml-pipeline-steps

This is a client-tooling change, not retirement of Azure Machine Learning or a required workspace upgrade. CLI v1, the azure-cli-ml extension, separately reached end of support on September 30, 2025; Microsoft no longer provides technical support or updates for it.

Current product guidance recommends Python SDK v2 (azure-ai-ml) and CLI v2 (ml). The announcement's recommendation to migrate to V1 contradicts its own V1 end-of-life statement; it does not establish a supported companion-package migration mapping.

Existing workspaces can support v1 and v2 clients, subject to compatibility and networking constraints. New service features are available only through v2. The supplied content specifies no regional exceptions or post-support maintenance or security-update commitment.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify dependencies on the five retiring packages and inventory v1 client code, pipelines, training and deployment automation. Use pip show azureml-core, pip show azure-ai-ml and az extension list to identify installed core tooling. These checks cover only the environment examined and do not discover every companion-package dependency or workflow.
2. Use current product guidance to plan a move to SDK v2, or CLI v2 for CI/CD automation. REST is another documented option for applications needing minimal dependencies or languages without an SDK. Clarify package-specific replacement paths where needed: the announcement's instruction to migrate to V1 is contradictory.
3. Resolve migration constraints. Review the v1_legacy_mode restriction for private-endpoint workspaces. Export database datastores to object storage because v2 does not support them. Replace v1 SDK secret-management methods with direct Key Vault client-library access, using the documented identity approach. Check designer compatibility and data-asset directionality.
4. Adapt code and commands using the referenced v1-to-v2 guidance. V1 and v2 packages and CLI commands are not interchangeable. Microsoft recommends against installing both SDK versions in the same environment or mixing them in the same code. Compatible workspace resources can be reused.
5. As a team-owned validation step, exercise migrated jobs, pipelines, data access, secrets and deployment scoring before switching dependent automation. The supplied content does not provide a complete cutover, backup or cleanup procedure.

Microsoft recommends moving SDK v1 workflows before June 30, 2026 and CLI v1 workflows as soon as possible. For clarification, use Microsoft Q&A or Azure support. Technical support requires a support plan and the documented subscription-level support permissions.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if your workloads depend on the five retiring companion SDKs or Python SDK v1. CLI v1 has a separate, earlier support milestone. Your environment has not been inspected.

Continuity and support

Existing v1 workflows, model deployments and web services continue functioning according to product guidance. Unsupported clients may face security risks or breaking changes following product architecture changes. The companion-SDK notice separately warns that those packages may stop working without notice after June 30, 2026; continuity is not guaranteed.

The supplied content does not announce a service, workspace or data-access shutdown, retirement-related data deletion, retention changes or cost estimates.

Migration constraints

- Compatible workspaces, compute, models, environments and object-storage datastores can be reused; adopting v2 does not inherently require a new workspace.
- V1 datasets can be consumed in v2, but v2 data assets cannot be used in v1. Database datastores are unsupported in v2.
- Private-endpoint workspaces may require changes to the v1_legacy_mode setting before v2 API use.
- Designer classic prebuilt components cannot consume v2 data assets or share pipelines with v2 custom components. Classic pipelines using v1 datasets remain available.
- V1 SDK Key Vault secret-management methods are unavailable in v2.
- Legacy ACI and AKS web-service deployment tooling differs from v2 managed or Kubernetes endpoints. Local endpoints are for testing, not production.

records.title: Retirement: Azure CDN will be retired on December 1 2025 in China
records.summary: Azure CDN in China stopped serving traffic on December 1, 2025, according to the retirement FAQ. Compatible profiles were scheduled for automatic migration to Azure Front Door; eligibility does not confirm completion. Migration timing differs across sources: the notice required migration, validation and deletion before November 15, 2025, while the FAQ recommended migration before November 30, 2025. No extension is explicitly documented. Auto-migrated customers also needed to update automation and replace legacy mcchcdn.com CNAME targets before February 1, 2026. Standard Azure Front Door billing applies from October 1, 2026. The supplied sources do not establish your profiles' current status.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure CDN retired in China, with existing CDN profiles stopping traffic on December 1, 2025, according to the FAQ. The sources do not establish a retirement outside China or identify affected versions.

Microsoft recommended Azure Front Door, available in China East 2 and China North 3, or an alternative CDN. Compatible profiles were scheduled for automatic in-place migration. After migration, those resources could no longer be viewed as Azure CDN profiles.

Automatic migration excluded disabled, inactive and incompatible configurations. The FAQ provides additional exclusions, including unsupported global acceleration or overseas configurations. The separate migration guide describes customer-managed overseas delivery through public Azure Front Door; that procedure does not establish automatic-migration eligibility.

The sources do not document maintenance or security-update commitments.

The sources do not document maintenance or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your profiles and status. Use the Azure portal eligibility indicator and View details to inspect incompatibilities. Eligibility alone does not confirm that migration completed. The referenced comparison page was unavailable, so its compatibility details cannot be verified from the supplied inputs.
2. Choose a destination for your delivery scope. The FAQ directs compatible profiles to Azure Front Door and noneligible profiles, including global acceleration or overseas configurations, to a third-party CDN. Separately, the migration guide describes mainland delivery through Azure China Front Door, overseas delivery through public Azure Front Door with a public Azure subscription, and combined delivery through both deployments plus Azure Traffic Manager. These sources do not fully reconcile the overseas recommendations; confirm compatibility with support before selecting that path.
3. Create and validate the replacement. For its Azure Front Door procedure, the guide directs you to Premium if you need Web Application Firewall and Private Link to origins, otherwise Standard. It describes functionality testing by binding the local host IP to the relevant Azure Front Door IP, testing both deployments for combined delivery. This is not a complete production-validation checklist.
4. Cut over traffic and integrations. For mainland-only or overseas-only delivery, the guide directs you to change custom-domain DNS after successful validation. For combined delivery, it directs you to add both endpoints to Azure Traffic Manager but omits further setup and final cutover details. After Azure Front Door migration, update DevOps automation to use Azure Front Door APIs or applicable command-line tooling. Replace legacy mcchcdn.com CNAME targets; they became unusable on February 1, 2026.
5. Clean up after validation. The notice required deletion of CDN resources after successful validation. The FAQ specifically directs deletion after validated migration to an alternative CDN to avoid unnecessary charges. No export or backup procedure is supplied.

The notice required migration, validation and deletion before November 15, 2025; the FAQ recommended migration before November 30, 2025 without explicitly documenting an extension. Contact support or your sales contact for unresolved migration questions.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
Your exposure depends on your Azure CDN configuration in China and whether migration completed. According to the FAQ, unmigrated profiles stopped serving traffic on December 1, 2025. Portal visibility did not mean continued service, and the sources do not establish your resources' current status.

Automatic-migration limits

The FAQ excludes:

- Disabled profiles, active profiles without endpoints, and disabled endpoints within active profiles.
- Domains not directly CNAME-mapped to an Azure CDN endpoint.
- Endpoints without active requests in the preceding three months.
- Unsupported features, including global acceleration or overseas configurations.

Microsoft described automatic migration as downtime-free for eligible instances, but eligibility is not evidence of completion. After migration, Azure CDN profile views disappeared and automation needed Azure Front Door APIs or tooling. Legacy CDN CNAME targets became unusable on February 1, 2026.

Customer-managed overseas Azure Front Door deployment requires a public Azure subscription. The guide's combined-delivery approach requires separate China and public Azure deployments and Azure Traffic Manager; the FAQ separately directs noneligible overseas configurations to a third-party CDN.

Azure Front Door billing includes base, edge-to-client egress, edge-to-origin ingress and request fees, rather than CDN egress-only billing. Costs may increase depending on traffic; no customer-specific estimate is supplied. Standard billing applies from October 1, 2026. The FAQ describes a customer-requested, time-bound discount through sales, not an automatic entitlement.

The FAQ documents portal visibility through January 31, 2026 for certain unmigrated profiles, but not subsequent retention or deletion behavior. No unaffected Azure China CDN configuration is established.

Microsoft is retiring Confidential VM series DCesv5, DCedsv5, ECesv5 and ECedsv5, with a stated deadline of September 12, 2025. The notice identifies DCesv6 and ECesv6 as successors available through public preview.

Moving to these successors requires preview enablement and redeployment in available regions. Sizes with persistent local storage are described as coming to preview later, without a date. The supplied content does not establish their subsequent availability or document maintenance, support or security-update commitments for the retiring series.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your VMs and associated resources using DCesv5, DCedsv5, ECesv5 or ECedsv5. The notice provides no inventory method.
2. Check whether the documented successor preview meets your regional, OS, capacity and storage requirements. Choose DCesv6 for a balanced memory-to-vCPU ratio or ECesv6 for a higher ratio. Persistent-local-storage sizes are described as forthcoming, without a date.
3. Sign up for the successor preview. The retirement notice required signup by September 12, 2025; the preview announcement says Microsoft will contact applicants. The supplied signup-page content does not confirm current enrollment availability.
4. After preview enablement, redeploy in an available region. Microsoft also directed deletion of affected v5 VMs and resources by September 12, 2025.

The supplied content provides no backup, data-transfer, cutover or validation procedure. For technical help, create a support request or contact azconfidentialpm@microsoft.com.

impact.guidance:

- ECesv6: up to 64 vCPUs and 512 GiB of memory.

The supplied material identifies no regional exceptions or retirement-related maintenance or security-update commitments.

records.title: Retirement: Spark Native Connector for Semantic Link
records.summary: Microsoft scheduled full retirement of the Spark native connector for Semantic Link for October 1, 2028. Retirement began on October 1, 2025, after which Microsoft states no major connector versions will be released. Review connector usage across your Microsoft Fabric tenants and plan migration to the Semantic Python SDK. The connector supports Spark runtimes through 3.5, not 4.0 or later. The notice does not specify whether full retirement stops existing workloads. The supplied Semantic Link overview does not independently establish a retirement or deadline.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring the Spark native connector for Semantic Link, with full retirement scheduled for October 1, 2028. Microsoft recommends the Semantic Python SDK as the replacement, describing it as offering comparable functionality and enhanced support.

The connector supports Spark runtimes through 3.5; Microsoft will not support Spark 4.0 or later. No major connector versions will be released after October 1, 2025. Interim maintenance, security updates and post-retirement availability are not specified.

This notice concerns the Spark native connector, not a documented retirement of Semantic Link as a whole. The supplied Semantic Link overview does not independently announce a retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Assess your Image Analysis usage, dependencies, business scenarios and technical requirements. The guidance supplies no discovery commands or automated inventory method.
2. Make a transition plan by September 25, 2026 and select alternatives based on capabilities, integration, cost and support:
  - OCR and Read: Azure Document Intelligence.
  - Face scenarios: Face API. The supplied Face overview separately says emotion and gender inference have retired and access to certain attributes is limited; it does not announce retirement of the entire Face service. Face access has eligibility requirements.
  - Image embeddings: Cohere Embed in Microsoft Foundry or SigLIP. The migration page names Cohere Embed v3 but references v4 material, leaving the intended version unclear. It suggests SigLIP for zero-shot classification and image-text retrieval.
  - Other image analysis: GPT models in Microsoft Foundry for custom solutions, or Azure Content Understanding for managed generative image analysis.
3. Plan model migration and test the replacement in staging against your requirements. The sources do not guarantee feature parity across alternatives.
4. Update production workflows, retrain stakeholders and complete migration by September 25, 2028.

Alternative-specific constraints

For Document Intelligence, Microsoft directs new development to v4.0 API (2024-11-30). Its v3.0 API (August 31, 2022) separately reaches end of support on March 30, 2029; that is not an Image Analysis deadline or a documented workload shutdown date.

The retirement announcement describes Content Understanding as preview, and the migration guidance labels its cited image solutions material preview. The supplied Content Understanding overview separately recommends API version 2025-11-01 (GA) for production and 2026-06-01-preview for evaluation. Do not treat every capability as production-ready. Using Content Understanding requires a Foundry Azure Resource and your own supported model deployments where applicable.

The supplied sources do not provide detailed Image Analysis export, backup, cutover or cleanup procedures.

records.title: Retirement: Prompt Flow in Azure ML and Foundry
records.summary: Prompt Flow in Azure Machine Learning and Microsoft Foundry, including web authoring, VS Code extensions and related container images, retires on April 20, 2027. Migrate existing applications and deployments before that date. Microsoft’s migration guidance says these experiences and images will no longer be supported or available afterward, but does not specify exactly when existing workloads stop running. Runtime images already receive no security or package updates. Microsoft recommends Agent Framework for most orchestration scenarios; migration requires code-based workflows rather than visual authoring. Review Foundry options for evaluation and tracing dependencies, validate replacement workflows, switch traffic and decommission old resources after stable operation.

what.announcement:

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Complete migration before April 20, 2027:

1. Inventory your Prompt Flow applications, deployments and runtime-image dependencies. Export flow.dag.yaml, map every node to its replacement and identify custom logic, evaluation and tracing dependencies.
2. Select your replacement by use case. Microsoft recommends Agent Framework for most orchestration scenarios; review Foundry options for evaluation and tracing. Plan for code-based authoring rather than a visual editor.
3. Prepare the prerequisites for your chosen migration path. The Foundry guide requires Python 3.10 or later, an Azure subscription with a Foundry project and deployed chat model, the Agent Framework SDK, and an installed, authenticated Azure CLI. Use FoundryChatClient for Foundry project endpoints; AzureOpenAIChatClient does not support those URLs. Store production secrets in Azure Key Vault.
4. Rebuild with WorkflowBuilder and Executor, starting with a linear path before adding branches and parallel execution. The samples specify MAF packages 1.0.1 or later; RAG samples additionally require an Azure AI Search index, and tracing samples require Application Insights. Some multi-agent orchestration and Azure AI Search sample packages are preview.
5. Run both workflows with identical inputs. The Foundry guide recommends SimilarityEvaluator and a mean similarity score of at least 3.5 out of 5 in parity_results.csv before proceeding. Validate the capabilities your workloads require; the supplied content does not establish complete parity.
6. Deploy, enable tracing and add a CI/CD parity-evaluation gate. Confirm a healthy deployment, visible traces and a passing pipeline. The Foundry guide specifies Azure Container Apps or Foundry Agent Service; the samples instead describe managed online endpoints on Azure ML or AI Foundry. These hosting instructions differ, so confirm the applicable path before deployment rather than treating the options as interchangeable.
7. Switch production traffic before retirement. After confirming stable operation, decommission old Prompt Flow endpoints, connections and compute resources.

The detailed Foundry prerequisites and examples do not establish an equivalent procedure for every Azure Machine Learning configuration. Flow export is documented, but broader backup and data-retention procedures are not.

records.title: Retirement: Support for Node.js 20 ends on April 30, 2026 – upgrade your apps to Node.js 22
records.summary: Support for Node.js 20 in Azure Functions ended on April 30, 2026. Apps can continue running, but Microsoft no longer provides security updates, performance optimizations or customer support for Node.js 20. Upgrade affected apps to Node.js 22. The supplied language-update reference provides migration guidance but does not establish a different Node.js retirement date.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Functions ended support for Node.js 20 on April 30, 2026, in alignment with the end of community support. The notice directs you to upgrade to Node.js 22.

Apps can continue running afterward, but Microsoft no longer provides security updates, performance optimizations or customer support for Node.js 20. The general language-support policy says retired-language apps can still be created and deployed; this does not restore support.
what.html:
Azure Functions ended support for Node.js 20 on April 30, 2026, in alignment with the end of community support. The notice directs you to upgrade to Node.js 22.

Apps can continue running afterward, but Microsoft no longer provides security updates, performance optimizations or customer support for Node.js 20. The general language-support policy says retired-language apps can still be created and deployed; this does not restore support.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Upgrade your Azure Functions apps using Node.js 20 to Node.js 22; the documented deadline was April 30, 2026.

1. Identify each app's configured language version, operating system, hosting plan and Functions runtime. The FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME setting identifies the language stack, not its version.
2. Review dependencies, extension bundles, binding extensions, local tools and build/deployment settings for compatibility. Ensure the app uses Functions runtime 4.x; follow the applicable migration guidance for older runtimes. Rebuild and test locally.
3. Back up your configuration. Where supported, use a staging slot for testing and rollback. Flex Consumption does not support slots, so test in a non-production app instead. Plan a maintenance window for a direct production update.
4. Publish updated code before changing the language-stack configuration. Target the correct app or slot. Linux Consumption requires Azure CLI rather than the portal for stack updates.
5. Confirm the selected version, check that the app shows Running, and test function behavior. If using staging, validate it before swapping into production.

The reference documents rollback by swapping slots back or restoring the previous language configuration and redeploying previous code. Returning to Node.js 20 does not restore its support.

impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
This retirement affects Azure Functions apps using Node.js 20. The supplied content does not identify your resources or establish how many apps are affected.

Without an upgrade, apps can continue running after April 30, 2026, but Microsoft no longer provides Node.js 20 security updates, performance optimizations or customer support. The notice identifies potential security vulnerabilities as a reason to upgrade. The general policy also says retired-language apps may face instance-allocation limits, potentially down to one instance; it does not establish that such a limit applies to your apps.

The update reference says changing the language version restarts the app, with typical unavailability of 30–60 seconds. In-flight requests terminate and new requests fail until restart succeeds. Dependencies and deployment settings may also need changes.

The supplied content does not specify data deletion, retention changes or cost consequences for this retirement.

records.title: Retirement: Licensing changes for future Azure VMware Solution subscriptions starting October 16, 2025.
records.summary: Microsoft is retiring Azure VMware Solution (AVS) license-included SKUs, not AVS itself. PayGo SKUs retire on October 31, 2026. License-included Reserved Instance customers must transition before August 30, 2027 to avoid documented service disruption on August 31, 2027. AV36 separately retires on August 30, 2027, moved from September 30, 2027. Current product guidance distinguishes PayGo from Reserved Instances, unlike the broader announcement's August 30, 2027 deadline and unreconciled RI-term statement. Continue on AVS with portable VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) subscriptions or migrate to another destination. New or additional nodes purchased from October 16, 2025 already require portable VCF subscriptions.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring AVS license-included SKUs, not AVS itself. PayGo retires on October 31, 2026; license-included RI service ends on August 30, 2027. AV36 also retires on August 30, 2027.

You can continue using AVS with customer-provided portable VCF subscriptions purchased from Broadcom or a channel partner. Microsoft describes this as a licensing change without technical AVS product changes and will continue managing infrastructure and VMware host software, patches and upgrades.

Product guidance says existing license-included PayGo nodes can operate unchanged through October 31, 2026, and qualifying RIs purchased on or before October 15, 2025 until August 30, 2027. BYOL is available in all 39 AVS regions identified by the supplied guidance.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your license-included PayGo nodes, license-included RIs, RI purchase and expiry dates, and AV36 usage. Azure Migrate is referenced for environment assessment, but the supplied content gives no SKU-inventory procedure.
2. Choose your destination: continue on AVS with portable VCF subscriptions, use Nutanix Cloud Clusters on Azure, or migrate to another Azure service such as Azure native infrastructure, Azure Red Hat OpenShift or Azure App Services.
3. For AVS BYOL, purchase portable VCF subscriptions from Broadcom or a channel partner. Where applicable, use the self-service process to exchange license-included RIs for VCF BYOL RIs, then add your VCF license key in the Azure portal. Microsoft permits exchanges for reservations expiring after August 30, 2027.
4. Transition PayGo by its October 31, 2026 retirement and license-included RIs before August 30, 2027. Address AV36 retirement separately by August 30, 2027. Contact your Microsoft account team to clarify RI-term treatment, PayGo transition requirements and transition assistance.

The guidance describes BYOL as the least disruptive option and Nutanix Move as a no-cost migration tool. It supplies no detailed backup, cutover, cleanup or validation procedures.

what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Microsoft recommends that you:

1. Review your current AV36 SDDCs.
2. Work with your Microsoft Account Team to plan migration and confirm applicable AV36 PayGo dates.
3. Identify available replacement AVS node types using the Azure Product Availability by Region page. Its geography and availability filters help you assess options; the supplied page does not itself identify specific replacement nodes or retirement-affected regions.
4. Consult AVS documentation for HCX migrations between node types.

The supplied HCX reference describes these migration options:

- Cold Migration: long downtime; small-scale VM copy.
- HCX vMotion: no downtime; serial, small-scale migrations.
- Bulk Migration: minimal downtime, including source VM shutdown and destination VM power-on; parallel migrations at the largest scale.
- Replication Assisted vMotion: no downtime; parallel migrations at larger scale.
- OS Assisted Migration: conversion downtime for Hyper-V and KVM workloads.

That reference primarily covers on-premises workloads moving to AVS; it does not establish that every option applies to your AV36 node migration. Its documented architecture uses HCX as an AVS add-on and an HCX Service Mesh connecting sites, including a Layer 2 network extension.

The supplied content does not provide complete migration prerequisites, validation, backup, cutover or cleanup procedures.

records.title: Retirement: Support for Python 3.10 ends on October 1st, 2026
records.summary: Extended support for Python 3.10 on Azure App Service ends on October 1, 2026. Apps will continue to run, but Microsoft will stop providing Python 3.10 security updates and customer service. The retirement notice directs you to upgrade to Python 3.11 before that date. Python on Windows App Service has a separate, earlier support cutoff of December 23, 2021; upgrading its Python version alone is not documented as a supported migration.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure App Service is ending extended support for Python 3.10 on October 1, 2026. After that date, Microsoft will no longer provide security updates or customer service for Python 3.10, although apps using it will continue to run. The notice directs you to upgrade to Python 3.11.

Separately, App Service removes end-of-life Python versions from the Runtime Stack selection dropdown. Existing apps targeting those versions should not be affected by that removal; this does not establish continued support.

Python on Windows App Service is already unsupported. The Python guidance identifies Linux as the supported OS going forward and also recommends a Windows container as a migration option.

Python on Windows App Service is already unsupported. The Python guidance identifies Linux as the supported OS going forward and also recommends a Windows container as a migration option.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify each App Service app's configured Python version and whether it runs on Linux or Windows, using the referenced language-version guidance.
2. For Python 3.10 apps, follow the retirement notice's direction to upgrade to Python 3.11 before October 1, 2026. You can list currently supported Linux runtimes with az webapp list-runtimes --os-type linux.
3. For Python apps on Windows, use the separately documented migration options: supported Python on Linux App Service or a Windows container. Changing the Python version alone is not documented as an OS migration.
4. For a Python stack-version change in the Azure portal, open the app's Configuration, select General settings, choose the Python version under Stack Settings > Minor version, and save. Changing stack settings restarts the app.

The Python 3.10 notice does not provide migration prerequisites, compatibility checks, backup instructions or validation procedures.

records.title: Retirement: Deprecation of Custom Resource Providers
records.summary: Microsoft announced retirement of Azure Resource Manager Custom Resource Providers (CuRP) by October 31, 2026, with creates, updates, patches and actions blocked from July 31, 2026. These dates have passed, but the supplied content does not confirm implementation or establish post-retirement workload, data or read/delete availability. Microsoft lists Deployment Scripts, Bicep Extensions and Azure Functions as alternatives for specific scenarios; the references do not establish equivalent support for persistent resource management.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft announced retirement of Azure Resource Manager Custom Resource Providers (CuRP) by October 31, 2026.

From July 31, 2026, the notice said custom resources and resource providers would support only read and delete operations. It does not specify what remains available after retirement, regional or version exceptions, or maintenance, support and security-update commitments.

Deployment Scripts, Bicep Extensions and Azure Functions are listed as scenario-specific alternatives. Their supplied reference pages do not independently announce a CuRP retirement or establish equivalent replacement capabilities.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify workflows that use CuRP and distinguish endpoint triggering from persistent resource-management requirements. The supplied content provides no CuRP resource-discovery method.
2. Evaluate Microsoft's listed alternatives: Deployment Scripts for endpoint triggering without persistent resource management; Bicep Extensions for that scenario when you use Bicep; or Azure Functions for triggering several endpoints or services. The content does not establish a replacement for persistent resource management.
3. Plan replacement of affected workflows. No CuRP migration procedure, export or backup instructions, cutover steps or cleanup steps are supplied. For Deployment Scripts, the reference recommends testing the selected version and checking execution status, outputs and logs.

If you select Bicep Extensions, extensions requiring OAuth On-Behalf-Of can fail in nested modules configured as Template Specs or using templateLink with manually authored parent templates. The documented workaround is to import the extension in the root Bicep file.

For clarification, ask your Microsoft account manager to email curpdeprecation@microsoft.com with your name, company name, email contact and subscription ID.

records.title: Update: The retirement date for default outbound access has been extended to March 31, 2026.
records.summary: Azure is changing default outbound connectivity for new virtual networks, not shutting down default outbound access everywhere. The update explicitly extends its earlier September 30, 2025 date to March 31, 2026. Current product guidance scopes the change to new VNets using an API version released after March 31, 2026; its release date is unspecified, so this is not a universal migration deadline. The portal already defaults to private subnets. Existing VNets remain unchanged. Workloads in private subnets need explicit outbound connectivity to reach public endpoints.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure is making subnets private by default in new VNets created with an API version released after March 31, 2026. Default outbound access is disabled by default, not removed. VMs in private subnets need explicit outbound connectivity to reach internet and Microsoft public endpoints.

The Batch notices particularly identify pools using Simplified compute node communication without public IP addresses that rely on default Internet outbound access.

- Existing VNets, including new VMs added to them, retain their behavior unless you make their subnets private.
- Earlier API versions retain the previous default; supported subnets can explicitly remain nonprivate.
- Existing explicit outbound methods continue operating. Batch pools already configured with explicit outbound access are exempt from the older notice.
- Delegated or managed PaaS subnets are outside this private-subnet configuration; the individual service manages outbound connectivity.

The supplied material does not document a blanket workload shutdown or support and security-update commitments.
what.html:

The Batch notices particularly identify pools using Simplified compute node communication without public IP addresses that rely on default Internet outbound access.

  • Existing VNets, including new VMs added to them, retain their behavior unless you make their subnets private.
  • Earlier API versions retain the previous default; supported subnets can explicitly remain nonprivate.
  • Existing explicit outbound methods continue operating. Batch pools already configured with explicit outbound access are exempt from the older notice.
  • Delegated or managed PaaS subnets are outside this private-subnet configuration; the individual service manages outbound connectivity.

The supplied material does not document a blanket workload shutdown or support and security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your deployment API versions, subnet settings and outbound methods. For Batch, check whether pools use Simplified compute node communication without public IP addresses and depend on default outbound access. Azure Advisor can identify VM and scale set NICs with default outbound IP allocations, but allocation does not prove use.
2. Before workloads need public endpoints from a private subnet, configure explicit outbound connectivity. Options include NAT Gateway, which Microsoft recommends for most scenarios; Standard Load Balancer outbound rules; a Standard public IP on a VM NIC; or a firewall/NVA reached through a user-defined route.
3. Check routing and configuration constraints. Internet-next-hop routes need explicit egress in private subnets. For the documented issue with IP-address-based load balancer backend pools using default outbound access, Microsoft recommends NAT Gateway.
4. If you choose to make an existing subnet private, set its portal Default outbound access setting to Disabled and save. Stop and deallocate affected existing VMs so their NIC state updates; plan for the interruption.
5. As team-owned validation, confirm required public-endpoint connectivity and review NIC flags and portal alerts. Record the configuration and results.

Existing VNets do not require migration because of this default change alone. The supplied material provides no export, backup or cleanup procedure.

impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
New VNets using the post-March 31, 2026 API version are affected unless you explicitly configure supported subnets as nonprivate or provide outbound connectivity. VMs in private subnets cannot rely on default outbound access for public endpoints, including Windows activation and updates.

For dependent Batch pools without explicit egress, loss of internet connectivity can affect pools, compute nodes, jobs and tasks. The older notice says these resources may stop working, not that every workload fails immediately. Current guidance does not establish a shutdown of existing VNets.

- Existing VNets, including newly added VMs, remain unchanged. Existing explicit outbound connectivity continues operating.
- Internet-next-hop routes, including service-tag exceptions intended to bypass an NVA/firewall, need explicit outbound connectivity in private subnets.
- That routing limitation does not apply to service endpoints. VMs can still access same-region Azure Storage accounts without an explicit outbound method.
- Flexible-orchestration scale set instances already require explicit outbound connectivity.
- A default outbound IP allocation or alert does not establish that traffic uses that IP; explicit egress can take precedence.

Deployment API versions and portal defaults affect new deployments differently. The supplied material establishes no regional exception, general console/API removal, data-deletion event or cost estimate. It does not establish whether your resources are affected.

records.title: Retirement: End of life reminder of NVv3 and NVv4-series Azure virtual machine in Azure Batch pools
records.summary: NVv3- and NVv4-series VM support in Azure Batch pools retired on September 30, 2026. The Batch notice says new pools using these series are blocked after retirement; existing pools cannot scale out and are subject to forced resize to zero nodes, with no exact resizing time specified. Azure VM guidance explicitly extends NVv3 use for existing Azure UAE North users through January 31, 2027, but the supplied sources do not confirm that this extension applies to Azure Batch pools. Migrate affected pools to a suitable Batch-supported size. Batch SKU and image queries can help review support status, but do not establish migration completion or application health.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired NVv3- and NVv4-series VM support in Azure Batch pools on September 30, 2026. The notice provided a migration window through that date; afterward, Batch blocks new affected pools, prevents scale-out of existing affected pools, and can force them to zero nodes.

Affected sizes are:

- NVv3, powered by NVIDIA Tesla M60: Standard_NV12s_v3, Standard_NV12hs_v3, Standard_NV24s_v3, Standard_NV24ms_v3, Standard_NV32ms_v3 and Standard_NV48s_v3.
- NVv4, powered by AMD Radeon Instinct MI25: Standard_NV4as_v4, Standard_NV4ahs_v4, Standard_NV8as_v4, Standard_NV8ahs_v4, Standard_NV16as_v4, Standard_NV16ahs_v4, Standard_NV32as_v4 and Standard_NV32ahs_v4.

Azure VM guidance documents an NVv3 extension for existing Azure UAE North users through January 31, 2027, but its applicability to Batch pools is unconfirmed. It also states that retired VMs lose SLA coverage and included support. The sources do not document pre-retirement maintenance or security-update commitments.

The retirement does not announce removal of other Batch VM sizes. The VM guidance identifies NVadsA10_v5 and NVadsV710_v5, written as NVads_V710_v5 in the NVv4 guidance, as outside these retirements.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify Batch pools using the affected NVv3 or NVv4 sizes. Check regional SKU support and end-of-life information with az batch location list-skus --location <azure-region>, then compare the results with your pool configurations. This command lists regional SKUs; it does not inventory your pools.
2. Select a replacement that supports your workload and is available through Batch in your region. The Batch notice recommends a newer series in what it calls the “same NC product line,” or another Batch-supported size, but does not explain that wording for the affected NV series.
3. Use Azure VM recommendations as candidates, not confirmation of Batch compatibility. For NVv3, Microsoft recommends NVadsA10_v5; graphics, virtual desktops, visualization and small AI alternatives include NC_RTXPRO6000BSE_v6. NCasT4_v3 is listed for offline inference when latency is not a priority. For NVv4, Microsoft recommends NVads_V710_v5; alternatives include NVadsA10_v5 for small AI or graphics workloads and NGads_V620 for graphics or gaming.
4. Check target-region availability, pricing, Batch image compatibility and core quota; request target quota where needed. Review supported images with az batch pool supported-images list, including verificationType and batchSupportEndOfLife.
5. Migrate affected Batch pools to a suitable supported size. The general deadline was September 30, 2026. Do not assume the NVv3 UAE North VM extension permits continued Batch use without confirmation.

For VM resizing to NVads_V710_v5, the NVv4 guidance requires registering the subscription for VMTempDiskResizePreview and confirming registration to address a known resize error. That guidance does not establish a Batch pool migration procedure.

The supplied sources do not provide a Batch-specific migration, backup, cutover, cleanup or post-migration validation procedure. Customers with a support plan can request VM resizing assistance under Virtual Machine running Windows/Linux, selecting Assistance with resizing my VM; the sources do not establish a Batch-specific escalation route.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
Your Batch pools are affected if they use one of the listed NVv3 or NVv4 sizes. No tenant resources have been inspected. Regional supported-SKU results can help you compare support status with your configurations, but do not identify your deployed pools automatically.

After September 30, 2026, the Batch notice says new affected pools cannot be created and existing affected pools cannot scale out. Forced resize to zero nodes threatens workload continuity, not just support availability; its exact timing is unspecified.

Separately, Azure VM guidance states that remaining retired VMs are deallocated, stop running, cease incurring VM billing charges, and lose SLA coverage and included support. Existing NVv3 users in Azure UAE North have a documented VM extension through January 31, 2027; Batch coverage remains unconfirmed. The VM billing statement does not establish whether associated resources continue to incur charges.

The sources do not specify retirement-related data deletion, retention, continued data access, migration costs or separate console, API, integration and deployment-tooling changes.

Batch image verification is a separate consideration: an image becoming unverified means regular Batch interoperability testing has stopped, not that the image has stopped working. Verification does not cover every application or usage scenario.

records.title: Retirement: Migration of Azure Batch Low-Priority VMs to Spot VMs in early March
records.summary: Azure Batch retired Low-Priority VMs on September 30, 2025. Automatic migration of remaining instances to Spot VMs was scheduled to start on March 1, 2026 and finish within several days; no exact completion date or completion confirmation is supplied. Microsoft expected no workload interruption. No action was required to accept Spot VMs; avoiding the transition required moving to dedicated compute before the end of February 2026. Spot-based billing begins with the March invoice. Spot VMs have no SLA or availability guarantee and can lose local data and unsaved work when evicted.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Batch announced automatic migration of all remaining Low-Priority VMs to Spot VMs starting March 1, 2026, following their retirement on September 30, 2025. The notice lists no regional or version exceptions.

Batch-managed pool allocation handles the transition. Existing API/SDK references to Low-Priority VM properties allocate Spot capacity without code or configuration changes. The notice does not specify a separate pre-migration availability or support commitment.

The separate Spot guidance describes operating constraints, not another retirement: Spot capacity varies by VM family, size, region and time, with no SLA or availability guarantee. Batch Spot VMs support neither maximum prices nor price-based evictions; eviction is capacity-driven. Some clouds, VM sizes and subscription offers are unavailable, and ephemeral OS disks are unsupported.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
No action was required to accept the automatic Spot transition. Avoiding it required moving your Batch workloads to dedicated, on-demand compute before the end of February 2026. The notice supplies no detailed migration procedure or prerequisites.

For ongoing Spot use, the supplied guidance recommends:

1. Identify Spot usage through pool current and target Spot counts and the SDK node property distinguishing dedicated from Spot nodes. Check quota, regional capacity, supported VM options and fallback capacity.
2. Choose Spot-only pools for flexible, restartable work. Use a dedicated baseline or mixed pool when continued progress matters; favor dedicated VMs for strict deadlines, unresumable work or long-running, tightly coupled multi-node MPI jobs.
3. Implement durable checkpoints where needed. Checkpointing is optional and your responsibility; automatic task requeueing does not preserve unsaved progress.
4. Test a representative job before production. In a nonproduction pool, remove a running Spot node using the requeue deallocation option, then verify recovery and output correctness. Test reduced capacity and measure cost per completed job, including repeated compute, checkpoint storage and extra runtime.
5. Assign an alert owner and a condition for increasing dedicated capacity if interruptions threaten completion.

These are Spot-readiness checks, not additional retirement requirements. No retirement-specific export, cutover or cleanup procedure is supplied.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
The migration notice covers all remaining Azure Batch Low-Priority VMs. Microsoft expected no interruption to existing workloads during the several-day transition; the notice does not describe workload shutdown. Existing API/SDK Low-Priority property references continue to allocate capacity as Spot without code or configuration changes.

If you took no action, the announced outcome was automatic migration and Spot-based billing beginning with the March invoice. The notice does not quantify the price difference.

Once using Spot, your workloads face separate operational risks: nodes can be evicted for capacity reasons, including immediately after creation. Local data and work not durably checkpointed can be lost. Batch automatically requeues interrupted tasks and attempts to replace capacity, but execution depends on availability. Azure attempts to restore a preempted VM only during the first 48 hours after preemption, without guaranteeing restoration; this is not a retirement deadline.

Dedicated nodes can provide a baseline when Spot capacity is unavailable. Job and task submission can remain unchanged across pool VM types, although job-manager placement can require configuration. Repeated work can offset lower VM prices; no tenant-specific impact or cost estimate is established.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
This retirement affects Azure Functions apps using Python 3.10. Without an upgrade, your apps continue running after October 1, 2026, but lose the documented security updates, performance optimizations and customer service. The general language-support policy says retired-language apps can still be created and deployed, but lose eligibility for new features and may face instance-allocation limits, including scaling to one instance in some cases. During supported language updates, changing the version restarts the app. A direct production update typically causes 30–60 seconds of unavailability, terminates in-flight requests and causes new requests to fail until restart succeeds. progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use the supplied language-update checks to validate individual app upgrades:

1. Check the Functions runtime under Settings > Configuration > Function runtime settings. The Azure portal, Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell can check runtime versions; this alone does not establish the Python version.

3. Test function behavior. For failures, inspect Monitoring > Log stream and review dependency compatibility.

These checks validate an app update, not retirement-wide completion. Any inventory, upgrade-status record and test evidence you maintain are team-owned tracking. records.title: Retirement: NP-series Azure Virtual Machines will be retired on May 31, 2027
records.summary: Microsoft Azure will retire Standard_NP10s, Standard_NP20s and Standard_NP40s VMs on May 31, 2027. After that date, remaining affected VMs will be deallocated, stop working and no longer incur VM billing charges; NP-series will lose SLA coverage and included support. Resize or replace affected VMs before retirement. Purchases of 1-year and 3-year NP-series reserved instances end separately on April 2, 2026. The supplied replacement-size reference pages describe capabilities, not additional retirements or deadlines.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft Azure will retire these NP-series VM sizes on May 31, 2027:

- Standard_NP10s
- Standard_NP20s
- Standard_NP40s

Remaining affected VMs will be deallocated after that date. The notice does not specify regional exceptions, pre-retirement availability restrictions beyond reserved-instance purchases, or maintenance and security-update commitments.

The notice recommends evaluating NDv2, NCads_H100_v5 or NCasT4_v3 replacements by workload. Their supplied reference pages describe capabilities; they do not announce retirement of those alternatives.
what.html:
Microsoft Azure will retire these NP-series VM sizes on May 31, 2027:

  • Standard_NP10s
  • Standard_NP20s
  • Standard_NP40s

Remaining affected VMs will be deallocated after that date. The notice does not specify regional exceptions, pre-retirement availability restrictions beyond reserved-instance purchases, or maintenance and security-update commitments.

The notice recommends evaluating NDv2, NCads_H100_v5 or NCasT4_v3 replacements by workload. Their supplied reference pages describe capabilities; they do not announce retirement of those alternatives.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Resize or replace affected VMs before May 31, 2027 to avoid disruption.

1. Identify your Standard_NP10s, Standard_NP20s and Standard_NP40s VMs. The notice provides no inventory method.
2. Select a replacement that meets your workload requirements. Microsoft recommends NDv2 for demanding GPU-accelerated AI, machine learning, simulation and HPC; NCads_H100_v5 for Azure Applied AI training and batch inference; or NCasT4_v3 for real-time AI inference, interactive graphics and visualization.
3. Check applicable replacement constraints. NCads_H100_v5 supports Generation 2 VMs, but not Generation 1 VMs, live migration, memory-preserving updates or nested virtualization; its reference also points to vCPU quota checks. For NCasT4_v3 graphics and visualization, you must manually install Azure-supported GRID drivers; the NVIDIA GPU driver extension installs CUDA drivers.
4. Resize affected VMs, or deallocate them and change their sizes, before retirement.

The inputs do not establish feature equivalence or provide a complete compatibility assessment, backup/export procedure, cutover sequence, cleanup instructions or migration-validation steps.

records.title: Retirement: Support for Windows Server 2016 Marketplace images on Azure Batch pools will end on January 12, 2027
records.summary: Azure Batch support for Windows Server 2016 ends on January 12, 2027, and the affected Marketplace images become unavailable. Migrate affected pools before that date. The notice does not confirm that existing workloads shut down then. The notice also dates Windows Server 2016 extended-support end to January 12, 2027, while the lifecycle page lists January 13, 2027 Pacific Time; use the earlier date for planning. A licensed custom image with Azure ESU may be an option, but it does not extend Azure Batch support.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Batch is retiring Windows Server 2016 support on January 12, 2027. The notice identifies Windows Server 2016 Marketplace images under MicrosoftWindowsServer / WindowsServer as becoming unavailable.

A Windows Server 2016 custom image may remain an option with appropriate licensing and Azure ESU, but it does not preserve Azure Batch support. The supplied custom-image reference explains configuration requirements; it does not independently establish retirement dates or ESU eligibility.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Batch pools using the affected Marketplace image SKUs listed under impact. The notice supplies no inventory command.
2. Select a supported Windows Server image. Microsoft recommends the latest Windows Server version where possible. If you must retain Windows Server 2016, assess appropriate licensing and Azure ESU before choosing a custom image; this does not extend Batch support.
3. Plan the pool-property changes using the referenced update guidance, and migrate before January 12, 2027. The supplied reference does not provide a complete Windows Server 2016 migration procedure. Do not treat its separate disk-encryption migration example as instructions for this retirement.
4. Test the migration before changing production configurations, as Microsoft recommends. Specific retirement completion checks, backup, cutover and cleanup requirements are not supplied.

If you choose a custom image

Use a generalized Azure Compute Gallery image; specialized images are unsupported. Use Microsoft Entra ID authentication, not Shared Key. Ensure the image has a replica in the Batch account region. Cross-subscription images require the same Entra tenant and Microsoft.Batch registration in the image subscription.

The creating application needs image access including Microsoft.Compute/disks/beginGetAccess/action; Reader alone is insufficient. Prepare the image with a supported Batch base image, managed disks, the default temporary drive and an unencrypted OS disk. Do not preinstall Azure extensions. Match purchase-plan information and the node-agent SKU to the image.

Microsoft recommends at least one image replica per 300 instances for large pools and at least 15 minutes of resize timeout per 1,000 VMs for fixed-size pools. These are configuration recommendations, not retirement requirements.
