progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use the migration guide's discovery script to list containers with analytical storage enabled in each account you run it against. Check transactional TTL separately: the enabled-container list alone does not establish whether you need historical preservation.

Keep team-owned migration evidence for each container: the selected migration path, initial replication completion, expected Delta tables, row-count and sample-data comparisons, schema checks, and downstream cutover results. For historical preservation, also retain the cutover timestamp, backfill row counts and evidence that timestamp ranges have no gaps or overlaps.

Confirm downstream workflows succeed before disabling analytical storage. These are checks your team performs, not an automatic retirement tracker.

The guide points to the mirroring limitations page for support updates and Troubleshoot mirrored Azure Cosmos DB for common issues. For retirement or migration-path questions, contact your Microsoft account manager or cosmosdbsynapselink@microsoft.com.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Functions runtime v3 on Linux Consumption will stop running September 30, 2026
records.summary: Azure Functions runtime v3 apps on Linux Consumption stop running after September 30, 2026 under the documented retirement. Migrate affected apps to runtime v4. Separately, .NET in-process support ends on November 10, 2026, and Linux Consumption hosting retires on September 30, 2028, requiring migration to Flex Consumption. These later milestones do not extend the v3 shutdown deadline.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Functions runtime v3 apps on Linux Consumption will no longer start or process executions after September 30, 2026. Existing deployments in that configuration stop functioning. Microsoft directs affected customers to runtime v4.

V4 is highly backward compatible with v3, but language requirements and breaking changes require review. For .NET apps, Microsoft recommends the isolated worker model because in-process support ends on November 10, 2026.

Separately, Linux Consumption hosting receives no new features or language versions and retires on September 30, 2028. Upgrading to v4 does not replace the required move to Flex Consumption. Windows Consumption apps are not currently affected by that hosting-plan retirement.

The supplied sources do not document maintenance or security-update commitments for v3 before shutdown.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify apps using both runtime v3 and Linux Consumption. The supplied PowerShell inventory covers a selected subscription and filters version settings containing 3; it does not identify v2 apps or establish Linux Consumption scope. Check operating systems and hosting plans separately.
2. Select a supported v4 language target and review hosting restrictions and breaking changes. For .NET, Microsoft recommends the isolated worker model and .NET 10 in this guide. A supported .NET Framework target is an alternative for required Framework-only dependencies. Convert C# script apps to the project model before following C# project steps. No first-class Go v3 migration path is documented.
3. Update local tooling to Azure Functions Core Tools v4, then migrate project dependencies, bindings and settings using the language-specific guidance. Non-.NET apps need extension bundle 2.x or later. For isolated .NET, migrate startup configuration, replace incompatible WebJobs packages, update the worker setting, and review serialization and logging changes.
4. Test locally on v4. In Azure portal, open Diagnose and solve problems, run Functions 4.x Pre-Upgrade Validator, and resolve its recommendations.
5. Update the Azure host to v4 and configure the language stack to match the project's target framework before publishing. Code and application-setting changes restart the app. If you use deployment slots, follow the slot-specific configuration, staging validation, swap and rollback constraints.
6. Publish and verify the migrated app. Separately, migrate Linux Consumption apps to Flex Consumption before September 30, 2028. Microsoft encourages this move, but the referenced plan-migration guide was unavailable in the supplied material; its procedure and completion checks are not established here.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
Your apps face the documented shutdown after September 30, 2026 if they use runtime v3 on Linux Consumption. Without migration, they no longer start or process executions. The supplied sources do not establish this shutdown for v2 or v3 on other hosting configurations, although both versions are out of extended support.

Windows Consumption apps are not currently affected by the Linux Consumption plan retirement. This exception does not restore support for retired runtimes or the .NET in-process model.

Migration has documented availability and compatibility effects:

- Code and application-setting changes restart apps. Staging slots can reduce downtime but require the documented swap configuration.
- V4 does not support Azure Functions Proxies or Azure Storage logging through AzureWebJobsDashboard; the guide directs logging to Application Insights.
- V4 enforces Linux Consumption timeouts and extension minimums. Apps sharing storage with identical host IDs fail to start.
- Node.js 10 and 12 and Python 3.6 are unsupported on v4. Validate threading, bindings, serialization and worker-model changes. In isolated .NET, System.Text.Json ignores Newtonsoft.Json attributes, potentially leaving properties at default values without errors.

The supplied material does not establish whether you have affected apps, regional exceptions, retention or deletion effects, cost changes, or separate console/API impacts.

records.title: Retirement: End of life reminder of HBv2/HC-Series/NP-Series Azure Virtual Machine in Azure Batch Pool

records.title: Retirement: Azure Reserved Virtual Machines Instances for select VM series
records.summary: From July 1, 2026, Microsoft ends purchases and renewals of Azure Reserved VM Instances for selected VM series and terms. Existing reservations, including those renewed before the cutoff, retain discounts through their individual expiration dates. Without replacement coverage, continued usage moves to pay-as-you-go pricing at expiration, even if auto-renew is enabled. This reservation change does not shut down workloads; separate VM-series retirement deadlines apply.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft ends purchases and renewals of these Azure Reserved VM Instances from July 1, 2026:

- One-year terms: Av2, Amv2, Bv1, D, Ds, Dv2, Dsv2, F, Fs, Fsv2, G, Gs, Ls and Lsv2.
- One-year and three-year terms: Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3 and Esv3.

Existing reservations, including renewals completed before the cutoff, continue providing discounts through their full terms. This billing change does not disrupt running workloads.

The transition guide broadly discusses one-year and three-year renewals, but its explicit affected list limits the first group to one-year terms. That wording remains unclear and does not establish a three-year restriction for the first group. The reservation notice identifies no regional exceptions; cloud exclusions in the separate VM retirement guide must not be assumed to apply to this purchase cutoff.

Microsoft ends purchases and renewals of these Azure Reserved VM Instances from July 1, 2026:

  • One-year terms: Av2, Amv2, Bv1, D, Ds, Dv2, Dsv2, F, Fs, Fsv2, G, Gs, Ls and Lsv2.
  • One-year and three-year terms: Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3 and Esv3.

Existing reservations, including renewals completed before the cutoff, continue providing discounts through their full terms. This billing change does not disrupt running workloads.

The transition guide broadly discusses one-year and three-year renewals, but its explicit affected list limits the first group to one-year terms. That wording remains unclear and does not establish a three-year restriction for the first group. The reservation notice identifies no regional exceptions; cloud exclusions in the separate VM retirement guide must not be assumed to apply to this purchase cutoff.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. In the Azure portal, open Reservations, filter Product type to Virtual Machines, and compare VM family, reservation term and expiration date with the affected list. Reservation permissions are separate from subscription permissions.
2. Review utilization and active usage in Cost Management + Billing > Reservations. Confirm which workloads will continue after their reservations expire. Do not rely on auto-renew to preserve discounts.
3. Choose coverage based on your workloads: evaluate a one-year or three-year savings plan for eligible hourly compute spend, assess newer VM SKUs and supported reservations, or deliberately accept pay-as-you-go pricing. The transition guide presents self-service reservation trade-in as an option; exchanges and refunds have limitations that the supplied management page does not detail.
4. Align replacement coverage with reservation expiration and any VM modernization. The guide recommends planning 6–12 months before expiration and working with your Microsoft account team to model costs. Renewal before July 1, 2026 was a time-limited option, not an available post-cutoff action.
5. If you also migrate VMs, check the separate series deadline, target specifications, regional capacity and quota. For v6, the supplied guide requires Generation 2, an NVMe-supported OS, and MANA with a supported OS. Its resize sequence is to stop and deallocate, resize, then start the VM; plan for interruption and loss of in-memory and temporary-disk data.

The reservation cutoff itself does not require workload migration. The supplied transition guidance does not provide detailed backup, cutover or cleanup procedures.

- November 15, 2029: Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3 and Esv3, excluding Azure Government, Azure operated by 21Vianet and sovereign cloud regions.

Microsoft says retired VMs will be deallocated. Separate capacity-growth restrictions for Dv3/Dsv3/Ev3/Esv3 begin in July 2026, with no exact day supplied.

The migration table also labels earlier three-year dates, May 1, 2025 or November 15, 2025 for other listed series, as “RI expiration.” Their meaning is unclear; they do not establish cancellation dates for active reservations. The management page's July 17, 2026 update date is not a retirement deadline.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use the documented reservation inventory and utilization reviews to identify affected VM families, terms, expiration dates and continuing usage. In the Azure portal, All services > Reservations shows Utilization (%) and usage trends; appropriate reservation permissions are required.

Enterprise Agreement customers can inspect usage data programmatically, including unused reservation hours in amortized cost data. For other subscription types, the management page identifies the Reservations Summaries - List By Reservation Order And Reservation API. These methods measure reservation use, not complete VM inventory or migration readiness.

For team-owned tracking, record each affected order, its expiration date, chosen coverage approach and completion evidence. If you migrate workloads, also record prerequisite checks and workload-validation results. This is local planning advice, not a website-provided tracker or saved checklist.

records.title: Retirement: GPv1 and Legacy Blob storage account creation
records.summary: Azure Storage lists October 13, 2026 as the retirement date for GPv1 and legacy Blob storage accounts, with remaining accounts moving to GPv2. Microsoft describes GPv1 upgrades as permanent, in-place changes without downtime or data loss, but pricing can increase. Review remaining accounts, deployment artifacts and costs, then upgrade customer-managed accounts and validate workloads and billing. Databricks-managed DBFS accounts require no customer migration action and have a separate conversion window extending into Q1 2027. The supplied guidance conflicts on new-account restrictions and general conversion timing; it does not confirm completed conversion or establish a workload shutdown.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Storage is retiring GPv1 and legacy Blob storage account types and moving remaining accounts to GPv2. The stated retirement date is October 13, 2026; Microsoft says it will automatically convert accounts that customers do not migrate.

GPv1 retirement applies globally, across redundancy options, including accounts supporting Blobs, Tables, Queues and Files. Legacy BlobStorage accounts are also in scope. Existing GPv2 accounts are not identified as requiring migration.

Microsoft describes the GPv1 upgrade as a permanent, in-place account-type change that preserves data and endpoints, with no downtime or data-loss risk. The upgrade guide says existing applications and tools continue working without changes. For legacy Blob accounts, the overview says most blob-only workloads need no code changes, not that every workload is guaranteed compatible.

Databricks-managed DBFS accounts are a separate population that Microsoft migrates automatically. The supplied sources do not document pre-retirement maintenance, support or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
For customer-managed accounts, migrate remaining affected accounts to GPv2 rather than relying on an unspecified automatic-conversion schedule.

1. Identify account types and ownership. Use Azure Resource Graph, Azure CLI, Azure Inventory or the Azure portal. In the portal, review Settings > Configuration > Account kind. Distinguish GPv1's Storage, legacy BlobStorage and GPv2's StorageV2. The supplied Resource Graph query has coverage limits; do not treat it as a complete inventory.
2. Separate Databricks-managed DBFS accounts. Confirm the managed resource group and customer read-only status; a dbstorage name prefix alone is insufficient. No customer migration action is required for these accounts.
3. Review compatibility and costs. Assess capacity, transactions, read/write/list activity, pricing assumptions and tier-aware behavior. Use Azure Monitor metrics and the Azure Pricing Calculator or the documented cost estimator. The estimator excludes contract-specific discounts, taxes and reservations. Include applicable tier minimum-retention, early-deletion and lifecycle-operation charges.
4. Review deployment artifacts. Update infrastructure-as-code, pipelines, templates, modules, scripts and policies for GPv2 while preserving networking, security, redundancy, access tier, encryption, identity, data protection and tags. Validate changes outside production or through your normal change-review process.
5. Upgrade customer-managed accounts. The portal procedure is to select Upgrade under Account kind, enter the account name and confirm. Alternatives include the latest Azure CLI, PowerShell with the latest Az.Storage module, or documented automation. Policy guidance mixes account-type terminology, so verify its scope before use. GPv2 is the documented upgrade path; the announcement also mentions BlockBlobStorage or FileStorage for suitable workloads but supplies no capability comparison.
6. Validate the result. Confirm the resulting account kind, application operation, deployment behavior and billing. Continue monitoring metrics, usage and costs.

The upgrade is irreversible. Choose the default Hot or Cool tier for block blobs deliberately; Hot is the default when omitted, and these access tiers do not apply to other data objects. The supplied guidance does not establish an export, backup, separate cutover or cleanup requirement.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are in scope if you have GPv1 accounts, including Files hosted on GPv1, or legacy BlobStorage accounts. GPv1 scope is global and includes all redundancy options. The supplied material does not establish whether your accounts are affected or already converted.

Workloads and deployment tooling

Microsoft describes GPv1 conversion as in-place, preserving data and endpoints without downtime or data loss. Most legacy blob-only workloads can migrate without code changes. However, the upgrade guide also warns of disruption if you do not upgrade and does not reconcile that warning with automatic conversion.

Stale deployment artifacts can cause validation or deployment failures or unintended configuration changes even when running workloads continue normally. The sources do not establish a retirement-related console/API outage, data deletion or retention change.

Billing

The upgrade itself is free, but GPv2 transaction charges can increase costs, particularly for read-, write- or list-heavy Blob workloads. Lower capacity prices do not guarantee lower total costs. Cooler tiers increase access and transaction charges, and subsequent tier changes can incur charges.

GPv1 guidance expects GPv2 pricing shortly after retirement regardless of backend conversion completion. The legacy Blob overview lists billing changes beginning in November 2026. The GPv1 overview says conversion does not change Azure Files or Azure Disks pricing. No account-specific cost estimate is supplied.

If you take no action, Microsoft treats non-migration as consent to conversion. Databricks-managed DBFS accounts require no customer migration action and follow their separate automatic-conversion schedule.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance:
October 13, 2026 is the stated retirement date for GPv1 and legacy Blob storage accounts. The retirement overviews also identify October 2026. These dates have passed, but the supplied material does not confirm that conversion has completed.

Separate milestones and conflicts

- Announcement: the notice lists October 1, 2025; the migration overviews list September 2025. The announcement timing remains inconsistent.
- New GPv1 account creation: the notice lists September 1, 2026 and the GPv1 overview lists September 2026, but the upgrade guide says Q1 2026. Current guidance conflicts, so the restriction date is unconfirmed. For legacy Blob accounts, the notice lists September 1, 2026 and the overview lists September 2026.
- GPv1 automatic conversion: sources describe conversion after October 13, 2026 or under the October 2026 milestone. No exact completion date is established. GPv2 pricing is expected shortly after retirement, even if backend conversion is unfinished.
- Legacy Blob conversion and billing: the overview says automatic migration follows October 13, 2026 and billing changes begin in November 2026. Its general conversion window runs from early November through “Q1CY26,” an internally inconsistent end period. Completion timing is unconfirmed; this does not establish an extension.
- Databricks-managed DBFS accounts: Microsoft converts these separately after October 13, 2026, in waves extending into Q1 2027. No customer migration action is required.

The upgrade guide warns of service disruption if GPv1 accounts are not upgraded, while other guidance describes non-disruptive conversion. The sources do not reconcile those statements or establish a separate workload shutdown date.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use Azure Resource Graph, CLI, Azure Inventory or the portal to identify remaining affected account types and review their post-upgrade kind. The GPv1 overview also documents Azure Policy detection and in-place upgrades; verify the account-type scope before applying policy guidance.

Discovery has limits. The supplied Resource Graph query is subscription-scoped, filters specific Standard SKUs and selects non-StorageV2 kinds rather than only the retiring types. Its results do not prove complete coverage. The portal's Settings > Configuration > Account kind provides an account-level check, not a fleet-wide completion report.

For team-owned tracking, record each account's original type, ownership, migration outcome, confirmed resulting type, deployment-artifact review, workload validation and billing checks. Monitor storage metrics and costs after migration; usage metrics alone do not prove completion. These are local migration records, not progress inspected or saved by this website.

Track confirmed Databricks-managed DBFS accounts separately. The supplied page provides their automatic-conversion window but no dedicated completion tracker.

For help, use Microsoft Q&A or your Microsoft representatives. With a support plan, create an Azure portal technical support request for Storage Account Management, choosing Upgrade or change account type, tier or replication, then Upgrade to general purpose v2 storage account.

records.title: Retirement: Azure VMware Solution AV36 node End of Support now August 30, 2027
records.summary: Microsoft will retire all Azure VMware Solution AV36 SDDCs after August 30, 2027 and remove access on August 31, 2027, regardless of reserved instance expiration dates. Review your AV36 deployments and work with your Microsoft Account Team to plan migration to another available AVS node type. Microsoft will retain data for up to 60 days for retrieval, but the supplied content does not specify retrieval procedures or an exact deletion date.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft will retire all Azure VMware Solution AV36 SDDCs after August 30, 2027, with access removed on August 31, 2027. Individual reserved instance expiration dates do not provide an exception.

AV36 is not compatible with VMware Cloud Foundation 9. The retirement notice connects the transition to Broadcom's support roadmap and the AVS License-included service retirement. It does not document maintenance or security-update commitments before retirement.

The regional availability and HCX reference pages do not independently establish retirement dates or additional affected populations.
what.html:
Microsoft will retire all Azure VMware Solution AV36 SDDCs after August 30, 2027, with access removed on August 31, 2027. Individual reserved instance expiration dates do not provide an exception.

AV36 is not compatible with VMware Cloud Foundation 9. The retirement notice connects the transition to Broadcom's support roadmap and the AVS License-included service retirement. It does not document maintenance or security-update commitments before retirement.

The regional availability and HCX reference pages do not independently establish retirement dates or additional affected populations.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Review your current AV36 SDDCs and plan migration before access is removed on August 31, 2027.
2. Work with your Microsoft Account Team on the transition and obtain applicable AV36 PayGo key dates.
3. Use Azure Product Availability by Region to identify alternative AVS node types available in your geography. The supplied availability content does not name a specific replacement or confirm its suitability.
4. Review the AVS HCX migration documentation and select a method appropriate to your workload, downtime and scale requirements.

The HCX reference describes these options:

- Cold Migration: long downtime; small-scale VM copy.
- HCX vMotion: no downtime; serial, small-scale migrations.
- Bulk Migration: minimal downtime with source shutdown and destination power-on; parallel migrations at the largest scale.
- Replication Assisted vMotion: no downtime; parallel migrations at larger scale.
- OS Assisted Migration: conversion downtime for Hyper-V and KVM workloads.

The reference primarily covers on-premises-to-AVS migration, not a complete AV36 node-to-node procedure. Its documented architecture uses HCX as an AVS add-on and an HCX Service Mesh connecting sites, including a Layer 2 network extension. The supplied content does not provide complete migration prerequisites, backup, cutover, validation, cleanup or data-retrieval procedures.

records.title: Retirement: D-series, Ds-series, Dv2-series, Dsv2-series, and Ls-series Virtual Machines for Azure Batch pools
records.summary: Azure Compute will retire D-, Ds-, Dv2-, Dsv2- and Ls-series VMs on May 1, 2028, affecting Azure Batch pools that use them. Migrate before this date. Existing pools continue running before retirement. Afterward, affected pools cannot be created or scale out, pools may be forcibly resized to zero, and remaining VMs will be stopped/deallocated without SLA coverage.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Compute will retire D-series, Ds-series, Dv2-series, Dsv2-series and Ls-series VMs on May 1, 2028. This affects Azure Batch pools that use these series.

Existing pools continue running before retirement. Afterward, affected pool creation and scale-out are blocked, and existing workloads face shutdown. The supplied notice does not specify regional exceptions or maintenance and security-update commitments.
what.html:
Azure Compute will retire D-series, Ds-series, Dv2-series, Dsv2-series and Ls-series VMs on May 1, 2028. This affects Azure Batch pools that use these series.

Existing pools continue running before retirement. Afterward, affected pool creation and scale-out are blocked, and existing workloads face shutdown. The supplied notice does not specify regional exceptions or maintenance and security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Azure Batch pools that use D-, Ds-, Dv2-, Dsv2- or Ls-series VMs. The supplied notice does not provide an identification procedure.
2. Select a supported replacement for your workload from the alternatives below.
3. Migrate before May 1, 2028. Either scale the pool to zero and update its VM size using Batch API version 2024-07-01 or later, or create a new pool with supported VM sizes and migrate workloads.

Replacement options:

- General-purpose D/Ds/Dv2/Dsv2 pools: Dsv5/Ddsv5 or Dasv5/Dadsv5.
- NVMe workloads: Dsv6/Ddsv6 or Dasv6/Dadsv6.
- Storage-optimized Ls pools: Lsv3/Lasv3 or Lsv4/Lasv4.

VM pricing may change after migration; consult Azure VM pricing. The notice does not provide validation, backup or cleanup procedures.

records.title: Retirement: Migrate from Azure Blueprints by January 31, 2027
records.summary: Azure Blueprints (Preview) retires on January 31, 2027, explicitly extending the previous July 11, 2026 retirement date. Creation and modification restrictions begin on July 31, 2026 and expand on October 31, 2026 and December 31, 2026. Export blueprint data you want to retain before retirement and migrate to Azure deployment stacks using ARM JSON or Bicep templates. At retirement, Blueprints management access and lock enforcement stop, and unexported blueprint data is permanently deleted. Resources deployed through blueprints remain.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Azure Blueprints (Preview) on January 31, 2027, covering definitions, versions, assignments and blueprint locks.

Reading and deletion through the portal and PowerShell/REST APIs remain available before retirement, subject to the phased creation and modification restrictions. At retirement, Blueprints management interfaces and commands stop working, and Microsoft permanently deletes unexported blueprint data.

Deployed resources remain, but blueprint Do Not Delete and Read Only locks stop enforcing protection.

Microsoft recommends Azure deployment stacks for deployment, lifecycle management and deny-assignment enforcement. Template specs optionally provide template storage and versioning; they are not required for deployment stacks. The supplied content does not document regional exceptions or maintenance, support and security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your definitions, versions and assignments using View Impacted Blueprints Resources, Azure Advisor and the Azure Blueprints portal. Include management-group definitions without subscription assignments: the subscription-based impacted view excludes them.
2. Export all blueprint definitions, versions and assignments you want to retain before January 31, 2027, including policy, role-assignment and template artifacts. Export preserves blueprint data; deployed resources remain without it.
3. Convert exported definitions into a single ARM JSON template or Bicep file. Convert policy and role assignments, and incorporate template artifacts through Bicep modules, nested templates or template links. You can also embed policy definitions.
4. Choose storage and versioning if needed: optionally publish converted templates as template specs, or use Git for versioning, code review and pipeline-based deployment. Template specs alone do not provide lifecycle management or lock enforcement.
5. Deploy the converted template or template spec through a deployment stack at the intended scope. If you need protection similar to blueprint locks, configure deployment-stack deny settings through Azure CLI or Azure PowerShell; you need the corresponding roles.

Act before phased restrictions block operations you need. Deployment stacks support resource-group, subscription and management-group scopes; template specs have resource-group scope. The supplied guidance does not provide detailed cutover, migration-validation or cleanup procedures.

records.title: Retirement: Azure VPN Client for Linux (Preview) will be retired on August 31, 2026
records.summary: Azure VPN Client for Linux (Preview) retired on August 31, 2026. Current product guidance says Microsoft no longer provides fixes, security patches or technical support and has removed the package from its Linux repository. The announcement separately places the end of P2S support on September 1, 2026; use the earlier date for planning. Existing installations might still work, but production connectivity should move to a supported alternative. OpenVPN and strongSwan alternatives do not support Microsoft Entra ID authentication for Azure VPN Gateway P2S. Azure VPN Gateway, Site-to-Site VPN, and Windows and macOS clients are unaffected.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired the Microsoft-provided Azure VPN Client for Linux preview application, distributed as the microsoft-azurevpnclient package, on August 31, 2026. It remained in preview with no path to general availability.

Current guidance says Microsoft no longer provides bug fixes, security patches or technical support and has removed the package from Microsoft's Linux repository. Existing installations might still function.

Azure VPN Gateway itself, existing P2S gateway configuration, Site-to-Site VPN, and Azure VPN Client for Windows and macOS are unaffected by the retirement. Migration can nevertheless require gateway configuration changes. Virtual WAN users are directed to separate guidance; the supplied content does not establish that scope's details.
what.html:
Microsoft retired the Microsoft-provided Azure VPN Client for Linux preview application, distributed as the microsoft-azurevpnclient package, on August 31, 2026. It remained in preview with no path to general availability.

Current guidance says Microsoft no longer provides bug fixes, security patches or technical support and has removed the package from Microsoft's Linux repository. Existing installations might still function.

Azure VPN Gateway itself, existing P2S gateway configuration, Site-to-Site VPN, and Azure VPN Client for Windows and macOS are unaffected by the retirement. Migration can nevertheless require gateway configuration changes. Virtual WAN users are directed to separate guidance; the supplied content does not establish that scope's details.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
If you still use the retired Linux client, migrate rather than relying on it for production connectivity.

1. Identify Linux users relying on the client and check their gateway tunnel type and authentication method.
2. Select OpenVPN with certificate authentication, or strongSwan with IKEv2 and certificate or RADIUS authentication.
3. Update gateway settings where needed. OpenVPN-only gateways already using certificates require no gateway change for the OpenVPN replacement. For strongSwan, enable IKEv2; IKEv2 and OpenVPN can coexist.
4. Generate new VPN client profiles from the gateway, then install and configure the replacement on each Linux device.
5. Test connectivity, roll out the replacement, then uninstall Azure VPN Client for Linux.

Neither Linux alternative supports Microsoft Entra ID authentication for Azure VPN Gateway P2S. Entra ID-only configurations need an alternative authentication method for Linux clients. If you require Entra ID authentication, evaluate using a Windows or macOS client that supports it instead.

Consult Azure VPN Gateway documentation for configuration steps and use your standard change-management process for gateway and client updates.

records.summary: Azure Load Balancer Inbound NAT Pools for Virtual Machine Scale Sets retire on September 30, 2027. New pool creation is blocked starting November 15, 2026; existing configurations continue to function until retirement. Complete migration to Inbound NAT rules V2 before September 30, 2027. Migration interrupts active NAT-rule traffic, but not load-balancing or outbound-rule traffic. Single-VM V1 rules are unaffected. Exact post-retirement behavior is not documented.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Load Balancer is retiring Inbound NAT Pools, the Virtual Machine Scale Sets-specific feature of Inbound NAT rules V1, on September 30, 2027. New pool creation stops on November 15, 2026; existing configurations continue to function until retirement.

Replace affected pools with Inbound NAT rules V2. NAT Pools automatically create and delete per-instance rules as a scale set scales. V2 instead targets a load balancer backend pool, removes the need for a NAT-pool reference on each scale set NIC configuration and exposes instance port mappings in the load balancer configuration.

Single-VM V1 rules are outside this retirement and require no migration. The sources do not document maintenance or security-update commitments, or exact post-retirement availability.

Azure Load Balancer is retiring Inbound NAT Pools, the Virtual Machine Scale Sets-specific feature of Inbound NAT rules V1, on September 30, 2027. New pool creation stops on November 15, 2026; existing configurations continue to function until retirement.

Replace affected pools with Inbound NAT rules V2. NAT Pools automatically create and delete per-instance rules as a scale set scales. V2 instead targets a load balancer backend pool, removes the need for a NAT-pool reference on each scale set NIC configuration and exposes instance port mappings in the load balancer configuration.

Single-VM V1 rules are outside this retirement and require no migration. The sources do not document maintenance or security-update commitments, or exact post-retirement availability.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify affected load balancers by inspecting their inboundNatPools arrays using the documented Azure CLI or PowerShell listing procedure. A nonempty array requires migration. Single-VM V1 rules without NAT Pools require no action.
2. Plan an interruption for active NAT-rule traffic. Size the frontend port range for the maximum backend-instance count. Each backend instance is exposed on the new rule's configured port. NAT rules cannot overlap port ranges or share a backend port; NAT and load-balancing rules also cannot share a backend port.
3. Choose the manual or automated migration path below and complete migration before September 30, 2027.
4. Confirm that no NAT Pools remain, the new rule targets the intended backend pool and every expected backend instance has a port mapping.

Manual migration

The documented procedure assumes a Manual scale-set upgrade policy. Delete the NAT Pool from the load balancer, remove the loadBalancerInboundNatPools reference from the scale set NIC configuration, update all scale set instances, then deploy a V2 rule against the intended backend pool.

Automated migration

Automation requires a Standard SKU load balancer, a Manual or Automatic scale-set upgrade policy, the latest PowerShell, Azure PowerShell modules and the AzureLoadBalancerNATPoolMigration module. Rolling upgrade policy is unsupported. Upgrade a Basic load balancer to Standard first if necessary.

Connect to Azure, collect the target load balancer and resource-group names, and run the documented migration command with those names.

By default, the script reuses a backend pool whose membership matches the NAT Pools; if none matches, it exits without changes. Alternatively, select NoReuse to always create new backend pools or OptionalFirstMatch to create one when no match exists. You can adjust backend-pool membership and NAT-rule associations after migration.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if you use Azure Load Balancer Inbound NAT Pools for Virtual Machine Scale Sets. A nonempty inboundNatPools array identifies affected load balancers; scale set NIC configurations reference those pools through loadBalancerInboundNatPools.

Starting November 15, 2026, you cannot create new pools. Existing configurations continue to function until September 30, 2027. Microsoft warns of potential service disruptions without migration, but the sources do not specify exact post-retirement workload behavior.

Migration interrupts active NAT-rule traffic. Traffic through load-balancing rules and outbound rules is unaffected during migration. The downtime duration is not specified. V2 changes the configuration target to a backend pool and requires sufficient frontend ports for the planned instance count.

Single-VM V1 rules without NAT Pools are unaffected. A V1 rule's Azure Virtual Machine type or backendIPConfiguration property alone does not establish that it is affected.

The sources do not document retention, deletion or cost effects.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use the migration guide's configuration checks to identify affected resources and confirm completion. These checks cover only the load balancers and instances you examine; they do not establish a tenant-wide inventory.

1. Before migration, inspect each load balancer's inboundNatPools array using the documented Azure CLI or PowerShell listing procedure. Any returned pools require migration.
2. After migration, confirm that the NAT Pool listing returns an empty result.
3. Confirm that the new rule shows the intended Target backend pool in the Azure portal, or that its backendAddressPool property is populated.
4. In the new inbound NAT rule's Port mapping section, check the expected mapping for every backend instance.

For team-owned tracking, record these results against your resource inventory. The sources do not describe a centralized retirement tracker or dedicated migration help or escalation route.

records.title: Retirement: Support for Node 22 LTS ends on April 30, 2027
records.summary: Support for Node 22 LTS on Azure App Service ends on April 30, 2027. Apps will continue running, but Microsoft will stop providing security updates and customer service for that runtime version. Upgrade to Node 24 LTS before that date. Changing runtime settings restarts your app.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft will end support for Node 22 LTS on Azure App Service on April 30, 2027. Your apps will continue running afterward, but Microsoft will no longer provide security updates or customer service for Node 22 LTS.

The Node.js runtime policy covers Windows and Linux. At end of life, App Service removes a version from the Runtime Stack dropdown; existing apps targeting it should not be affected. Dropdown removal does not establish workload shutdown or continued support.

App Service automatically applies the latest platform-available patch for your configured Node.js runtime. The retirement notice does not specify maintenance commitments before the deadline or regional exceptions.
what.html:

The Node.js runtime policy covers Windows and Linux. At end of life, App Service removes a version from the Runtime Stack dropdown; existing apps targeting it should not be affected. Dropdown removal does not establish workload shutdown or continued support.

App Service automatically applies the latest platform-available patch for your configured Node.js runtime. The retirement notice does not specify maintenance commitments before the deadline or regional exceptions.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify apps configured for Node 22 LTS. Check WEBSITE_NODE_DEFAULT_VERSION on Windows or linux-fx-version on Linux.
2. Check available supported runtimes with az webapp list-runtimes --os-type windows or az webapp list-runtimes --os-type linux.
3. Upgrade affected apps to Node 24 LTS before April 30, 2027. On Windows, update the runtime app setting through the portal or Azure CLI. On Linux, use Azure CLI or select the app in the portal, then Configuration → General settings → Stack Settings → Major version, and save.

Changing runtime settings restarts your app. For Windows, Microsoft recommends tilde syntax rather than pinning a specific minor or patch version, whose availability is not guaranteed. Older Node.js 14 and 16 examples in the reference do not establish current support.

The supplied sources do not document Node 22-to-24 compatibility prerequisites, capability gaps, or a post-upgrade validation procedure. As a team-owned precaution, test application behavior before completing your cutover.

impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:

If you do not upgrade, your apps will continue running after April 30, 2027, but Node 22 LTS will lose security updates and customer service from Microsoft. Under the general App Service policy, you must upgrade an unsupported runtime before receiving related App Service support.

records.title: Retirement: Support for Python-2.7; 3.8 and PowerShell- 7.1; 7.2 will be retired on September 30, 2026
records.summary: Azure Automation is retiring support for Python 2.7, Python 3.8, PowerShell 7.1 and PowerShell 7.2. The announcement title gives September 30, 2026; its body says unsupported status begins on October 1, 2026. Runbooks can continue running, but lose security updates, bug fixes and official support. Upgrade to supported Azure Automation runtimes to retain support eligibility. The supplied lifecycle references do not establish replacement-runtime availability in Azure Automation or extend this retirement.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Automation is ending support for Python 2.7, Python 3.8, PowerShell 7.1 and PowerShell 7.2, with retirement dated September 30, 2026 and unsupported status beginning on October 1, 2026.

Affected runbooks may continue running afterward, but Microsoft will no longer provide security updates, bug fixes or official support for these runtimes. The general policy also makes retired runtimes ineligible for new features and performance optimizations, while allowing you to create, deploy and run runbooks and environments using them.

The notice specifies no regional exceptions or retirement of other runtime versions.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Review Azure Automation retirement notification emails for affected versions and applicable timelines. Identify your runbooks using Python 2.7, Python 3.8, PowerShell 7.1 or PowerShell 7.2; the supplied material gives no inventory procedure.
2. Select a supported runtime available in Azure Automation. Consult the supplied PowerShell and Python lifecycle references, but do not treat upstream support as proof that Azure Automation offers a particular version. The material does not identify service-supported replacement versions or migration prerequisites.
3. Upgrade affected runbooks to retain support eligibility, using September 30, 2026 as your planning deadline before unsupported status begins on October 1, 2026.
4. As team-owned migration planning, validate your scripts, modules and integrations before cutover and record the results. The retirement material provides no validation criteria, backup, rollback or cleanup procedure.

An upgrade is needed for supported status, not because the policy requires existing runbooks to stop running.

records.title: Retirement: Microsoft Dev Box will be retired on September 18, 2028
records.summary: Microsoft Dev Box will retire on September 18, 2028 and will no longer be available afterward. The closing-down process begins on September 14, 2026; intermediate restrictions are not specified. Existing deployments remain supported during the transition. Microsoft recommends evaluating Windows 365 and planning migration.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Microsoft Dev Box on September 18, 2028. The service is in maintenance mode, with no new feature development planned.

You can continue using existing deployments during the transition; the service will no longer be available after retirement. Microsoft recommends evaluating Windows 365 as the replacement. The notice identifies no regional exceptions or separate version-specific timelines and makes no specific security-update commitment.
what.html:
Microsoft is retiring Microsoft Dev Box on September 18, 2028. The service is in maintenance mode, with no new feature development planned.

You can continue using existing deployments during the transition; the service will no longer be available after retirement. Microsoft recommends evaluating Windows 365 as the replacement. The notice identifies no regional exceptions or separate version-specific timelines and makes no specific security-update commitment.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Plan to replace workflows that depend on Dev Box before September 18, 2028. Microsoft recommends that you:

1. Review your Dev Box usage, including dev centers, projects, pools, images and developer workflows.

records.title: Retirement: AzureDnsEndpoints for Azure storage accounts will be retired March 2027
records.summary: Azure Storage DNS zone endpoints (preview), called AzureDnsZone endpoints in the announcement, enter retirement in March 2027; no exact retirement day is stated. Microsoft separately asks customers to transition new and existing Blob storage account deployments to Standard endpoints by April 1, 2027. The overview describes broader preview coverage but does not establish additional migration requirements.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Storage DNS zone endpoints (preview) enter retirement in March 2027. Microsoft recommends Standard endpoints, which the announcement describes as generally available and fully supported for production workloads.

The announcement addresses Azure Blob storage account deployments. The storage account overview describes the preview more broadly: Azure Resource Manager storage accounts in all public regions, excluding government cloud regions, with endpoint formats for Blob Storage, static websites, Data Lake Storage, Azure Files, Queue Storage and Table Storage. It does not establish separate migration requirements for those additional services.

Microsoft will remove creation of new accounts with AzureDnsZone endpoints on an unspecified date. The announcement says existing accounts will not be impacted or deleted. The overview still describes the preview as available but provides no post-retirement support or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify affected accounts. The announcement describes an Azure Resource Graph query selecting accounts with kind StorageV2 and parsed dnsEndpointType equal to AzureDnsZone. The overview also documents endpoint discovery through the get properties operation; DNS zone endpoint hostnames contain a zone identifier from z1 through z50 and use the storage.azure.net domain.
2. Use Standard endpoints for new accounts. Check capacity before planning deployments: Standard endpoints allow 250 accounts per region per subscription by default, or up to 1,000 with a quota increase, compared with 5,000 for the preview.
3. Follow the announcement's referenced deployment-update instructions to transition new and existing Blob storage account deployments to Standard endpoints by April 1, 2027. Consult the referenced retirement FAQ for existing-account guidance.

The supplied content does not include those update instructions or FAQ contents. It does not establish an endpoint-conversion procedure, migration prerequisites, required data-copy steps, cutover checks or cleanup requirements. General account-creation and account-type migration pages do not establish a procedure for this endpoint retirement. Deleting existing accounts is not a documented requirement.

records.title: Retirement: Azure App Service on Azure Stack Hub
records.summary: Azure App Service on Azure Stack Hub retires on September 30, 2029. Migrate affected applications before that date to avoid remaining on an unsupported deployment. Since September 30, 2026, new installations are unsupported and no new product releases, features or enhancements are provided. Existing supported deployments can continue running and upgrade to the latest available release until retirement. The sources do not establish automatic workload shutdown or data deletion. This retirement does not apply to Azure Stack Hub as a whole.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure App Service on Azure Stack Hub retires on September 30, 2029, ending Microsoft support. Existing supported deployments can continue running and upgrade to the latest available release until retirement.

Since September 30, 2026, new installations are unsupported and no new product releases, features or enhancements are provided. The sources do not document a security-update commitment for the retiring service.

Microsoft recommends Azure App Service in Azure as the migration destination. This notice does not retire Azure Stack Hub as a whole or Azure App Service in Azure. The sources identify no version-specific or regional exceptions.
what.html:
Azure App Service on Azure Stack Hub retires on September 30, 2029, ending Microsoft support. Existing supported deployments can continue running and upgrade to the latest available release until retirement.

Since September 30, 2026, new installations are unsupported and no new product releases, features or enhancements are provided. The sources do not document a security-update commitment for the retiring service.

Microsoft recommends Azure App Service in Azure as the migration destination. This notice does not retire Azure Stack Hub as a whole or Azure App Service in Azure. The sources identify no version-specific or regional exceptions.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Complete migration before September 30, 2029.

1. Inventory your applications, owners, runtimes, dependencies and business requirements. Assess compatibility, compliance and data residency. Decide which supporting services will move, remain on-premises or on Azure Stack Hub, or be replaced; retained dependencies may require hybrid connectivity.
2. Select hosting by application requirements. Standard Azure App Service suits cloud-ready applications that fit its sandbox constraints. Use Windows for existing ASP.NET Framework applications; ASP.NET Core can use Windows or Linux. The guidance lists Linux for Java, Node.js, Python and PHP. Assess Managed Instance on Azure App Service for complex Windows dependencies such as registry access, COM components or custom runtimes. Container options include App Service Containers, Azure Container Apps and AKS; App Service Environment is listed for single-tenant isolation. Modernization is not required for every workload.
3. Validate target-region availability, capacity, networking, identity and compliance requirements. Design and provision your landing zone, hosting and supporting services. Define migration waves, acceptance criteria, rollback procedures and cutover plans; use pilots and lower-risk workloads before business-critical workloads where appropriate.
4. Migrate code, configuration, connection strings, authentication, certificates, databases and files. The execution guidance recommends Azure Key Vault for secrets and Azure Files or Azure Blob Storage to replace Azure Stack Hub file-share dependencies. Validate database compatibility and network rules, and configure backup, redundancy and recovery policies.
5. Test functionality, performance, security, compliance and integrations. Validate authentication, scaling, certificates and network controls, and obtain business sign-off.
6. Before retirement, synchronize final data changes, freeze changes to the source deployment, update DNS and monitor production traffic. Retain rollback options until validation is complete; the guidance recommends deployment slots for cutover and rollback.
7. Validate production workloads, enable monitoring and alerts, update operational runbooks and confirm backup policies. Retire the old deployment only after successful migration.

what.question: What is changing?

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Current product guidance directs you to migrate to the supported SAP agentless connector before October 14, 2026, the separate container-image removal milestone. The retirement itself occurred on September 14, 2026.

2. Compare connector capabilities and configuration options. Review the SAP Sentinel user and role: the agentless connector requires fewer but different authorizations. Consult the referenced configuration guide and minimum-authorization role sample.
3. Review billing exclusions for selected SAP SIDs and contact your account representative before migrating. Connector system-identification methods differ, although retirement does not change pricing or billing meters.

records.title: Retirement: Support for Java 8, 11 and 17 will end on September 1, 2027
records.summary: Support for Java 8, 11 and 17 on Azure App Service ends on September 1, 2027. Apps will continue running, but Microsoft will stop providing security updates and customer service for those versions. Upgrade to Java 25 before that date. Changing Java stack settings restarts the application.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure App Service will end support for Java 8, 11 and 17 on September 1, 2027. Apps using these versions will continue running afterward, but Microsoft will no longer provide security updates or customer service for them.

The retirement notice does not specify regional exceptions. The Java configuration reference covers Linux and Windows; it provides runtime-change instructions rather than independently announcing this retirement.
what.html:
Azure App Service will end support for Java 8, 11 and 17 on September 1, 2027. Apps using these versions will continue running afterward, but Microsoft will no longer provide security updates or customer service for them.

The retirement notice does not specify regional exceptions. The Java configuration reference covers Linux and Windows; it provides runtime-change instructions rather than independently announcing this retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Azure App Service apps using Java 8, 11 or 17. The policy page references language-version guidance for checking configured runtimes, but the supplied material does not provide a fleet-wide inventory method.
2. Upgrade affected apps to Java 25 before September 1, 2027, as directed by the retirement notice. Test that the replacement meets your app's needs; the supplied material does not detail Java 25 compatibility prerequisites or migration gaps.
3. To change the runtime in the Azure portal, select your App Service app, open Settings, then Configuration and Stack settings. Select the target under Major version on Linux or Java version on Windows, then select Save.
4. Test the updated app to confirm that it meets your needs.

Changing stack settings restarts your application. The supplied material does not document retirement-specific backup, rollback or cleanup steps.

records.title: Retirement: Always Encrypted with Intel SGX Enclaves
records.summary: Always Encrypted with Intel SGX enclaves in Azure SQL Database retires on October 31, 2027 as Microsoft phases out support for SGX-enabled DC-series hardware. Affected workloads will lose enclave functionality. Move to a supported Standard-series non-DC compute tier and enable VBS enclaves, or consider SQL Server on Confidential VMs.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Always Encrypted with Intel SGX enclaves in Azure SQL Database on October 31, 2027 as support for SGX-enabled DC-series hardware is phased out.

The notice identifies Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) enclaves as a hardware-independent alternative. SQL Server on Confidential VMs is another option to consider. The notice does not specify regional exceptions or interim maintenance, support or security-update commitments.
what.html:
Microsoft is retiring Always Encrypted with Intel SGX enclaves in Azure SQL Database on October 31, 2027 as support for SGX-enabled DC-series hardware is phased out.

The notice identifies Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) enclaves as a hardware-independent alternative. SQL Server on Confidential VMs is another option to consider. The notice does not specify regional exceptions or interim maintenance, support or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Complete your transition before October 31, 2027 to avoid losing enclave functionality.

1. Identify your Azure SQL databases using Intel SGX enclaves and DC-series compute tiers. The notice provides no inventory procedure.
2. Choose VBS enclaves in Azure SQL Database, or consider SQL Server on Confidential VMs. The notice provides no selection criteria or migration steps for the latter.
3. For VBS, move to a supported Standard-series non-DC compute tier and enable VBS enclaves. No attestation is required.
4. Update client drivers to versions that support VBS enclaves.
5. Update connection strings to remove SGX attestation parameters and use VBS enclave mode.
6. Validate your migration before retirement. The notice does not specify validation procedures or minimum driver versions.

records.summary: Azure VMware Solution (AVS) is retiring its license-included offerings, not AVS itself. License-included PayGo SKUs retire on October 31, 2026; license-included Reserved Instance service ends on August 30, 2027. RI customers must complete their transition before August 30, 2027 to avoid disruption on August 31, 2027. AVS continues with portable Broadcom VMware Cloud Foundation licenses. AV36 retirement was separately moved from September 30, 2027 to August 30, 2027.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure VMware Solution is retiring its license-included SKUs: PayGo on October 31, 2026 and license-included RI service on August 30, 2027. AVS continues with portable VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) subscriptions purchased from Broadcom or a channel partner.

New node purchases after October 15, 2025 require a Broadcom VCF subscription. RIs purchased on or before that date can retain their existing licensing until the RI retirement milestone, subject to the requirement to transition before it. AV36 also retires on August 30, 2027.

The blog describes this as a licensing change, not an AVS product change. It states that portable VCF subscriptions are supported in all 39 AVS regions and that Microsoft continues managing AVS infrastructure and VMware host-level software, including patches and upgrades. The supplied content does not identify regional exceptions.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your license-included PayGo nodes, license-included RIs and AV36 usage. Establish whether your RIs were purchased on or before October 15, 2025. The guidance points to Azure Migrate for environment assessment but provides no SKU-identification procedure.
2. Choose your destination. Continue on AVS with portable VCF licenses, switch to Nutanix Cloud Clusters on Azure, or migrate to another Azure service such as Azure native infrastructure, Azure Red Hat OpenShift or Azure App Services. The guidance describes VCF BYOL as the least disruptive option; it identifies Nutanix Move as a no-cost migration tool.
3. For AVS VCF BYOL, purchase portable VCF subscriptions from Broadcom or a channel partner. Use the documented self-service exchange path for existing license-included RIs, then add your VCF license key in the Azure portal. Microsoft permits exchanges for reservations expiring after August 30, 2027; the supplied content does not give full exchange terms.
4. Complete your transition for the applicable SKU deadline. For license-included RIs, finish before August 30, 2027. Contact your Microsoft account team for transition assistance, including PayGo and AV36 planning.

Detailed validation, backup, cutover and cleanup procedures are not supplied. Do not treat the licensing steps as a complete migration runbook.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
Your exposure depends on your AVS configuration:

- License-included PayGo: retirement is October 31, 2026; detailed post-retirement behavior is not specified.
- License-included RIs: failure to transition before August 30, 2027 risks the documented service disruption on August 31, 2027. Bringing portable VCF licenses allows continued AVS use without technical changes according to the blog.
- AV36: retirement is August 30, 2027. The supplied content does not detail the required AV36 replacement procedure.
- Nodes already using portable VCF subscriptions: the licensing notice identifies no required licensing conversion. This does not establish an exception from the separate AV36 retirement.

AVS itself continues. Microsoft’s management of infrastructure and host-level software is distinct from your responsibility to obtain VCF licensing. Although the blog states that BYOL pricing is lower than bundled pricing, it provides no total-cost comparison including the separately purchased Broadcom subscription.

The sources do not specify data retention or deletion, console/API or integration effects, or your actual resource exposure.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance:
The main license-included retirement milestone is August 30, 2027, but PayGo retires earlier. Keep these scopes separate:

- License-included PayGo SKUs: retire on October 31, 2026. The blog documents unchanged operation through that date; the retirement notice and guidance explicitly identify it as retirement. They do not specify subsequent disruption timing.
- License-included Reserved Instances (RIs): August 30, 2027 is the last service day. The guidance nevertheless requires you to complete the transition before August 30, 2027 to avoid service disruption on August 31, 2027.
- AV36: retirement moved from September 30, 2027 to August 30, 2027. The former date aligned with Broadcom’s stated vSphere 8 end of support; that support milestone is separate from AV36 retirement.

Microsoft stopped selling AVS with included VCF subscriptions after October 15, 2025. Broadcom’s licensing-policy change began on November 1, 2025; neither date is the retirement milestone. These changes do not mean AVS itself is shutting down.

records.title: Retirement: DCsv3 and DCdsv3-series Azure Virtual Machines will be retired on October 31, 2029
records.service: Linux Virtual Machines · Virtual Machines · Windows Virtual Machines
records.summary: Microsoft retires Azure DCsv3/DCdsv3-series VMs on October 31, 2029, including Linux, Windows, Dedicated Host, AKS and Virtual Machine Scale Sets uses. Migrate before that date: remaining subscriptions stop working and stop incurring billing charges afterward. Separate restrictions apply earlier: purchases and renewals of one-year and three-year Reserved VM Instances end after October 31, 2026; capacity restrictions and a ban on new subscriptions begin on November 1, 2026. Microsoft continues support, SLA assurance, infrastructure updates and maintenance until retirement, but adds no new features or regions. Select a suitable confidential VM or container alternative, check capabilities, regional availability and quota, and review pricing and reservations.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring DCsv3/DCdsv3-series Azure VMs on October 31, 2029, including Linux, Windows, Dedicated Host and uses through AKS and Virtual Machine Scale Sets. These series will no longer be available for use or purchase afterward.

Until retirement, Microsoft continues workload support, SLA assurance, infrastructure updates and maintenance. Microsoft is not accepting feature requests, adding new features or expanding these series to new regions. Existing-region availability remains subject to capacity restrictions starting November 1, 2026.

Newer confidential VMs and confidential container services are documented alternatives. Their reference pages describe capabilities, not additional retirements.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Migrate your affected workloads before October 31, 2029.

1. Identify DCsv3/DCdsv3 workloads, including Linux, Windows, Dedicated Host, Virtual Machine Scale Sets and app-enclave-aware containers on AKS. The supplied guidance provides no inventory query or discovery procedure.
2. Select an alternative for your workload and performance requirements:
  - AMD VM-based workloads: DCasv6/DCadsv6 or memory-optimized ECasv6/ECadsv6.
  - Intel VM-based workloads: DCesv6/DCedsv6 or memory-optimized ECesv6/ECedsv6.
  - Lift-and-shift containerized applications: Azure Confidential Container Instances (C-ACI).
  - AKS container orchestration: Virtual nodes on Azure Container Instances (C-VN2).
3. Check compatibility, target-region availability and target-family vCPU quota. Request additional quota through the Azure portal if needed. If suitable confidential VMs are unavailable locally, check nearby regions or contact Azure Support.
4. Follow the documentation for your selected option and complete migration before retirement. The supplied guidance does not provide detailed backup, cutover, validation or cleanup procedures.
5. Review pricing and active one-year or three-year reservations in the Azure portal. The migration guide lists penalty-free reservation exchanges, trade-in for an Azure Savings Plan for compute, or reservations aligned with the replacement series as options. Shorter one-year terms are optional advice, not a migration requirement.

Replacement constraints

The supplied AMD VM references do not support Generation 1 VMs, Live Migration, Memory Preserving Updates, Accelerated Networking or Nested Virtualization. DCasv6 and ECasv6 have no local storage.

The DCesv6/DCedsv6/ECedsv6 references do not support Generation 1 VMs, Accelerated Networking, Ephemeral OS Disk, Nested Virtualization or Memory Preserving Updates; Live Migration is listed as coming soon. DCesv6 has no local storage. The ECesv6 reference URL names v5 series while its content describes ECesv6, so confirm the intended series when using it.

For C-ACI, Windows containers are in preview. Enforcement policies must be generated with the Azure CLI confcom extension; manual policy creation is unsupported. Enclaves are separately in preview, support Linux containers only, and have no network access; they communicate with their parent container group through port forwards. Confidential virtual nodes are supported where confidential ACI is available.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
The announcement points to the Azure Retirement Workbook for retirement information and warns that retirements may take up to two weeks after announcement to appear. Absence during that period does not establish that you are unaffected. The supplied workbook page contains no usable detail, so its resource coverage and completion checks cannot be confirmed.

The migration guide documents target-family quota checks and active-reservation review in the Azure portal. These checks do not prove that all affected workloads have migrated. No retirement-specific inventory query or automated migration-completion check is supplied.

For team-owned tracking, record affected workloads, replacement choices, capability checks, region and quota readiness, reservation decisions and migration completion evidence. This is local planning advice, not tracking provided by this website.

For help, use Microsoft Q&A or an Azure portal support request. The documented technical-support route requires a support plan: select Technical, My services, Virtual Machine running Windows/Linux, your VM, and Assistance with resizing my VM, then complete the applicable subtype and request. The referenced Q&A page was unavailable in the supplied material.

records.title: Retirement: Azure IoT Central will be retired on September 20, 2029
records.summary: Azure IoT Central will retire on September 20, 2029 and remains available until then. Microsoft recommends completing your transition before retirement. The migration playbook describes moving connectivity and provisioning to IoT Hub and DPS, using Microsoft Fabric for analytics, and replacing application capabilities. Post-retirement workload behavior and data retention are not specified.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft will retire Azure IoT Central on September 20, 2029. The service remains available until then. The notice identifies no regional, version, or customer-population exceptions and makes no specific maintenance or security-update commitments.

Microsoft recommends Azure IoT Hub, Device Provisioning Service (DPS), and Azure Device Registry as its Azure-native platform for connected operations. The migration playbook describes IoT Hub for connectivity and operations, DPS for provisioning, and Microsoft Fabric for analytics and dashboards.

This transition requires mapping or recreating IoT Central application capabilities, including templates, properties, commands, jobs, rules, integrations, and operator experiences. Device administration requires a custom portal or internal tooling.
what.html:
Microsoft will retire Azure IoT Central on September 20, 2029. The service remains available until then. The notice identifies no regional, version, or customer-population exceptions and makes no specific maintenance or security-update commitments.

Microsoft recommends Azure IoT Hub, Device Provisioning Service (DPS), and Azure Device Registry as its Azure-native platform for connected operations. The migration playbook describes IoT Hub for connectivity and operations, DPS for provisioning, and Microsoft Fabric for analytics and dashboards.

This transition requires mapping or recreating IoT Central application capabilities, including templates, properties, commands, jobs, rules, integrations, and operator experiences. Device administration requires a custom portal or internal tooling.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Microsoft recommends completing your transition before September 20, 2029. Use the migration playbook to plan and execute these steps:

1. Inventory your templates, devices, groups, jobs, exports, dashboards, integrations, and roles. Define required user journeys and success criteria.
2. Provision IoT Hub, DPS, routes, and monitoring in nonproduction. For Fabric analytics, use the recommended solution accelerator or build the ingestion and analytics path manually. Confirm telemetry reaches dashboards and establish side-by-side comparisons.
3. Map or recreate application capabilities and administration tools. Use direct methods for immediate online commands and desired properties for durable state changes.

- Fabric dashboards, alerts, and support views show migrated devices.
- Replacement operational capabilities are ready before cleanup.

records.title: Retirement: Microsoft HPC Pack
records.summary: Microsoft is retiring all versions of HPC Pack, with support ending on August 27, 2027. Existing deployments will remain operational afterward but receive no updates, fixes or technical support. Until then, Microsoft provides limited retirement-only support, including security/CVE response and necessary security updates, but excludes non-security fixes and migration services. Assess your workloads and transition options. Azure Batch is a documented option for managed parallel and HPC scheduling, but no alternative guarantees one-to-one feature parity.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring all versions of HPC Pack. Until August 27, 2027, Microsoft provides limited retirement-only support covering:

- Security/CVE response and necessary security updates.
- Guidance from existing documentation and validated configurations.
- Assistance with supported components and documented functionality.
- Case-by-case evaluation of long-term support options where available, without guaranteed availability.

This support excludes non-security fixes, product improvements, new features, custom code, design changes, validation of new platforms or integrations, new product investigation or documentation, migration planning or execution, consulting and unsupported configurations.

After end of support, existing deployments remain operational without updates, fixes or technical support.
