records.title: Azure Multi-Factor Authentication Server will be deprecated 30 September 2024
records.summary: Beginning September 30, 2024, Azure Multi-Factor Authentication Server deployments no longer service MFA requests, so authentications that depend on them could fail. Microsoft directs existing customers to cloud-based Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication. Migration must address federation, applications, RADIUS, hardware tokens and password-reset dependencies—not just registered authentication data. The migration references provide implementation guidance but do not independently establish or change the retirement date.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Multi-Factor Authentication Server stops servicing MFA requests beginning September 30, 2024. Microsoft directs existing customers to cloud-based Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication. MFA Server is also unavailable for new deployments.

The migration guidance describes three choices:

- Replace MFA Server while retaining federation and application authentication through AD FS.
- Move MFA and user authentication to Microsoft Entra ID while retaining AD FS for applications.
- Move applications, MFA and user authentication to Microsoft Entra ID and decommission AD FS.

The guides describe staged migration with groups, but that routing capability is not an exception to the announced retirement. The supplied content does not document continued maintenance or security-update commitments.
what.html:
Azure Multi-Factor Authentication Server stops servicing MFA requests beginning September 30, 2024. Microsoft directs existing customers to cloud-based Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication. MFA Server is also unavailable for new deployments.

The migration guidance describes three choices:

  • Replace MFA Server while retaining federation and application authentication through AD FS.
  • Move MFA and user authentication to Microsoft Entra ID while retaining AD FS for applications.
  • Move applications, MFA and user authentication to Microsoft Entra ID and decommission AD FS.

The guides describe staged migration with groups, but that routing capability is not an exception to the announced retirement. The supplied content does not document continued maintenance or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify every MFA Server dependency: federation and AD FS claims rules, applications, Conditional Access policies, registered authentication methods, RADIUS clients, hardware OATH tokens, MIM self-service password reset and Privileged Access Management (PAM).
2. Choose your migration scope. You can retain federation, move user authentication to Microsoft Entra ID, or also migrate applications and decommission AD FS. If you plan to migrate applications, move as many as possible before migrating MFA. Microsoft recommends password hash synchronization (PHS); pass-through authentication (PTA) is another documented option.
3. Prepare the selected route. For the documented MFA-and-user-authentication route, complete PHS or PTA prerequisites and seamless SSO preparation. Use cloud-only groups for Staged Rollout; nested and dynamic membership groups are unsupported. Preserve the security goals of MFA-enforcing AD FS claims rules in Conditional Access before enabling Staged Rollout. Keep groups protecting high-value applications dedicated to that purpose.
4. If remaining AD FS applications require MFA, back up claims rules and configure every AD FS server for Microsoft Entra MFA. Group-based provider selection requires AD FS 2019 with farm behavior level 4 and on-premises security groups; access control policies cannot select a provider by group membership. The general guide also describes Windows Server 2016 with level 3 migration, but users must select their MFA provider during transition. Configuring the farm requires Enterprise Administrator permissions; managing the feature requires a Global Administrator. Skip this preparation if no remaining AD FS applications require MFA.
5. Plan test and pilot groups and a rollback approach. Use the latest Migration Utility included in the most recent Azure MFA Server update to synchronize supported authentication data. Microsoft recommends combined security-information registration because migrated phone numbers can be stale. Protect registration with Conditional Access; documented options for users outside the trusted device or location include a Temporary Access Pass or temporary policy exclusion.
6. Resolve integration-specific gaps before cutover:
  - Hardware-OATH-only migration requires a CSV seed file containing token secret keys, which MFA Server cannot export. Contact the hardware vendor if keys are missing. The Web Service SDK can export assigned serial numbers; users must supply device OTP information to complete registration.
  - MIM cannot use Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication directly. Evaluate Microsoft Entra SSPR. If you cannot move SSPR, or use MFA Server for PAM, Microsoft recommends an alternative third-party MFA option.
  - For RADIUS clients, prefer supported SAML, OpenID Connect or OAuth integrations. Otherwise, evaluate NPS with the Microsoft Entra MFA extension and confirm supported versions and capabilities with the service provider. Register users before NPS use and verify their default authentication methods with each client.
7. Add users to applicable Conditional Access and AD FS claims-rule groups before adding them to Staged Rollout. Validate registration, sign-ins, application access and each dependent integration before expanding migration.
8. Before decommissioning, review MFA Server logs for remaining users or applications. For the cloud-user-authentication route, convert federated domains to managed authentication, remove Staged Rollout, restore or adjust AD FS claims rules, and disable the MFA Server authentication provider. Decommission servers using your enterprise process. Back up residual logs and data before optional cleanup; remove applicable Web Server SDK components and check pre-8.0.x deployments for Phone App Web Service removal.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if your authentication flows depend on Azure Multi-Factor Authentication Server, including through AD FS, applications, RADIUS, MIM password reset or PAM. Beginning September 30, 2024, those deployments no longer service MFA requests, so dependent authentications could fail. The supplied content does not inventory your environment or identify deployment-specific exceptions.

Replacing MFA Server does not inherently require replacing AD FS or moving every application. For users moved to cloud authentication, PHS or PTA replaces the federated authentication path, and Microsoft Entra MFA applies when required. Existing Conditional Access policies can remain unchanged if they already determine MFA prompts; MFA enforced through AD FS claims rules needs equivalent coverage.

Important compatibility limits include:

- MIM cannot use Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication directly.
- MFA Server cannot export hardware OATH secret keys; token-only migration requires seed keys and user participation.
- The NPS extension does not use Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies. All authentication requests reaching NPS require MFA, and unregistered users fail authentication.
- NPS uses the user's default MFA method without offering an alternative during authentication, even if that method is disabled in tenant authentication-method or MFA policies. Users may not see an on-screen indication that an MFA request was sent.
- RADIUS client capabilities and password-encryption methods constrain available MFA methods. Methods requiring input need access-challenge support; some clients support only Authenticator push notifications and phone calls.

The supplied content does not document retirement-specific data deletion, retention changes or costs.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:

records.title: Retirement: Network security group flow logs in Azure Network Watcher will be retired
records.summary: Azure Network Watcher network security group (NSG) flow logs retire on September 30, 2027. Migrate to virtual network flow logs before retirement. After that date, Azure deletes existing NSG flow log resources and no longer supports traffic analytics enabled for them. Existing records in Azure Storage remain subject to configured retention policies and storage charges. New NSG flow log creation ended on June 30, 2025, a separate milestone. Use Network Watcher's migration view and reports to assess your selected subscriptions and regions and confirm replacement resource state; validate log delivery and downstream consumers separately.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Network Watcher is retiring network security group (NSG) flow logs on September 30, 2027. Microsoft directs you to replace them with virtual network flow logs. No version-specific or regional retirement exceptions are documented.

Existing NSG flow logs can remain in use before retirement, but you can no longer create new ones. The sources provide no separate maintenance or security-update commitment.

After retirement, Azure deletes NSG flow log resources and no longer supports their traffic analytics. This does not delete existing log records from Azure Storage.

Virtual network flow logs record supported Layer 4 traffic and add security admin rule decisions and virtual network encryption status. Their reference page describes replacement capabilities and limits; it does not independently establish the retirement or guarantee equivalent coverage for every configuration.

After retirement, Azure deletes NSG flow log resources and no longer supports their traffic analytics. This does not delete existing log records from Azure Storage.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Migrate to virtual network flow logs before September 30, 2027.

1. Open Network Watcher > Logs > Migrate flow logs in Azure portal. Select your subscriptions and regions, then review total and selected NSG flow log counts. As team-owned preparation, identify traffic analytics, storage and downstream consumer dependencies.
2. Choose a migration method. Use the script for partial interface/subnet coverage or differing configurations. Use Azure Policy for uniform configurations, where the same NSG applies across all interfaces or subnets, or when you want virtual-network-level logging. The script does not support PaaS scenarios where NSG flow logs are in your subscription but target resources are in other subscriptions; manually enable replacement logging on the PaaS virtual network or subnet instead.
3. Check replacement workload and regional support, including separate Traffic Analytics limits. Prepare a standard storage account in the virtual network's region, in the same subscription or another subscription associated with the same Microsoft Entra tenant. Premium storage is unsupported. If choosing version 5, verify region and subscription support and parser compatibility; availability is limited to West Central US, East Asia and Canary regions, subject to subscription support. Azure PowerShell provisioning of version 5 requires Az PowerShell 16.4.0 or later.
4. For script migration, prepare an active Azure subscription, PowerShell 7, the Az PowerShell module and required RBAC permissions for flow log subscriptions and any Traffic Analytics Log Analytics workspaces. Download and extract the script and JSON configuration from the portal. Do not change topology in selected subscriptions and regions once script execution starts.
5. Run analysis and review its report. Choose migration with or without aggregation: aggregation can replace multiple interface-level configurations with one virtual-network-level flow log. Review the migration summary before accepting changes. The script offers rollback before acceptance, but not afterward. Keep the script and reports for troubleshooting.
6. Confirm that migrated NSG flow logs are disabled and replacement virtual network flow logs exist. As team-owned validation, verify expected storage delivery, parsing and downstream analysis. Then delete the migrated NSG flow log resources. For manual migration, Microsoft recommends disabling NSG flow logs before enabling replacement logging on the same workloads to avoid duplicate recording and additional costs.
7. Review retained records and storage retention settings. Export or backup is optional, not a documented retirement requirement; retirement itself does not delete stored records.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if you use NSG flow logs or traffic analytics enabled for them. Without migration, Azure deletes those logging resources after September 30, 2027 and no longer supports their traffic analytics. The supplied guidance does not announce shutdown of VMs, virtual networks or NSG traffic filtering.

Existing Azure Storage records remain subject to configured retention policies and storage charges. The NSG flow log retention feature requires general-purpose v2 storage accounts.

Migration scope and limits

- Portal counts cover only selected subscriptions and regions. Review subnet and NIC configurations; missing records do not prove that no dependency exists.
- Aggregation can expand interface-level logging to virtual-network scope. For a scale set with a load balancer, the script enables subnet logging. If interface coverage is partial or configurations differ, it uses one interface's configuration for that subnet flow log.
- Existing NSG flow logs do not support Application Gateway v2 subnets or D, E and F family v6 VMs. Private endpoint traffic is captured only at the source VM, and ExpressRoute gateway-subnet logging can miss traffic. Do not assume the replacement resolves every existing gap.

Replacement constraints

Virtual network flow logs do not support Azure Container Instances, Azure Container Apps, Azure Logic Apps, Azure Functions, Azure DNS Private Resolver, App Service, Azure Database for MariaDB, MySQL and PostgreSQL, Azure SQL Managed Instance, Azure NetApp Files or Microsoft Power Platform.

ExpressRoute gateway-subnet logging misses outbound VM-to-circuit flows, which require VM subnet or NIC logging, and traffic bypassing the gateway through FastPath. For API Management, Traffic Analytics supports VNet Injection, not VNet Integration.

Rotating customer-managed storage encryption keys stops flow logging until you disable and re-enable it. Modifying an actively ingested blob's block structure can prevent further writes to that hour's blob.

Broader coverage and overlapping logging can increase volume and costs. Virtual network flow-log collection is charged per gigabyte with a 5 GB/month free tier per subscription; storage is separate. Optional Traffic Analytics has separate processing charges and no free tier. The sources do not establish your affected resource count or migration cost.

records.title: Retirement: Azure PostgreSQL migration extension in Azure Data Studio (ADS)
records.summary: The Azure PostgreSQL migration extension in Azure Data Studio retired on November 15, 2024. Microsoft no longer enhances or supports the extension, and it lacks the latest security and compliance features. Microsoft recommends migration services for Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server through the Azure portal or Azure CLI. The notice does not announce database workload shutdown or retirement of Azure Data Studio. The supporting migration-service page describes alternatives, not another retirement milestone.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired the Azure PostgreSQL migration extension in Azure Data Studio on November 15, 2024, ending enhancements and support for that extension.

The notice describes limited functionality and lack of support for the latest Azure Database for PostgreSQL SKUs, without naming those SKUs. Microsoft recommends migration services for Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server through the Azure portal or Azure CLI.

This retirement concerns the extension, not Azure Data Studio or Azure Database for PostgreSQL. The supporting page's comparison with Azure Database Migration Service (Classic) does not establish a retirement of Classic.

Microsoft retired the Azure PostgreSQL migration extension in Azure Data Studio on November 15, 2024, ending enhancements and support for that extension.

The notice describes limited functionality and lack of support for the latest Azure Database for PostgreSQL SKUs, without naming those SKUs. Microsoft recommends migration services for Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server through the Azure portal or Azure CLI.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Microsoft recommends transitioning away from the retired extension:

1. Identify whether your migration process uses the Azure PostgreSQL migration extension in Azure Data Studio. The supplied content provides no discovery procedure.
2. Review migration services for Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server through the Azure portal or Azure CLI. The supporting page lists offline and online migration from Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, Google Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, on-premises environments and Azure virtual machines.
3. Choose offline migration if you can stop connected applications while databases are copied. Choose online migration when you need minimal downtime; it requires primary keys in all tables and has additional replication restrictions not detailed in the supplied overview.
4. Review the referenced premigration validations and source-specific guidance. For online migration, monitor source storage and compute during replication, then perform cutover after the destination synchronizes with the source.

The supplied content does not provide complete prerequisites, detailed post-migration validation, backup, export or cleanup procedures.

records.title: Azure QnA Maker will be retired on 31 March 2025
records.summary: Azure QnA Maker fully retired on October 31, 2025 according to the supplied current product guidance. Runtime and inferencing requests fail, dependent applications and bots stop functioning, and projects and knowledge bases are inaccessible and cannot be updated. Microsoft directs customers to Custom Question Answering in Azure Language. Earlier sources give March 31, 2025 and conflicting March 15, 2025 dates; this synthesis prefers current product guidance for full retirement, but the supplied sources do not explicitly document an extension. Creation of new QnA Maker resources and knowledge bases stopped on October 1, 2022. Post-retirement content recovery and migration feasibility are not established.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure QnA Maker fully retired on October 31, 2025. Microsoft directs customers to Custom Question Answering in Azure Language. QnA Maker runtime and inferencing requests now fail, and its projects and knowledge bases are no longer accessible or editable.

The earlier announcement states that resources and knowledge bases created before October 1, 2022 remained supported until March 31, 2025. It describes the replacement as providing all QnA Maker capabilities, improved relevance ranking, availability across 31 regions, and support for unstructured content from documents and public URLs.

The full-retirement guidance documents no version, region or customer exceptions. This retirement does not establish retirement of Azure Language or Custom Question Answering.

records.title: Azure Red Hat OpenShift 3.11 will be retired on 30 June 2022
records.summary: Azure Red Hat OpenShift 3.11 retired on June 30, 2022. Microsoft stated that remaining 3.11 clusters would be shut down following retirement, without specifying a separate shutdown date. The notice directs customers to OpenShift 4 to avoid service disruption. Support for creating new 3.11 clusters continued through November 30, 2020, a separate milestone. The other supplied pages do not establish another retirement date or an extension.

records.title: Azure S8 and S9 Analysis Services SKUs retiring on 31 August 2023
records.summary: After August 31, 2023, Azure Analysis Services S8 and S9 SKUs are unavailable for new deployments. Existing servers continue on old hardware; no shutdown or migration-completion deadline is stated. Microsoft recommends S8v2 or S9v2, subject to regional availability and query replica limits. This retirement does not apply to Azure Analysis Services as a whole.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Analysis Services retired S8 and S9 SKUs from new deployments after August 31, 2023. Existing S8 and S9 servers continue on old hardware.

Microsoft recommends S8v2 and S9v2. Each provides twice the QPUs of its corresponding deprecated plan, with the same memory:

- S8v2: 640 QPUs and 200 GB of memory.
- S9v2: 1280 QPUs and 400 GB of memory.

The supplied sources do not announce retirement of Azure Analysis Services as a whole or its other plans. They do not specify changes to support or security-update commitments.

Microsoft recommends S8v2 and S9v2. Each provides twice the QPUs of its corresponding deprecated plan, with the same memory:

  • S8v2: 640 QPUs and 200 GB of memory.
  • S9v2: 1280 QPUs and 400 GB of memory.

The supplied sources do not announce retirement of Azure Analysis Services as a whole or its other plans. They do not specify changes to support or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Review your Azure Analysis Services server's selected plan in the Azure portal to identify S8 or S9 servers.
2. Review S8v2 or S9v2 availability and query replica limits in your region before selecting a replacement. For new servers, use an available replacement or review the pricing page for another suitable SKU.
3. Plan the change using the documented Azure portal or PowerShell plan-changing capabilities. The service supports changing plans within a tier. Microsoft's retirement notice recommends starting migration before August 31, 2023, but sets no completion deadline.

The supplied sources do not provide S8/S9-specific migration prerequisites, backup, cutover, downtime or validation procedures.

records.title: Azure Scheduler will be retired on 31 January 2022
records.summary: Azure Scheduler’s standalone-service retirement was explicitly extended to January 31, 2022. Microsoft directs you to move configured jobs to Azure Logic Apps before that date. A supplied Q&A answer instead reports full retirement on December 31, 2019; the explicit extension notices establish the applicable date. Earlier Free SKU shutdown and portal restrictions are separate milestones. Internally scheduled WebJobs are unaffected, while WebJobs triggered through Azure Scheduler require migration. The original timeline associates full retirement with stopping all jobs and deleting all data, but the extension does not separately confirm revised deletion timing. The supplied migration-reference content is a Logic Apps quickstart and does not establish migration completion checks.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Scheduler is retiring as a standalone service on January 31, 2022. Microsoft identifies Azure Logic Apps as its replacement and directs you to migrate scheduled jobs for continued use.

The retained timeline separates Free SKU shutdown and portal removal from continued API and SDK operation of existing Standard, P10 and P20 resources. The extension does not explicitly revise those earlier restrictions or guarantee availability before retirement.

For WebJobs, the supplied Q&A distinguishes Scheduler-triggered jobs from internal scheduling: WebJobs using Azure Scheduler are affected; internally scheduled WebJobs are not affected by this retirement.

The original full-retirement timeline says all Scheduler jobs stop and all data is deleted. The extension does not separately confirm revised deletion timing. Regional exceptions and maintenance, support or security-update commitments are not documented.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Move Azure Scheduler jobs you need to continue using to Azure Logic Apps before January 31, 2022.

1. Identify your configured Scheduler jobs. For WebJobs, distinguish internal scheduling from Azure Scheduler calls to the WebJobs API; the supplied content provides no inventory tool or discovery command.
2. Move Scheduler-dependent jobs to Logic Apps. For Scheduler-triggered WebJobs, the supplied Q&A describes using a Logic App HTTP Action to invoke the WebJobs API.
3. Consult the migration guidance and FAQ referenced by the notices. The supplied content at the migration-reference URL is instead a Logic Apps Consumption quickstart, so it does not supply retirement migration procedures or establish completion.

Internally scheduled WebJobs do not require migration for this retirement. The Q&A moderator states that their website must have Always On configured for scheduling to work.

The inputs do not provide detailed compatibility checks, migration prerequisites, export or backup procedures, cutover, validation or cleanup steps. The historical instruction to disable or delete job collections before October 31, 2019 applied to customers who did not want jobs to continue after portal removal; it was not the final retirement deadline.

records.title: Azure Service Fabric Mesh Preview Retirement
records.summary: Microsoft is retiring Azure Service Fabric Mesh Preview, with support for existing deployments ending on April 28, 2021. The announcement also prohibits new deployments through the Service Fabric Mesh API, without specifying a separate effective date. Plan your workload migration to a suitable alternative. Azure-deployed Service Fabric clusters and Service Fabric Standalone are unaffected. The supplied content does not establish a workload shutdown date.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Azure Service Fabric Mesh Preview, its fully managed offering for containerized applications. Existing deployments remain supported until April 28, 2021; the announcement prohibits new deployments through the Service Fabric Mesh API.

Azure-deployed Service Fabric clusters and Service Fabric Standalone are unaffected and remain supported and available, according to the announcement. The supplied content does not specify when Mesh workloads stop running.
what.html:
Microsoft is retiring Azure Service Fabric Mesh Preview, its fully managed offering for containerized applications. Existing deployments remain supported until April 28, 2021; the announcement prohibits new deployments through the Service Fabric Mesh API.

Azure-deployed Service Fabric clusters and Service Fabric Standalone are unaffected and remain supported and available, according to the announcement. The supplied content does not specify when Mesh workloads stop running.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Azure Service Fabric Mesh workloads. The supplied content provides no resource-inventory method.
2. Choose a destination based on your requirements:
  - Azure Container Instances for quickly deploying serverless containers.
  - Azure Kubernetes Service for additional control over your environment.
  - Service Fabric managed clusters for the full Service Fabric feature set, including stateful programming models, with reduced cluster-management overhead.
  - Azure-deployed Service Fabric clusters or Service Fabric Standalone, which remain available.
3. Plan and carry out your migration with the April 28, 2021 support-end milestone in mind. The supplied content does not provide Mesh migration procedures, backup, cutover or validation steps.

If you choose Service Fabric managed clusters, create a new managed cluster. The reference explicitly states that existing Service Fabric clusters have no migration path to that resource type; it does not document a Mesh migration procedure. Manual changes to a managed cluster's underlying resources are unsupported.

For managed-cluster sizing, Basic requires at least 3 nodes, supports one node type and up to 100 nodes per node type, and does not support adding or removing node types or zone redundancy. Standard requires at least 5 nodes, supports up to 50 node types and 1,000 nodes per node type, and supports node-type changes and zone redundancy.

The retirement announcement offers a “Contact Us” route for questions.

records.title: Retirement: Retirement of Classic Alerts for Azure Site Recovery
records.summary: Classic Alerts for Azure Site Recovery will retire on September 23, 2027. Microsoft recommends moving to Azure Monitor alerts through the guided migration experience in Business Continuity Center or Recovery Services Vault. Configure notification routing and validate delivery before disabling classic alerts. The notice does not specify post-retirement alert behavior or effects on recovery workloads.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Classic Alerts for Azure Site Recovery on September 23, 2027 and recommends Azure Monitor alerts as the replacement. The notice does not specify pre-retirement maintenance or support commitments, regional exceptions, or post-retirement availability.

Built-in Azure Monitor alerts are enabled by default and do not require alert-rule configuration. Sending notifications requires an alert processing rule and an action group.

Coverage depends on the replication scenario:

- Disaster-recovery enablement failures, critical replication health and failover failures: Azure VM, Hyper-V and VMware replication.
- Agent version expiry: Azure VM and Hyper-V replication.
- Unreachable agents: Hyper-V replication.
- Auto certification expiry: Azure VM replication.

Azure Monitor supports multiple notification channels, selection of notification scenarios, programmatic alert and notification management, and consistent alert management across services.

Azure Monitor supports multiple notification channels, selection of notification scenarios, programmatic alert and notification management, and consistent alert management across services.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
If you use Classic Alerts for Azure Site Recovery, Microsoft recommends moving to Azure Monitor alerts for the September 23, 2027 retirement.

1. Identify affected vaults. In Business Continuity Center, open Monitoring + Reporting > Alerts > Manage alerts > Manage built-in alert settings for resources to review settings across subscriptions. Backup Center also exposes a Site Recovery Classic Alerts column.
2. Use the guided migration experience in Business Continuity Center or Recovery Services Vault. Review alert coverage for your Azure VM, Hyper-V or VMware replication scenarios.
3. Configure notifications in Azure Monitor > Alerts > Alert processing rules. Set the intended resource scope and filters, apply an existing or new action group with your notification destinations, and select Always for continuous scheduling. Built-in alert generation alone does not enable notifications.
4. Validate alert visibility and notification delivery. Allow the documented 24-hour registration period before testing. The reference's test disables public network access on a test VM's cache storage account to generate a critical replication-health alert; keep that test confined to test resources.
5. Update and save each vault's monitoring settings to disable classic alerts when switching to Azure Monitor alone. Leaving both systems enabled generates duplicate alerts.

Security alerts cannot be disabled. If you use optional suppression rules, they take precedence over notification rules for the same scope during their scheduled window. The supplied content does not document export, backup or additional cleanup requirements.

records.title: Azure Site Recovery data encryption feature will be retired April 30, 2022
records.summary: Azure Site Recovery retired its data encryption feature on April 30, 2022. VMs still using it after that date lose failover operations and cannot use Azure Site Recovery. The documented migration requires disabling replication, creating a new replication policy and completing initial replication to a storage account with Storage Service Encryption (SSE) enabled. The retirement notice establishes the deadline; the supporting reference pages do not independently establish it.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Site Recovery retired its data encryption feature on April 30, 2022. The documented replacement is Encryption at Rest with Azure Site Recovery, which uses Storage Service Encryption (SSE).

SSE encrypts data before storage and decrypts it on retrieval. Upon failover to Azure, migrated VMs run from encrypted storage accounts. The notice states that this improves recovery time objective (RTO), but provides no quantified improvement.

The supplied notice does not specify affected versions or regions. Separate reference material about client-side encryption and unmanaged disks does not establish additional scope for this retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
To retain Azure Site Recovery failover capability, the notice required you to migrate each affected VM by April 30, 2022:

1. Identify VMs using the retired data encryption feature. The notice references an affected-VM list, but that list and a feature-specific identification method are absent from the supplied content.
2. Disable replication for the affected VM.
3. Create a new replication policy.
4. Enable replication and select a storage account with SSE enabled.
5. Complete initial replication to that storage account. The VM then uses Encryption at Rest with Azure Site Recovery.

Disabling protection stops replication. The supporting removal guidance has scenario-specific prerequisites and cleanup requirements; it is not itself a retirement migration procedure. The supplied content does not document a retirement-specific backup, cutover or cleanup sequence.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Sphere is retiring Legacy service interfaces on September 27th, 2027
records.summary: Microsoft will retire Azure Sphere Legacy service interfaces—the Legacy API (PAPI) and azsphere CLI—on September 27, 2027. Complete migration to Azure Sphere (Integrated) before retirement; afterward, Legacy interfaces will no longer manage devices. Legacy remains fully supported until retirement and can run alongside Integrated during migration. Integrating your tenant does not migrate workflows or automation. The supplied content does not describe device-workload shutdown.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring the Azure Sphere Legacy API (PAPI) and Legacy CLI (azsphere) on September 27, 2027. Move device-management workflows to Azure Sphere (Integrated).

Integrated provides management through Azure portal, the Azure Sphere extension for Azure CLI, Azure Sphere for PowerShell, and the Integrated API. The notice states that Integrated supports all Legacy features.

Integrating a Legacy tenant turns it into an Azure Sphere catalog. Existing resources remain the same and receive Azure resource IDs. Integration also proposes mappings from Legacy user roles to Azure RBAC roles for your review.

You can use Legacy and Integrated interfaces together during migration. The supplied content describes management-interface retirement, not retirement of devices or shutdown of device workloads.

You can use Legacy and Integrated interfaces together during migration. The supplied content describes management-interface retirement, not retirement of devices or shutdown of device workloads.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify workflows, scripts, custom applications, and automation using PAPI or azsphere, including manufacturing, operations, and development tasks. The supplied content provides no automatic inventory method.
2. Before other migration work, use the Azure portal Integrate feature to turn your Legacy tenant into a catalog. Review the proposed Azure RBAC role mappings; you can accept, modify, or reject them.
3. Move interactive workflows to Integrated interfaces. Choose portal or command-line tools for each use case, update scripts and internal documentation, and train users. Learning Azure RBAC scope and resource hierarchy is recommended.
4. Rework automation and API integrations. Each interface built on the Integrated API requires a Microsoft Entra access token. Develop and test alongside existing production automation, taking care with irreversible operations such as claiming devices into a catalog.
5. Verify that users can perform all required tasks, then deploy and validate updated automation. The blog strongly recommends removing migrated users' Legacy permissions and recommends removing Legacy service-principal access after production cutover. Users testing automation may need Legacy access longer.
6. Complete remaining Legacy-access cleanup when supported. At the time of the blog, at least one active Legacy Administrator was required, and removing the last administrator was unsupported. The supplied content does not confirm that this restriction has changed.

Complete migration before September 27, 2027. Adopting Azure Monitor is optional, not a migration prerequisite.

impact.guidance:

records.title: Retirement: Azure Spring Apps will be retired on March 31, 2028
records.service: Azure Container Apps · Azure Spring Apps
records.summary: Azure Spring Apps Basic, Standard and Enterprise retire on March 31, 2028; support and access to workloads and the service end afterward. Standard consumption and dedicated (preview) retired on March 31, 2025. Migrate by your plan's deadline. Current product guidance places the Basic, Standard and Enterprise new-customer cutoff at March 17, 2025, while the announcement says after March 31, 2025. Enterprise destination guidance for retaining Spring commercial support or Tanzu components remains conflicting and needs confirmation.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Azure Spring Apps: Basic, Standard and Enterprise on March 31, 2028, following Standard consumption and dedicated (preview) on March 31, 2025. After each retirement, support and access end.

Existing Basic, Standard and Enterprise customers can generally continue operating until retirement. Microsoft documents workload support, SLA assurance, infrastructure maintenance, OSS/Tanzu component management and application container-image updates, subject to the Enterprise exceptions below. Microsoft will not add new features or accept feature requests.

App Live View, App Accelerator and App Configuration Service have been unsupported since September 2025. Microsoft may remove these components if a critical vulnerability is identified.

Microsoft recommends Azure Container Apps or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) as replacements. The retirement concerns Azure Spring Apps, not Microsoft's broader Java on Azure offering.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Azure Spring Apps instances, plans, applications and dependencies. Apply the correct retirement deadline: March 31, 2028 for Basic, Standard and Enterprise; March 31, 2025 for Standard consumption and dedicated (preview).
2. Select a destination using the referenced migration guidance. Microsoft recommends Azure Container Apps for managed, serverless container hosting or AKS for Kubernetes-based hosting. Product guidance also lists Azure App Service as a PaaS alternative. Azure Container Apps meets most Spring hosting needs; full feature parity is not established.
3. For Enterprise, check your use of Spring commercial support and Tanzu components. Destination guidance conflicts: several passages recommend AKS, while another passage and the announcement specify Tanzu Platform Spring Essentials on Azure Container Apps. Confirm your supported destination with Microsoft support and Broadcom before committing. Contact your Broadcom sales representative for Tanzu purchasing guidance.
4. Migrate by your plan's retirement date. The Azure CLI spring extension can assist with Azure Container Apps environment setup; it is not documented as a complete migration tool. The supplied content does not provide detailed export, backup, cutover or cleanup procedures.
5. As a team-owned completion check, validate required application behavior and dependencies on the destination. This is planning advice, not a documented automated completion check.

Use the Azure Pricing Calculator to assess destination costs. For technical migration help, open an Azure portal support ticket.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
All listed Azure Spring Apps plans are affected. Without migration, you lose support and access to instances after your plan's retirement: March 31, 2028 for Basic, Standard and Enterprise, or March 31, 2025 for Standard consumption and dedicated (preview). Product guidance explicitly includes loss of access to workloads and the service.

Customer eligibility and operations

Current product guidance defines an existing Basic, Standard or Enterprise customer as one who created an instance before March 17, 2025. It also classifies customers with no instance in the past three months as new customers. New customers cannot sign up.

Existing customers can continue creating, updating and deleting instances until retirement, but the boundary is unclear: the guidance says “within the same tenant in 2025 or within the same subscription” without fully explaining how those conditions interact.

Enterprise dependencies and costs

App Live View, App Accelerator and App Configuration Service have been unsupported since September 2025 and may be removed if a critical vulnerability is identified. That milestone did not itself shut down all Enterprise workloads.

Billing for commercial Tanzu components resumed on April 21, 2025 at the pre-promotion price, with Microsoft collecting payment for Broadcom. Destination costs depend on service selection, pricing and resource use; no customer-specific estimate is supplied.

The sources do not establish which resources you have, provide an automated discovery method, distinguish console/API loss from other access, or specify data retention, deletion or post-retirement recovery arrangements.

what.html:

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Microsoft strongly recommends migrating your Azure SQL Edge workloads. The supplied guidance supports the following planning steps, but provides no detailed migration procedure:

1. Identify your Azure SQL Edge workloads and assess their capacity and feature requirements. No resource-discovery method is documented.
2. Select a destination:
  - SQL Server Express: Described as free, using the same database engine as Azure SQL Edge, and able to run in containers. The notice lists limits of the lesser of 1 socket or 4 cores, 1,410 MB RAM, and 10 GB per database. It states five years of full support plus five years of extended support, without specifying a version or lifecycle dates.
  - SQL Server Standard: Recommended for applications that exceed Express limits and need essential database management capabilities without advanced enterprise features.
  - SQL Managed Instance enabled by Azure Arc: A managed option on infrastructure of your choice, described as maintaining data sovereignty and providing built-in management capabilities. Its stated near-100% compatibility with the latest SQL Server database engine does not guarantee complete compatibility.
3. Plan migration and validation for your selected destination. The supplied material does not provide retirement-specific prerequisites, export or backup procedures, cutover instructions, validation checks, or cleanup steps.

records.title: Azure Stack Edge Pro FPGA is retiring on 29 February 2024
records.summary: Azure Stack Edge Pro FPGA retired on February 29, 2024. Microsoft no longer provides replacement devices, security patches, critical updates or phone, email and web support for these devices. The migration guide identifies end-of-life as February 2024, consistent with the notice's exact date; neither source establishes a workload shutdown date. Migrate data and workloads to Azure Stack Edge Pro 2 or Pro GPU after checking availability, capacity and compatibility. Migration requires a new resource, data protection, workload redeployment and verification before erasing and returning the source device. The supplied GPU overview limits device availability to validated partner workloads and large-scale deployments of at least 100 nodes.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired Azure Stack Edge Pro FPGA devices on February 29, 2024, ending replacement devices, security patches, critical updates and phone, email and web support. The supplied sources do not state that existing FPGA workloads shut down or identify regional exceptions.

The migration guide documents moving data and workloads to Azure Stack Edge Pro 2 or Pro GPU. This requires a new device order and Azure resource, data restoration or copying, and workload redeployment—not an in-place hardware replacement.

The supplied Pro GPU overview is not a retirement announcement. It limits device availability to validated partner workloads and large-scale deployments of at least 100 nodes; partner workloads may not be supported on every device. Microsoft states that it continues to facilitate and support Azure Government customers and the Defense Industrial Base, but this is not an exception to FPGA retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Inventory and plan. Record the FPGA device configuration, cloud and local shares, users, bandwidth schedules and IoT Edge modules using the local UI and Deployment checklist. Microsoft recommends a recent backup and a maintenance window because migration is disruptive; communicate expected downtime.
2. Choose an eligible, compatible target. The migration guide identifies Pro 2 and Pro GPU. Check capacity: documented usable storage is 720 GB–2.5 TB for Pro 2 and 4.19 TB for Pro GPU, versus 12.5 TB for Pro FPGA. The targets support NFS 3.0, not NFS 4.1. FPGA-dependent models require changes; IoT Edge modules may also need modification. CPU-only custom models should work unchanged using CPU.
3. Check ordering restrictions. The supplied GPU overview limits availability to validated partner workloads and large-scale deployments of at least 100 nodes. Consult your Azure Stack Edge partner about device compatibility. Existing customers with qualified workloads can submit the Azure Stack Edge sign-up form through the Azure portal. The overview lists Azure Arc, Azure Local infrastructure and the Azure Local Integrated Systems catalog as alternatives, but does not establish feature equivalence or migration procedures for them.
4. Protect source data. Fully tier cloud shares to Azure and confirm their status in the Azure portal. Copy local-share data to another on-premises server or use an existing supported backup solution. The guide identifies robocopy for SMB and rsync for NFS.
5. Prepare the target. Order the device and create a new Azure resource; you cannot activate it against the FPGA resource. Configure networking with different static IP addresses where applicable, the same device name and a DNS domain, and certificates. Activate it with the new resource's activation key. Source and target preparation can run in parallel.
6. Restore and redeploy. Recreate cloud shares using their existing blob containers, restore users, refresh cloud data and recreate bandwidth schedules. Configure compute and local storage, recreate local shares and restore or copy their data. Direct copying is possible when both devices are online. Use the target device name for SMB and its new IP addresses for NFS, then redeploy prepared IoT Edge workloads.
7. Verify before cleanup. Confirm that all data migrated and workloads were deployed on the target. Only after migration is complete, erase local data on the source and follow Microsoft's device-return procedure.

  • Deployment and access: You need a new Azure resource and activation, recreated settings and shares, and redeployed workloads. SMB access changes from source IP addresses to the target device name; NFS uses the target's new IP addresses.
  • Continuity and data: Microsoft describes migration as disruptive and recommends a downtime window. Cloud-share data must be fully tiered and refreshed on the target; local-share data must be copied or recovered. Erase source local data only after completing migration.
  • Replacement availability: The supplied GPU overview restricts device availability to validated partner workloads and large-scale deployments of at least 100 nodes. Do not assume a replacement order is available for every FPGA deployment.

The sources provide no quantified migration costs or separate retirement-related portal/API shutdown date.

records.title: Azure Storage classic metrics will be retired on 31 August 2023
records.summary: Azure Storage Analytics metrics, also called classic metrics, retired on January 9, 2024 according to the product migration guidance. The announcement lists August 31, 2023; the product-guidance date is used here, but the supplied content does not explicitly document an extension. Replace classic metric views and alert rules with Azure Monitor metrics. This retirement does not establish a shutdown of Azure Storage workloads or deletion of historical data.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired Azure Storage classic metrics. Use Azure Monitor metrics for replacement monitoring, including metric views and alert rules.

Classic metrics were collected, aggregated and stored in tables in your storage account. Azure Monitor manages the replacement metrics and supports multiple destinations; a storage account is optional. Collection is enabled by default, but you must create charts or dashboards to view the metrics and replace classic-metric alert rules.

The supplied content does not specify regional exceptions or support and security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Compile an inventory of the classic metrics, metric views and classic-metric alert rules you use. The guidance does not provide an automated discovery procedure.
2. Use the migration guidance's mappings to select equivalent Azure Monitor metrics and dimensions. For example, Capacity maps to BlobCapacity with BlobType set to BlockBlob or PageBlob. Many transaction metrics map to Transactions filtered by ResponseType and, where applicable, Authentication.
3. Create replacement Azure Monitor charts or dashboards. You do not need to enable metric collection; it is enabled by default.
4. Create replacement Azure Monitor alert rules for any rules based on classic metrics.
5. As a team-owned validation step, compare your replacement views and rules with your inventory. Account for Azure Monitor omitting data when no activity triggers a metric, rather than reporting the classic zero value.

The supplied guidance does not document historical-data migration, export, backup, cutover or cleanup procedures.

records.title: (updated) Azure StorSimple 8000/1200 series will no longer be supported starting December 31, 2022
records.summary: Azure StorSimple 8000/1200 series, Data Manager and Snapshot Manager reached end of life on December 31, 2022. The end-of-life notice states that cloud management, access to live data and backups, and customer support would no longer be available. An older notice marked potentially outdated says data would remain accessible; this conflicts with the end-of-life notice. Migrate required data, validate access and complete applicable decommissioning steps: powering off an appliance does not stop billing. The migration guide documents a backup-based workflow but does not confirm its availability after end of support.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure StorSimple reached end of life on December 31, 2022, covering:

- 8000 series: physical appliances 8100 and 8600, and virtual appliances 8010 and 8020.
- 1200 series.
- StorSimple Data Manager and StorSimple Snapshot Manager.

The end-of-life notice states that cloud management, access to live data and backups, and phone, email and web customer support would no longer be available. Hardware replacement and repair ended for 8000 series devices; software updates ended for 8000 and 1200 series devices. The migration guide also identifies StorSimple Device Manager for both series as out of support.

An older notice marked potentially outdated says data remains accessible, conflicting with the end-of-life notice. The supplied material documents no regional exceptions or continued-availability guarantees.

The migration guide describes moving 8000 series data to Azure file shares, optionally using Azure File Sync for an on-premises cache. The 1200 series requires separate guidance. The documented workflow uses Data Manager, itself out of support; its current availability is not confirmed.

Azure StorSimple reached end of life on December 31, 2022, covering:

  • 8000 series: physical appliances 8100 and 8600, and virtual appliances 8010 and 8020.
  • 1200 series.
  • StorSimple Data Manager and StorSimple Snapshot Manager.

The end-of-life notice states that cloud management, access to live data and backups, and phone, email and web customer support would no longer be available. Hardware replacement and repair ended for 8000 series devices; software updates ended for 8000 and 1200 series devices. The migration guide also identifies StorSimple Device Manager for both series as out of support.

An older notice marked potentially outdated says data remains accessible, conflicting with the end-of-life notice. The supplied material documents no regional exceptions or continued-availability guarantees.

The migration guide describes moving 8000 series data to Azure file shares, optionally using Azure File Sync for an on-premises cache. The 1200 series requires separate guidance. The documented workflow uses Data Manager, itself out of support; its current availability is not confirmed.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your scope. Inventory appliances, volumes, shares, required backups and remaining registrations. Use the supplied migration guide for 8100/8600 and 8010/8020 appliances; use separate guidance for the 1200 series or Virtual Array as applicable. Separate migration instructions for Data Manager and Snapshot Manager are not supplied. Contact Microsoft Support to clarify current migration availability; the guide documents a workflow, not a guarantee that it remains usable after retirement.
2. Choose and size the destination. Use direct Azure file share access when local caching is unnecessary, or Azure File Sync when you need an on-premises cache. Map folders to target shares and storage accounts, accounting for capacity, performance and sync limits. Resolve unsupported formats and file-fidelity gaps before migration.
3. Prepare encryption keys and backups. Retrieve each appliance's service data encryption key. If regeneration is necessary, follow the documented authorization and multi-device rollover procedure: initiate it within four hours of authorization and update remaining devices. Rollover blocks management operations until complete, but the guide says host I/O continues. Select the most recent backup and required historical backups, up to 50. Source volumes must be online for selection. Jobs copy backups, not live volumes; selections cannot change after job creation, and older backups cannot be inserted later. The guide recommends suspending retention policies to protect selected backups during migration.
4. Meet deployment and network prerequisites. Target subscriptions must use the StorSimple subscription's Microsoft Entra tenant. Deploy Data Manager in the source storage account's subscription, resource group and region. Use LRS or ZRS, not GRS or geo-zone redundancy. Source and target public storage endpoints must remain accessible without firewall or virtual-network restrictions during migration. Private endpoints may coexist but cannot replace public access; apply network restrictions afterward.
5. Run and review migration jobs. Process backups oldest first. Run only one job per source volume and per target share, with no more than four concurrent jobs per Device Manager. Before starting another job, ensure previous jobs have shown file-copy progress for at least 30 minutes. Review copy logs and resolve required missing data; job completion alone does not establish a complete migration.
6. Configure destination access. Wait for the share's migration jobs to finish before configuring direct access or Azure File Sync. For File Sync, use a separate Windows Server with direct-attached storage—not NAS or the server fronting the physical StorSimple appliance. Keep storage and the Storage Sync Service in the same region. Enable cloud tiering and wait for the full namespace download before local RoboCopy.
7. Cut over and validate. Plan downtime, stop source writes and run final RoboCopy catch-up before redirecting users. Match source and destination folder structures exactly: mirror mode deletes destination items absent from the source. The guide recommends Windows Server 2022 and documents additional restrictions and a retry workaround for low-free-space mode. Review logs, resolve failures and verify user access and dependencies. For archival workloads, a final backup migration can replace catch-up copying, but downtime may last days or longer.
8. Decommission only after validation. The guide recommends observing the destination for at least a few days. Save needed copy logs before deleting Data Manager. Follow applicable decommissioning steps to unregister migrated appliances, remove empty Device Managers, delete the old storage account and retire or return hardware. Deprovisioning is irreversible; optional volume cleanup does not forensically erase disks. Turning off an appliance does not stop billing.

Azure StorSimple 8000/1200 series will no longer be supported starting 31st December 2022
StorSimple 8000 series migration to Azure File Sync | Microsoft Learn

actions.html:
1. Identify your scope. Inventory appliances, volumes, shares, required backups and remaining registrations. Use the supplied migration guide for 8100/8600 and 8010/8020 appliances; use separate guidance for the 1200 series or Virtual Array as applicable. Separate migration instructions for Data Manager and Snapshot Manager are not supplied. Contact Microsoft Support to clarify current migration availability; the guide documents a workflow, not a guarantee that it remains usable after retirement.
  2. Choose and size the destination. Use direct Azure file share access when local caching is unnecessary, or Azure File Sync when you need an on-premises cache. Map folders to target shares and storage accounts, accounting for capacity, performance and sync limits. Resolve unsupported formats and file-fidelity gaps before migration.
  3. Prepare encryption keys and backups. Retrieve each appliance's service data encryption key. If regeneration is necessary, follow the documented authorization and multi-device rollover procedure: initiate it within four hours of authorization and update remaining devices. Rollover blocks management operations until complete, but the guide says host I/O continues. Select the most recent backup and required historical backups, up to 50. Source volumes must be online for selection. Jobs copy backups, not live volumes; selections cannot change after job creation, and older backups cannot be inserted later. The guide recommends suspending retention policies to protect selected backups during migration.
  4. Meet deployment and network prerequisites. Target subscriptions must use the StorSimple subscription's Microsoft Entra tenant. Deploy Data Manager in the source storage account's subscription, resource group and region. Use LRS or ZRS, not GRS or geo-zone redundancy. Source and target public storage endpoints must remain accessible without firewall or virtual-network restrictions during migration. Private endpoints may coexist but cannot replace public access; apply network restrictions afterward.
  5. Run and review migration jobs. Process backups oldest first. Run only one job per source volume and per target share, with no more than four concurrent jobs per Device Manager. Before starting another job, ensure previous jobs have shown file-copy progress for at least 30 minutes. Review copy logs and resolve required missing data; job completion alone does not establish a complete migration.
  6. Configure destination access. Wait for the share's migration jobs to finish before configuring direct access or Azure File Sync. For File Sync, use a separate Windows Server with direct-attached storage—not NAS or the server fronting the physical StorSimple appliance. Keep storage and the Storage Sync Service in the same region. Enable cloud tiering and wait for the full namespace download before local RoboCopy.
  7. Cut over and validate. Plan downtime, stop source writes and run final RoboCopy catch-up before redirecting users. Match source and destination folder structures exactly: mirror mode deletes destination items absent from the source. The guide recommends Windows Server 2022 and documents additional restrictions and a retry workaround for low-free-space mode. Review logs, resolve failures and verify user access and dependencies. For archival workloads, a final backup migration can replace catch-up copying, but downtime may last days or longer.
  8. Decommission only after validation. The guide recommends observing the destination for at least a few days. Save needed copy logs before deleting Data Manager. Follow applicable decommissioning steps to unregister migrated appliances, remove empty Device Managers, delete the old storage account and retire or return hardware. Deprovisioning is irreversible; optional volume cleanup does not forensically erase disks. Turning off an appliance does not stop billing.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are in scope if you use StorSimple 8000 series models 8100, 8600, 8010 or 8020, the 1200 series, Data Manager or Snapshot Manager. The supplied material does not inspect your environment or provide regional exceptions.

Retirement consequences

From December 31, 2022, the end-of-life notice says cloud management, live-data and backup access, and customer support would no longer be available. Management changes include losing the ability to view or change volume, share, backup and backup-policy settings or install updates. Hardware replacement and repair ended for 8000 series devices; software updates ended for both device series.

The older, potentially outdated notice says data remains accessible, which conflicts with the end-of-life notice. Do not interpret end of support alone as proof of workload shutdown, but do not assume continued data access given the explicit end-of-life warning. The sources do not specify data-retention or deletion timing, separate API changes, or distinct operational consequences for Data Manager and Snapshot Manager.

Migration limits and data fidelity

The supplied 8000 series workflow supports NTFS volumes only. ReFS, Windows Server Dynamic Disks, BitLocker-encrypted volumes, deduplication-enabled volumes and corrupted backups are unsupported. Jobs migrate backups, so later live changes require catch-up copying or a final backup migration; cutover requires downtime.

Windows ACLs, common metadata and some timestamps migrate, but alternate data streams are stripped. Links, junctions, reparse points, corrupt files, files larger than 4 TiB and paths longer than 2048 characters are skipped. EFS-encrypted files fail to copy. File change time, last-access timestamps and auditing information are not preserved. System Volume Information and $Recycle.Bin contents are excluded. Review logs for unsupported names and other item-level failures.

Azure File Sync supports up to 30 Azure file shares per server or cluster. The guide reports testing at 100 million items per share but recommends staying below roughly 20–30 million. Storage-account performance is shared across its shares.

Costs and cleanup risks

The guide says Data Manager migration jobs are free, but target storage, snapshots and file-share transactions incur charges. Cross-region migration incurs egress charges; same-region migration does not. StorSimple storage, backup and appliance costs continue until relevant resources are deprovisioned; powering off alone does not stop billing.

Deprovisioning permanently removes access to resource configuration and data. Deleting Data Manager also deletes its jobs and makes copy logs difficult to retrieve. Preserve required data and evidence before cleanup.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance:
Azure StorSimple reached end of life on December 31, 2022, according to the supplied end-of-life notice. It identifies that date as the end of support and availability of cloud management, live data and backups.

Both supplied notices give the same date, but their stated consequences conflict: the older notice, marked potentially outdated, says data remains accessible; the end-of-life notice says access to live data and backups would no longer be available. Use the end-of-life notice for planning rather than treating this as support-only retirement. Neither notice establishes a data-deletion schedule.

The migration guide confirms end of support without supplying an effective date. Its reference to a 2019 announcement and its January 12, 2023 update date are not retirement deadlines. No separate migration deadline or documented extension is supplied.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
The migration guide documents checks, but does not confirm that its tools remain available after retirement. Contact Microsoft Support for current availability, end-of-support details, fatal migration-job failures or unresolved issues; the end-of-life notice says StorSimple customer support ended, so a continuing support route is not guaranteed.

1. Maintain a team-owned appliance and volume inventory, namespace-mapping worksheet and required-backup checklist. Reconcile each source with its target share and migration job. These are local planning records, not website-managed tracking.
2. Where available, review Data Manager Job definitions, job states and per-backup results. Check for paused jobs and inspect Copy errors, Unsupported files and CSV copy logs. Retry recoverable errors; retrying does not make unsupported items migratable. Complete means selected backups were processed—not that every required item or later live change transferred. Complete with warnings requires log review.
3. Reconcile target share snapshots with your backup checklist. Their Comments field records the original StorSimple backup date.
4. For Azure File Sync, confirm the server appears under Registered servers. Before local RoboCopy, verify that the server endpoint's download status has left Initial sync. Alternatively, inspect Event Viewer under Microsoft\FileSync\Agent\Telemetry for event 9102 with Download direction and FullGhostedSync with HResult = 0, or a subsequent RegularSync event. These checks establish namespace arrival, not that all file contents are cached locally.
5. Review final RoboCopy logs, resolve required missing files and verify user access and dependencies. Save migration and decommissioning evidence separately, and export needed copy logs before deleting Data Manager.
6. Review remaining device registrations during decommissioning. The end-of-life notice says continued notification emails after migration mean at least one device remains registered. This signals remaining registration work; it does not prove whether data migration is complete.

records.title: Azure support for TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 will end by 31 October 2024
records.summary: Microsoft announced that Azure support for TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 would end on October 31, 2024, with interactions requiring TLS 1.2 or later from that date. Older-protocol dependencies could cause service disruptions. The supplied announcement does not confirm current enforcement or service-specific rollout dates. Resources already using TLS 1.2 or later exclusively need no further action under the announcement.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft announced the end of Azure support for TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 on October 31, 2024, requiring TLS 1.2 or later for interactions with Azure services.

The announcement does not specify regional or individual service exceptions, pre-deadline maintenance commitments, or service-specific enforcement behavior. The linked legacy-TLS guidance provides migration recommendations; it does not independently announce a universal Microsoft shutdown.
what.html:
Microsoft announced the end of Azure support for TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 on October 31, 2024, requiring TLS 1.2 or later for interactions with Azure services.

The announcement does not specify regional or individual service exceptions, pre-deadline maintenance commitments, or service-specific enforcement behavior. The linked legacy-TLS guidance provides migration recommendations; it does not independently announce a universal Microsoft shutdown.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify resources, applications, clients and partner integrations that interact with Azure using TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1. The supporting guidance recommends endpoint scans, negotiated-traffic analysis, and reviews of source code and configuration for hardcoded protocol versions.
2. Transition affected interactions to TLS 1.2 or later. Upgrade operating systems or frameworks where necessary. Remove hardcoded protocol selection only after confirming that operating-system defaults support your required configuration; some applications need source changes, recompilation and deployment.
3. Following the supporting guidance, disable protocols older than TLS 1.2 in staging and run full-stack regression tests, including mutual TLS, service dependencies and partner integrations. Coordinate rollout with affected customers and partners. If you must retain FIPS Mode, follow the separate FIPS-preserving guidance.
4. Confirm that resources interacting with Azure exclusively use TLS 1.2 or later. If they already do, the announcement says no further action is needed.

The announcement's transition deadline was October 31, 2024. The supporting migration guidance primarily covers Microsoft operating systems and Windows cryptography libraries; it is not a service-specific Azure migration procedure.

progress.guidance:
Use exclusive TLS 1.2-or-later communication with Azure as your team-owned completion check. The supporting migration guidance documents these discovery and validation methods:

records.title: Retirement: Azure Synapse Runtime for Apache Spark 3.3
records.summary: Microsoft announced retirement and disablement of Azure Synapse Runtime for Apache Spark 3.3 for March 2025, without an exact day. Current lifecycle guidance lists end of support as March 31, 2025 but still describes disablement as forthcoming, so actual disablement timing remains unconfirmed; no extension is documented. Assess migration to a supported runtime such as Synapse Spark 3.5. The original recommendation to use Spark 3.4 is outdated: that version reached end of support on March 31, 2026.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft announced that Azure Synapse Runtime for Apache Spark 3.3 would retire and be disabled in March 2025. Lifecycle guidance confirms end of support on March 31, 2025 but describes disablement as forthcoming, without confirming when workloads stop running.

The original notice recommends Spark 3.4, but that version separately reached end of support on March 31, 2026. It is not a supported migration destination under the supplied guidance. Synapse Spark 3.5 is listed as generally available with no announced end-of-support date.

The sources do not announce retirement of Azure Synapse Analytics or Spark 3.5. They do not specify regional exceptions or establish continued Spark 3.3 patch availability after end of support.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify Synapse pools using Spark 3.3. The lifecycle page documents enumeration with Get-AzSynapseWorkspace and Get-AzSynapseSparkPool to report pool runtime versions.
2. Assess migration to a supported runtime such as Synapse Spark 3.5. Do not rely on the original Spark 3.4 recommendation: Spark 3.4 is now unsupported. Evaluating Fabric is optional for this Spark 3.3 retirement; the supplied sources provide no use-case selection criteria.
3. Review Spark migration guidance and check SQL, UDFs, deprecated APIs, libraries and dependencies. Create a new target-runtime pool with compatible libraries, update your code and test in an Azure Synapse development environment, not only locally.
4. After validation, deploy to the new pool and monitor application behavior and performance with Azure Synapse monitoring tools.

The UI does not support an in-place upgrade to 3.5. The documented PowerShell alternative using ForceApplySetting decommissions existing old-version clusters. The lifecycle page explicitly warns against the PowerShell upgrade method when workspace custom libraries are installed.

For attached-library upgrade errors, the page lists pool recreation or downgrading, removing attached packages and upgrading again, without explaining how to choose between them. The supplied material does not document backup, detailed cutover or cleanup procedures.

records.title: Azure Synapse Runtime for Apache Spark 3.2 End of Support
records.summary: Microsoft scheduled Azure Synapse Runtime for Apache Spark 3.2 for retirement and disablement on July 8, 2024. what.question: What is changing?

what.announcement:

The original notice recommends upgrading to 3.3 or 3.4. Its forecast of 3.4 general availability is not confirmation, although the supplied 3.3 guidance subsequently identifies 3.4 as generally available.

Those alternatives have their own lifecycle limits: 3.3 was scheduled for disablement on March 31, 2025, and 3.4 has been unsupported since March 31, 2026. For 3.4, Microsoft no longer provides bug fixes, security updates or vulnerability remediations; workloads may continue temporarily, but execution is not guaranteed.

records.title: Retirement: Azure unmanaged disks will be retired on 31 March 2026 (formerly 30 September 2025)

what.announcement:
Microsoft retired Azure unmanaged disks on March 31, 2026 and directs you to Azure Managed Disks. The migration guidance covers Windows and Linux VMs, converting their unmanaged OS disks and attached data disks.

Page blobs are unaffected. VMs already using managed disks are outside this disk-conversion scope; that does not establish whether they have separate deployment-model requirements.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
