records.title: Azure Virtual Desktop (classic) will be retired on 30 September 2026 - Please transition to Azure Virtual Desktop
records.summary: Azure Virtual Desktop (classic) retires on September 30, 2026. Microsoft states that connections to classic resources will be blocked afterward. Migrate to Azure Resource Manager-based Azure Virtual Desktop host pools before that date. Automatic migration supports US-geography service objects only and has application-group and user-assignment limits; manual migration is recommended for small, simple deployments. New classic tenant creation ended on September 30, 2023, with request-based exceptions that do not extend retirement.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Virtual Desktop (classic) retires on September 30, 2026, after which Microsoft will block connections to classic resources. Azure Resource Manager-based Azure Virtual Desktop is the replacement, not a service being retired.

Migration replaces classic service objects with Azure-integrated objects managed through the Azure portal. Existing classic resources remain manageable, migratable and supported through the retirement date; the supplied material does not document security-update commitments.

With automatic migration, virtual machines remain available through both existing and new host pools during migration, allowing users to connect to the same session. Completing migration deletes the classic service objects and leaves users with the new application-group feeds.

With automatic migration, virtual machines remain available through both existing and new host pools during migration, allowing users to connect to the same session. Completing migration deletes the classic service objects and leaves users with the new application-group feeds.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Migrate your remaining classic resources before September 30, 2026.

1. Identify your classic tenants, host pools, application groups and session hosts. For automatic migration, you can optionally export a destination-resource mapping with Get-RdsHostPoolMigrationMapping; the supplied material does not establish a tenant-wide automated discovery method.
2. Select a migration approach. Manual migration is recommended for small test deployments, small production deployments planning to grow, and simple configurations; the guide advises against it for advanced configurations or deployments with many users. Automatic migration creates service objects only in the US geography and supports no more than 500 application groups. Above that limit, the guide requires rebuilding the environment to reduce the application-group count within your Microsoft Entra tenant.
3. Prepare an Azure subscription with Contributor and User Access Administrator roles. Automatic migration also requires at least RDS Contributor permissions on the classic tenant or relevant host pools. Use PowerShell or PowerShell ISE, not PowerShell Core, for the classic RDPowershell module. Install and import the documented migration and dependency modules. The guide requests the latest RDPowershell module in its prerequisites but explicitly installs version 1.0.3414.0 in setup; this discrepancy is unresolved.
4. For automatic migration, sign in to classic and Azure Resource Manager, select the target subscription, register Microsoft.DesktopVirtualization, and use Start-RdsHostPoolMigration for the intended tenant or host pool. Choose whether to copy user assignments. Copying is subject to the documented 2,000-user-assignment limit per subscription, reduced by existing assignments. If you skip copying, assign access separately; users initially see only the classic feed.
5. For manual migration, authenticate with the replacement service's new application ID, create the new host pools and high-level objects, register any reused virtual machines, recreate RemoteApp application groups, and assign users or groups. Update Conditional Access policies for the new objects. Move session hosts and users in small groups to reduce downtime.
6. For automatic migration, verify new service objects, application-group access and initial user connections. Manually configure RBAC permissions and diagnostic settings. Moving application groups to another resource group after assigning access removes their RBAC roles, so you must reassign them.
7. After validating automatic migration, run Complete-RdsHostPoolMigration for the intended scope, then explicitly delete the classic tenant after finalizing migration. Set-RdsHostPoolHidden supports testing only; it does not complete migration. If you need to revert instead, Revert-RdsHostPoolMigration deletes newly created Azure service objects but leaves the created workspace and resource group for manual cleanup.

The supplied manual guide does not provide explicit backup, validation, rollback or classic-resource cleanup steps.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if you still depend on Azure Virtual Desktop (classic). Microsoft states that connections to classic resources will be blocked after September 30, 2026. The supplied material does not establish whether your environment contains classic resources or document automatic deletion of virtual machines or user data.

Azure Resource Manager-based host pools are the migration destination and are not identified as retiring. The automatic tool's US-geography restriction limits that migration method; it is not a regional exception to retirement.

Automatic migration has these practical limits and configuration changes:

- More than 500 application groups requires the documented environment rebuild to reduce the count before using the tool. A classic tenant-creation exception does not waive this limit.
- Copying user assignments is constrained by the documented 2,000-assignment limit per subscription and existing assignments. Copying exposes both feeds during migration; skipping it requires separate access assignments.
- Virtual machines remain available through both host-pool versions during migration. Completing migration deletes classic service objects and removes the classic feed.
- New-object RBAC permissions and diagnostic settings require manual configuration. Moving application groups between resource groups after assigning access removes their RBAC roles.

Manual migration requires recreating application groups and assignments, registering reused virtual machines, and updating Conditional Access policies. The supplied material gives no migration cost estimates or retirement-related data-retention details.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use the automatic migration guide's checks as team-owned migration evidence. These checks require the documented permissions and supported PowerShell environment; they are not a tenant-wide retirement dashboard.

1. Optionally export a destination-resource mapping with Get-RdsHostPoolMigrationMapping and record the tenants and host pools in your migration scope.
2. After Start-RdsHostPoolMigration, check the new Azure service objects, workspace resource group, host-pool/application-group resource group and intended user access. Service-object creation can take up to 15 minutes; assignment processing adds time.
3. Verify initial user connections, RBAC permissions and diagnostic settings before finalizing. Hiding classic resources with Set-RdsHostPoolHidden can support testing but is not completion.
4. After Complete-RdsHostPoolMigration, confirm that only the new application-group feeds remain, then explicitly delete the classic tenant after finalizing migration. Retain the results as team-owned completion evidence.

For manual migration, locally record the new host pools, reused-host registrations, recreated application groups, assignments, Conditional Access updates and staged movement of hosts and users. These records are planning evidence, not documented automated completion checks.

records.title: Preparing for TLS 1.2 in Microsoft Azure
records.summary: The supplied Azure notice recommends making TLS 1.2 the default but does not announce an Azure-wide TLS 1.0/1.1 retirement or migration deadline. Services that still accept TLS 1.0/1.1 will continue supporting them until further notice; services whose customers use only TLS 1.2 have switched to TLS 1.2-only traffic. Evaluate Azure-hosted workloads and on-premises applications that connect to Azure, update dependencies and validate compatibility before disabling older protocols.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft recommends configuring Azure-connected workloads to use TLS 1.2 by default. The notice states that all Azure services fully support TLS 1.2 and that Azure has removed its dependency on TLS 1.0/1.1.

- Services whose customers use only TLS 1.2 have switched to accepting only TLS 1.2 traffic.
- Services still accepting TLS 1.0/1.1 will continue supporting them until further notice.
- Azure Guest OS Family 6 disables TLS 1.0/1.1.

This notice does not announce a scheduled Azure-wide shutdown of older TLS versions.
what.html:
Microsoft recommends configuring Azure-connected workloads to use TLS 1.2 by default. The notice states that all Azure services fully support TLS 1.2 and that Azure has removed its dependency on TLS 1.0/1.1.

  • Services whose customers use only TLS 1.2 have switched to accepting only TLS 1.2 traffic.
  • Services still accepting TLS 1.0/1.1 will continue supporting them until further notice.
  • Azure Guest OS Family 6 disables TLS 1.0/1.1.

This notice does not announce a scheduled Azure-wide shutdown of older TLS versions.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
These are migration recommendations, not requirements tied to an announced Azure-wide deadline.

1. Inventory your Azure-hosted workloads and on-premises applications that connect to Azure. Review operating systems, frameworks, libraries, client dependencies and hardcoded protocol settings.
2. Update incompatible components to support TLS 1.2 or later. The referenced guidance recommends removing hardcoded protocol selection and preferring operating-system defaults; older .NET and WinHTTP applications may need changes.
3. Review applicable FIPS requirements before changing protocol settings. The guidance documents additional restrictions for Windows Server 2016.
4. Test in staging with protocols older than TLS 1.2 disabled. Include service dependencies, mutual TLS certificate selection, third-party integrations and non-Windows clients. Resolve failures and repeat regression testing.
5. Coordinate rollout with customers and partners, and configure workloads to use TLS 1.2 by default.

Microsoft discourages re-enabling legacy protocols. The Guest OS troubleshooting workaround is not a retirement migration.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
Review Azure-hosted workloads and on-premises applications connecting to Azure, particularly those using TLS 1.0/1.1. The supplied content does not identify your affected resources or provide a service-by-service inventory.

Services that still accept older TLS versions continue doing so until further notice; the Azure notice announces no workload shutdown. Services already accepting only TLS 1.2 reject older-protocol traffic. Applications using the Windows TLS stack on Guest OS Family 6 cannot communicate using TLS 1.0/1.1 under its documented default configuration.

Disabling older protocols can prevent incompatible clients from connecting. An operating system's TLS 1.2 support does not establish application compatibility: hardcoded settings, older frameworks, custom mutual TLS handling and third-party integrations may still require changes.

The separate Cloud Services (classic) shutdown notice in a reference article does not establish an Azure-wide TLS retirement or its consequences.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Review service-specific TLS announcements and further Azure updates, as the Azure notice recommends.

For team-owned tracking, the referenced migration guidance documents these methods:

- Maintain an operating-system, application and dependency inventory; record remediation work.
- Use endpoint scans and network-edge traffic analysis to identify older TLS usage. Traffic analysis shows successfully negotiated protocol versions, not encrypted payloads.
- Use IIS custom logging to correlate clients, TLS versions and cipher suites where applicable.
- Use SSL Labs Handshake Simulation to assess simulated client compatibility; it does not replace testing actual applications and clients.
- Record passing regression and partner-interoperability tests with protocols older than TLS 1.2 disabled as local completion evidence.

The supplied content defines no universal Azure migration dashboard or completion certification. Office 365-specific SecureScore guidance does not establish coverage for Azure services.

records.title: Azure Active Directory B2C is deprecating login.microsoftonline.com
records.summary: Azure AD B2C retired access through login.microsoftonline.com with a stated revised deadline of August 31, 2022, replacing the original December 4, 2020 deadline. Move affected policy-based authentication to b2clogin.com or a custom domain. Policy-free Microsoft Entra endpoints must remain on login.microsoftonline.com; Azure AD tenants are unaffected. The supplied reference guidance provides migration details but no independent retirement date or precise post-retirement failure behavior.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure AD B2C is retiring login.microsoftonline.com for policy-based user authentication. Move affected applications and APIs to b2clogin.com or a custom domain. The retirement update states that functionality remains the same on b2clogin.com.

The transition covers policy-based authorization, logout and token endpoints, related identity-provider redirects, and token-issuer references. Azure AD tenants are unaffected.

Policy-free Microsoft Entra endpoints, including token requests for Microsoft Graph access to the B2C tenant, must remain on login.microsoftonline.com; they cannot move to the replacement domains. The supplied content does not document maintenance, security-update or continued-support commitments.
what.html:
Azure AD B2C is retiring login.microsoftonline.com for policy-based user authentication. Move affected applications and APIs to b2clogin.com or a custom domain. The retirement update states that functionality remains the same on b2clogin.com.

The transition covers policy-based authorization, logout and token endpoints, related identity-provider redirects, and token-issuer references. Azure AD tenants are unaffected.

Policy-free Microsoft Entra endpoints, including token requests for Microsoft Graph access to the B2C tenant, must remain on login.microsoftonline.com; they cannot move to the replacement domains. The supplied content does not document maintenance, security-update or continued-support commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify applications and APIs using login.microsoftonline.com for B2C user flows or custom policies. Review endpoint and issuer references, identity-provider trusted redirects, authentication-library configuration and UI-customization CORS settings. Exclude policy-free Microsoft Entra endpoints.
2. Select your tenant's b2clogin.com hostname or a custom domain. Update identity-provider trusted redirect URLs. The documented b2clogin.com formats accept a tenant ID or tenant domain name; remove /te if present. The authresp endpoint may not contain a policy name.
3. For APIs validating token issuers, configure acceptance of both old and new issuers before switching applications. With existing user flows or custom policies, use the Azure portal's Run user flow view or relying party policy to open each domain's OpenID Connect discovery endpoint and record its issuer. The OWIN/Katana example uses ValidIssuers in TokenValidationParameters and retains audience validation. Other OWIN libraries have no equivalent examples in the supplied content.
4. Update applicable authorization, logout and token endpoints, user-flow references and token-issuer settings. Update Allowed Origins if you use UI customization. For OWIN applications and B2C-protected Azure API Management APIs, use the referenced migration guidance; the OWIN sample requires additional tenant-specific configuration.
5. Apply the documented library-specific settings: MSAL.NET v2 or earlier requires ValidateAuthority set to false; v3 or later does not. MSAL.js v1.2.2 or earlier requires validateAuthority set to false. For MSAL.js v1.3.0 or later, specify a valid token issuer through knownAuthorities when validateAuthority is true, its default.
6. Move applications in stages, then remove API acceptance of login.microsoftonline.com-issued tokens. As a team-owned validation step, check affected sign-in, sign-out and token flows before removing old-issuer acceptance. The supplied pages do not provide a formal validation procedure.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are in scope if your applications or APIs use login.microsoftonline.com for Azure AD B2C policy-based authentication. Configuration changes can extend beyond application endpoints to API issuer validation, identity-provider redirects, authentication-library settings and customized-UI CORS origins.

APIs must recognize the new issuer before applications switch. Accepting both issuers supports staged migration; removing the old issuer means those APIs no longer accept tokens issued by it.

Unaffected: Azure AD tenants and policy-free Microsoft Entra endpoints used for shared enterprise-tenant capabilities, including Microsoft Graph token acquisition for a B2C tenant. Keep those endpoints on login.microsoftonline.com.

B2C tenants created after the original announcement cannot use the old endpoint. It does not establish your tenant's migration status.

records.title: Batch Service in select regions will be retired on 31 March 2026
records.summary: Microsoft announced Azure Batch retirement on March 31, 2026 in India West, China North 1, China East 1, USDoD East and USDoD Central, with affected workloads to migrate before that date. Other regions are outside scope. Accounts cannot move directly between regions: deploy a separate destination account, recreate features that do not export, and verify quotas and operation before optionally deleting the source.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Azure Batch on March 31, 2026 because of regional constraints in:

- India West
- China North 1
- China East 1
- USDoD East
- USDoD Central

Azure Batch is not retiring in other regions. The notice does not document changes to availability, maintenance or support before retirement.

You cannot move a Batch account directly between regions. Migration creates a separate destination account from an exported Azure Resource Manager template; some features must be recreated.
what.html:
Microsoft is retiring Azure Batch on March 31, 2026 because of regional constraints in:

  • India West
  • China North 1
  • China East 1
  • USDoD East
  • USDoD Central

Azure Batch is not retiring in other regions. The notice does not document changes to availability, maintenance or support before retirement.

You cannot move a Batch account directly between regions. Migration creates a separate destination account from an exported Azure Resource Manager template; some features must be recreated.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Azure Batch workloads in the five affected regions. The retirement notice does not provide a resource-discovery method.
2. Select another region that supports the services and features you use. Moving associated regional resources is recommended, not required; the migration procedure assumes they are already aligned with the destination.
3. In the source Batch account in the Azure portal, use Automation > Export template, then download and extract the template.
4. Load it through a custom template deployment. Update the account name, associated storage account resource ID and location, then deploy the destination account.
5. Recreate required jobs and tasks, job schedules, certificates and application packages; these do not export. Confirm sufficient destination quota before migrating workloads. Microsoft's stated migration target was before March 31, 2026.
6. Verify that the destination account works and all required features are restored. Only then optionally delete the source account.

what.html:
Microsoft is retiring the legacy built-in analytics dashboard and associated reports in Azure API Management classic tiers in March 2027. The announcement specifies March 15, 2027 for the dashboards.

The replacement Azure Monitor-based dashboard uses Log Analytics workbooks and gateway logs stored in a Log Analytics workspace. Microsoft describes closely similar data, not guaranteed feature parity. The replacement dashboards do not consume API Management instance capacity.

The monitoring article applies broadly, but its retirement statement specifically concerns classic tiers. It does not explicitly establish whether or when REST API Reports operations retire. API analytics is currently unavailable in API Management workspaces, which are distinct from the Log Analytics workspace required by the replacement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify classic-tier API Management instances where you use Monitoring > Analytics (classic). Review dependencies on REST API Reports operations separately because their retirement scope is unclear.
2. Begin using Monitoring > Analytics, the Azure Monitor-based dashboard, before March 15, 2027. You need a Log Analytics workspace receiving API Management gateway logs.
3. If logging is not configured, open Monitoring > Diagnostic settings > + Add diagnostic setting. Name the setting, select Logs related to ApiManagement Gateway, choose Send to Log Analytics, select a workspace, set the destination table to Resource specific, and save. The workspace can be in the same or a different subscription. For LLM analytics, also select Logs related to generative AI gateway.
4. Allow up to two hours for a new workspace to receive data, or approximately 15 minutes for an existing workspace. In Monitoring > Analytics, check the time ranges and report categories you need. Inspect gateway logs through Monitoring > Logs.

Creating a diagnostic setting might fail if the service’s MinApiVersion property is higher than 2022-09-01-preview. If data is missing, review all-API and per-API logging settings; sampling and disabled logging can limit coverage. Request and response details are not collected by default.

The supplied guidance provides no retirement-specific historical-data migration, backup, cutover or cleanup procedure.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if you rely on the legacy built-in analytics dashboard or associated reports in API Management classic tiers. Without transitioning, you will lose access to the retiring analytics experiences. The sources do not describe API traffic stopping or API Management workloads shutting down, and they do not clearly establish the future of REST API Reports operations.

The replacement requires gateway logs in a Log Analytics workspace. Data arrival delays, sampling and logging settings can limit coverage. Closely similar data does not establish full report parity or automatic transfer of historical analytics.

Gateway log entries have a 32 KB limit. Collected request and response payloads can each be up to 8,192 bytes; API Management removes body and trace content if the full entry exceeds 32 KB. Generative AI messages larger than 32 KB are split into chunks, with a 2 MB limit each for request and response messages.

The sources do not specify retirement-related historical-data retention, deletion or migration costs. They do not assess your resources.

records.title: Bing Search APIs will transition from Azure Cognitive Services to Azure Marketplace on 31 October 2023
records.summary: Bing Search APIs transitioned from Azure Cognitive Services to Azure Marketplace on October 31, 2023. The notice states that existing Azure Cognitive Services instances are no longer supported after that date and directs you to Azure Marketplace for new instances. This is an end-of-support milestone, not a documented workload shutdown. The supplied reference pages do not establish another retirement date or an existing-instance migration procedure.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Bing Search APIs transitioned from Azure Cognitive Services to Azure Marketplace on October 31, 2023. The notice covers existing Azure Cognitive Services instances of:

- Bing Auto Suggest
- Bing Custom Search
- Bing Entity Search
- Bing Spell Check
- Bing Web Search

Those instances are no longer supported after that date. The notice says new instances can continue to be created through Azure Marketplace; it does not document maintenance or security-update commitments. The supplied setup page explains resource creation, but does not independently establish a retirement or continued availability today.

records.title: Changes to My Groups admin controls
records.summary: Starting June 2024, Microsoft will replace the Microsoft Entra admin center control for enabling or disabling My Groups with a setting controlling end-user access to security groups in My Groups. The change is automatic and preserves the existing Yes/No configuration as described. Deployment may take up to two weeks to reach your organization. My Groups is not shutting down, and no exact retirement day or required action deadline is documented.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft will replace the Microsoft Entra admin center setting used to enable or disable My Groups with a setting that controls whether end users can view and manage security groups in My Groups.

This is a control replacement, not a shutdown of My Groups. Admins retain separate group settings controlling whether end users can create Microsoft 365 and security groups.
what.html:

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
You do not need to take action. Microsoft will apply the change automatically for admins and users.

To understand the resulting access, check your existing Restrict user ability to access groups features in the Access Panel setting:

- Yes: The replacement setting will restrict users from seeing and editing security groups in My Groups.
- No: The replacement setting will expose security groups in My Groups.

The notice does not require migration or document migration validation steps.

records.title: Change tracking and inventory with Log Analytics agent in Azure Automation will be retired on 31 August 2024
records.summary: Azure Automation Change Tracking and Inventory with the Log Analytics agent had a retirement date of August 31, 2024. The supplied Microsoft Q&A announcement identifies the same date as end of support and LA agent deprecation. Microsoft directed customers to migrate to the Azure Monitor Agent-based version to avoid service disruption. The sources do not establish an exact workload shutdown date. Migration requires manual handling of file-content tracking settings and, when changing workspaces, alerts. Same-workspace script migration removes extension-installed legacy agents, which can affect other solutions.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Automation Change Tracking and Inventory with the LA agent reached its stated retirement and support-end date on August 31, 2024. Microsoft named Change Tracking and Inventory with Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) as the replacement.

The affected migration scope includes Windows VMs, Linux VMs and Azure Arc-enabled servers using LA-based Change Tracking and Inventory. This is not a retirement of Azure Automation as a whole or of the AMA-based replacement.

The AMA overview requires Change Tracking extension version 2.20.0.0 or later and describes Azure Policy onboarding and data collection rule management. The supplied sources do not specify regional retirement exceptions, pre-retirement maintenance or security-update commitments, or exact post-retirement availability.
what.html:
Azure Automation Change Tracking and Inventory with the LA agent reached its stated retirement and support-end date on August 31, 2024. Microsoft named Change Tracking and Inventory with Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) as the replacement.

The affected migration scope includes Windows VMs, Linux VMs and Azure Arc-enabled servers using LA-based Change Tracking and Inventory. This is not a retirement of Azure Automation as a whole or of the AMA-based replacement.

The AMA overview requires Change Tracking extension version 2.20.0.0 or later and describes Azure Policy onboarding and data collection rule management. The supplied sources do not specify regional retirement exceptions, pre-retirement maintenance or security-update commitments, or exact post-retirement availability.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Microsoft directed you to migrate affected configurations to AMA by August 31, 2024 to avoid service disruption.

1. Identify LA-based Change Tracking and Inventory machines and their workspaces. The Automation account onboarding workflow lists Azure and Azure Arc machines ready for migration. A workspace's JSON View provides its resource ID.
2. Choose a migration route: Azure portal workflows for selected machines or an Automation account's machines, or the documented PowerShell script for workspace-wide migration, including same-workspace migration. A Q&A user reported a same-subscription restriction in portal onboarding; the supplied thread does not resolve it.
3. For the script, install PowerShell and the latest Az module, including Az.Accounts and Az.OperationalInsights. Obtain write access to workspace and machine resources and Azure credentials for Connect-AzAccount and Select-AzContext. PowerShell 7 or later is recommended; Azure Cloud Shell is not supported. Ensure the AMA-based configuration meets the documented Change Tracking extension requirement of version 2.20.0.0 or later.
4. Before same-workspace script migration, migrate other solutions that depend on the legacy agent. The script removes extension-installed MMA/OMS agents and may stop dependent solutions; it does not remove MSI-installed MMA agents. Provide the destination workspace and initiate migration.
5. Manually migrate file-content tracking settings. If you change workspaces, manually configure workspace-based alerts. Review the referenced support matrix for supported operating systems, regions, collection limits and frequencies; those details are not supplied here. Enable individual registry keys you need to track; preconfigured keys are not enabled by default.
6. Compare incoming LA and AMA data after AMA onboarding using matching change-type and time-range filters. After validation, you may optionally disable LA-based Change Tracking for selected VMs or the entire workspace.

The supplied content does not document a retirement-specific export or backup procedure.

impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are in scope if you use LA-agent-based Change Tracking and Inventory on Windows VMs, Linux VMs or Azure Arc-enabled servers. The supplied sources do not establish which of your resources are affected. The AMA-based replacement and Azure Automation as a whole are not identified as retiring.

Migration has these documented constraints:

- The script migrates settings for Windows services, Windows files, Windows registry, Linux files and Linux daemons, but file-content tracking settings require manual migration.

For AMA data visibility, system-level application data is always logged. User-level applications appear only while a user is signed in and are marked as Removed when the user signs out; account for this limit when comparing inventory.

records.summary: Azure Monitor classic monitoring and alerting is replaced by the newer Azure Monitor platform. Current supplied retirement guidance identifies February 29, 2024 for Azure Government and Azure China 21Vianet; the structured deadline applies only to those clouds. For public cloud, guidance describes retirement as already completed, with limited use until May 31, 2021. Historical notices give June 30, 2019, explicitly postponed to August 31, 2019; automatic migration starting in July 2019 was a separate phase. These dates must not be treated as one universal shutdown deadline. Classic metric alert migration changes management interfaces and notification payloads. what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Monitor replaces classic monitoring and alerting with its newer platform. The supplied guidance gives February 29, 2024 for Azure Government and Azure China 21Vianet and describes public-cloud retirement separately as already completed.

The principal migration scope is classic metric alert rules exposed through Alerts (classic) and the microsoft.insights/alertrules resource type. A historical notice also includes classic Application Insights platform/custom metrics and classic Failure Anomalies; the supplied material does not separately map every historical feature to the later cloud-specific dates.

Microsoft's guidance says most classic metric rules migrate automatically without downtime or loss of monitoring coverage. Some rules require manual action. Migration changes rule-management interfaces and notification payloads and creates action groups. Existing classic rules continue running until their replacements take effect; classic rules become unavailable in a subscription after migration completes.

Exceptions:

- Classic Activity Log alert rules are not deprecated or migrated under this change and remain usable through Azure Monitor – Alerts.
- Service Health alerts remain usable in Service Health.

The supplied material does not document maintenance or security-update commitments. Reference pages about dynamic thresholds, multi-resource alerts and legacy log search APIs do not independently establish additional retirements under this notice.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify classic metric alert rules in Alerts (classic) or as microsoft.insights/alertrules resources. Inventory deployment scripts and webhook, logic app and runbook consumers. Keep Activity Log and Service Health alerts separate.
2. Review migration eligibility and the referenced preparation and unsupported-rule guidance. Some rules require manual migration or recreation; the supplied excerpts do not identify every unsupported configuration or replacement procedure.
3. Update deployment automation to the new metric-alert REST API, CLI, PowerShell or Azure Resource Manager interfaces. Update notification handlers for the new payload. The deployment guidance describes an Azure Monitor - Metrics Alert Handler logic app template and a runbook parser supporting classic and new payloads. The payload-preparation reference reports a disagreement between its field mapping and parser about the time-aggregation field location; treat that mapping as unresolved.
4. If the documented migration tool is available, open Monitor > Alerts, select Manage alert rules or View classic alerts, then Migrate to new rules. You need the Monitoring Contributor role at subscription level. Select a subscription marked Ready to migrate, preview its rules, optionally download the CSV, supply notification email addresses and review the confirmation before starting.
5. Account for the cutover constraint: starting migration prevents creation or editing of classic rules in that subscription. Existing rules continue running until their replacements take effect. Automatic migration does not remove your responsibility to update integrations or handle unsupported rules.
6. Check portal status and notification emails. As team-owned validation, confirm notification delivery and downstream processing. The guide lists PagerDuty, OpsGenie and Signl4 as compatible; confirm other integrations with their providers.

The references describe phased tool availability but do not confirm its current availability. They do not provide a complete backup, rollback or cleanup procedure.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are in scope if you use Azure Monitor classic metric alert rules or automation that manages or consumes them. The supplied material does not establish whether your subscriptions contain these configurations.

Separate the effects:

- Management: classic APIs and portal interfaces retire. Starting subscription migration blocks classic-rule creation and editing; completing migration makes classic rules unavailable in that subscription.
- Monitoring: retirement guidance says existing rules continue notifying during migration and most migrate without downtime. Rules that cannot migrate automatically require manual action to continue running. This does not establish a shutdown of monitored application workloads.
- Integrations: deployment interfaces and notification schemas change. Unchanged scripts or payload parsers can be incompatible with migrated alerts.
- Exceptions: Activity Log and Service Health alerts remain usable through their newer interfaces.

Migrated alert rules and corresponding migrated email, webhook or LogicApp action groups remain free with their existing functionality, including threshold, aggregation-type and aggregation-granularity edits. Adding newer features, notifications or action types can introduce charges. New non-migrated rules, ingestion, retention and custom metrics beyond included free units can also incur charges. The material provides no tenant-specific cost estimate or retirement-related data-deletion schedule.

The guidance describes closure of classic APIs, portal interfaces and related services, including new classic rule creation, while also stating that existing rules continue executing and notifying during migration. It does not establish one date when every existing alert stops firing.

records.title: Azure classic storage accounts will be retired on 31 August 2024
records.summary: Azure classic storage accounts retired on August 31, 2024. Microsoft required migration to Azure Resource Manager before that date to avoid service disruptions. New classic storage account creation stopped on August 1, 2022; existing accounts were supported through retirement. The supplied notice does not specify exact post-retirement behavior or whether the documented migration process remains available.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure classic storage accounts retired on August 31, 2024 because they depended on Azure Cloud Services (classic), which the notice identifies as having the same retirement date.

Microsoft directed customers to migrate to Azure Resource Manager. The notice describes Resource Manager as providing the same capabilities, plus resource lifecycle management, resource grouping and group-level access control.

The supplied content does not document regional exceptions or post-retirement maintenance and security-update commitments. It does not establish a retirement of general-purpose v1 or v2 storage accounts as a whole.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify classic storage accounts and their dependencies. The retirement notice does not provide an inventory procedure. Determine whether each account contains disks or VM data and whether associated classic VMs or virtual networks need migration first.
2. Review prerequisites and pricing. The migration overview requires associated VMs and virtual networks to migrate before their storage accounts. Accounts without associated disks or VM data can migrate independently. Review Azure Resource Manager pricing; the supplied content provides no cost comparison.
3. Address dependent configurations where applicable. Storage migration affects Site Recovery replication, which must be disabled and enabled again afterward. For VMs with Backup or snapshot extensions, the overview directs you to its referenced migration FAQ for preserving earlier backups; those details are not supplied.
4. Use the documented storage migration flow. In the Azure portal, open the classic storage account, select Settings > Migrate to ARM, run Validate, then Prepare if validation passes. Type yes and select Commit to finish. The supplied page does not establish whether this process remains available after retirement.
5. Validate the result. As team-owned checks, confirm storage access and dependent application operation, and restore affected replication and configuration. Classic disk and image objects disappear from the portal after storage migration, but their backing VHDs remain.

The required migration deadline was before August 31, 2024. For questions, use Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and need technical help, create a support request.

records.title: Classic experience to protect VMware machines using Azure Site Recovery will be retired on 30 March 2026
records.summary: Microsoft retired Azure Site Recovery’s classic experience for protecting VMware VMs and physical servers on March 30, 2026. Classic is unsupported, new classic protection is unavailable, and remaining replications may experience disruption; the supplied guidance does not establish a separate workload shutdown date. Migrate eligible existing replications to the modernized experience only when the upgrade action is available; otherwise, contact Microsoft Support for recovery guidance. Recovery plans must be recreated. Pricing remains the same, but classic-vault billing continues until recovery-point retention expires and cleanup completes.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired Azure Site Recovery’s classic experience for protecting VMware VMs and physical servers on March 30, 2026. Classic is no longer supported, and you cannot enable new classic protection. New Recovery Services vaults use the modernized experience and cannot switch to classic.

The replacement is the modernized experience, launched in October 2022. Microsoft describes it as including classic capabilities, a stateless replication appliance, and automatic upgrades for the Mobility service agent and replication appliance. Pricing remains the same.

The supplied migration reference applies only to eligible existing replications where Upgrade to modernized VMware replication is available. If that action is unavailable, contact Microsoft Support for recovery guidance. Recovery plans do not migrate and must be recreated.
what.html:
Microsoft retired Azure Site Recovery’s classic experience for protecting VMware VMs and physical servers on March 30, 2026. Classic is no longer supported, and you cannot enable new classic protection. New Recovery Services vaults use the modernized experience and cannot switch to classic.

The replacement is the modernized experience, launched in October 2022. Microsoft describes it as including classic capabilities, a stateless replication appliance, and automatic upgrades for the Mobility service agent and replication appliance. Pricing remains the same.

The supplied migration reference applies only to eligible existing replications where Upgrade to modernized VMware replication is available. If that action is unavailable, contact Microsoft Support for recovery guidance. Recovery plans do not migrate and must be recreated.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your existing classic VMware or physical-machine replications and check whether Upgrade to modernized VMware replication is available. If it is unavailable, contact Microsoft Support for recovery guidance rather than proceeding with this migration.
2. Check migration eligibility. Replication must run through a configuration server from on-premises to Azure using managed disks. Initial replication must be complete. Items must not be failed over, failed back, resynchronizing, or replicating from Azure to on-premises. Check noncritical replication health and successful recovery-point creation.
3. Prepare the configuration server and source Mobility service agent. Both must run currently supported N-4 or later versions. The configuration server must have noncritical health and a healthy heartbeat.
4. Prepare a modernized Recovery Services vault in the same geographical location as the classic vault. Deploy and register the on-premises replication appliance. Its components must run currently supported N-4 or later versions, have noncritical health, and report a healthy heartbeat. Add the relevant vCenter Server or vSphere host details for discovery, and confirm support for your vCenter and source Linux or Windows Server versions.
5. Size and register the infrastructure before migration. Microsoft recommends the same number of replication appliances as classic process servers. Healthy protection with a recovery point less than 50 minutes old is listed as taking 1–2 hours to migrate; otherwise, duration depends on disk size and replication status.
6. Follow the referenced migration instructions using the available upgrade action. Recreate recovery plans in the modernized vault, then review destination replication health and recovery-point creation.

Vaults with managed identities or Private Endpoints enabled are supported. The supplied infrastructure reference does not include the full cutover procedure or a complete validation procedure. For technical help, use Microsoft Q&A or create a support request if you have a support plan.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are potentially affected if you use Azure Site Recovery’s classic experience to protect VMware VMs or physical servers. Check your replicated items and upgrade-action availability; the supplied material does not establish whether your resources are affected or eligible for migration.

Classic has been unsupported since March 30, 2026, and remaining classic replications may experience disrupted replication health or service interruption. The guidance does not establish that protected workloads themselves shut down or that workload data is deleted.

The documented migration excludes unmanaged-storage replication, Azure-to-on-premises replication, and items in failed-over, failed-back, initial-replication, or resynchronization states. These are migration limitations, not retirement exemptions. Vaults with managed identities or Private Endpoints are supported. Recovery plans do not transfer and must be recreated.

Pricing remains the same. Classic-vault Site Recovery license charges continue until all recovery-point retention periods expire and the recovery points are cleaned up. A system-triggered purge replication operation then removes the replicated item. Modernized-vault license charges start only after the first recovery point exists and the old vault has been cleaned up, subject to remaining trial days carried over. Microsoft states that only one vault is billed at a time; the supplied guidance provides neither a retention duration nor a cost estimate.

records.title: Classic VM retirement: extending retirement date to September 1st 2023
records.summary: Microsoft announced an extension of classic Linux and Windows IaaS VM retirement to September 1, 2023, requiring migration from Azure Service Manager to Azure Resource Manager. The migration overview instead gives September 6, 2023 for full retirement. These same-milestone dates differ by five days, so this summary uses the earlier date; the supplied material does not establish a further extension. The notice warns of potential service disruption, but neither source confirms retirement execution or exact shutdown behavior. Migration prerequisites and disruption depend on VM, network and storage configuration. Cloud Services (classic) Web/Worker Roles are outside this guidance's retirement scope.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring classic Linux and Windows IaaS VMs managed through Azure Service Manager, with migration to Azure Resource Manager. The selected retirement date is September 1, 2023, although the migration overview gives September 6, 2023.

The migration guidance covers associated compute, networking and storage. It explicitly excludes Cloud Services (classic) Web/Worker Roles from its IaaS VM guidance; their appearance in a supported-resource list does not establish the same retirement milestone. This notice does not establish retirement of Azure Resource Manager VMs.

The sources do not document regional exceptions, maintenance or security-update commitments during the extension, current migration availability, or precise post-retirement service behavior.
what.html:
Microsoft is retiring classic Linux and Windows IaaS VMs managed through Azure Service Manager, with migration to Azure Resource Manager. The selected retirement date is September 1, 2023, although the migration overview gives September 6, 2023.

The migration guidance covers associated compute, networking and storage. It explicitly excludes Cloud Services (classic) Web/Worker Roles from its IaaS VM guidance; their appearance in a supported-resource list does not establish the same retirement milestone. This notice does not establish retirement of Azure Resource Manager VMs.

The sources do not document regional exceptions, maintenance or security-update commitments during the extension, current migration availability, or precise post-retirement service behavior.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your classic IaaS VMs and associated virtual networks, storage accounts, availability sets, extensions and network dependencies. Separate VMs already in a virtual network from those outside one. The supplied sources provide no automated inventory procedure.
2. Plan migration to Azure Resource Manager against the selected September 1, 2023 deadline. Resource Manager requires VMs to use a virtual network; for VMs outside one, choose a platform-created network or an existing Resource Manager network. Migrate classic ExpressRoute circuits first. ExpressRoute gateway migration requires the gateway and virtual network to share a subscription.
3. Resolve unsupported configurations. These include multiple availability sets, or mixed availability-set and non-availability-set VMs, within one cloud service. Review multiple-subnet configurations, endpoint ACLs, Application Gateway and VNet peering dependencies. Separate Web/Worker Roles from a shared VM network. Networks containing App Service environments, HDInsight services or Dynamics Lifecycle Services-managed VMs are unsupported. Move API Management to another network before migrating its IaaS network.
4. Prepare dependent configuration and protection. Update RBAC policies for changed resource URIs; reconfigure dropped alerts and Autoscale settings. Remove unsupported XML extensions or expect them to be dropped. Disable Premium-storage boot diagnostics before migration and re-enable afterward; Microsoft recommends deleting its screenshot and serial-log blobs to stop their charges. For Defender for Cloud extensions, follow the documented requirement to disable the subscription policy to remove the monitoring extension. Backup/snapshot extensions require FAQ procedures not included in the supplied content to preserve earlier backups. Disable and re-enable Site Recovery VM replication around storage migration.
5. Migrate compute and networking, then associated storage accounts. Storage without associated disks or VM data can migrate independently, as can unattached network security groups, route tables and reserved IPs. For classic storage in the Azure portal, select Migrate to ARM, run Validate, select Prepare if validation passes, then type yes and select Commit.
6. As team-owned completion checks, verify application operation and required RBAC, alerts, Autoscale, extensions, diagnostics and replication. Recreate Application Gateway and restore applicable settings after migration. Detailed compute migration, backup preservation and troubleshooting procedures are not included in the supplied content.

For assistance, the retirement notice names Azure Migration Support, migration-specific free support for customers without technical support, and Microsoft Q&A. The supplied dedicated-support page contains no usable instructions. The notice also mentions eligibility-based FastTrack assistance, but the supplied destination describes Frontier Accelerate rather than confirming that retirement-specific offer.

Resource Manager requires VMs to use a virtual network; for VMs outside one, choose a platform-created network or an existing Resource Manager network. Migrate classic ExpressRoute circuits first. ExpressRoute gateway migration requires the gateway and virtual network to share a subscription.
  3. Resolve unsupported configurations. These include multiple availability sets, or mixed availability-set and non-availability-set VMs, within one cloud service. Review multiple-subnet configurations, endpoint ACLs, Application Gateway and VNet peering dependencies. Separate Web/Worker Roles from a shared VM network. Networks containing App Service environments, HDInsight services or Dynamics Lifecycle Services-managed VMs are unsupported. Move API Management to another network before migrating its IaaS network.
  4. Prepare dependent configuration and protection. Update RBAC policies for changed resource URIs; reconfigure dropped alerts and Autoscale settings. Remove unsupported XML extensions or expect them to be dropped. Disable Premium-storage boot diagnostics before migration and re-enable afterward; Microsoft recommends deleting its screenshot and serial-log blobs to stop their charges. For Defender for Cloud extensions, follow the documented requirement to disable the subscription policy to remove the monitoring extension. Backup/snapshot extensions require FAQ procedures not included in the supplied content to preserve earlier backups. Disable and re-enable Site Recovery VM replication around storage migration.
  5. Migrate compute and networking, then associated storage accounts. Storage without associated disks or VM data can migrate independently, as can unattached network security groups, route tables and reserved IPs. For classic storage in the Azure portal, select Migrate to ARM, run Validate, select Prepare if validation passes, then type yes and select Commit.
  6. As team-owned completion checks, verify application operation and required RBAC, alerts, Autoscale, extensions, diagnostics and replication. Recreate Application Gateway and restore applicable settings after migration. Detailed compute migration, backup preservation and troubleshooting procedures are not included in the supplied content.

For assistance, the retirement notice names Azure Migration Support, migration-specific free support for customers without technical support, and Microsoft Q&A. The supplied dedicated-support page contains no usable instructions. The notice also mentions eligibility-based FastTrack assistance, but the supplied destination describes Frontier Accelerate rather than confirming that retirement-specific offer.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
The affected scope is your classic Linux or Windows IaaS VMs and their dependent compute, network and storage resources. The supplied material does not establish which resources you own or how many are affected.

- No migration: the announcement warns of potential service disruption after the deadline. It does not specify exact shutdown behavior, retirement-related data retention or deletion, or costs of inaction.
- VMs outside a virtual network: migration stops, deallocates and restarts the VMs. Management and application/data operations may be temporarily unavailable.
- VMs already in a virtual network: for most supported configurations, migration changes metadata while VMs remain on the same hardware, network and storage. Applications continue running, but management operations may be temporarily unavailable. This is not a blanket no-downtime guarantee.
- Storage and data access: after storage migration, classic images and disks disappear from the Azure portal, while their backing VHDs remain in the storage account. This describes migration behavior, not retirement-related retention guarantees.
- Configuration and integrations: changed resource URIs affect RBAC policies. Alerts, Autoscale settings and unsupported XML extensions can be lost. Storage migration affects Site Recovery replication; security, backup and network dependencies may require preparation.

The sources do not establish that Resource Manager VMs or Cloud Services Web/Worker Roles share this retirement milestone. They also do not document separate post-retirement console, API or deployment-tooling behavior.

records.title: Cloud-based load testing features will be retired on March 31, 2020
records.summary: Azure DevOps cloud-based load testing retired on April 29, 2021 according to the product guidance and the blog's official-retirement statement. The original announcement and retained blog text instead identify March 31, 2020; no supplied source explicitly documents an extension or reconciles the shutdown dates. Cloud testing, dependent pipeline tasks and Azure portal performance-test options are affected. On-premises Visual Studio testing follows a separate support lifecycle, and Application Insights Availability tests are excluded. Replace affected cloud execution and pipeline dependencies, and preserve needed tests and results where exports remain available.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure DevOps cloud-based load testing retired, with April 29, 2021 identified by product guidance and the blog's official-retirement statement, subject to the conflicting shutdown dates described above.

The affected features include:

- Visual Studio cloud execution using auto-provisioned or self-provisioned agents.
- Azure DevOps web-based URL, HAR, Apache JMeter and Visual Studio web tests.
- Dependent Azure Pipelines cloud load-testing tasks.
- Performance-test options in the App Service and Application Insights Azure portal experiences.

Visual Studio web performance and load-testing functionality, including .webtest files, is also deprecated. Visual Studio 2019 is the last version containing these capabilities and the last Test Controller/Test Agent release for on-premises rigs. Microsoft states that it receives no new load-testing features, with issue support following the applicable product lifecycle. Visual Studio Enterprise on-premises testing is separate from cloud retirement.

Application Insights Availability tests are explicitly excluded. The supplied content does not specify regional exceptions or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify tests and pipelines that use Visual Studio cloud execution, the Azure DevOps Load Test Portal, cloud-backed pipeline tasks or Azure portal performance-test options. Separate these from on-premises rigs and Application Insights Availability tests.
2. Select a replacement for your test type. The sources identify self-hosted Test Controller/Test Agent for Visual Studio tests, subject to the applicable Visual Studio Enterprise lifecycle; Apache JMeter or compatible services for JMeter workloads; and SOAP UI as an alternative for API testing with .webtest files. The blog's October 3, 2022 update also names Azure Load Testing. Another reference calls it Preview; the supplied content does not establish its current status, feature parity or a conversion path for Visual Studio projects.
3. Where the historical export paths remain available, export URL-, HAR- and Visual Studio webtest-based tests using Export test to Visual Studio. Existing JMeter scripts can be reused with compatible alternatives; automatic conversion of Visual Studio tests is not promised.
4. Preserve historical results you need. The guidance describes downloading Visual Studio, URL and HAR reports through Visual Studio Enterprise for offline viewing, and downloading JMeter results as .csv files for JMeter reporters. Current export availability is not confirmed.
5. Replace cloud execution and affected pipeline tasks. As a team-owned completion check, validate replacement test runs and pipeline execution. Detailed cutover and cleanup procedures are not supplied.

The original announcement required a replacement by March 31, 2020; later guidance recommends migration as soon as possible. The sources do not document an extension of that original action target.

records.title: Cloud Services (classic) deployment model is retiring on 31 August 2024
records.summary: Microsoft announced retirement of Azure Cloud Services (classic) on August 31, 2024, requiring migration before that date. The announcement stated that classic deployments would be stopped and deallocated beginning September 1, 2024, with permanent data loss. Its named destination, Cloud Services (extended support), has a separate lifecycle: deprecation on March 31, 2025 and full retirement on March 31, 2027. That later date does not extend the classic deadline. Community guidance describes resource-discovery methods, but does not confirm that an empty retirement workbook proves migration is complete.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft announced retirement of the Azure Cloud Services (classic) deployment model on August 31, 2024. Its announcement named Cloud Services (extended support) in Azure Resource Manager as the migration destination and stated that classic deployments would be stopped and deallocated beginning September 1, 2024.

The supplied migration reference separately states that extended support was deprecated on March 31, 2025 and will fully retire on March 31, 2027. Classic-to-extended-support migration therefore does not complete remediation for the destination’s own retirement.

The sources do not document regional exceptions or retirement-specific maintenance and security-update commitments. They do not establish that the historical classic migration paths remain available.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your deployment model. Community guidance recommends searching the Azure portal for Cloud Services (classic) with all subscriptions selected. Cross-check Advisor → Workbooks → Service Retirement, selecting the relevant retirement and setting subscription, resource group and location filters to all.
2. Separate the two retirement scopes. Microsoft’s classic announcement required migration to Cloud Services (extended support) before August 31, 2024. The destination itself retires on March 31, 2027; review the deprecation and migration guidance referenced by its notice. That guidance’s contents and a complete migration-away procedure are not supplied.
3. Check migration constraints before using the documented classic-to-extended-support procedure. All Cloud Services within a migrating virtual network migrate together. Preparation blocks create, update and delete operations while reads remain available through both APIs. Abort is unavailable after a commit attempt. After migration, local configuration files must use the Azure Resource Manager virtual-network ID; the old naming scheme fails validation. These are historical migration-tool constraints, not evidence that the path remains available.
4. Validate and record completion. The classic migration reference describes validation for common unsupported scenarios and testing after preparation before committing. Keep deployment-level migration status and workload-validation evidence as team-owned records; these checks do not establish readiness for extended-support retirement.

The supplied content does not provide complete retirement-specific backup, export, cutover or cleanup instructions. It names Virtual Machine Scale Sets, Azure Container Apps, App Service, Azure Kubernetes Service and Azure Service Fabric in a classic-migration discussion, but does not establish their suitability or migration steps for leaving extended support.

For classic-retirement questions, use Microsoft Q&A. Technical support requests require a support plan.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify classic deployments. Community guidance recommends searching the Azure portal for Cloud Services (classic) with all subscriptions selected, then cross-checking Azure Advisor > Workbooks > Service Retirement with subscription, resource group and location filters set to all. These checks are not confirmed as exhaustive.
2. Distinguish classic deployments from extended-support deployments. The original requirement was to migrate classic services to extended support before August 31, 2024; extended support itself retires on March 31, 2027.
3. Evaluate the alternatives listed in the supplied guidance: Virtual Machine Scale Sets, Azure Container Apps, App Service, Azure Kubernetes Service and Azure Service Fabric. Select against your application requirements; the supplied page establishes neither feature equivalence nor migration procedures to these destinations.
4. As team-owned planning, record your destination, migration outcome and application-validation evidence. The supplied content provides no retirement-wide completion criteria or backup procedure.

For the separately documented classic-to-extended-support migration, prerequisites include subscription coadministrator access and registration of Microsoft.ClassicInfrastructureMigrate. In-place migration follows validate, prepare, test, then commit or abort; abort is unavailable after a commit attempt. Migrate Microsoft Entra Domain Services separately first if it shares the virtual network, promote staging deployments to production beforehand, and update local .cscfg virtual-network references to Azure Resource Manager IDs afterward. Redeployment requires traffic cutover and validation before removing the old classic service.

These procedures do not complete migration away from extended support. Their presence does not establish that classic migration remains available today.

what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft announced retirement of the Azure Cloud Services (classic) deployment model on August 31, 2024. The notice required affected services to move to Cloud Services (extended support) in Azure Resource Manager to continue operating.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your classic deployments. Community guidance recommends searching for Cloud Services (classic) in the Azure portal with all subscriptions selected. Cross-check Azure Advisor > Workbooks > Service Retirement with subscription, resource group and location filters set to all. These checks are not confirmed as exhaustive.
2. Distinguish classic deployments from extended-support deployments. The classic announcement required migration to extended support before August 31, 2024; it does not establish whether that migration remains available now.
3. Account for extended support's separate March 31, 2027 retirement. Evaluate the alternatives listed in the product guidance: Virtual Machine Scale Sets, Azure Container Apps, App Service, Azure Kubernetes Service and Azure Service Fabric. Select according to your application requirements; the supplied page does not establish feature equivalence or provide migration procedures to these alternatives.
4. As team-owned planning, record your destination, migration outcome and application-validation evidence. Use Microsoft Q&A for questions, or create a technical support request if you have a support plan.

Documented classic-to-extended-support procedure

This procedure is not a migration away from extended support. It requires subscription coadministrator access and registration of Microsoft.ClassicInfrastructureMigrate. In-place migration follows validate, prepare, test, then commit or abort; abort is no longer allowed after a commit attempt.

For applicable configurations, migrate Microsoft Entra Domain Services separately first when sharing a virtual network, promote staging deployments to production before migration, and update local .cscfg virtual-network references to Azure Resource Manager IDs afterward. Redeployment requires you to direct traffic to the new deployment and validate it before removing the old classic service.

The supplied material does not provide retirement-specific backup procedures or a complete migration procedure away from extended support.

records.title: Community support for Azure Functions Proxies will end on 30 September 2025
records.summary: Azure Functions Proxies community support ended on September 30, 2025. Microsoft recommends migrating to Azure API Management. The announcement states that Proxies would remain in maintenance mode until that date, with no further investment; it does not establish a workload shutdown or data-deletion date. Product guidance covers legacy proxies in runtime versions 1.x–3.x and temporary re-enablement in 4.x for runtime upgrades.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Functions Proxies community support ended on September 30, 2025, with no further investment announced. Microsoft recommends Azure API Management as the long-term supported alternative.

Product guidance identifies proxies as a legacy feature for Functions runtime versions 1.x–3.x. It permits temporary re-enablement in 4.x to support runtime upgrades, but gives no duration or scheduled withdrawal for that option. This does not establish an extension of Proxies support.

The announcement described planned 4.x compatibility work by October 2022; the product guidance documents temporary re-enablement. Neither establishes continued support or a separate security-update commitment.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your function apps that use Azure Functions Proxies. The supplied guidance provides no discovery procedure.
2. Assess Azure API Management for your scenarios. Microsoft strongly recommends moving as soon as possible; no separate dated migration target is documented.
3. Integrate your function app with a new or existing API Management instance, then import its HTTP-triggered endpoints. Import excludes endpoints with admin-level authorization.
4. Configure API Management to reproduce your previous proxy behavior using the referenced API editing and policy guidance.

Temporary re-enablement of proxies in Functions 4.x supports runtime upgrades; it is not presented as the long-term replacement. The product reference states that migration documentation and tools for an existing Proxies implementation are not currently available, although integration articles and equivalent-task hints are provided. Detailed validation, cutover and cleanup steps are not supplied.

For migration challenges or scenarios API Management does not cover, the announcement directs you to an Azure Functions GitHub issue labeled proxy-deprecation; the product reference directs you to the API Management feedback forum.

records.title: Community support for Node 14 LTS is ending on 30 April 2023
records.summary: Node 14 LTS support on Azure App Service ends on April 30, 2023. Microsoft will stop providing patches and customer service for that version, but existing applications will continue to run. The notice directs you to upgrade to Node 16 LTS before that date; it does not establish that Node 16 remains supported today. General App Service guidance provides runtime-identification methods and warns that changing runtime settings restarts your app.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
After April 30, 2023, Microsoft will no longer provide patches or customer service for Node 14 LTS on Azure App Service. The notice states that existing applications will continue to run.

General App Service guidance covers Windows and Linux and says end-of-life Node.js versions are removed from the Runtime Stack dropdown without affecting existing applications targeting them. This guidance does not independently establish a Node 14 retirement date or promise updates after end of life.

The notice names Node 16 LTS as its upgrade target. It documents no regional exceptions or support commitments for other versions.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your App Service apps using Node 14 LTS. General runtime guidance identifies WEBSITE_NODE_DEFAULT_VERSION for Windows and linux-fx-version for Linux as the configured-runtime settings.
2. Check available supported runtimes with az webapp list-runtimes --os-type windows or az webapp list-runtimes --os-type linux. The retirement notice directed an upgrade to Node 16 LTS before April 30, 2023; its recommendation and the reference page's examples do not establish Node 16's current support status.
3. Update affected apps. For Windows, change the runtime app setting through the portal or Azure CLI. For Linux, use Azure CLI or the portal's Configuration → General settings → Stack Settings → Major version, then save. Changing runtime settings restarts the app.

For Windows, the runtime guidance recommends tilde syntax rather than pinning a specific minor or patch version, whose availability is not guaranteed. The supplied content does not document compatibility prerequisites, backup requirements or post-change validation procedures.

records.title: Community support for PHP 7.3 is ending on 6 December 2021
records.summary: PHP 7.3 extended support on Linux and Windows ended on December 6, 2021. Azure App Service applications using PHP 7.3 can continue running unchanged, but are unsupported and receive no further PHP patches. The notice recommended updating to PHP 7.4 before that date; it does not establish PHP 7.4's current support status. The general App Service reference describes runtime-selection behavior, not a separate retirement deadline.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
PHP 7.3 on Azure App Service on Linux and Windows lost support and further PHP patches after December 6, 2021. The announcement says existing applications continue running unchanged; it does not announce a workload shutdown or runtime removal.

Separately, the general App Service reference says end-of-life PHP versions are removed from the Runtime Stack selection dropdown and existing apps targeting them should not be affected. Automatic installation of available PHP patch updates does not establish continued patches for end-of-life versions.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your apps using PHP 7.3 in the Azure portal under App Service > your app > Configuration > General settings > Stack Settings.
2. Check the official PHP support timeline before selecting a replacement. The retirement notice recommended PHP 7.4, but the supplied content does not establish its current support status. To list currently supported Linux runtimes, run:
az webapp list-runtimes --os-type linux


3. Review migration guidance and compatibility requirements before changing versions. The announcement references a migration document, but its contents are not supplied. PHP 8 requires an App Service Linux instance; no Windows-to-Linux migration procedure is provided.
4. To change the configured version, select a supported version under Minor version and click Save. Saving the stack-setting change restarts your app.

The supplied content provides no compatibility-validation procedure or documented backup, cutover or cleanup steps.
