records.title: Retirement: transition to the Authentication methods policy for Azure Active Directory
records.summary: Microsoft announced September 30, 2024 as the retirement date for managing Azure Active Directory MFA and self-service password reset authentication methods through legacy policies. Move this management to the unified Authentication methods policy. The supplied migration guide describes continued legacy-policy use during migration and reversible completion, but gives no revised retirement date or extension. Current enforcement is therefore unconfirmed; neither source establishes an authentication-service shutdown.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft announced retirement of legacy MFA and SSPR authentication-method management on September 30, 2024, replacing it with the unified Authentication methods policy.

The migration guide says you can use legacy policies while configuring the replacement. After you select Migration Complete, Microsoft Entra follows the unified policy; legacy method settings no longer apply or remain editable, except SSPR security questions, which remain managed in legacy SSPR settings.

The automated guide migrates tenant policy settings, not individual user settings. Already-configured methods available only in the unified policy, including FIDO2 security keys, Temporary Access Pass and Microsoft Entra certificate-based authentication, need no migration changes.

The sources do not establish an authentication-service shutdown, regional exceptions, or maintenance, support and security-update commitments.
what.html:
Microsoft announced retirement of legacy MFA and SSPR authentication-method management on September 30, 2024, replacing it with the unified Authentication methods policy.

The migration guide says you can use legacy policies while configuring the replacement. After you select Migration Complete, Microsoft Entra follows the unified policy; legacy method settings no longer apply or remain editable, except SSPR security questions, which remain managed in legacy SSPR settings.

The automated guide migrates tenant policy settings, not individual user settings. Already-configured methods available only in the unified policy, including FIDO2 security keys, Temporary Access Pass and Microsoft Entra certificate-based authentication, need no migration changes.

The sources do not establish an authentication-service shutdown, regional exceptions, or maintenance, support and security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Sign in to the Microsoft Entra admin center with at least the Authentication Policy Administrator role. Audit and record enabled methods across legacy MFA, SSPR and the unified policy, including SSPR scope, user/group targeting and method-specific settings, so you can restore settings if needed.
2. Choose automated or manual migration. For automation, open Entra ID > Authentication methods > Policies, open the migration guide, review or edit its recommendations, then select Migrate and confirm. This migrates tenant policy settings only and marks migration complete.
3. For manual migration, open Manage migration and select Migration in progress before changing methods. Configure methods and targeting from your audit. Resolve MFA/SSPR differences: a method enabled in the unified policy can apply to both sign-in and password reset.
4. Preserve security questions in legacy SSPR. Map OATH usage to the separate Authenticator OTP, third-party software OATH and hardware OATH controls. For SSPR mobile phone, enable SMS and Voice calls; for office phone, enable Voice calls and its Office phone option. Review Email OTP member password-reset targeting separately from external-user sign-in settings.
5. Review SMS sign-in, which is enabled by default in SMS settings. Disable it for target users if you use cross-tenant synchronization or do not want SMS sign-in; users enabled for SMS sign-in are skipped from cross-tenant synchronization.
6. For manual migration, remove legacy methods one at a time and test each change. Select Migration Complete only after MFA and SSPR work as intended. You can return to Migration in Progress to re-enable legacy settings.

You do not have to reproduce every existing setting, but disabling a method can require users to register another method. Enabling additional modern methods is Microsoft's recommendation, not a migration prerequisite.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are in scope if your tenant uses legacy MFA or SSPR policies to control authentication methods. Inspect:

- Legacy MFA: Entra ID > Users > Per-user MFA > service settings.
- SSPR: Entra ID > Users > Password reset > Authentication methods.
- Unified policy: Entra ID > Authentication methods > Policies.

Legacy MFA settings are tenant-wide. SSPR scope and unified-policy group inclusions, exclusions and configuration parameters also affect your migration. This summary does not inspect your tenant.

Consolidating different MFA and SSPR settings requires deciding which methods should be available across both scenarios. Keeping previously enabled methods available is intended to preserve users' options; disabling them can prevent use of existing registrations and require new registrations. SMS sign-in can also exclude affected users from cross-tenant synchronization.

Migration Complete changes policy enforcement and prevents legacy method-setting edits, except for SSPR security questions. The automated guide does not migrate individual user settings. Already-configured methods unique to the unified policy need no changes.

The notice retires management capability, not explicitly authentication itself. The sources do not establish a dated no-action workload shutdown, data deletion, retention changes or cost effects.

records.title: Retiring version Async 2.x of the Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK on 31 August 2024
records.summary: Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK Async 2.x for SQL API retired on August 31, 2024. Microsoft states that requests using Async 2.x continue to be served after retirement, but the SDK receives no further updates. Migrate affected applications to Java SDK 4.x and use 4.x for new subscriptions/accounts. Migration requires dependency and API changes, including moving asynchronous code from RxJava to Reactor.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK Async 2.x for SQL API on August 31, 2024 and directs customers to Java SDK 4.x. Async 2.x requests continue to be served after retirement, but Microsoft makes no further updates to that SDK.

Java SDK 4.x combines synchronous and asynchronous APIs, provides TCP-based direct mode and supports all throughput modes, including autoscale. Async 2.x provides asynchronous requests only, HTTP-based direct mode and manual throughput only.

The supplied sources do not identify regional exceptions. The v4 general-availability announcement describes the replacement SDK; it does not independently establish a retirement deadline.
what.html:
Microsoft retired Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK Async 2.x for SQL API on August 31, 2024 and directs customers to Java SDK 4.x. Async 2.x requests continue to be served after retirement, but Microsoft makes no further updates to that SDK.

Java SDK 4.x combines synchronous and asynchronous APIs, provides TCP-based direct mode and supports all throughput modes, including autoscale. Async 2.x provides asynchronous requests only, HTTP-based direct mode and manual throughput only.

The supplied sources do not identify regional exceptions. The v4 general-availability announcement describes the replacement SDK; it does not independently establish a retirement deadline.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify affected applications by checking Maven dependencies and imports for Async 2.x. The migration guide maps Async 2.x.x to azure-cosmosdb.
2. Review the v4 migration guide and choose the synchronous or asynchronous API appropriate for your application. For asynchronous migrations, follow the RxJava-to-Reactor guidance. The supplied v4 release page lists JDK 8 as the minimum supported runtime.
3. Remove the prior SDK dependency from pom.xml, add the latest available v4 com.azure:azure-cosmos dependency and update imports to com.azure.cosmos. Adapt client and resource access, accessors and document representations; v4 uses POJOs or JsonNode rather than publicly exposing CosmosItemProperties.
4. Run mvn dependency:tree to identify dependency conflicts. Resolve incompatible versions through dependency management or targeted exclusions, then rebuild and thoroughly test application functionality and runtime dependencies.
5. Use Java SDK 4.x for new subscriptions/accounts, as Microsoft directs.

The announced migration deadline was August 31, 2024. The supplied sources do not prescribe export, backup, cutover or cleanup procedures.

records.title: Some Azure Service Bus SDK libraries will be retired on 30 September 2026—migrate to the latest SDKs
records.summary: Microsoft retired WindowsAzure.ServiceBus for Service Bus messaging, Microsoft.Azure.ServiceBus and the legacy Java Service Bus SDK on September 30, 2026, ending official support and updates. SBMP also retired that day and is no longer usable. Applications using AMQP can continue functioning with the retired libraries, but without support or updates. Migrate to the supported SDK for your service and language. WindowsAzure.ServiceBus use with Event Hubs also requires migration; its Azure WCF Relay support continues until further notice.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired these older Azure Service Bus SDK libraries on September 30, 2026, ending official support and updates:

- WindowsAzure.ServiceBus for Service Bus messaging.
- Microsoft.Azure.ServiceBus.
- The Java library com.microsoft.azure:azure-servicebus, whose packages begin with com.microsoft.azure.servicebus. The Java guide covers migration from version 3 and identifies legacy versions as 3.x.x or below.

SBMP retired on the same date. WindowsAzure.ServiceBus applications using AMQP, and applications using the other two libraries, can continue functioning without support or updates.

WindowsAzure.ServiceBus applications using Event Hubs also need to migrate. Azure WCF Relay is an exception: its WindowsAzure.ServiceBus support continues until further notice, and Azure.Messaging.ServiceBus is not its replacement.
what.html:
Microsoft retired these older Azure Service Bus SDK libraries on September 30, 2026, ending official support and updates:

  • WindowsAzure.ServiceBus for Service Bus messaging.
  • Microsoft.Azure.ServiceBus.
  • The Java library com.microsoft.azure:azure-servicebus, whose packages begin with com.microsoft.azure.servicebus. The Java guide covers migration from version 3 and identifies legacy versions as 3.x.x or below.

SBMP retired on the same date. WindowsAzure.ServiceBus applications using AMQP, and applications using the other two libraries, can continue functioning without support or updates.

WindowsAzure.ServiceBus applications using Event Hubs also need to migrate. Azure WCF Relay is an exception: its WindowsAzure.ServiceBus support continues until further notice, and Azure.Messaging.ServiceBus is not its replacement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify affected applications through package references and namespaces. Include WindowsAzure.ServiceBus applications using Event Hubs. Separate Service Bus messaging from Azure WCF Relay, and check whether WindowsAzure.ServiceBus messaging applications use SBMP or AMQP.
2. Select the replacement for your service and language:
  - Service Bus .NET: migrate directly to Azure.Messaging.ServiceBus version 7. Do not use Microsoft.Azure.ServiceBus as an intermediate destination; it is also retired.
  - Service Bus Java: replace com.microsoft.azure:azure-servicebus with com.azure:azure-messaging-servicebus.
  - Event Hubs .NET: replace WindowsAzure.ServiceBus with Azure.Messaging.EventHubs.
3. Follow the applicable migration guide and update application code, not just package references. Move SBMP messaging to AMQP. Update client construction, message types, receiving, settlement and administration APIs. Connection strings remain supported; Azure Active Directory authentication uses Azure.Identity for .NET or azure-identity for Java.
4. Review the features your application uses. The .NET replacement lacks batch-settlement APIs and automatic activity-baggage propagation; WindowsAzure.ServiceBus migration also requires attention to cross-partition batching and stable message identifiers for duplicate detection. Java asynchronous APIs use Project Reactor instead of CompletableFuture. Cross-entity transactions require explicit enablement and the documented send-via ordering and receiver constraints.
5. As team-owned validation, test authentication, sending, receiving, settlement and any sessions, duplicate detection, dead-letter handling, lock renewal, transactions or tracing you use. For Java SAS-token connection strings, replace SharedAccessSignatureToken with SharedAccessSignature and do not also specify SharedAccessKeyName or SharedAccessKey.

The supplied guides provide comparisons and samples, but no complete backup, deployment cutover, rollback or cleanup procedure. Do not apply the Service Bus replacement to WCF Relay.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if your applications use one of the retired libraries. Review package references, legacy namespaces and transport configuration; this summary does not inspect your resources or establish tenant-wide coverage.

- SBMP: you can no longer use this protocol after September 30, 2026.
- AMQP and retired SDKs: applications can continue functioning, but Microsoft no longer provides official support or updates. Continued operation does not restore support.
- Event Hubs: WindowsAzure.ServiceBus use is included even if you do not use Service Bus.
- Azure WCF Relay: WindowsAzure.ServiceBus support continues until further notice.

Migration requires code and integration changes. In .NET, batch settlement is unavailable, individual settlement can partially succeed, and activity baggage does not propagate automatically. For WindowsAzure.ServiceBus migration, batches cannot span partitions; on partitioned entities with duplicate detection enabled, leaving SessionId, PartitionKey and MessageId all unset causes sends to fail. Java client construction, asynchronous programming and authentication options change. Transaction routing constraints require review in both languages.

The supplied content does not document a general Service Bus shutdown, retirement-related data deletion, retention changes or cost changes. Questions in the Q&A listing do not confirm Power Automate connector impact.

records.title: Retirement of SQL Server Native Client (SNAC) OLE DB provider for linked servers in Azure SQL Managed Instance
records.summary: Microsoft scheduled retirement of SQLNCLI for Azure SQL Managed Instance linked servers across all Azure regions during late May and June 2023. One notice describes the start as late May and early June; the other describes the broader rollout window and supplies June 2023 as structured metadata. Neither establishes an exact date or a single retirement month, and rollout completion is not confirmed. Existing linked servers automatically use MSOLEDBSQL without recreation, while their metadata continues to show SQLNCLI. New linked servers and creation scripts must use MSOLEDBSQL after deactivation.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure SQL Managed Instance was scheduled to retire the SQL Server Native Client OLE DB provider, identified as SNAC or SQLNCLI, for linked servers during late May and June 2023 across all Azure regions.

Microsoft documents automatic rerouting of existing SQLNCLI linked servers to MSOLEDBSQL, described as fully compatible, without manual migration. Stored metadata remains unchanged, so sys.servers continues to report SQLNCLI.

After deactivation, new linked servers to other managed instances or SQL Server instances must specify MSOLEDBSQL. This retirement concerns Azure SQL Managed Instance linked servers; the supplied content does not establish retirement dates for other SNAC uses.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Review your Azure SQL Managed Instance linked-server creation scripts for SQLNCLI provider settings.
2. Change those scripts to pass MSOLEDBSQL as the Provider parameter to sp_addlinkedserver. After deactivation, new linked-server creation with SQLNCLI fails.
3. If you use the SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) linked-server wizard, install the latest SSMS version as directed by the reference and select Microsoft OLE DB Driver for SQL Server.

You do not need to recreate or manually migrate existing SQLNCLI linked servers: Microsoft documents automatic rerouting. The supplied content does not specify additional prerequisites, validation, backup, cutover or cleanup procedures.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
This retirement affects SQLNCLI linked servers in Azure SQL Managed Instance across all Azure regions, along with tooling that creates new linked servers.

- Existing linked servers: Microsoft documents automatic rerouting to MSOLEDBSQL without manual changes. SQLNCLI remains visible in sys.servers because stored metadata does not change; that value alone does not indicate a migration failure.

- SSMS: The linked-server wizard removes SQL Server Native Client 11.0, SQL Server Native Client 10.0 and Microsoft OLE DB Provider for SQL Server from its provider list. Their corresponding identifiers also disappear from the Object Explorer provider list.

The supplied content describes a provider change, not existing workload shutdown. It does not document downtime, data deletion, additional charges or effects on other SNAC uses.

records.title: Retirement: Support for Application Gateway Web Application Firewall v2 Configuration is ending
records.summary: Legacy WAF configuration on Azure Application Gateway WAF v2 retires on March 15, 2027; the WAF v2 SKU itself is not retiring. Migrate to WAF policy before that date. Microsoft states that existing configurations remain usable and supported through retirement and that the direct WAF v2 configuration upgrade preserves configuration and rules without downtime. New legacy configuration deployments were discontinued on March 15, 2025. Post-retirement traffic and shutdown behavior are not specified.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring legacy WAF configuration on Azure Application Gateway WAF v2 on March 15, 2027, not the WAF v2 SKU itself. Use WAF policy instead. Gateways already using WAF policy are outside this retirement's scope.

Microsoft is making no further investments in legacy configuration; latest features and future enhancements are available only through WAF policies. Existing configurations remain usable and supported through retirement, but the supplied content gives no specific security-update commitment or regional exceptions.

WAF policies support gateway, listener and path-based scopes and can be shared across gateways, listeners and URL paths. Microsoft describes equivalent functionality and additional Policy features as available at no extra cost.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Migrate affected Application Gateway WAF v2 gateways to WAF policy before March 15, 2027.

1. In the Azure portal, open each relevant gateway and select Web Application Firewall. Identify gateways using legacy configuration and the Upgrade from WAF configuration option.
2. Select Upgrade from WAF configuration.
3. Enter a name for a new WAF policy and select Upgrade, or associate an existing WAF policy. Creating a new policy carries over the previous configuration and rules.
4. As a team-owned validation step, confirm that the intended policy is associated with the gateway and review its settings and rules.

The guidance also identifies Azure Firewall Manager and Azure PowerShell as upgrade options. Microsoft documents the direct legacy WAF v2 configuration upgrade as having no downtime.

Application Gateway v1 does not support WAF policy: upgrade to v2 first. If starting from Standard v2, change the tier to WAF V2 and save before following the policy upgrade path. The no-downtime statement does not explicitly cover these other transitions.

The supplied content does not document backup, rollback or cleanup steps.

records.title: Retirement: Support for .NET 6 ends on 12 November 2024—upgrade your Azure Functions apps to .NET 8
records.summary: Support for .NET 6 in Azure Functions ended on November 12, 2024. Apps continue running, but Microsoft no longer provides security updates or customer service for .NET 6. The retirement notice directed customers to upgrade to .NET 8 by that date. Separate guidance requires in-process .NET apps to migrate to the isolated worker model before November 10, 2026; that requirement does not change the .NET 6 end-of-support date.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft ended support for .NET 6 in Azure Functions on November 12, 2024. Affected apps continue running, but Microsoft no longer provides security updates or customer service for .NET 6. The retirement notice names .NET 8 as the upgrade target and documents no regional exceptions.

The general language-support policy says retired language apps can still be created and deployed, but are no longer eligible for new features, security patches or performance optimizations until upgraded.

The separate requirement to migrate from the in-process model to the isolated worker model applies to in-process .NET apps. Apps already using the isolated worker model are outside that model-migration requirement.

The general language-support policy says retired language apps can still be created and deployed, but are no longer eligible for new features, security patches or performance optimizations until upgraded.

The separate requirement to migrate from the in-process model to the isolated worker model applies to in-process .NET apps. Apps already using the isolated worker model are outside that model-migration requirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Azure Functions apps using .NET 6 and their worker models. The supplied content does not provide a complete inventory method. Azure portal, Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell can check the Functions runtime version; FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME identifies the language stack, not its version.
2. Upgrade affected apps. The retirement notice specified .NET 8 by November 12, 2024. Check Supported languages in Azure Functions and runtime compatibility when selecting your target.
3. If an app uses the in-process model, follow the referenced isolated-worker migration guidance before November 10, 2026. Changing the .NET version alone does not establish completion of that migration.
4. For apps already using the isolated worker model, install the target SDK and update the target framework, SDK and worker packages, binding extensions, dependencies and build/deployment tooling. Rebuild and test locally. Confirm Functions runtime 4.x; follow the runtime migration guidance if needed rather than only changing its setting.
5. Publish updated code before changing the Azure stack configuration, targeting the correct app or staging slot. Linux Consumption apps require Azure CLI for stack updates.
6. Verify the configured .NET version, Running status and function behavior. If using a staging slot, validate it before swapping into production.

The version-update guidance recommends backing up configuration and using a staging slot for testing and rollback. Flex Consumption does not support slots; use a non-production function app instead. For rollback, swap the slot back, or restore the previous language configuration and redeploy the previous code. These version-update steps are not a complete worker-model migration procedure.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
Your Azure Functions apps using .NET 6 are affected: they continue running after November 12, 2024 but no longer receive Microsoft security updates or customer service for .NET 6. Continued use leaves potential security vulnerabilities without those updates. The supplied content does not establish which of your apps are affected.

Under the general language-support policy, retired language apps lose eligibility for new features, security patches and performance optimizations. Microsoft may limit allocated instances in certain cases, including scaling to one instance, and requires an upgrade before providing support. These are general policy conditions, not evidence that a specific app has been limited.

For the documented language-version update, changing the stack configuration restarts the app. A direct production update typically causes 30–60 seconds of unavailability, terminates in-flight requests and rejects new requests until restart succeeds. Staging slots can minimize downtime, but Flex Consumption does not support them. Dependencies, bindings and CI/CD settings may also need updates.

The sources do not document retirement-related data deletion or additional costs. The separate in-process migration reference does not specify the consequences of missing its deadline.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use the documented configuration checks to build a team-owned inventory and record upgrade and validation results. These checks have limits:

1. Check the Functions runtime through Azure portal, Azure CLI or Azure PowerShell. The version-update guide identifies FUNCTIONS_EXTENSION_VERSION with a target of ~4; this verifies the Functions runtime, not the .NET version or worker-model migration.
2. Compare your language version with Supported languages in Azure Functions and the applicable support timeline. FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME alone does not establish language-version support.
3. After updating, confirm the selected .NET version under General settings and Running status in Overview. Test function behavior; inspect Monitoring > Log stream for runtime mismatches, dependency errors and binding conflicts.
4. Record worker-model migration status separately. A configured language version and Running status alone do not prove that migration is complete.

The general policy documents notification emails from the Functions team about upcoming language retirements affecting your apps, but no migration-progress dashboard or automated completion check.

For questions, the retirement notice directs you to Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and need technical help, open the Azure portal and select the question mark icon at the top of the page.

records.summary: Support for .NET 7 in Azure Functions ended on May 14, 2024, also the notice's deadline to upgrade affected apps to .NET 8. Hosted apps continue running, but Microsoft no longer provides .NET 7 security updates or customer service. Upgrade and validate affected apps using guidance appropriate to their worker model, operating system and hosting plan.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft ended support for .NET 7 in Azure Functions on May 14, 2024. Affected apps continue running, but Microsoft no longer provides security updates or customer service for .NET 7. The retirement notice directs you to upgrade these apps to .NET 8.

The general Azure Functions language policy says retired language stacks remain available for app creation and deployment, but lose eligibility for new features, security patches and performance optimizations. This does not establish a shutdown date.
what.html:

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Azure Functions apps using .NET 7 and record their worker model, target framework, Functions runtime, operating system and hosting plan. The retirement notice does not provide a .NET 7 inventory method. The FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME setting identifies the language stack, not its version.
2. Upgrade affected apps to .NET 8, as required by the notice by May 14, 2024. Check the supported-language guidance and compatibility of the Functions runtime, worker packages, binding extensions and dependencies. The supplied version-upgrade procedure primarily covers isolated-worker apps; use the referenced model-migration guidance where needed rather than assuming it covers every worker model.
3. Install the target SDK, update the target framework and required code or deployment settings, then rebuild and test locally. Ensure the app uses Functions runtime 4.x; older runtime migrations require the relevant migration guide.
4. Back up the app configuration as recommended. Where supported, test in a staging slot. Flex Consumption does not support slots, so verify changes in a non-production app instead.
5. Publish updated code before changing the Azure language-stack configuration, targeting the correct app or slot. Linux Consumption requires Azure CLI for stack updates; supported Linux plans otherwise allow portal updates.
6. Verify the configured language version, Running status and function behavior before completing cutover. If using staging, verify it before swapping into production. For rollback, swap back or restore the previous language configuration and redeploy the previous code.

records.title: Retirement: Support for the in-process model for .NET apps in Azure Functions ends 10 November 2026.
records.summary: Microsoft ended support for the in-process model for .NET apps in Azure Functions on November 10, 2026. Apps can continue running, but Microsoft no longer provides security or feature updates for this model. Migrate affected apps to the isolated worker model and a supported target framework, then validate application behavior and deployment configuration. This is an end-of-support milestone, not a workload shutdown.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft ended support for the in-process model for .NET apps in Azure Functions on November 10, 2026. The replacement is the isolated worker model. Existing in-process apps can continue running without support or security and feature updates for that model.

The migration guide covers C# function apps and assumes Functions runtime 4.x. Apps on runtime 1.x, 2.x or 3.x need the corresponding host-version migration guidance. No regional restrictions or customer exceptions are documented.

The notice describes the isolated model as offering the same functionality, dependency-chain control, isolation from platform lifecycle activities and support for targeting STS .NET versions. Migration still requires reviewing documented code, binding, serialization and logging differences.
what.html:
Microsoft ended support for the in-process model for .NET apps in Azure Functions on November 10, 2026. The replacement is the isolated worker model. Existing in-process apps can continue running without support or security and feature updates for that model.

The migration guide covers C# function apps and assumes Functions runtime 4.x. Apps on runtime 1.x, 2.x or 3.x need the corresponding host-version migration guidance. No regional restrictions or customer exceptions are documented.

The notice describes the isolated model as offering the same functionality, dependency-chain control, isolation from platform lifecycle activities and support for targeting STS .NET versions. Migration still requires reviewing documented code, binding, serialization and logging differences.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
To regain a supported configuration, migrate affected apps to the isolated worker model and a supported target framework.

1. Identify in-process apps using the migration guide's Azure PowerShell inventory script. It filters function apps whose Runtime value equals dotnet in the currently selected subscription. Repeat discovery for every subscription in scope.
2. Review dependencies and execution-model differences. Choose a supported .NET target, or a supported .NET Framework target if you require Framework-only libraries or APIs. Use host-version migration guidance for Functions runtimes earlier than 4.x. Convert C# script files to a C# project before following the project migration steps.
3. Update the project SDK and worker packages, replace WebJobs extension packages, move startup and dependency-injection configuration into Program.cs, and update function attributes, logging, triggers, bindings and affected types. Remove remaining WebJobs and Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Extensions package references.
4. Review serialization attributes, host/application log filtering and extension configuration. For HTTP functions using ASP.NET Core integration, replace synchronous stream I/O with asynchronous operations or evaluate the documented compatibility option. Extension upgrades can require host.json changes.
5. Set the local worker runtime to dotnet-isolated and fully test with Azure Functions Core Tools 4.x. Check build paths, deployment tooling and CI/CD configuration. The .NET Upgrade Assistant is optional; verify its supported targets before using it.
6. Coordinate deployment with the Azure worker-runtime and, if needed, .NET stack configuration changes. Changing the worker-runtime setting and deploying code each restart the app; an interim mismatch produces AZFD0013 errors.
7. When feasible, use a staging slot. Set its worker runtime to dotnet-isolated without making that setting slot-specific, deploy and validate the app, then swap into production. Validate production behavior and update infrastructure automation to preserve the new configuration.

The supplied .NET policy lists .NET 10 and .NET 11 as supported through November 14, 2028, subject to current patches and operating-system eligibility. These are framework lifecycles, not extensions of the in-process retirement.

Use host-version migration guidance for Functions runtimes earlier than 4.x. Convert C# script files to a C# project before following the project migration steps.
  3. Update the project SDK and worker packages, replace WebJobs extension packages, move startup and dependency-injection configuration into Program.cs, and update function attributes, logging, triggers, bindings and affected types. Remove remaining WebJobs and Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Extensions package references.
  4. Review serialization attributes, host/application log filtering and extension configuration. For HTTP functions using ASP.NET Core integration, replace synchronous stream I/O with asynchronous operations or evaluate the documented compatibility option. Extension upgrades can require host.json changes.
  5. Set the local worker runtime to dotnet-isolated and fully test with Azure Functions Core Tools 4.x. Check build paths, deployment tooling and CI/CD configuration. The .NET Upgrade Assistant is optional; verify its supported targets before using it.
  6. Coordinate deployment with the Azure worker-runtime and, if needed, .NET stack configuration changes. Changing the worker-runtime setting and deploying code each restart the app; an interim mismatch produces AZFD0013 errors.
  7. When feasible, use a staging slot. Set its worker runtime to dotnet-isolated without making that setting slot-specific, deploy and validate the app, then swap into production. Validate production behavior and update infrastructure automation to preserve the new configuration.

The supplied .NET policy lists .NET 10 and .NET 11 as supported through November 14, 2028, subject to current patches and operating-system eligibility. These are framework lifecycles, not extensions of the in-process retirement.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if your .NET Azure Functions apps use the in-process model. The documented inventory script covers only the currently selected subscription; it does not establish your tenant-wide exposure or assess migration readiness.

Without migration, apps can continue running after November 10, 2026, but Microsoft no longer supports the model or provides its security and feature updates. The sources do not announce workload shutdown, data deletion, retention changes or cost effects.

Migration affects application code, extension packages, runtime configuration and potentially build/deployment automation. Compatibility risks include changed binding types, Newtonsoft.Json attributes being silently ignored by System.Text.Json, separate host/application logging configuration and synchronous HTTP stream I/O failing under ASP.NET Core integration.

Runtime-setting changes and code deployment each restart the app. A temporary mismatch produces AZFD0013 errors; a validated staging-slot swap avoids introducing that interim mismatch in production.

You do not need to change AzureWebJobsStorage solely for this migration. No general host.json change is required, although extension upgrades or logging requirements can require updates. Apps already using the isolated worker model are outside this model retirement, but their target frameworks have separate support lifecycles.

records.title: Retirement: Upgrade from Azure API Management stv1 to stv2 by Aug. 31, 2024
records.summary: Azure API Management retired the stv1 compute platform in global Azure on August 31, 2024. The separate retirement date for Azure Government and Azure operated by 21Vianet was February 24, 2025. This affects classic Developer, Basic, Standard and Premium instances using stv1, not those tiers themselves. Existing stv2 instances, Consumption and v2 pricing tiers are unaffected. Global Azure stv1 instances lost SLA guarantees and related service credits from September 1, 2024; retirement did not itself shut down or delete instances. Migrate remaining stv1 instances to stv2. Microsoft schedules automatic migration, which can cause downtime and, under special conditions, remove virtual network settings and block endpoints.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure API Management retired the stv1 compute platform for classic Developer, Basic, Standard and Premium instances in global Azure on August 31, 2024, and in Azure Government and Azure operated by 21Vianet on February 24, 2025. You need to move remaining stv1 instances to stv2; the service tiers themselves are not retiring.

Before retirement, stv1 instances continued operating normally but did not receive the latest stv2 features. After global Azure retirement, SLA commitments ended and remaining instances became subject to automatic migration, rather than immediate shutdown or deletion. Microsoft states that it will make no new security and compliance investments in stv1; the supplied guidance does not specify a security-update schedule.

Existing stv2 instances, Consumption instances using mtv1, and v2 pricing tiers are unaffected. Qatar Central supports only stv2. The stv2 platform supports availability zones, private endpoints and Azure DDoS protection unavailable on stv1.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Migrate any remaining Azure API Management stv1 instances to stv2. The retirement dates were August 31, 2024 for global Azure and February 24, 2025 for Azure Government and Azure operated by 21Vianet.

1. Identify each instance's platform in the Azure portal under Overview > Essentials > Platform Version. Separate instances by cloud because the retirement dates differ.
2. For stv1 instances, follow Microsoft's referenced migration guide. The supplied platform guidance identifies a migration API for instances not injected into a virtual network and manual steps for VNet-injected instances. You can migrate your instances before automatic migration occurs.
3. Confirm that each migrated instance reports stv2. As team-owned validation, check API access and your intended network configuration separately.

The supplied content does not include the full migration procedure, prerequisites, backup steps or detailed workload-validation checks.

If automatic migration blocks endpoints

Under special conditions, automatic migration removes virtual network configuration and blocks service endpoints. For the documented portal recovery, select Unblock my service on the instance's Overview page, then redeploy into your virtual network. Unblocking is irreversible and makes endpoints publicly accessible from the internet, so restore network protection as soon as possible. Microsoft strongly recommends a new subnet with stv2-compatible settings.

To recover original virtual network and subnet names, open Diagnose and solve problems > Availability and performance > VNet Verifier and select a pre-migration time range. The referenced guidance also documents an Azure CLI recovery procedure.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if an Azure API Management instance uses stv1 in the classic Developer, Basic, Standard or Premium tier. Check its platform version rather than relying on its tier or creation date. Existing stv2 instances, Consumption using mtv1, and v2 pricing tiers are unaffected.

For global Azure, retirement on August 31, 2024 did not itself shut down or delete instances, but SLA guarantees and related service credits ended from September 1, 2024. Remaining stv1 instances are subject to automatic migration, which can cause downtime for upstream API consumers. Azure Government and Azure operated by 21Vianet had a separate retirement date of February 24, 2025; their SLA transition dates are not separately documented in the supplied content.

Automatic migration usually retains virtual network settings. Under special conditions, it removes those settings and blocks the API gateway, developer portal, direct management API and Git repository. The portal then reports that all service endpoints are blocked. Portal unblocking exposes endpoints publicly until you restore network protection.

The supplied content does not establish your resource inventory, quantify downtime or migration costs, or provide a separate data-retention policy.

records.title: Retirement: Upgrade your Azure Logic Apps Integration Service Environment workloads
records.summary: Azure Logic Apps Integration Service Environment (ISE) had a documented retirement deadline of August 31, 2024, with migration to Logic Apps Standard required to preserve workload continuity. Microsoft stated that afterward ISE access and support would end, workflows would stop, workflow history would be permanently deleted, and linked integration accounts would be removed. Logic Apps Consumption is unaffected. The retirement notice and product guidance support August 31, 2024; a Q&A also gives August 1, 2024, without documenting an extension. Sources separately conflict on when new ISE creation stopped: September 14, 2022 versus after November 1, 2022. The supplied content documents announced consequences, not independently verified retirement execution.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Logic Apps Integration Service Environment (ISE) was scheduled to retire on August 31, 2024. Microsoft directs you to migrate ISE workloads to Logic Apps Standard, rather than expect a transparent infrastructure migration.

The change covers deployed ISE instances, their workflows, workflow history and associated integration accounts. Product guidance attributes retirement to ISE's dependency on retiring Classic Cloud Services and identifies infrastructure and virtual-network interdependencies as migration considerations.

Microsoft documented support for existing instances during the transition and allowed logic app deployments into existing ISE environments until decommissioning within the retirement timeline. The supplied content does not specify regional exceptions or detailed security-update commitments.

Logic Apps Consumption is unaffected. Logic Apps Standard is the recommended destination, not a retiring service.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Microsoft required you to migrate ISE workloads to Logic Apps Standard by August 31, 2024 to preserve continuity.

1. Identify your ISE instances, workflows, connections and associated integration accounts. The supplied sources provide no inventory procedure.
2. Plan workflow grouping, network dependencies and connector compatibility. The March 2023 connector-parity target is a historical plan, not confirmation of current availability.
3. Use Export to Logic Apps Standard in the Logic Apps Standard extension for Visual Studio Code. Product guidance calls for the latest extension version. Review export validation and the referenced known issues. Conversion to built-in connectors depends on availability; the tool also exports managed connector actions and connection configuration and generates a destination-connection ARM template.
4. Update, test and debug the exported workflows locally, then package and deploy directly or through your DevOps processes. Validate the deployed workflows in Azure.

The Standard development guide documents an Azure account, subscription and internet access as prerequisites for Azure deployment and managed connector scenarios. It specifies Project Runtime ~4, required for Inline Code Operations actions; this is not a separate runtime retirement.

The supplied content does not provide detailed workflow-history preservation, integration-account migration, production cutover or cleanup procedures. Do not treat workflow export alone as a complete migration. Migration documentation, an FAQ, Microsoft Q&A and Azure support are documented help routes.

deadline.html:
The documented ISE retirement deadline was August 31, 2024. Microsoft required migration off ISE by that date. Afterward, Microsoft stated that ISE access and support would end, workflows would stop, workflow history would be permanently deleted, and associated integration accounts would be removed.

The retirement notice and product guidance identify August 31, 2024. A Q&A title and announcement instead identify August 1, 2024, while an employee reply on that page gives August 31, 2024. This synthesis uses the applicable product-guidance date, August 31, 2024; the supplied content does not explicitly establish an extension.

A separate new-instance restriction has an unresolved date discrepancy: the Q&A says creation stopped on September 14, 2022, while product guidance says after November 1, 2022. Product guidance documents a support-request exception for existing customers needing to recreate an environment, not an exception to retirement.

No exact shutdown time or time zone is supplied. The sources do not independently confirm that retirement occurred as announced.

records.title: Retiring Azure Batch AI
records.summary: Microsoft retired Azure Batch AI Preview on March 31, 2019 and advised migration to Azure Machine Learning before that date to avoid application disruptions. Subsequent product guidance describes an unspecified grace period for existing subscriptions without SLA support, blocked new registrations and shutdown without further notice; it supplies no shutdown date. Government clouds had a separate historical support exception whose end date is unconfirmed. Migration requires reviewing capability gaps and conflicting CLI guidance.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired Azure Batch AI Preview on March 31, 2019 and directs customers to Azure Machine Learning, including Azure Machine Learning Compute for at-scale training and batch scoring.

The product guidance describes continued use by existing subscriptions only during an unspecified grace period, with no SLA support, further investment or updates. New registrations are blocked, and shutdown is described as forthcoming without further notice; the supplied material does not establish when shutdown occurred.

Government clouds had a separate historical support exception until Azure Machine Learning availability, with no confirmed end date here. The documented replacement has capability and interface differences, so you should not assume unchanged workload compatibility.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Batch AI workspaces, clusters, file servers, experiments and jobs. Check regional availability in the Azure portal, particularly for Government clouds; the historical availability plan does not confirm the exception's current status.
2. Use Microsoft's migration guide to map workspaces to workspaces, clusters to AmlCompute, file servers to Datastores, experiments to experiments, and jobs to runs.
3. Review compatibility before migrating. The comparison lists container-only execution, no Node Prep or OS-family choice, JobPreparation as not yet available, and job-level mounting limited to FileShares and Blobs. The replacement SDK is listed as Python rather than Batch AI's Java, C#, Python and Node.js SDKs.
4. Configure an Azure Machine Learning Compute target and migrate your workloads using the referenced code mappings. Confirm your submission interface: the guidance conflicts on CLI availability and excludes portal job submission.
5. Validate migrated training and batch-scoring workloads. Run History supports job monitoring, and the Artifact service retrieves logs, files and models.

Microsoft's notice advised migration before March 31, 2019; the product guidance urges immediate migration without another dated target. The supplied material does not detail backup, export, cutover or cleanup procedures. For migration troubleshooting, contact AzureBatchAITrainingPreview@service.microsoft.com.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
If you use Azure Batch AI Preview, your workloads fall within the retirement scope, subject to the separately documented historical Government-cloud exception. The notice warns of application disruptions without migration before March 31, 2019. Later guidance allows existing subscriptions only an unspecified grace period without SLA support and blocks new registrations; it does not establish an exact shutdown date or detailed shutdown behavior.

Migration can affect more than workload execution:

- Execution is container-only, with preparation, OS-selection and storage-mounting limitations documented in the comparison.
- The replacement SDK is listed as Python, REST APIs are distributed across microservices, and portal job submission is excluded. CLI availability is inconsistent within the guidance.
- Monitoring changes from GetJob to Run History; log, file and model retrieval changes from ListFiles and Storage APIs to the Artifact service.

The guidance says previous VM-family quota capacity carries forward and underlying infrastructure pricing should not vary between the services. This is not a workload-specific cost estimate. No data-retention or deletion policy is supplied, and these sources do not establish whether your resources are affected.

records.title: App Service support for Ruby is ending 12 April 2023
records.summary: App Service support for Ruby 2.7 ended on April 12, 2023. App Service will not support Ruby 2.7 or future Ruby versions after that date. Applications continue to run unchanged but no longer receive patches. Microsoft recommends migrating to a custom container before that date. This is an end-of-support milestone, not an application shutdown.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
App Service ended support for Ruby 2.7 on April 12, 2023 and will not support future Ruby versions. Your applications continue to run unchanged, but they no longer receive patches after that date.

Microsoft recommends custom containers as the migration option. The supplied deployment tutorial demonstrates Ruby on Rails in a custom Linux container; its Ruby 2.7.6 example does not establish that version's support status.
what.html:

Microsoft recommends custom containers as the migration option. The supplied deployment tutorial demonstrates Ruby on Rails in a custom Linux container; its Ruby 2.7.6 example does not establish that version's support status.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Microsoft recommends migrating your applications to a custom container before April 12, 2023 to minimize risk. The supplied tutorial covers Ruby on Rails and requires a Rails application and Docker.

1. Identify applications using App Service's Ruby 2.7 support. The notice provides no inventory method.
2. Add a Dockerfile beside your Gemfile. The tutorial's example installs dependencies, exposes port 3000 and starts Rails bound to 0.0.0.0. Its Ruby 2.7.6 base image is an example, not a support recommendation.
3. Build and run the container locally, then check that your application is accessible.
4. Tag and push the image to Azure Container Registry.
5. Create an App Service Web App with Docker Container publishing and Linux, then select your registry and image. Check that the application becomes available.

The supplied material does not document cutover, backup, rollback or cleanup steps, assess capability gaps, or provide migration instructions for non-Rails applications.

records.title: Service Management REST APIs and support will be retired on November 1, 2021
records.summary: Classic Azure Service Manager management REST APIs for Azure Service Bus, Relay and Event Hubs are identified for retirement on December 1, 2021 in the supplied migration guidance, with migration to Azure Resource Manager requested by November 30, 2021. The announcement and REST references instead state November 1, 2021. The migration guidance is preferred for the structured retirement date, but the discrepancy remains unresolved; no supplied source explicitly documents an extension. The Event Hubs reference also says Event Hubs has no RDFE REST APIs, leaving its precise affected scope unclear. This concerns classic management interfaces, not an announced shutdown of the underlying messaging services.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Resource Manager replaces the classic Azure Service Manager management model covered by this retirement. The migration guidance names Azure Service Bus, Relay and Event Hubs and gives December 1, 2021 as the retirement date; the announcement and REST references give November 1, 2021.

The change concerns classic management REST APIs and their support, with migration guidance also mapping deprecated PowerShell commands to replacements. It does not announce retirement of the underlying messaging services, Resource Manager APIs or direct service APIs.

Event Hubs scope needs care: the migration guidance includes it, but its REST reference explicitly says Event Hubs has no RDFE REST APIs. The supplied content does not resolve that inconsistency or document regional exceptions, pre-retirement availability, maintenance or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify management integrations and scripts for the named services that call management.core.windows.net or use deprecated PowerShell commands listed in the migration guidance. Distinguish classic management calls from Resource Manager and direct service calls; do not assume all Event Hubs integrations are affected.
2. Replace affected classic REST operations with service-specific Azure Resource Manager operations using the supplied migration mappings. Some mapping entries have no replacement listed, so confirm coverage for each operation before cutover.
3. Update affected PowerShell scripts using the listed Resource Manager replacements, including newer Az commands where provided.
4. As a team-owned validation step, verify that changed management operations work and no longer depend on classic endpoints or deprecated commands.

The migration guidance requested completion by November 30, 2021, ahead of its stated retirement on December 1, 2021. Other supplied sources give November 1, 2021; no explicit extension is documented. Detailed prerequisites, resolution of unmapped operations and a complete cutover procedure are not supplied.

Microsoft directed customers to migrate to PostgreSQL 13 or higher on Flexible Server by that date to avoid workload disruption. The notice does not specify a shutdown date. Its destination guidance is historical: the supplied upstream policy now marks PostgreSQL 13 and earlier as unsupported, and the supplied migration reference contains no usable migration guidance.

what.announcement:
Microsoft ended support for PostgreSQL 11 on Azure Database for PostgreSQL Single Server on November 9, 2024. The notice states that support, including creation of new version 11 servers, continued through that date.

The specified migration destination was PostgreSQL 13 or higher on Flexible Server. The supplied upstream policy marks PostgreSQL 13 and earlier as unsupported; the historical destination guidance does not establish current support for a particular Flexible Server version.

The notice does not describe post-deadline server availability or security-update commitments.

Both options support EHR launch. Enhanced also supports standalone launch and scope restrictions, but requires you to integrate Azure Health Data and AI open-source samples with the FHIR service and Azure products such as Azure API Management.

The notice says Enhanced can be considered for SMART on FHIR Implementation Guide v1.0.0 and §170.315(g)(10) requirements; it does not establish that your implementation meets certification requirements. No regional exceptions or retirement-related maintenance and security-update commitments are documented.

records.title: Retirement: SQL Data Sync will be retired on September 30th, 2027
records.summary: Microsoft will retire SQL Data Sync on September 30, 2027. The retirement notice says you can continue using it without disruption until that date, when workloads running SQL Data Sync will be deleted and associated application data will be lost. Complete migration by retirement, choosing an alternative that matches your synchronization requirements and platforms. SQL Data Sync does not support Azure SQL Managed Instance. The supplied guidance lists alternatives but does not provide complete migration procedures or service-specific completion checks.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring SQL Data Sync on September 30, 2027. This Azure SQL Database service synchronizes selected data bidirectionally across databases on premises and in the cloud.

Affected scenarios include hybrid SQL Server/Azure SQL Database synchronization, distributed applications with separate reporting databases, and globally distributed applications. SQL Data Sync does not support Azure SQL Managed Instance; its inclusion among replacement platforms does not indicate existing support.

The notice permits continued use without disruption until retirement. It does not specify regional or customer exceptions, or separate maintenance, support and security-update commitments.
what.html:
Microsoft is retiring SQL Data Sync on September 30, 2027. This Azure SQL Database service synchronizes selected data bidirectionally across databases on premises and in the cloud.

Affected scenarios include hybrid SQL Server/Azure SQL Database synchronization, distributed applications with separate reporting databases, and globally distributed applications. SQL Data Sync does not support Azure SQL Managed Instance; its inclusion among replacement platforms does not indicate existing support.

The notice permits continued use without disruption until retirement. It does not specify regional or customer exceptions, or separate maintenance, support and security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify where you use SQL Data Sync, your source and destination platforms, and the synchronization behavior your applications require.
2. Select a replacement suited to your scenario and platforms. For hybrid synchronization, the guidance lists Always On availability groups, Managed Instance link, Azure Data Factory, transactional replication and linked servers. For distributed read workloads, it lists read replicas, Always On availability groups and database copy. For cross-region read workloads, it lists Azure Data Factory and readable active geo-replication. Other options include Azure Functions and Microsoft Fabric mirrored databases.
3. Use the referenced solution guidance to plan and complete migration by September 30, 2027.

The alternatives are not established as equivalent replacements for bidirectional synchronization. The supplied content does not provide complete prerequisites, capability comparisons, export or backup procedures, validation criteria, or cutover and cleanup steps.

records.title: Retirement: SQL Server Connector V1 Actions and Triggers to Be Retired on June 30, 2025 – Transition to V2 Actions and Triggers
records.summary: Microsoft set June 30, 2025 as the retirement date for SQL Server connector V1 actions and triggers, explicitly extending the original March 31, 2024 date. The notice permits V1 use through June 30, 2025 but directs migration to V2 before that date; it does not specify post-retirement execution behavior. Use the supplied migration guidance for affected Logic Apps, Power Automate flows and Power Apps, including backups, compatibility checks and validation. SQL Server itself and the entire connector are not identified as retiring.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft set June 30, 2025 as the retirement date for SQL Server connector V1 actions and triggers and directs you to replace them with V2 operations. The notice allows V1 use through that date but does not document subsequent execution, maintenance or security-update commitments.

The migration guidance covers SQL Server managed connector operations in Logic Apps, Power Automate and Power Apps: row creation, retrieval, update and deletion; table listing; SQL queries; and item-created and item-modified triggers. It also maps Execute stored procedure to V2, although that V1 operation is not explicitly marked deprecated in its operation reference.

V2 adds Server name and Database name parameters and supports Microsoft Entra ID authentication. Managed identity authentication is supported only in Logic Apps.

This is not a retirement of SQL Server itself or the entire connector. The SQL Server built-in connector for Standard logic app workflows is distinct from the managed connector described here. Default authentication has a separate deprecation label, with no supplied removal date.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Migrate affected V1 operations to V2; the notice's action target was before June 30, 2025. Check compatibility before replacing operations.

1. Identify V1 operations. In Power Automate, inspect each SQL operation's Code View and compare host.operationId with the documented V1 IDs. For Logic Apps, run the supplied Azure Resource Graph queries separately for actions and triggers, supplying your subscription ID.
2. Save a backup copy of each affected logic app, flow or Power App before changing it.
3. For Logic Apps and Power Automate, select the matching V2 operation and connection, supply server and database names, and preserve the remaining parameters. The guidance also documents Logic Apps Code View changes and Power Automate package-definition editing as alternatives. For the package route, update operation IDs, add server and database parameters with the documented value default, preserve the ZIP structure with Microsoft.Flow and manifest.json at its root, and select the intended connections during import.
4. Reconnect downstream dynamic content to V2 outputs when replacing V1 actions. The designer guidance contains a contradictory instruction to delete V2 after configuring V1; that cleanup instruction remains unresolved. The documented definition-editing routes provide alternatives.
5. For Power Apps, remove SQL data sources, enable the enhanced Microsoft SQL Server connector in Settings, and re-add the sources. Temporary formula errors are expected while sources are removed. Verify behavior, especially DateTime handling, and save. New apps already have the enhanced connector enabled.
6. Verify server, database and remaining parameters. Save and test migrated Logic Apps, inspect imported flow actions and connections, and validate Power Apps behavior before treating migration as complete.

Execute a SQL query (V2) does not support on-premises SQL Server or gateway connections. Microsoft Entra ID guest users are unsupported for Entra ID connections; the reference identifies SQL Server or Windows authentication as alternatives. Authentication changes require the corresponding identity setup and database permissions. Review the additional trigger and virtual-network constraints below.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are in scope if your apps or workflows use SQL Server managed connector V1 actions or triggers. The retirement date is June 30, 2025, but the supplied notices do not establish whether unmigrated workflows stop executing afterward. No assessment of your resources or affected resource count is supplied.

Existing V2 operations and SQL Server databases themselves are not identified as retirement targets. No retirement-specific regional restrictions or customer exceptions are documented.

Migration constraints include:

- Replacing V1 actions can break downstream dynamic-content references until you reconnect them to V2 outputs.
- V2 requires server and database parameters. Managed identity authentication is limited to Logic Apps, and Microsoft Entra ID guest users are unsupported for Entra ID connections.
- Execute a SQL query (V2) is unavailable for on-premises SQL Server and gateway connections.
- Power Platform environments linked to a virtual network support only the eight V2 actions listed in the reference. Other actions return 403 Unauthorized, and the on-premises data gateway is unsupported.
- V2 item-created triggers require an IDENTITY column. Item-modified triggers require ROWVERSION and fire on inserts and updates. Turning a flow off and on does not reset trigger state.
- Power Apps migration temporarily causes formula errors while SQL data sources are removed; the guidance specifically calls for checking DateTime behavior.

The supplied content does not specify retirement-related data deletion, retention changes, costs, or post-retirement API and tooling behavior.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use the supplied connector reference's identification and validation methods to track your migration from V1. These checks do not certify tenant-wide retirement readiness.

1. In Power Automate, inspect SQL operation IDs in Code View and compare them with the documented V1 and V2 IDs. This is an operation-level check, not a documented tenant-wide inventory.
2. In Logic Apps, run both Azure Resource Graph queries for each subscription you review. They report matching V1 action and trigger counts by workflow. They target microsoft.logic/workflows resources and specific connection and definition patterns; coverage of every hosting model or nested configuration is not established, and they do not inventory Power Apps or Power Automate.
3. Verify migrated operations, populated server and database parameters, and remaining settings. Save and test Logic Apps; inspect updated actions and connection selections after Power Automate imports; and verify Power Apps behavior, especially DateTime tables.

For team-owned tracking, retain the reviewed resource list, remaining V1 findings, backups and validation results as migration evidence. The supplied content documents no automatic progress dashboard.

The connector reference lists idcknowledgeeco@microsoft.com as a contact, but does not document a retirement-specific escalation process.

records.title: Standard and High-Performance VPN Gateway SKUs will be retired on 30 September 2025
records.summary: Azure VPN Gateway Standard and High Performance legacy SKUs retire on June 30, 2026 according to the supplied product guidance, preferred over the original announcement's September 30, 2025 date. The sources do not explicitly document an extension, and the product page points to separate latest-timeline guidance that was not supplied. Migrate Standard to VpnGw1AZ and High Performance to VpnGw2AZ using the Azure portal Basic IP migration tool to retain your IP address. Microsoft supports existing gateways and customer-initiated migration through retirement and says it will attempt automatic migration after June 2026; constraints can prevent completion. No guaranteed workload shutdown date is documented. VPN Gateway Basic is excluded, and the migration path for classic gateways remains unresolved.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure VPN Gateway is retiring the legacy Standard and High Performance SKUs on June 30, 2026, according to the supplied product guidance. The Azure portal Basic IP migration tool upgrades both the public IP and gateway SKU:

- Standard becomes VpnGw1AZ.
- High Performance becomes VpnGw2AZ.

Microsoft states that existing legacy gateways remain supported until retirement. The original announcement links this change to these SKUs accepting only Basic IP.

VPN Gateway Basic is not retiring. The product guidance says it currently supports only Basic SKU public IP addresses. The separate public-IP retirement notice must not be treated as a retirement of VPN Gateway Basic.

The guidance says classic gateways cannot move to newer SKUs, leaving their retirement migration path unresolved. No regional exceptions or specific security-update commitments are documented.

  • High Performance becomes VpnGw2AZ.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Migrate affected gateways before June 30, 2026, the retirement date in the supplied product guidance, rather than relying on attempted automatic migration.

1. Identify gateways using Standard or High Performance, their deployment model and associated Basic public IP addresses. The supplied content provides no inventory procedure.
2. For an eligible gateway, use the Azure portal Basic IP migration tool to retain your IP address. It upgrades the public IP to Standard and moves Standard gateways to VpnGw1AZ or High Performance gateways to VpnGw2AZ. Check for and resolve constraints such as insufficient subnet size.
3. If you choose the documented delete-and-recreate route instead, the gateway must use Azure Resource Manager. Remove its connections, delete the gateway, create the replacement, update on-premises VPN devices and connected network-to-network local network gateways with the new IP address, download new point-to-site client configuration packages, and recreate connections. This route causes connectivity downtime and changes the IP address even if you reuse its public IP resource.
4. Review applicable VPN Gateway pricing. The supplied content does not establish pricing for automatic AZ-SKU upgrades or provide a retirement-specific completion-check procedure.

For classic gateways, do not assume the tool or newer SKUs are supported: the supplied guidance leaves their migration path unresolved. Microsoft Q&A is available for questions; customers with a support plan can create a technical support request.

impact.guidance:

records.title: Start using new alerts in Azure Monitor for Azure China 21Vianet
records.summary: Azure Monitor classic alerts on Azure China 21Vianet retired on February 29, 2024. Migrate affected classic metric rules to newer alerts, update Resource Manager templates and adapt notification integrations. Activity log alerts, including Service Health alerts, and log search alerts are unaffected. Some metrics require manual recreation, threshold changes or alternatives; migration-tool completion alone does not establish full coverage. The supplied guidance describes historical tool availability and migration continuity, not verified current availability or a universal shutdown date for every existing rule.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Monitor retired classic alerts on Azure China 21Vianet on February 29, 2024, replacing classic metric alert rules with newer alerts and reusable action groups. Affected rules appear in Alerts (classic) and use the Microsoft.Insights/alertRules resource type.

Activity log alerts, including Service Health alerts, and log search alerts are unaffected.

The documented migration tool creates equivalent rules and action groups where supported, then deletes the classic rules. During migration, existing rules continue evaluating and notifying until replacements take effect; this does not establish availability after retirement. Notification payloads and management APIs change, and new action-group emails are English-only.

Some metrics require manual changes or have no replacement identified in the supplied guidance. The pages describe historical migration-tool availability, not verified current availability. They provide no maintenance or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your China subscriptions' classic rules through Monitor > Alerts > View classic alerts and inventory templates using Microsoft.Insights/alertRules. Separate unaffected activity log and log search alerts. Flag rules targeting deleted resources or deprecated metrics; these cannot migrate.
2. Select newer metric alerts for supported metric rules. For VM guest metrics, send guest metrics to Azure Monitor Logs and follow the log search alert path. The China notice also excludes what it calls “retirement metrics” from the tool without clarifying that term.
3. Review metric-specific gaps before migration. Storage percentage metrics need absolute thresholds. AnonymousThrottlingError, SASThrottlingError and ThrottlingError each need two replacement alerts and adjusted thresholds. Azure Cosmos DB Http 2xx, Http 3xx and Service Availability rules require manual recreation and threshold adjustment. Other Cosmos DB metrics have no replacement identified in the supplied guidance.
4. Use manual migration or the documented tool where available. Triggering the tool requires subscription-level Monitoring Contributor, or a custom role with the documented read and action-group, classic-rule, metric-alert and smart-detector permissions. Migrating Application Insights Failure Anomaly alerts also requires Microsoft.AlertsManagement resource-provider registration.
5. In Migrate to new rules, select subscriptions marked Ready to migrate, preview each subscription and optionally download its details as CSV. Resolve reported locks and blocking policies. Listed locks must be removed, not merely disabled; policies require an appropriate exclusion, enforcement-mode change, exemption or policy change. Supply notification email addresses before starting. Starting migration prevents creating or editing classic rules in that subscription.
6. Update affected Resource Manager templates to newer alert resource types and adapt integrations to the new notification payloads and management APIs. As team-owned validation, compare conditions, dimensions, units, thresholds, aggregation, evaluation windows, recipients and downstream automation. Check completion emails and resolve required actions. The tool deletes classic rules after creating replacements; no separate manual export, cutover or cleanup procedure is supplied.
