actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Inventory your application's SDK dependencies and imports. Compare them with the referenced retired-library lists and migration resources. The retirement-list reference was unavailable in the supplied material, so package-family names alone are not a complete retirement inventory.
2. Select replacements for each affected dependency. For .NET management code, follow the applicable non-Fluent or Fluent migration guidance to Azure.ResourceManager, Azure.Identity and ArmClient. Check individual package READMEs for feature differences; the examples do not establish complete capability parity.
3. For Go management code, select the corresponding current resource-management modules. Track 2 uses separate modules by resource provider and one API version per module. Choose stable, non-beta modules for production. The repository states support for the two most recent major Go releases; the migration guide gives no fixed minimum version.
4. Update integration code. For .NET, adapt authentication, resource models and management operations. For Go, update authentication, client initialization, error handling, polling, pagination and any custom policies, endpoints or HTTP transport. Updating Go management packages without changing authentication code can cause authentication failures.
5. As a team-owned completion check, validate the operations and configurations your applications actually use. Do not copy examples unchanged: the supplied .NET Fluent VM examples differ in configuration, and the replacement example pairs an Ubuntu image with a Windows OS-type value.

Microsoft's recommended upgrade date was September 30, 2023. If you retain affected libraries, the announcement says their source is available on GitHub for your own fixes; this does not restore official support or updates. The sources provide no complete migration-wide acceptance checklist or cutover procedure.

records.title: Update your scripts to use Az PowerShell modules by 29 February 2024
records.summary: AzureRM PowerShell retired on February 29, 2024; Microsoft’s migration guidance describes this as deprecation and the end of maintenance and support. AzureRM may still function, and the sources do not establish a workload shutdown date. Migrate scripts and script modules to Az for continued support and updates. Migration can require changes beyond cmdlet names, and compatibility aliases do not resolve every breaking change.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
AzureRM PowerShell is deprecated and no longer maintained or supported. Microsoft advises migrating your scripts and script modules to Az for continued support and updates.

AzureRM scripts do not automatically work with Az. Migration can involve changes to modules, cmdlets, parameters and return values. Az’s Enable-AzureRmAlias compatibility feature is not deprecated with AzureRM, but it does not resolve every breaking change.

The supplied sources document no regional or customer exceptions or version-specific exemption from deprecation.
what.html:
AzureRM PowerShell is deprecated and no longer maintained or supported. Microsoft advises migrating your scripts and script modules to Az for continued support and updates.

AzureRM scripts do not automatically work with Az. Migration can involve changes to modules, cmdlets, parameters and return values. Az’s Enable-AzureRmAlias compatibility feature is not deprecated with AzureRM, but it does not resolve every breaking change.

The supplied sources document no regional or customer exceptions or version-specific exemption from deprecation.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify installed AzureRM versions with Get-Module -Name AzureRM -ListAvailable -All, and search your scripts for *-AzureRM*. These checks cover only the systems and files you examine.
2. Check the prerequisites for your chosen migration procedure. The general migration guide identifies AzureRM 6.13.2 as the latest release and says scripts should work with it before migration. The automatic-migration quickstart instead specifies 6.13.1. The supplied sources do not reconcile these differing prerequisites; do not treat them as interchangeable. Older versions may require additional major-version migration changes.
3. Prefer the AzureRM-to-Az migration toolkit to generate and review a change plan before modifying scripts. The automatic quickstart documents installing it with Install-Module -Name Az.Tools.Migration and selecting individual files or folders for analysis.
4. Review plan entries whose PlanResult is not ReadyToUpgrade, and manually resolve blocking issues. Generating a plan does not change files.
5. Back up scripts and modules before applying changes: the upgrade has no undo operation. The documented SaveChangesToNewFiles mode preserves originals and creates copies with _az_upgraded appended to filenames; ModifyExistingFiles changes files in place.
6. Review execution entries whose UpgradeResult is not UpgradeCompleted, resolve failures and validate migrated scripts. Unusual encodings can cause problems, and the tool does not detect AzureRM cmdlets passed to Pester mock statements. The supplied guide provides no runtime-validation, cutover or cleanup procedure.

As a transitional alternative, you can use Az with Enable-AzureRmAlias while updating scripts. Aliases apply only to the current session by default and do not resolve renamed parameters or changed return values.

records.title: Update your Traffic Analytics queries by 31 August 2022
records.summary: Traffic Analytics retired support for nine older log-schema fields after August 31, 2022, according to the retirement notice. Update affected queries to the replacement schema. The schema reference provides version 2 migration examples but no retirement date; it does not document an extension. Neither source establishes a Traffic Analytics service shutdown or when older fields stop returning data.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Traffic Analytics updated its log schema and retired support for nine older fields after August 31, 2022, according to the retirement notice:

- VMIP_s
- Subscription_g
- Region_s
- NSGRules_s
- Subnet_s
- VM_s
- NIC_s
- PublicIPs_s
- FlowCount_d

The schema reference introduces SrcPublicIPs_s, DestPublicIPs_s and NSGRule_s, with examples for moving queries from schema version 1 to version 2. The updated schema separates source and destination information and no longer aggregates data across an NSG; NSGList_s contains one NSG.

The sources do not announce a Traffic Analytics service shutdown, identify regional exceptions, or establish when older fields become unavailable. They provide no maintenance or security-update commitments.
what.html:
Traffic Analytics updated its log schema and retired support for nine older fields after August 31, 2022, according to the retirement notice:

  • VMIP_s
  • Subscription_g
  • Region_s
  • NSGRules_s
  • Subnet_s
  • VM_s
  • NIC_s
  • PublicIPs_s
  • FlowCount_d

The schema reference introduces SrcPublicIPs_s, DestPublicIPs_s and NSGRule_s, with examples for moving queries from schema version 1 to version 2. The updated schema separates source and destination information and no longer aggregates data across an NSG; NSGList_s contains one NSG.

The sources do not announce a Traffic Analytics service shutdown, identify regional exceptions, or establish when older fields become unavailable. They provide no maintenance or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Traffic Analytics queries that reference the nine retiring fields or depend on their schema version 1 representation.
2. Adapt affected queries using the schema version 2 examples. Use explicit source/destination fields rather than inferring them from FlowDirection_s for AzurePublic and ExternalPublic flows. The reference also warns that direction-based inference can be inappropriate for a network virtual appliance.
3. Replace parsed NSGRules_s values with NSGRule_s, FlowDirection_s and FlowStatus_s. Calculate flow counts by adding AllowedInFlows_d, DeniedInFlows_d, AllowedOutFlows_d and DeniedOutFlows_d.
4. As a team-owned validation step, check that revised queries return the source/destination, NSG rule and flow-count results you expect.

The version 2 NSG example still splits NSGRules_s even though its projected output uses replacement fields. This is an example inconsistency, not evidence that the old field must remain a dependency. The sources do not provide a complete field-by-field replacement mapping or a service cutover procedure.

If you have a support plan and need technical support, contact Microsoft support.

  3. Replace parsed NSGRules_s values with NSGRule_s, FlowDirection_s and FlowStatus_s. Calculate flow counts by adding AllowedInFlows_d, DeniedInFlows_d, AllowedOutFlows_d and DeniedOutFlows_d.
  4. As a team-owned validation step, check that revised queries return the source/destination, NSG rule and flow-count results you expect.

The version 2 NSG example still splits NSGRules_s even though its projected output uses replacement fields. This is an example inconsistency, not evidence that the old field must remain a dependency. The sources do not provide a complete field-by-field replacement mapping or a service cutover procedure.

If you have a support plan and need technical support, contact Microsoft support.

records.title: On 31 August 2024, both the update management feature of Azure Automation and the Log Analytics agent it uses will be retired
records.summary: Azure Automation Update Management and the Log Analytics agent it uses had a retirement date of August 31, 2024. The Q&A describes this as Update Management end of support and agent deprecation; neither source establishes that running virtual machines shut down. Microsoft directed affected customers to migrate assessment and patching to Azure Update Manager. Check OS compatibility, Azure Arc prerequisites and pricing exemptions before migrating, and account for assessment and Hybrid Worker removal when cleaning up the old solution.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Automation Update Management reached its documented retirement/end-of-support milestone on August 31, 2024, alongside retirement/deprecation of the Log Analytics agent it uses. Microsoft identifies Azure Update Manager as the replacement for virtual-machine assessment and patching.

This notice concerns the Update Management solution, not Azure Automation as a whole or every virtual machine. Azure Update Manager manages Windows and Linux servers on Azure VMs and Azure Arc-connected machines without depending on Azure Automation or Log Analytics.

The supplied content does not establish pre-retirement maintenance or security-update commitments, regional exceptions or exactly which old-service functions remained available afterward.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify whether you use Azure Automation Update Management and its Log Analytics agent. No complete inventory method is supplied. The Q&A moderator says customers without Automation accounts can ignore this Update Management notification.
2. Check replacement prerequisites and capability gaps. Non-Azure machines require Azure Arc. Azure Update Manager does not support Windows 10/11 patching; the FAQ recommends Microsoft Intune for those devices. Azure Lighthouse integration is unsupported. Check the OS support matrix; the Q&A leaves CIS-hardened Windows 2019/2022 support unresolved and does not validate the proposed workaround.
3. Migrate assessment and patching to Azure Update Manager using the referenced migration guide. Microsoft's documented target was before/by August 31, 2024. The supplied content does not reproduce the procedure or establish whether its script is required.
4. Review pricing eligibility before onboarding Arc-enabled servers. The FAQ identifies exemptions, including eligible existing Automation Update Management servers that used the service for free as of September 1, 2023. Newly onboarded machines in the same subscription are not automatically exempt.
5. Account for cleanup effects before deleting the old updates solution from the Log Analytics workspace: this removes VMs from the old solution, stops its assessments and deletes associated system Hybrid Workers, including when automatic inclusion of available and future machines was enabled.

Detailed migration validation, export, backup and cutover instructions are not supplied.

records.title: Upgrade Azure Database for MySQL to MySQL v8.0 before support for v5.7 ends
records.summary: Azure Database for MySQL 5.7 Standard Support ended on September 30, 2026 under the supplied current version policy. Servers remaining on 5.7 automatically entered paid Extended Support on October 1, 2026, through March 31, 2029; these are support milestones, not scheduled workload shutdown dates. Older announcement and Q&A content instead gives September 30, 2025 as the Flexible Server 5.7 support endpoint, with the Q&A calling it extended-support end. This synthesis uses the applicable current product guidance without treating the discrepancy as an explicitly documented extension. Single Server separately retired on September 16, 2024. Upgrade to a version within Standard Support to avoid Extended Support charges. Although the original notice recommends 8.0, its Standard Support ends on January 31, 2027; the supplied upgrade guide also supports 5.7-to-8.4 upgrades.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Database for MySQL 5.7 moved from Standard Support to automatically enrolled, paid Extended Support on October 1, 2026, following Standard Support end on September 30, 2026. This changes version support and billing; it does not retire the entire service.

The current version policy says Microsoft provides critical security updates during Extended Support, but does not guarantee new features or minor-version upgrades. After Extended Support ends on March 31, 2029, Microsoft stops database-engine security updates and support while continuing maintenance and patching of service components such as the host and operating system.

Single Server separately retired on September 16, 2024. The original notice directed its customers to migrate to Flexible Server before upgrading from 5.7. Existing Flexible Server customers need a version upgrade rather than that deployment migration.

The original notice recommends MySQL 8.0. Current supplied guidance also lists MySQL 8.4 as generally available and documents Flexible Server upgrades from 5.7 to either 8.0 or 8.4. The upgrade procedure alone does not establish a retirement date. No regional exceptions are documented.
what.html:
Azure Database for MySQL 5.7 moved from Standard Support to automatically enrolled, paid Extended Support on October 1, 2026, following Standard Support end on September 30, 2026. This changes version support and billing; it does not retire the entire service.

The current version policy says Microsoft provides critical security updates during Extended Support, but does not guarantee new features or minor-version upgrades. After Extended Support ends on March 31, 2029, Microsoft stops database-engine security updates and support while continuing maintenance and patching of service components such as the host and operating system.

Single Server separately retired on September 16, 2024. The original notice directed its customers to migrate to Flexible Server before upgrading from 5.7. Existing Flexible Server customers need a version upgrade rather than that deployment migration.

The original notice recommends MySQL 8.0. Current supplied guidance also lists MySQL 8.4 as generally available and documents Flexible Server upgrades from 5.7 to either 8.0 or 8.4. The upgrade procedure alone does not establish a retirement date. No regional exceptions are documented.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your deployment and version. Inspect each Flexible Server's version, compute tier, read replicas and high-availability configuration in the Azure portal. If you still have an unresolved Single Server migration, the original sequence was migration to Flexible Server 5.7, stabilization, then a major-version upgrade. Its retirement date has passed; the inputs do not establish a current recovery path for remaining Single Server deployments.
2. Choose a supported target. To avoid or stop Extended Support charges, choose a version within Standard Support. The policy's exit FAQ more narrowly requires community support; a target satisfying both avoids that ambiguity. The supplied guide supports Flexible Server 5.7-to-8.0 and 5.7-to-8.4 upgrades. Consider that 8.0 Standard Support ends on January 31, 2027, rather than following the original 8.0 recommendation without checking its lifecycle.
3. Test compatibility before production. Review removed features and test an upgrade on a restored server copy. Check drivers, authentication, connections, queries and performance. Remove unsupported sql_mode values identified by the guide: NO_AUTO_CREATE_USER, NO_FIELD_OPTIONS, NO_KEY_OPTIONS and NO_TABLE_OPTIONS. Use the documented compatibility checks as applicable; online 8.0-to-8.4 validation is in preview, can lock tables, and is not a substitute for application testing. The guide directs you to the community upgrade checker for pre-upgrade validation.
4. Prepare recovery and dependencies. Take an on-demand production backup, commit or roll back all XA transactions, and upgrade associated read replicas before the primary. A successful upgrade cannot be downgraded in place; returning to the previous version requires restoring a pre-upgrade backup to a new server.
5. Schedule downtime and upgrade. In-place upgrades preserve connection strings but interrupt access, including with HA. Microsoft upgrades the HA standby and primary as one operation; do not upgrade the standby separately. Portal upgrades are documented; Azure CLI requires version 2.40.0 or later. REST API or SDK upgrade requests must not change other service properties simultaneously.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected by the 5.7 support transition if your Azure Database for MySQL servers still use that version. The supplied material does not inspect your resources or establish your exposure. Single Server retirement is a separate deployment-level change.

Support and charges

Remaining on 5.7 triggers automatic paid Extended Support from October 1, 2026 under current guidance. Billing is per vCore per hour for servers in succeeded state, not stopped servers. Read replicas and HA add chargeable vCores. No rates or environment-specific estimate are supplied.

After Extended Support ends on March 31, 2029, database-engine security updates, bug fixes and engine-related support stop. Service-component maintenance continues. Current policy says new servers cannot use the retired version, while point-in-time recovery and read-replica creation remain available for existing servers. New capabilities might require supported versions, and uptime SLAs do not cover downtime caused by database-engine bugs.

These milestones do not establish automatic workload shutdown or data deletion. Microsoft may stop a compute node if a retired engine vulnerability seriously threatens the service and require an upgrade before bringing it online; that is a conditional intervention.

Upgrade effects

In-place upgrades cause downtime based on database size and table count, even with HA, but preserve connection strings. Replica-promotion and restored-server cutovers require new connection strings. Older clients and removed features can cause connection or compatibility failures. Online validation can lock tables and cause query timeouts.

For failed HA upgrades, the guide documents rollback; that does not make a successful upgrade reversible in place. Burstable upgrades incur General Purpose charges during actual use and remain on that tier after failure unless changed.

Historical deployment restrictions

The older Q&A lists ordinary 5.7 portal creation ending in January 2024 and CLI creation ending in April 2024, with replica, restore and MariaDB-migration exceptions through September 2025. Its Single Server migration exception is inconsistent: September 2024 in the table versus support end in the narrative. Current policy allows recovery and replica creation for existing servers after Extended Support ends, so the older restrictions should not be treated as confirmed current limits.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance:
Azure Database for MySQL 5.7 Standard Support ended on September 30, 2026 under the supplied current version policy. Servers still running 5.7 automatically entered paid Extended Support on October 1, 2026, which runs through March 31, 2029. The structured deadline represents the 5.7 Standard Support endpoint, not a workload shutdown or separate migration target.

Different scopes and conflicting guidance

- Single Server: retirement and its 5.7 support endpoint were September 16, 2024, according to the original notice and Q&A. The supplied pages with Single Server URLs contain Flexible Server announcements and do not independently confirm that retirement date.
- Older Flexible Server guidance: the announcement gives September 30, 2025 as the 5.7 support endpoint; the Q&A calls it extended-support end. Current version-policy guidance instead specifies Standard Support through September 30, 2026, followed by paid Extended Support. This synthesis prefers that applicable current guidance; the inputs do not explicitly document an extension reconciling these descriptions.
- Upgrade-target consideration: MySQL 8.0 Standard Support ends on January 31, 2027; its paid Extended Support runs from February 1, 2027 through May 31, 2029. These are not 5.7 deadlines.

Oracle's 5.7 retirement on October 31, 2023 is a separate community milestone. Neither Azure Standard Support end nor Extended Support end is documented as an automatic workload shutdown.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
The supplied upgrade guide documents upgrade tracking, but no retirement-wide inventory command, migration dashboard or automated progress report.

1. Monitor the upgrade in the Azure portal, review its operation result and check the reported MySQL version. For read replicas, confirm the target version on Overview before upgrading the primary.
2. Verify application connections, reads and writes; also check HA health where applicable. Review and resolve reported errors before retrying a failed upgrade.
3. For replica cutover, stop new operations on the original primary and confirm Slave_IO_Running and Slave_SQL_Running are yes and Seconds_Behind_Master is 0 before promotion. These checks show catch-up at that point, not overall migration completion.
4. Confirm the resulting version meets the policy's Extended Support exit requirements. The policy says upgrading to a version with community support automatically ends enrollment and billing, but supplies no billing-verification procedure.

For team-owned tracking, retain deployment and version inventories, the selected target, compatibility-test results, backup evidence, operation results and application checks. For Single Server migrations, also record migration and stabilization on Flexible Server. These are local planning records, not evidence that this website inspects resources or saves checklist progress. Schema validation alone does not establish application compatibility or performance.

For help, use Microsoft Q&A or, if you have a support plan, create a technical support request. The version policy also names Ask Azure Database For MySQL for Extended Support questions or feedback.

records.title: Upgrade to Standard SKU public IP addresses in Azure by 30 September 2025—Basic SKU will be retired
records.summary: Azure Basic SKU public IP addresses retired on September 30, 2025. Microsoft's upgrade guidance states that affected addresses remain operational after retirement, but without support or SLA guarantees; it gives no shutdown date. Upgrade to Standard SKU as soon as possible and plan for downtime and resource-specific requirements. Existing and new Cloud Services Extended Support deployments are exempt. VPN Gateway has separate migration timelines not supplied here. The announcement restricted new Basic SKU creation after March 31, 2025; the upgrade guidance permits creation for exempt Cloud Services Extended Support deployments through non-portal methods.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Basic SKU public IP addresses retired on September 30, 2025. For affected resources, Microsoft directs you to upgrade or migrate to Standard SKU to retain support. Basic addresses remain operational after retirement, but without support or SLA guarantees; no shutdown date is supplied.

Existing and new Cloud Services Extended Support (CSES) deployments are exempt. You can continue using Basic public IPs for those deployments and create them through non-portal methods such as Azure CLI or PowerShell.

Standard public IPs use static allocation and block inbound traffic by default when used as a frontend unless a network security group permits it. Standard supports zonal and zone-redundant configurations, with zone redundancy limited to regions supporting availability zones. Standard v2 currently works only with Standard v2 NAT Gateway, not other components.

The supplied content does not document security-update commitments or distinguish IPv4 and IPv6 retirement dates.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Basic SKU public IPs and associated resources. Exclude existing and new CSES deployments, which require no retirement migration. The supplied content does not provide a centralized inventory query.
2. Review Standard SKU pricing, allocation, security and compatibility requirements. Load balancer and public IP SKUs must match; a public IP used with a Standard Load Balancer must also match its tier. Standard v2 is currently limited to Standard v2 NAT Gateway. If you need a zone-redundant public IP, create a new Standard IP in a region supporting availability zones.
3. Plan downtime and follow the migration guidance for each resource:

- Virtual machines: use the applicable standalone-VM or availability-set script, or manually detach and upgrade the public IP.
- Virtual Machine Scale Sets: replace Basic instance public IPs with new Standard IPs. Uniform-model per-instance public IP configurations are not Public IP resources and cannot be upgraded in place.
- Basic Load Balancer: migrate to Standard Load Balancer using the referenced upgrade script.
- VPN Gateway: follow its separate migration guidance and timeline, which are not supplied here. The upgrade page states that all non-AZ SKUs become AZ SKUs.
- ExpressRoute gateway: use the gateway migration experience. For zone redundancy, select an availability zone-enabled gateway SKU; Azure assigns and manages the zone-redundant public IP.
- Application Gateway v1: migrate to v2; v1's separate retirement date was April 28, 2026.
- Azure Databricks: ephemeral workloads receive Standard IPs as VMs are replaced through regular usage. For long-running workloads, the page recommends restarting compute resources to replace Basic IPs.
- Disassociated public IPs: follow the referenced Azure portal, PowerShell or Azure CLI upgrade procedure.

4. Configure network security groups to permit required inbound traffic with Standard SKU.
5. As a team-owned validation step, confirm the resulting SKU, associated-resource compatibility and required connectivity.

Microsoft directs affected customers to upgrade as soon as possible. The supplied content references migration procedures but does not include detailed cutover, backup, rollback or post-migration validation steps.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if you use Azure Basic SKU public IP addresses outside the CSES exception. The migration path depends on the associated resource; some paths upgrade existing public IP resources, while others require replacement addresses or gateway/load-balancer migration. Standard SKU public IPs are not identified as retiring.

If you take no action, Microsoft's upgrade guidance states that Basic IPs remain operational after retirement, but without support or SLA guarantees. This is not a documented immediate workload shutdown.

Plan for migration downtime. Standard uses static allocation, while Basic supports dynamic allocation. Standard's inbound security model can interrupt required connectivity unless network security group rules permit traffic. Load balancer and public IP SKUs must match. Uniform-model VM Scale Set instance public IP configurations require new addresses rather than an in-place upgrade; address preservation is not established for all migration paths.

Existing and new CSES deployments remain unaffected, although creating Basic public IPs for CSES requires non-portal methods.

Review pricing before migrating. The pricing page states that ARM static public IPs remain chargeable regardless of the associated resource's state, but it does not support a migration cost estimate. The supplied content does not establish retirement-related data deletion or retention consequences, and it provides no assessment of your resources.

records.title: Custom views with view designer are migrating to Azure Monitor workbooks
records.summary: Azure Monitor is retiring View Designer custom views in Log Analytics workspaces in favor of workbooks. The transition began in March 2020, but the supplied sources give no final retirement date or existing-view shutdown date. The announcement says creation of new custom views through View Designer in the Azure portal would stop after an initial three-month phase, without an exact cutoff. Recreate your custom views in workbooks; the transition guide provides examples rather than an automatic conversion.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Monitor is retiring View Designer custom views in Log Analytics workspaces and transitioning them to workbooks. The staged transition began in March 2020; the final retirement date is unspecified.

Microsoft states that workbooks support the capabilities available in View Designer, with additional data sources, personal and shared views, custom layouts, cross-resource queries, parameters and templates. The transition guide describes recreating views, not automatic conversion.

The sources do not specify regional exceptions, how long existing views remain available, or retirement-related support and security-update commitments. The workbook overview describes the replacement service; it does not independently establish a retirement schedule.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify the View Designer views you need to recreate, including their queries, layouts and overview tiles. The sources provide no automated discovery method for affected views.
2. Recreate those views in Azure Monitor workbooks. The transition guide references sample JSON for vertical and tabbed layouts and examples for recreating visualization-and-list tiles.
3. Access, modify and save replacements through the workbook gallery. Viewing or editing requires appropriate permissions, including access to the resources used by each workbook. For shared editing, team members need the same access to the Azure resources.
4. As a team-owned validation step, compare replacement queries and visualizations with the original views.

Optionally, replace overview-tile navigation by pinning workbook visualizations or an entire workbook to an Azure dashboard. For individual visualizations, enable Always show the pin icon on this step.

The sources provide no required export, backup, cutover or cleanup procedure.

records.title: Version 2 of Translator is retiring on 24 May 2021
records.summary: Microsoft retired Translator V2 on May 24, 2021. Applications using V2 must move to V3, changing endpoints, API methods and XML payloads to JSON. Existing subscription keys remain valid, but some V2 capabilities have no V3 equivalent. The earlier April 30, 2019 end-of-support statement is a separate milestone, not evidence of an extended retirement date. The supplied guidance does not establish how V2 requests behave after retirement.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired Translator V2 on May 24, 2021 and directs V2 applications to V3, which the migration guidance describes as generally available and fully supported.

V3 changes the endpoint to api.cognitive.microsofttranslator.com and requires JSON requests and responses instead of XML. You can retain your existing Translator subscription and authentication key.

Important capability differences include:

- Translator text-to-speech methods are not supported in V3; Microsoft identifies Microsoft Speech Service for that functionality.
- AddTranslation, AddTranslationArray, GetTranslations and GetTranslationsArray have no supported V3 equivalent listed.
- V3 cannot access Translator Hub custom systems and does not support the standard categories SMT, speech, tech and generalnn. Microsoft identifies Custom Translator for neural customization.

The migration page's feature summary contains contradictory XML/JSON wording. Its detailed migration instructions explicitly require JSON and state that V3 neither accepts nor returns XML. The supplied pages do not document regional exceptions or V2 post-retirement maintenance and security-update commitments.

The supplied pages do not document regional exceptions or V2 post-retirement maintenance and security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify applications calling the V2 endpoint, api.microsofttranslator.com. Inventory their methods, XML handling, standard categories and Translator Hub dependencies.
2. Review the referenced V3 documentation and migration guidance. Change translation calls to api.cognitive.microsofttranslator.com and update request and response handling to JSON. Reuse your existing subscription and authentication key; a new subscription is not required.
3. Update method mappings: TranslateArray to Translate, DetectArray to Detect, GetLanguageNames and GetLanguagesForTranslate to Languages, and BreakSentences to BreakSentence.
4. Address capability gaps before treating migration as complete. Use Microsoft Speech Service for Speak and GetLanguagesForSpeak functionality. Assess Custom Translator for neural customization; it does not make existing Translator Hub systems directly accessible through V3. No supported V3 equivalent is listed for AddTranslation, AddTranslationArray, GetTranslations or GetTranslationsArray.
5. As a team-owned validation step, verify translation results, JSON compatibility, method replacements, customization and billing assumptions for each application.

The retirement notice required migration before May 24, 2021 to avoid disruption. The supplied material does not provide a complete cutover, rollback, export, backup or cleanup procedure. Historical guidance about mixing V2 and V3 during a migration period does not establish that V2 remains available.

records.title: Announcing Avere vFXT for Azure Retirement
records.summary: Avere vFXT for Azure retired on September 30, 2025. Microsoft ended software support and new-cluster creation after that date. Existing clusters can continue running unsupported; retirement does not automatically disable them. Billing continues until you remove all vFXT resources. Any Microsoft-initiated removal after retirement requires 90 days’ notice to owners; no removal date is specified.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Avere vFXT for Azure retired on September 30, 2025. Microsoft no longer provides software support, including setup, configuration and troubleshooting assistance, and you cannot create new clusters after retirement.

Existing clusters can continue running unsupported in your subscription; retirement does not automatically disable them.

Microsoft also hid the Marketplace offer during the retirement process. Hiding alone did not prevent existing customers from using existing workflows, including Terraform, but did not extend the new-cluster creation deadline.

records.title: Azure AI Video Indexer features adjustments following Media Services Retirement
records.summary: Azure AI Video Indexer retired Azure Media Services-dependent APIs and ended classic-account update and deletion support on June 30, 2024. Classic accounts required migration to ARM-based accounts; existing ARM-based accounts also required API changes to retain account access. Newly uploaded videos switched to single-bitrate encoding, while existing adaptive-bitrate videos remained playable. Creation of new classic accounts ended earlier, on January 15, 2024.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure AI Video Indexer removed its Azure Media Services dependencies on June 30, 2024. Updated APIs replaced Azure Media Services-dependent APIs, and classic-account update and deletion operations were no longer supported.

Newly uploaded videos switched to single-bitrate encoding. Existing adaptive-bitrate videos remained available for playback.

The notice covers classic accounts and existing ARM-based accounts. It does not specify affected API versions, regional exceptions or security-update commitments. The supplied documentation landing pages do not independently establish these retirement changes.

records.title: View Designer in Azure Monitor is retiring on 31 August 2023
records.summary: Azure Monitor View Designer retired on August 31, 2023, ending support for the feature and existing views under Log Analytics Workspace. Create and clone functionality had already been disabled on November 30, 2020. Microsoft directs you to recreate custom views in Workbooks. The supplied content does not establish that retirement shuts down workloads, deletes views or removes underlying data.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Monitor retired View Designer, including existing custom views under Log Analytics Workspace, on August 31, 2023. Microsoft no longer supports the feature and directs you to transition custom views to Workbooks.

The transition guide describes recreating common layouts and tiles, not an automatic conversion. Workbooks support logs, metrics, text, parameters, custom layouts, and personal or shared views. The supplied content does not establish complete feature parity, regional exceptions or security-update commitments.
what.html:
Azure Monitor retired View Designer, including existing custom views under Log Analytics Workspace, on August 31, 2023. Microsoft no longer supports the feature and directs you to transition custom views to Workbooks.

The transition guide describes recreating common layouts and tiles, not an automatic conversion. Workbooks support logs, metrics, text, parameters, custom layouts, and personal or shared views. The supplied content does not establish complete feature parity, regional exceptions or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify the View Designer custom views you need to recreate, including their queries, layouts and overview tiles. The supplied content provides no automated inventory method.
2. Recreate those views in Workbooks using the referenced transition guide. It describes sample JSON for vertical and tabbed layouts and ways to recreate visualization-and-list tiles.
3. Access, modify and save your replacements through the workbook gallery. For shared editing, team members need the same access to the Azure resources.
4. As a team-owned validation step, compare the recreated queries and visualizations with the original views.

Optionally, replace overview-tile navigation by pinning workbook visualizations or an entire workbook to an Azure dashboard. For individual visualizations, enable Always show the pin icon on this step.

The supplied content does not document a required export, backup, cutover or cleanup procedure. If you have a support plan and need technical support, contact Microsoft.

Azure Monitor Mobile Analytics is a migration option announced in Public Preview. The supplied guidance does not confirm general availability, complete Diagnostics replacement coverage or a separate security-update commitment for the extended App Center support period.

actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:

  - Test: BrowserStack App Automate, using its Device Testing CLI and migration guidance.
  - Distribution: App Store for iOS production, TestFlight for iOS testing, Google Play for Android production and Google Play Console for Android testing. Azure Pipelines tasks can distribute to these destinations. For Microsoft Store apps, use Partner Center Package Flights.
  - CodePush: Microsoft's independent version, integrated into your app and deployed separately from App Center.
  - Analytics & Diagnostics: Evaluate Azure Monitor mobile migration guidance. Mobile Analytics was announced in Public Preview; full Diagnostics coverage and general availability are not confirmed. Microsoft Store developers can use Partner Center analytics and diagnostics; custom events through the Microsoft Store Services SDK apply to UWP apps published in Microsoft Store.
3. Plan your Analytics & Diagnostics migration around the end-of-March-2027 support milestone. The supplied guidance gives no separate exact migration deadline or detailed validation, data-export, backup, cutover or cleanup requirements.

records.title: Retirement: VpnGw1-5 (Non-AZ SKUs) will be retired on Sep 30, 2026 – gateways will be automatically migrated to AZ SKUs
records.summary: Azure VPN Gateway is consolidating VpnGw1–5 Non-AZ SKUs into availability-zone-supported SKUs. The announcement explicitly sets retirement for September 30, 2026; product guidance instead says deprecation is scheduled after September 2026 without an exact date. The exact retirement timing therefore remains unconfirmed across the sources. Microsoft describes automatic migration, but its completion timing also conflicts. Product guidance recommends manual upgrades and says remaining Non-AZ gateways will reject management and configuration operations after an undated rollout; it does not announce a VPN traffic shutdown. Existing AZ SKUs need no consolidation migration, Basic gateway SKU is not retiring, and legacy Standard and High Performance SKUs require separate guidance.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure VPN Gateway is consolidating VpnGw1–5 Non-AZ SKUs into availability-zone-supported SKUs. Microsoft describes automatic migration and recommends manual upgrades. Product guidance says existing SKUs remain supported until migrated; it does not specify separate security-update commitments.

- Existing AZ SKUs need no consolidation migration.
- Standard and High Performance legacy SKUs require separate guidance.
- Basic gateway SKU is not retiring, and Gen1 has no announced retirement date.

Availability-zone-supported SKUs can be deployed in every region, but remain regional where availability zones are unavailable. Microsoft says it will enable zone redundancy when the region supports availability zones.
what.html:
Azure VPN Gateway is consolidating VpnGw1–5 Non-AZ SKUs into availability-zone-supported SKUs. Microsoft describes automatic migration and recommends manual upgrades. Product guidance says existing SKUs remain supported until migrated; it does not specify separate security-update commitments.

  • Existing AZ SKUs need no consolidation migration.
  • Standard and High Performance legacy SKUs require separate guidance.
  • Basic gateway SKU is not retiring, and Gen1 has no announced retirement date.

Availability-zone-supported SKUs can be deployed in every region, but remain regional where availability zones are unavailable. Microsoft says it will enable zone redundancy when the region supports availability zones.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify affected gateways. In the Azure portal, open the virtual network gateway and select Configuration, then check SKU. Alternatively, use Get-AzVirtualNetworkGateway and inspect the SKU name, or az network vnet-gateway show and query sku.name.
2. For VpnGw1–5 gateways without an AZ suffix, select the corresponding availability-zone-supported SKU. Microsoft recommends upgrading through the portal, PowerShell or Azure CLI. Existing AZ gateways need no consolidation migration.
3. Check the public IP SKU. For affected VpnGw1–5 gateways using Basic public IPs, use the VPN Gateway migration tool to upgrade to Standard. This also upgrades the gateway to Gen2; no separate Gen2 migration is needed. Legacy gateways need separate legacy-SKU guidance.
4. Keep Basic gateway SKU handling separate: if it references a Basic public IP, do not use the migration tool. Follow the documented procedure to remove that reference; the public IP address stays the same.
5. Recheck the resulting gateway SKU. As team-owned validation, confirm that required management and configuration operations succeed.

Microsoft also describes automatic migration, but conflicting completion statements leave its timing unconfirmed. Same-family migration has no expected downtime; cross-family upgrades may cause downtime. The supplied content does not document export, backup or detailed cutover steps.

records.title: We are retiring Azure Media Analytics preview processors on June 1, 2020
records.summary: Azure Media Analytics retired five preview processors on June 1, 2020: Motion Detection, Video Summarization, Video Optical Character Recognition, Face Detector and Content Moderator. The notice states that affected applications would begin experiencing errors or failed job submissions afterward. It recommended Video Indexer for OCR, face detection and content moderation, but provided no replacement for Motion Detection or Video Summarization. The historically recommended Video Analyzer preset later retired on September 14, 2023; Azure Media Services retired on June 30, 2024. These are separate milestones, not changes to the preview processors’ retirement date.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Media Analytics retired these preview processors on June 1, 2020:

- Motion Detection (Preview).
- Video Summarization (Preview), also called Azure Media Video Thumbnail MP.
- Video Optical Character Recognition (Preview).
- Face Detector (Preview).
- Content Moderator (Preview).

The retirement notice recommended Video Indexer capabilities for video OCR, face detection and content moderation. It stated that Motion Detection and Video Summarization were not being replaced at the time.

The supplied sources do not document pre-retirement maintenance or security-update commitments, regional exceptions, or current availability of every replacement capability.

  • Video Optical Character Recognition (Preview).

  • Content Moderator (Preview).

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify applications that use any of the five retired preview processors. The notice does not provide a discovery tool or inventory procedure.
2. For video OCR, face detection or content moderation, evaluate Azure Video Indexer against your application’s requirements. The original notice recommended the Video Indexer v2 REST API or the Video Analyzer preset in Azure Media Services v3, with migration before June 1, 2020. Do not treat the latter as a continuing migration destination: the supporting guidance identifies its retirement on September 14, 2023 and Azure Media Services retirement on June 30, 2024. The inputs do not establish current API-version availability or complete feature parity.
3. For Motion Detection or Video Summarization, assess how to address the capability gap; the notice supplies no replacement or migration path.
4. Before uploading videos to Video Indexer, ensure you have the necessary rights and appropriate consent, including for biometric data, and review the referenced service and privacy terms.
5. As team-owned validation, compare the replacement’s outputs with those your applications require before completing your cutover. This is planning advice, not a documented migration-completion check.

The supplied sources do not provide a complete migration procedure, export or backup instructions, cutover sequence, or cleanup requirements.

records.title: Azure Time Series Insights will be retired on 31 March 2025
records.summary: Microsoft's migration guidance identifies July 7, 2024 as the retirement date for Azure Time Series Insights Gen1 and Gen2 and warns of automatic resource deletion if migration is incomplete. This conflicts with the announcement's March 31, 2025 retirement and end-of-support date. The structured deadline follows the applicable product migration guidance; the supplied sources do not reconcile the dates or document an extension. Microsoft recommends Eventhouse in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence; Azure Data Explorer is another documented destination. Gen1 migration requires parallel ingestion for its fixed retention period. Gen2 cold-storage data remains accessible in your storage account after retirement, but this does not preserve the Time Series Insights service.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Azure Time Series Insights Gen1 and Gen2. The migration guidance identifies July 7, 2024 and automatic resource deletion for environments not migrated by then; the announcement instead identifies March 31, 2025 and loss of support afterward. The supplied sources leave this conflict unresolved.

Microsoft recommends Eventhouse in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence. Azure Data Explorer is another documented destination, with readiness guidance and migration tools referenced through the tsi2rti repository.

New feature releases stopped on March 31, 2022. The announcement says instances created before that date can continue to be used and supported through its stated retirement date. The sources do not establish regional exceptions, support eligibility for later-created instances or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Time Series Insights environments and whether they use Gen1 or Gen2. The supplied guidance provides no inventory command.
2. Select a destination. Microsoft recommends Eventhouse in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence; Azure Data Explorer is an alternative. Use the referenced tsi2rti readiness guidance and migration tools for your chosen destination.
3. Plan against the migration guidance's July 7, 2024 deadline while explicitly recording its unresolved conflict with the announcement's March 31, 2025 date.

Gen1 migration to Eventhouse

1. Create an Eventhouse.
2. Establish parallel ingestion from Azure Event Hubs.
3. Continue parallel ingestion for the full fixed retention period so Eventhouse contains the same retained data.
4. Start using Eventhouse, then delete the Time Series Insights environment.

Gen2 migration to Eventhouse

1. Create an Eventhouse.
2. Redirect ingestion to Eventhouse.
3. Import your subscription's cold-storage Parquet blobs using GetData.
4. Start using Eventhouse, then delete the Time Series Insights environment.

After migrating data and establishing continuous ingestion, connect consumption tools or applications. Documented options include Power BI, KQL Querysets, Real-Time Dashboards, KustoTrender and SDKs. For Gen2 hierarchies, the guidance describes Kusto Graph Semantics in Eventhouse.

For Azure Data Explorer, account for differences in query languages and visualization tools: Time Series Insights uses TSQ, while Azure Data Explorer offers KQL and SQL. Review destination pricing. The announcement references a Cost Estimator, but its supplied reference had no readable content. The pricing page documents an Azure pricing calculator; it does not establish a retirement deadline.

Use the referenced detailed Gen1/Gen2 guidance for implementation. The supplied material does not provide validation commands or a separate backup procedure.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
The migration guidance covers Time Series Insights Gen1 and Gen2 and warns of automatic resource deletion if migration is incomplete by July 7, 2024. The announcement instead states retirement and loss of support after March 31, 2025 without defining shutdown or deletion timing. These consequences must not be treated as a confirmed two-phase schedule.

- Gen1: There is no cold storage or hierarchy capability. Its fixed retention period requires parallel ingestion for that period in the documented migration sequence.
- Gen2: Cold data resides as Parquet blobs in your subscription. The guidance says this data remains accessible in your storage account after Time Series Insights resource deletion. It limits Azure Resource Manager access to management operations, such as changing storage-account settings, retrieving properties or keys, and deleting storage accounts; it does not specify the post-retirement data-reading interface.

Retained Gen2 data does not mean the Time Series Insights service remains available. Queries, visualizations, custom applications and hierarchy modeling need destination capabilities; automatic integration compatibility is not established.

For Azure Data Explorer capacity planning, the announcement compares Time Series Insights' 1 MB/s ingestion limit with an Azure Data Explorer example of 200 MB/s per node on a 16-core machine. That example is not a sizing estimate for your workload.

The supplied content does not assess your resources, quantify migration costs or establish storage-retention duration and costs.

progress.guidance:
The migration guidance provides Gen1/Gen2 sequences and references tsi2rti tools, but it does not document an automated retirement tracker, tenant inventory method or completion dashboard.

Maintain a team-owned migration record against the documented milestones:

- Gen1: destination created, parallel ingestion established, full retention period completed, consumption switched and old environment deleted.
- Gen2: destination created, ingestion redirected, cold data imported, consumption switched and old environment deleted.

As local completion evidence, record that migrated data is usable and continuous ingestion is established before switching consumption and deleting the old environment. These are team-owned checks, not a supplied automated assessment; validation commands and tool-coverage guarantees are not documented.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Plan migration of your classic IaaS resources to Azure Resource Manager. The product guidance states a September 6, 2023 retirement date, while the announcement required migration by March 1, 2023. The supplied sources do not reconcile those dates or establish whether this historical migration path remains available.

1. Identify affected resources. Inventory classic Linux and Windows VMs, their virtual networks, storage accounts and attached resources. Determine whether each VM is inside a virtual network. The supplied content does not provide a subscription-wide discovery method.
2. Resolve network prerequisites and blockers. Resource Manager VMs require a virtual network; for VMs outside one, choose a platform-created network or an existing Resource Manager network. Migrate classic ExpressRoute circuits first; ExpressRoute gateway migration requires the gateway and virtual network to share a subscription. Remove endpoint ACLs, remove and later recreate Application Gateway, and establish VNet peering after migration. Reduce each VM's subnet references to one and resolve unsupported availability-set arrangements, including cloud services mixing VMs inside and outside availability sets.
3. Check services sharing the network. Separate Web/Worker Roles from a shared VM network. Networks containing App Service environments, HDInsight services or Dynamics Lifecycle Services-managed VMs are unsupported. Move API Management deployments to another network before migrating their IaaS network.
4. Prepare integrations. Review RBAC policies because resource URIs change. Reconfigure alerts and Autoscale settings, which are dropped. Remove unsupported XML VM extensions or expect them to be dropped. Disable Premium-storage boot diagnostics before migration and re-enable it afterward; the guidance also instructs deletion of screenshot and serial-log blobs to stop their charges. For Defender for Cloud extensions, follow the requirement to disable the subscription policy to remove the monitoring extension. VMs with backup or snapshot extensions are unsupported; consult the referenced FAQ for preserving earlier backups. Disable and re-enable Site Recovery VM replication around storage migration.
5. Migrate compute, networking and storage. Compute and networking migrate independently of storage; migrate associated storage accounts to complete the process. Storage accounts without VM data or associated disks can migrate independently, as can unattached network security groups, route tables and reserved IPs. For classic storage accounts, the documented Azure portal workflow is Settings → Migrate to ARM → Validate → Prepare, then type yes and select Commit if validation passes.
6. Validate locally. As team-owned completion checks, verify migrated resources, application access, RBAC, alerts, Autoscale and affected backup, diagnostics and replication integrations. These checks are planning advice, not a documented retirement-wide completion certification.

The supplied content references additional migration guides and an FAQ but does not include their detailed procedures or a general backup, rollback or cleanup procedure.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are in scope if you use classic Linux or Windows IaaS VMs and their associated resources. The supplied sources do not inspect your subscription or establish how many resources you have.

Retirement consequences

The announcement states that, from March 1, 2023, classic VMs could no longer be started through ASM and Microsoft would move remaining running or stopped-allocated VMs to stopped-deallocated, disrupting running workloads. The product guidance instead schedules retirement for September 6, 2023 without specifying workload shutdown behavior. These conflicting milestones and consequences are not reconciled.

Customers not already using classic IaaS VMs were separately blocked from creating new classic VMs when the announcement took effect; the effective calendar date is not supplied.

Migration effects

- VMs outside a virtual network: Azure stops, deallocates and starts them during migration. Management-plane and data-plane operations may be temporarily unavailable.
- Supported VM configurations inside a virtual network: migration generally changes metadata while VMs remain on the same hardware, network and storage. Applications continue running without migration downtime, but management operations may be temporarily unavailable. This does not cover unsupported configurations.
- Management and integrations: resource URIs change, so RBAC policies may need updates. Alerts and Autoscale settings are dropped; unsupported extensions can also be dropped. Storage migration affects Site Recovery replication.
- Storage visibility: classic images and disks cease to appear in the Azure portal after storage migration, but their backing VHDs remain in the storage account. This does not mean those VHDs are deleted.

The guidance supports migration of virtual networks containing Microsoft Entra Domain Services, subject to other prerequisites. The announcement excludes Cloud Services and storage accounts or virtual networks not used by classic VMs from this retirement.

The sources do not establish general retention or deletion rules or quantify migration costs. The guidance specifically warns that retained boot-diagnostics screenshot and serial-log blobs continue to incur charges.

records.title: We’re retiring Azure Network Watcher Connection Monitor (classic) on 29 February 2024
records.summary: Microsoft retired Azure Network Watcher Connection Monitor (classic) on February 29, 2024 and instructed customers to migrate before that date. New classic monitors could not be created starting July 1, 2021. Current supplied guidance says classic is no longer available, but still includes migration instructions whose present availability is unconfirmed. Move classic monitoring to Connection Monitor and update dashboard and integration metrics manually. The sources do not establish that monitored workloads shut down or specify what happens to unmigrated configurations and historical data.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired Azure Network Watcher Connection Monitor (classic) on February 29, 2024. The replacement is the current Connection Monitor, which supports connectivity monitoring across Azure and hybrid environments using TCP, ICMP and HTTP tests.

The migration guidance describes zero-downtime migration with unchanged monitor names, regions, subscriptions and resource IDs. Migrated monitors appear only in the current Connection Monitor. Metric alerts migrate automatically; dashboards and external integrations require manual metric updates.

These migration descriptions remain alongside statements that classic is no longer available, so current migration availability is unconfirmed. The sources do not document regional retirement exceptions or classic maintenance and security-update commitments. They do not identify the current Connection Monitor or Azure Network Watcher as a whole as retired.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Microsoft instructed you to migrate classic monitoring before February 29, 2024. If you still depend on classic, use the supplied migration guidance, but confirm that its migration interface remains available: current guidance says classic is no longer available.

1. Identify classic monitors and their source endpoints, destinations, tests, alerts, dashboards and integrations. The documented interface is Connection monitor → Migrate Connection Monitors, followed by subscription selection; its present availability is unconfirmed.
2. Check prerequisites. Enable Network Watcher in applicable subscriptions and regions and install the Network Watcher extension on source Azure VMs and scale sets. For a custom Log Analytics workspace, enable Network Watcher in its subscription and region. The overview also requires the Network Performance Monitoring solution in the workspace. On-premises sources require Azure Arc and Azure Monitor Agent; you must enable Azure Arc yourself. Destination endpoints do not require the Network Watcher extension.
3. Check replacement constraints: 100 connection monitors per subscription per region, 20 test groups per monitor, 100 sources and destinations per monitor, and 20 test configurations per monitor. Cross-workspace monitoring has a regional boundary.
4. If the migration interface is available, select monitors and choose Migrate selected. Review monitor properties and workspace selection. Unless customized, migration creates a default Log Analytics workspace in the monitor's subscription and region. Resolve prerequisite errors and refresh before retrying.
5. Review migrated endpoints, test groups and configurations. Migration derives the protocol from port values and leaves success thresholds and optional properties blank. Manually replace ProbesFailedPercent with ChecksFailedPercent and AverageRoundtripMs with RoundTripTimeMs in dashboards and integrations, including Power BI, Grafana and SIEM systems.
6. Validate intended endpoint coverage, test states, logs, metrics and migrated alerts. Confirm that dashboards and integrations use the replacement metrics.

The older migration claim that agents remain unchanged does not override the overview's current requirement for Azure Monitor Agent on on-premises sources; it explicitly says the Log Analytics agent is unsupported there. No retirement-specific backup, cutover or cleanup procedure is supplied.

records.title: We’re retiring Azure Time Series Insights on 7 July 2024 – transition to Azure Data Explorer
records.summary: Microsoft retired Azure Time Series Insights Gen1 and Gen2 on July 7, 2024. The notice states that the service stops functioning and becomes inaccessible, with no support afterward; migration guidance warns of automatic resource deletion if migration is incomplete. Microsoft recommends Eventhouse in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence, with Azure Data Explorer as another documented destination. Gen1 migration requires parallel ingestion for its full fixed retention period. Gen2 cold-storage data remains accessible in your storage account, but this does not preserve the Time Series Insights service. A Q&A listing mentions support after March 2025 without supplying answers; it does not confirm an extension or alternative retirement date.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired Azure Time Series Insights Gen1 and Gen2 on July 7, 2024. This is service shutdown, not only end of support. The supplied guidance identifies no regional or customer exceptions and makes no maintenance or security-update commitment before retirement.

The announcement directs customers to Azure Data Explorer; the migration guidance recommends Eventhouse in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence and also documents Azure Data Explorer as an alternative. The tsi2rti repository provides readiness guidance and migration tools for both destinations.

The notice also states that Time Series Insights no longer receives the updates needed to meet the latest FedRAMP High requirements and can no longer be considered FedRAMP High compliant.
what.html:
Microsoft retired Azure Time Series Insights Gen1 and Gen2 on July 7, 2024. This is service shutdown, not only end of support. The supplied guidance identifies no regional or customer exceptions and makes no maintenance or security-update commitment before retirement.

The announcement directs customers to Azure Data Explorer; the migration guidance recommends Eventhouse in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence and also documents Azure Data Explorer as an alternative. The tsi2rti repository provides readiness guidance and migration tools for both destinations.

The notice also states that Time Series Insights no longer receives the updates needed to meet the latest FedRAMP High requirements and can no longer be considered FedRAMP High compliant.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
The documented migration deadline was July 7, 2024. The supplied guidance does not establish a post-retirement recovery procedure.

1. Identify whether your environments use Gen1 or Gen2. No inventory command is supplied.
2. Select your destination. Microsoft recommends Eventhouse in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence; Azure Data Explorer is another documented option. Use the tsi2rti readiness guidance for the selected destination.
3. Review replacement pricing. The notice references the Azure Data Explorer Cost Estimator, but its content was unavailable in the supplied material. The pricing page also documents the Azure pricing calculator; neither establishes your actual costs.

Gen1 migration sequence

1. Create an Eventhouse and establish parallel ingestion from Azure Event Hubs.
2. Continue parallel ingestion for the full fixed retention period so Eventhouse contains the same retained data.
3. Start using Eventhouse, then delete the Time Series Insights environment.

Gen2 migration sequence

1. Create an Eventhouse and redirect ingestion to it.
2. Import cold-storage Parquet blobs from your subscription using GetData.
3. Start using Eventhouse, then delete the Time Series Insights environment.

These sequences describe Eventhouse migration; use the referenced destination-specific guidance for Azure Data Explorer.

After migrating data and establishing continuous ingestion, connect your applications and consumption tools. Documented options include Power BI, KQL Querysets, Real-Time Dashboards, KustoTrender and SDKs. Plan for the change from TSQ to KQL/SQL. For Gen2 hierarchies, the guidance describes Kusto Graph Semantics in Eventhouse; it does not promise automatic integration or model compatibility.

The supplied material provides no separate backup procedure or validation commands.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
If you used Time Series Insights Gen1 or Gen2, the documented consequence from July 7, 2024 is loss of service access and support. Migration guidance also warns of automatic resource deletion if migration was incomplete. The supplied content does not identify your resources or establish unaffected versions, regions or customer groups.

- Gen1: There is no cold storage or hierarchy capability. Its fixed data-retention period makes parallel ingestion for that full period a prerequisite of the documented migration.
- Gen2: Cold data resides as Parquet blobs in your subscription. The guidance says that data remains accessible in your storage account after Time Series Insights resource deletion. It also limits Azure Resource Manager access to management operations, such as updating storage-account settings, retrieving properties or keys, and deleting storage accounts. It does not specify the post-retirement data-reading interface or retention duration.

Retained Gen2 blobs do not mean the Time Series Insights service remains available. Queries, visualizations, custom applications and hierarchy modeling must use destination capabilities; automatic compatibility is not established.

If you require FedRAMP High compliance, the notice states that Time Series Insights can no longer be considered compliant. Replacement and retained-storage costs are not established by the supplied material.

records.title: We’re retiring Classic Application Insights on 29 February 2024
records.summary: Classic Application Insights retired on February 29, 2024 according to the retirement notice. The migration guide separately documents phased automatic migration beginning in May 2024, without resource-specific dates or a final rollout deadline. Neither source establishes a monitoring shutdown date. Migrate to workspace-based Application Insights to choose your destination workspace, reviewing retention, permissions, exports, pricing and Terraform compatibility. Migration is irreversible and redirects new telemetry without moving historical data.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired Classic Application Insights on February 29, 2024, according to the notice, and is moving classic resources to workspace-based Application Insights. The migration guide documents phased automatic migration beginning in May 2024.

Migration permanently redirects new telemetry to a linked Log Analytics workspace. Historical telemetry stays in classic storage under its existing retention settings; new telemetry follows workspace retention settings. You can change the linked workspace later, but cannot reverse migration.

Microsoft states that migration should not require application downtime, restarts, or changes to instrumentation keys or connection strings. Workspace-based resources are available in all commercial regions and Azure US Government. Resources already linked to a workspace do not need classic-to-workspace migration.

The notice highlights customer-managed encryption keys, capacity reservations with discounted pricing, and diagnostic-settings exports to Azure Storage or Event Hub. It does not document pre-retirement maintenance or security-update commitments.

Workspace-based resources are available in all commercial regions and Azure US Government. Resources already linked to a workspace do not need classic-to-workspace migration.

The notice highlights customer-managed encryption keys, capacity reservations with discounted pricing, and diagnostic-settings exports to Azure Storage or Event Hub. It does not document pre-retirement maintenance or security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify classic resources in each relevant subscription. In Application Insights Overview, check for a missing linked workspace and the classic retirement warning. The guide also documents Azure Resource Graph, CLI and PowerShell inventory methods. Verify ambiguous inventory results against workspace linkage and the portal warning.
2. Choose a destination workspace if you want to control placement rather than wait for automatic migration. Select or create a Log Analytics workspace using Use resource or workspace permissions access control. It may be in another subscription within the same Microsoft Entra tenant and need not share the resource group. If security requirements prevent changing an incompatible workspace's access mode, create another workspace.
3. Review workspace pricing and configure the retention you need before migration. Classic retention settings do not carry over to new workspace telemetry.
4. Disable continuous export before migration. If you need uninterrupted automated exports, configure diagnostic settings beforehand. Validate downstream consumers because the export schema changes and existing Azure Stream Analytics integrations break. Diagnostic settings can also be configured afterward, but that does not provide the documented continuity precaution.
5. If you use Terraform, update the azurerm provider before migration. The guide recommends the latest version and identifies 3.89 or higher as preserving the resource, historical data and connection details. Older versions such as 3.12 can delete and recreate the resource.
6. In Application Insights, open Properties under Configure, select Migrate to Workspace-based, and choose the workspace. Migration is irreversible. Documented programmatic alternatives use Azure CLI with the application-insights extension, Azure PowerShell 8.0 or higher, or ARM templates.
7. Allow up to 24 hours while continuing to access telemetry through Application Insights. Confirm workspace linkage and new telemetry arrival, then validate workspace queries, historical-data access and diagnostic exports. Use the workspace daily cap rather than the Application Insights cap, recognizing that it is not a strict billing limit.
