impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
Classic Application Insights resources are affected; resources already linked to a workspace do not need this migration. If you take no action, the migration guide says Microsoft will automatically migrate classic resources, but gives no resource-specific timing. Manual migration lets you choose the destination workspace.

- Applications and monitoring: Microsoft documents no telemetry collection gaps and no impact to existing data API access, Live Metrics, ingestion-based sampling or pinned dashboards. Classic queries, workbooks and log-based alerts remain compatible within the Application Insights experience. Retirement is not documented as application shutdown.
- Queries and historical data: Direct workspace queries use different, case-sensitive table and column names and show only telemetry ingested after migration. Use the migrated Application Insights Logs tab to query classic and new data together. The guide warns that renaming the resource afterward hides pre-rename telemetry from that tab. Its separate statement that the associated workspace then shows all old and new data conflicts with its post-migration-only workspace limitation; historical-data access after renaming remains unclear.
- Retention: Migration does not move historical data. Classic data retains its existing retention settings and extended-retention charges until it exceeds its retention period. New telemetry follows workspace retention settings.
- Exports and tooling: Continuous export is unsupported after migration. Diagnostic settings change the export schema, can increase costs and require changes to Azure Stream Analytics integrations. An outdated Terraform provider can replace the resource, losing historical data and changing connection details.
- Pricing: The guide says costs usually do not change, but legacy resources lose the 1 GB monthly free allowance. Resources retaining pre-April 2018 nonregional basic-tier pricing move to current regional pricing. Workspace daily caps are not strict billing limits.

The supplied sources do not establish which of your resources are affected or quantify your costs.

Use the migrated Application Insights Logs tab to query classic and new data together. The guide warns that renaming the resource afterward hides pre-rename telemetry from that tab. Its separate statement that the associated workspace then shows all old and new data conflicts with its post-migration-only workspace limitation; historical-data access after renaming remains unclear.
  • Retention: Migration does not move historical data. Classic data retains its existing retention settings and extended-retention charges until it exceeds its retention period. New telemetry follows workspace retention settings.
  • Exports and tooling: Continuous export is unsupported after migration. Diagnostic settings change the export schema, can increase costs and require changes to Azure Stream Analytics integrations. An outdated Terraform provider can replace the resource, losing historical data and changing connection details.
  • Pricing: The guide says costs usually do not change, but legacy resources lose the 1 GB monthly free allowance. Resources retaining pre-April 2018 nonregional basic-tier pricing move to current regional pricing. Workspace daily caps are not strict billing limits.

The supplied sources do not establish which of your resources are affected or quantify your costs.

deadline.dateGuidance:

The migration guide separately says Microsoft began phased automatic migration in May 2024, continuing over several months. It provides no approximate migration dates for individual resources, subscriptions or regions. This later rollout is a different milestone, not a documented extension of the retirement date.

Neither source specifies a monitoring, data-access or workload shutdown date. A manually initiated migration can take up to 24 hours; that is a processing window, not a retirement deadline.

records.title: We’re retiring Network Performance Monitor on 29 February 2024
records.summary: Azure Network Performance Monitor retired on February 29, 2024. Microsoft instructed customers to migrate tests to Connection Monitor in Azure Network Watcher before that date. New tests in existing workspaces and enabling new workspaces were blocked from July 1, 2021. Current supplied guidance says Network Performance Monitor is no longer available, but retains migration procedures whose present availability is unconfirmed. Migration requires checking agent prerequisites, updating alerts and integrations, and disabling legacy tests to stop their documented charges. Connection Monitor does not support ExpressRoute bandwidth monitoring.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Network Performance Monitor retired on February 29, 2024. Microsoft identifies the current Connection Monitor in Azure Network Watcher as its replacement for Performance Monitor, Service Connectivity Monitor and ExpressRoute Monitor tests.

The migration guidance describes transferring tests into connection monitors, test groups, endpoints and configurations. Test and agent descriptions are not migrated. ExpressRoute loss and latency monitoring are supported, but ExpressRoute bandwidth monitoring is not available in Connection Monitor.

The guidance describes zero-downtime migration while also stating that Network Performance Monitor is no longer available; it does not establish that the older migration path remains usable. No regional retirement exceptions or ongoing support and security-update commitments are documented. Do not select Connection monitor (classic), which the supplied overview also says is no longer available.

Do not select Connection monitor (classic), which the supplied overview also says is no longer available.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your Network Performance Monitor workspaces, features, tests and agents. Resolve inactive agents before importing their tests, or record excluded tests and return to them later.
2. Check replacement capabilities and prerequisites. Enable Network Watcher in the workspace's subscription and region and in any different subscription and region containing an Azure VM endpoint. Azure VM sources require the Network Watcher extension. For on-premises sources, the current overview requires Azure Arc and Azure Monitor Agent and explicitly says the Log Analytics agent is unsupported; do not rely on the older migration article's unchanged-agent claim. Enable the Network Performance Monitoring solution in the Log Analytics workspace before creating monitors.
3. Check replacement limits: 100 connection monitors per subscription per region, 20 test groups per monitor, 100 sources and destinations per monitor, and 20 test configurations per monitor. The overview documents a regional boundary for cross-workspace monitoring. Account for the missing ExpressRoute bandwidth capability.
4. If the documented import path remains available, open Connection Monitor in Network Watcher, select Import tests from NPM, choose the subscription, workspace and feature, then select Import. Import requires an enabled Network Performance Monitor configuration with valid tests. The supplied pages do not confirm this path remains usable after service unavailability.
5. Verify the resulting monitors, test groups, endpoints, configurations and results. Update Network Performance Monitor log-based alerts, dashboards and external integrations to use NWConnectionMonitorTestResult and NWConnectionMonitorPathResult, or re-create alerts using metrics. The separate classic-monitor automatic alert migration claim does not establish automatic migration for these tests.
6. Manually disable legacy Network Performance Monitor tests after validating replacement coverage. The migration article says legacy tests remain chargeable until disabled.

No retirement-specific backup procedure is documented. For questions, use Microsoft Q&A; if you have a support plan and need technical help, create a support request.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if you use Network Performance Monitor tests or workspaces, including Performance Monitor, Service Connectivity Monitor or ExpressRoute Monitor. The supplied sources do not establish whether you have affected resources.

New tests and new workspace enablement were blocked from July 1, 2021. The service retired on February 29, 2024, and current guidance says it is no longer available. The sources do not establish that retirement shuts down your applications, VMs or network connections, or clarify current legacy-test continuity.

Migration creates one connection monitor per region and subscription, with test names becoming test group names. Test and agent descriptions are not transferred. ExpressRoute bandwidth monitoring has no documented replacement capability in Connection Monitor. Azure VM and on-premises sources must meet the current agent prerequisites; older unchanged-agent guidance conflicts with the current on-premises requirements.

Historical data remains in the original workspace's NetworkMonitoring table. The documented transition also writes results to NWConnectionMonitorTestResult and NWConnectionMonitorPathResult; after legacy tests are disabled, new data goes only to those two tables. Alerts, dashboards and integrations using the old table require updates.

The migration article says legacy tests incur charges until manually disabled. It provides no retirement-specific retention or deletion schedule, and no supported estimate of your costs.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
The migration guidance documents completion checks, not an automated retirement-wide tracker. Its present applicability is uncertain because it also states that Network Performance Monitor is no longer available.

1. Check that replacement connection monitors appear with the expected test groups, endpoints and configurations.
2. Verify results in NWConnectionMonitorTestResult and NWConnectionMonitorPathResult in the original Log Analytics workspace. Review test states, metrics and alerts, not just import success.
3. Reconcile all original tests against migrated test groups. Import errors can identify missing configurations, features without tests, invalid tests, missing Network Watcher prerequisites and inactive agents. An import that excludes inactive-agent tests is incomplete; enable those agents and migrate their tests again where the procedure remains available.
4. Keep team-owned migration evidence recording test coverage, updated alerts, dashboards and integrations, and confirmation that legacy tests are disabled.

Connection Monitor visibility is limited to resources you can access. Selected coverage levels can monitor only part of a compound resource, so a passing test does not prove complete coverage. Endpoint status is reevaluated every 24 hours; deallocated or scaled-down instances can temporarily appear indeterminate.

Use Microsoft Q&A for questions. If you have a support plan and need technical help, create a support request.

records.title: We’re retiring some Azure Site Recovery support options on March 1, 2023
records.summary: Azure Site Recovery retired support for disaster recovery between on-premises VMM-managed Hyper-V hosts after March 1, 2023. Support for recovery between on-premises VMware or physical server datacenters ended after December 31, 2020. After each applicable date, the affected scenario could no longer be viewed, managed or run in the portal, and replication data would be removed. The supplied reference's March 1, 2027 restrictions concern end-of-support Windows operating systems, not an extension of these scenario retirements.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Site Recovery retired two on-premises-to-on-premises disaster recovery scenarios: recovery between VMM-managed Hyper-V hosts after March 1, 2023, and recovery between VMware or physical server datacenters after December 31, 2020.

Disaster recovery to Azure is outside this retirement's scope. Microsoft recommends Azure as the recovery destination for VMware and Hyper-V VMs. Hyper-V Replica remains an alternative for Hyper-V site-to-site recovery, but Site Recovery cannot manage it.

records.title: Upgrade to Text-to-Speech Neural Voice  by 31 August 2024
records.summary: Microsoft retired Azure Text-to-Speech standard voices on August 31, 2024; they are unsupported from September 1, 2024 for cloud and on-premises speech synthesis. The documented migration deadline was August 31, 2024: replace standard voice names in synthesis requests with supported neural voice names. The supplied notices do not confirm that standard-voice requests stop working after retirement. Separate pricing-page deprecation details do not establish another retirement date or extend this deadline.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired Azure Text-to-Speech standard voices on August 31, 2024 and ended support from September 1, 2024, covering cloud and on-premises speech synthesis. Microsoft directs you to supported neural voices instead.

Existing users could use standard voices through the documented transition period; new users and new Speech resources were directed to neural voices. The retirement notices do not document exceptions, maintenance or security-update commitments.

The pricing page's broader deprecated Standard and Custom Web/Container listings are separate scope information, not evidence that every custom voice shares this retirement date. The product rebranding and language-support references do not independently establish a retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Review the voice names configured in your cloud and on-premises synthesis requests to identify standard-voice use. The notices provide no automated inventory method.
2. Review neural voice pricing and samples, then select supported neural voice names for your languages. Use the supplied language-support reference to check compatibility, including applicable regional or endpoint limits; consult separate documentation for containers or embedded speech.
3. Replace standard voice names with supported neural voice names in affected synthesis requests. The documented completion deadline was August 31, 2024.
4. As a team-owned validation step, test the updated requests in your applications and record the results.

The supplied content references migration instructions but does not include their detailed procedure. It does not establish feature parity, migration prerequisites, rollback or cleanup steps.

records.title: Retirement: We’re retiring v1.x of the JavaScript SDK for Azure Cosmos DB, on August 30, 2020
records.summary: Azure Cosmos DB JavaScript SDK v1.x retired on August 30, 2020. Microsoft’s product guidance states that retired SDKs continue sending requests but receive no support, bug fixes or new features. This conflicts with the original notice’s statement that v1.x would lose access; current product guidance takes precedence for the documented consequence. Upgrade to a supported SDK; the supplied guidance recommends v3. SDK v2’s separate retirement on September 24, 2021 does not change the v1.x deadline.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired Azure Cosmos DB JavaScript SDK v1.x on August 30, 2020. The supplied Node.js SDK guidance covers API for NoSQL and describes retirement as loss of SDK support, bug fixes and new features—not service shutdown.

The original notice offered v2.x or v3.x as upgrade options. Because v2 subsequently retired, the supplied product guidance recommends moving older SDKs to v3. It states no separate security-update commitment.
what.html:
Microsoft retired Azure Cosmos DB JavaScript SDK v1.x on August 30, 2020. The supplied Node.js SDK guidance covers API for NoSQL and describes retirement as loss of SDK support, bug fixes and new features—not service shutdown.

The original notice offered v2.x or v3.x as upgrade options. Because v2 subsequently retired, the supplied product guidance recommends moving older SDKs to v3. It states no separate security-update commitment.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify your applications using Azure Cosmos DB JavaScript SDK v1.x and record their versions. The supplied sources provide no inventory command.
2. Upgrade to a supported SDK. The original notice required upgrading by August 30, 2020; the supplied product guidance recommends v3 rather than the now-retired v2.
3. Plan migration changes using the referenced migration guide and release history. The supplied guide covers v2-to-v3 changes, not a complete direct v1-to-v3 procedure. It covers authentication options, query iteration, response handling, removed stored-procedure upsert usage and item reads that no longer throw on 404.
4. As team-owned validation, check affected application behavior before completing your rollout, including multi-region writes, which v3 enables by default when your account configuration supports them.

The guidance lists Node.js LTS versions as supported platforms. Its documented request-cancellation feature requires an AbortController polyfill for Node.js users.

impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if your applications use Azure Cosmos DB JavaScript SDK v1.x. The supplied sources do not establish which versions your applications use or retirement dates for other languages or APIs.

Under current product guidance, your applications can continue sending requests after retirement, but Microsoft no longer provides support, bug fixes or new features for the retired SDK. Migration can affect client configuration, query iteration, response and error handling, stored-procedure operations and multi-region write behavior. The supplied material does not describe data deletion or quantify migration costs.

records.title: We're retiring Memory Optimized Data Flows in Azure Data Factory - use General Purpose for better performance at a lower price.
records.summary: Azure Data Factory Memory Optimized Data Flows retire on April 1, 2027. New Memory Optimized creation was discontinued from April 1, 2024; existing pipelines can use existing Memory Optimized data flows before retirement. Assign General Purpose integration runtimes to your data flows. The notice includes a contradictory instruction to create a Memory Optimized runtime; ask Microsoft to clarify it. Automatic migration and exact post-retirement workload behavior are not documented. The supplied Front Door reference concerns a different service and does not corroborate this retirement.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft is retiring Azure Data Factory Memory Optimized Data Flows on April 1, 2027 and directs data flows to the General Purpose SKU. The notice does not describe automatic migration.

Existing pipelines can continue using existing Memory Optimized data flows before retirement. New Memory Optimized creation was discontinued from April 1, 2024.

Microsoft describes General Purpose as offering better performance at a lower price, but provides no workload-specific estimates. The notice also contradicts its migration direction by instructing you to create a Memory Optimized integration runtime despite the creation restriction.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
Prepare your affected data flows for retirement on April 1, 2027:

1. Identify data flows and pipelines using Memory Optimized integration runtimes. The notice does not provide a discovery method.
2. Assign General Purpose integration runtimes to existing and new data flows, following the notice's stated migration direction.
3. Ask Microsoft to clarify the contradictory instruction to create a Memory Optimized runtime rather than relying on it.

Detailed migration prerequisites, validation, cutover, backup and cleanup procedures are not provided.

records.title: We're retiring the Log Analytics agent in Azure Monitor on 31 August 2024
records.summary: The Azure Monitor Log Analytics agent (MMA/OMS) retired on August 31, 2024 and is no longer supported. Cloud ingestion is being shut down: after March 2, 2026, uploads can stop at any time without further notice. Migrate affected Windows and Linux machines to Azure Monitor Agent and data collection rules, validate monitoring and dependent services, then remove the old agent or its workspace configurations. Agents connected exclusively to on-premises SCOM are exempt.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) replaces the Log Analytics agent, also called Microsoft Monitoring Agent (MMA) or Operations Management Suite (OMS), which retired on August 31, 2024. This affects cloud data collection from Windows and Linux machines in Azure, on-premises and other clouds. AMA uses data collection rules (DCRs) instead of workspace-based collection configuration.

Microsoft no longer supports the old agent or provides new distributions or service packs. Azure portal installation is unavailable, although offline and extension-based installation still work. Cloud uploads can stop at any time after March 2, 2026.

Agents connected exclusively to on-premises SCOM are exempt. The supplied content does not establish retirement of Log Analytics workspaces or workspace-based Application Insights, or document regional exceptions or separate security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Inventory agents, workspaces, solutions and dependent services with the Azure Monitor Agent Migration Helper workbook. Stop automated Log Analytics agent deployments to new servers.
2. Check AMA prerequisites, permissions and support for your required collection. For non-Azure and on-premises servers, install the Azure Arc Connected Machine agent first.
3. Plan dependent-service changes. Use Azure Update Manager for Azure Automation Update Management; Azure Update Manager does not use AMA. Create an AMA change-tracking DCR for Change Tracking and Inventory. Switch Defender for Servers Plan 2 agent deployment to agentless scanning, create a custom DCR for Defender security-event collection, and update affected Microsoft Sentinel solutions to their latest versions.
4. Pilot AMA and DCRs. Use DCR Config Generator to convert existing workspace configuration, deploy AMA and the generated rules, and migrate VM insights if used. During testing, remove old-agent workspace configurations without uninstalling the agent to avoid duplicate ingestion where both agents collect the same data.
5. Validate collection by comparing data from both agents over the same period using workspace KQL queries. Check AMA heartbeats, expected data types, record counts and dependent-service operation before expanding deployment. Use built-in Azure Policy policies for AMA extensions and DCR associations at scale and on new machines.
6. After environment-wide validation, remove the old agent, using MMA Discovery and Removal where appropriate. On SCOM-managed machines, retain the agent and SCOM Management Group configuration; remove only its workspace configurations. The Operations Manager Admin Management Pack supports this at scale.

For IIS logs, enable the Service Name (s-sitename) W3C logging field if you need AMA to populate sSiteName. Account for SQL Assessment Solution deployment policies requiring one Log Analytics workspace per subscription.

For assistance, use Microsoft Q&A or create a technical support request if you have a support plan.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if Windows or Linux machines use the Log Analytics agent for cloud data collection, including machines outside Azure. The supplied content does not establish which resources you have.

Without migration, uploads can stop at any time after March 2, 2026 without further notice. This is a monitoring-data ingestion risk; the guidance does not state that monitored machines or workloads shut down. Microsoft no longer supports the agent. Portal installation is unavailable, while offline and extension-based installation still work.

Use the Migration Helper workbook to identify agents, workspaces and dependent solutions. For additional visibility, copy the Azure Monitor Workspace Auditing workbook from its repository and import it into your Log Analytics workspace. It shows data sources, heartbeats and resources sending data, including Application Insights resources; this visibility does not itself establish that every listed resource needs migration.

Migration also affects dependent services and deployment automation. Concurrent collection by both agents can cause duplicate ingestion. AMA IIS collection can omit sSiteName unless you enable the corresponding logging field. SQL Assessment Solution policies require one workspace per subscription. The supplied content does not quantify costs or establish retained-data deletion or data-access consequences.

Agents connected exclusively to on-premises SCOM are exempt. For SCOM-managed machines that also collect to workspaces, preserve the agent's SCOM configuration and remove workspace configurations after validating replacement collection.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use the Azure Monitor Agent Migration Helper workbook to inventory agents, audit workspaces, identify dependencies and track migration progress. It shows configured solutions, their last use and migration recommendations.

For detailed workspace analysis, copy the Azure Monitor Workspace Auditing workbook from its repository and import it into your Log Analytics workspace. Its data-source, heartbeat and resource views support discovery but do not replace collection validation.

Verify completion by comparing ingested data over the same period, checking AMA heartbeats in the Heartbeat table filtered by Category, confirming expected data types and record counts, and validating dependent services. Finish by removing the old agent or, for SCOM-managed machines, its workspace configurations while preserving SCOM configuration.

Record validation results and cleanup status as team-owned migration evidence. The guidance does not provide a single automatic completion check covering every dependency. The Q&A's suggested recent-heartbeat query is not confirmed to distinguish the retiring agent from other agents and is not proof of completion.

For help, use Microsoft Q&A or, if you have a support plan, create a technical support request.

records.title: Wire Data 2.0 (preview) will be retired on 31 March 2022
records.summary: Microsoft retired Wire Data 2.0 (Preview) in Azure Monitor and ended support on March 31, 2022. Customers were directed to transition to VM insights or Service Map before that date to avoid or minimize disruption to network connection monitoring and analysis. Migration includes replacement onboarding, WireData query updates and removal of the Wire Data solution while retaining the Dependency agent. The supplied guidance does not establish a workload shutdown date or historical-data deletion schedule.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
Microsoft retired Wire Data 2.0 (Preview) in Azure Monitor on March 31, 2022 and directs new and existing customers to VM insights or Service Map.

Both replacements use the Log Analytics agent and Dependency agent to collect network connection data and connect with Microsoft Sentinel. Their Map data set is described as comparable to Wire Data 2.0, not identical. VM insights also provides performance data and additional analysis features.

The supplied guidance does not document regional exceptions or post-retirement maintenance and security-update commitments.
what.html:
Microsoft retired Wire Data 2.0 (Preview) in Azure Monitor on March 31, 2022 and directs new and existing customers to VM insights or Service Map.

Both replacements use the Log Analytics agent and Dependency agent to collect network connection data and connect with Microsoft Sentinel. Their Map data set is described as comparable to Wire Data 2.0, not identical. VM insights also provides performance data and additional analysis features.

The supplied guidance does not document regional exceptions or post-retirement maintenance and security-update commitments.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify Log Analytics workspaces using Wire Data 2.0 and their reporting VMs. Check whether each VM already has VM insights or Service Map enabled.
2. Choose Service Map for its Map data set, or VM insights for that data set plus performance data and additional analysis features. Both require the Log Analytics agent and Dependency agent; consult the referenced deployment guidance for requirements and onboarding methods.
3. Onboard VMs that have only Wire Data enabled. Do not duplicate onboarding for VMs already using either replacement. The notice directed transition before March 31, 2022.
4. Migrate WireData queries using the documented replacement examples. Most use VMConnection; the IP-address inventory example uses VMComputer. Update field names, byte calculations and direction values as documented.
5. As a team-owned validation step, confirm replacement data and migrated queries meet your monitoring needs before removing Wire Data 2.0 from affected workspaces.

Keep the Dependency agent for VM insights or Service Map. Removing Wire Data removes its management pack unless another installed replacement uses it. No export or backup procedure is supplied.

VMs already using VM insights or Service Map have a replacement enabled, but WireData-based queries still need migration. The replacement data set is comparable; complete field and feature parity is not established.

records.title: Retirement notice: Windows Server 2022 will retire with k8s 1.34 in March 2027
records.summary: AKS product migration guidance sets Windows Server 2022 node-pool end of support at June 30, 2028 and node-image removal at June 30, 2029, when scaling operations will fail. This guidance takes precedence over the supplied announcement's March 15, 2027 retirement date; the inputs do not explicitly document an extension. Migrate to a supported Windows Server version. In-place migration to Windows Server 2025 is a constrained preview; manual migration uses a new node pool. Neither milestone establishes automatic workload shutdown.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement:
AKS is retiring support for Windows Server 2022 node pools on June 30, 2028, according to the product migration guidance. Microsoft will remove their existing node images on June 30, 2029, after which scaling operations will fail.

The announcement gives a conflicting retirement date of March 15, 2027. It allows continued use on Kubernetes 1.34 and earlier through March 14, 2027 and prohibits creating Windows Server 2022 pools on Kubernetes 1.35 or later. The product guidance instead documents lack of support on Kubernetes 1.37 or later; it does not explicitly resolve the announcement's creation restriction.

Windows Server 2025 is supported starting with Kubernetes 1.32.0. In-place migration from Windows Server 2022 to Windows Server 2025 is limited to Kubernetes 1.32–1.36 and is a preview. Other Windows Server version migrations require a new node pool.

The announcement also names Windows Server Annual Channel as a replacement Microsoft planned to support before retirement. The supplied Annual Channel announcement does not confirm current availability or provide an AKS migration procedure.
what.html:
AKS is retiring support for Windows Server 2022 node pools on June 30, 2028, according to the product migration guidance. Microsoft will remove their existing node images on June 30, 2029, after which scaling operations will fail.

The announcement gives a conflicting retirement date of March 15, 2027. It allows continued use on Kubernetes 1.34 and earlier through March 14, 2027 and prohibits creating Windows Server 2022 pools on Kubernetes 1.35 or later. The product guidance instead documents lack of support on Kubernetes 1.37 or later; it does not explicitly resolve the announcement's creation restriction.

Windows Server 2025 is supported starting with Kubernetes 1.32.0. In-place migration from Windows Server 2022 to Windows Server 2025 is limited to Kubernetes 1.32–1.36 and is a preview. Other Windows Server version migrations require a new node pool.

The announcement also names Windows Server Annual Channel as a replacement Microsoft planned to support before retirement. The supplied Annual Channel announcement does not confirm current availability or provide an AKS migration procedure.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance:
1. Identify Windows Server 2022 nodes with kubectl get nodes -o wide. Check your Kubernetes version, node-pool configuration and application compatibility with the target Windows Server version.
2. Select a supported replacement. The product guidance documents Windows Server 2025 starting with Kubernetes 1.32.0. Although the retirement announcement also names Windows Server Annual Channel, the supplied content does not confirm its current AKS availability or migration procedure.
3. Prepare and validate the application image: update the Dockerfile FROM statement, build the image, verify the application and deploy it to a development or test environment. Record the image name or tag.
4. Choose your migration method. In-place migration from Windows Server 2022 to Windows Server 2025 requires Kubernetes 1.32–1.36 and the aks-preview Azure CLI extension version 22.0.0b6 or later. This preview is not intended for production, is excluded from SLAs and limited warranty, and receives best-effort partial support. Use a new node pool for other version changes or unsupported configurations.
5. For in-place migration, use az aks nodepool update to change the OS SKU; the operation automatically reimages the pool. Include --enable-fips-image if the source pool is not already FIPS-enabled. For manual migration, create a new pool and match the original permissions and access. Windows Server 2025 requires a FIPS-enabled image.
6. For manual migration, update the workload YAML's OS SKU node selector and container image, then apply it using kubectl apply -f <filename>. Update pool-specific managed identity access, including gMSA access where used.
7. Verify the target OS, pod placement and application behavior. After manually moving and validating workloads, delete the old pool.

Complete migration before the product guidance's June 30, 2028 support end. The announcement instead directs migration by March 15, 2027; the supplied sources do not explicitly reconcile that conflict. No backup procedure is supplied.

1. Identify Windows Server 2022 nodes with kubectl get nodes -o wide. Check your Kubernetes version, node-pool configuration and application compatibility with the target Windows Server version.
  2. Select a supported replacement. The product guidance documents Windows Server 2025 starting with Kubernetes 1.32.0. Although the retirement announcement also names Windows Server Annual Channel, the supplied content does not confirm its current AKS availability or migration procedure.
  3. Prepare and validate the application image: update the Dockerfile FROM statement, build the image, verify the application and deploy it to a development or test environment. Record the image name or tag.
  4. Choose your migration method. In-place migration from Windows Server 2022 to Windows Server 2025 requires Kubernetes 1.32–1.36 and the aks-preview Azure CLI extension version 22.0.0b6 or later. This preview is not intended for production, is excluded from SLAs and limited warranty, and receives best-effort partial support. Use a new node pool for other version changes or unsupported configurations.
  5. For in-place migration, use az aks nodepool update to change the OS SKU; the operation automatically reimages the pool. Include --enable-fips-image if the source pool is not already FIPS-enabled. For manual migration, create a new pool and match the original permissions and access. Windows Server 2025 requires a FIPS-enabled image.
  6. For manual migration, update the workload YAML's OS SKU node selector and container image, then apply it using kubectl apply -f <filename>. Update pool-specific managed identity access, including gMSA access where used.
  7. Verify the target OS, pod placement and application behavior. After manually moving and validating workloads, delete the old pool.

Complete migration before the product guidance's June 30, 2028 support end. The announcement instead directs migration by March 15, 2027; the supplied sources do not explicitly reconcile that conflict. No backup procedure is supplied.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance:
You are affected if you use Windows Server 2022 node pools in AKS. Product guidance sets support end at June 30, 2028 and image removal at June 30, 2029, when scaling operations will fail. The announcement instead gives March 15, 2027 as retirement; this conflict is not explicitly explained.

The announcement prohibits creating Windows Server 2022 pools on Kubernetes 1.35 or later, while product guidance documents lack of support on Kubernetes 1.37 or later. These statements describe different constraints and do not establish that creation is available on Kubernetes 1.35–1.36.

Migration constraints include:

- Different Windows Server versions cannot coexist within one node pool.
- In-place migration reimages the pool. The documented configurations cover standard Windows Server 2022 containerd Generation 1 and Generation 2 pools. Generation 1-only VM sizes migrate to Windows Server 2025 Generation 1; Generation 2-capable sizes use Generation 2, which can affect image compatibility.
- Manual migration terminates existing pods and deploys replacements according to the updated node selector. A Windows-only selector does not restrict placement to the target Windows Server version.
- A new pool needs matching permissions and updated pool-specific managed identity access to Azure resources.

The sources do not establish automatic workload shutdown, data deletion or retention changes, or retirement-related costs. Your actual resource exposure cannot be determined from these pages.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance:
AKS product migration guidance sets Windows Server 2022 node-pool end of support at June 30, 2028. On June 30, 2029, AKS will remove existing Windows Server 2022 node images, causing scaling operations to fail. Neither milestone establishes automatic shutdown of running workloads.

The supplied retirement announcement instead identifies March 15, 2027, alongside Kubernetes 1.34 end of platform support, and directs migration by that date. The applicable product migration guidance takes precedence here, but the sources conflict and do not explicitly document an extension.

The version restrictions also differ in scope: the announcement prohibits creating Windows Server 2022 pools on Kubernetes 1.35 or later; the migration guidance says Windows Server 2022 is unsupported on Kubernetes 1.37 or later. The supplied content does not explicitly reconcile these restrictions.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance:
Use the documented checks as team-owned migration evidence:

1. Run kubectl get nodes -o wide to identify node OS images.
2. After an in-place migration, run kubectl describe node <node-name> and verify the Windows2025 OS SKU label and Windows Server 2025 OS image.
3. Run kubectl get pods -o wide to check pod status and node placement. Match those nodes to the target OS and validate application behavior. The supplied pod example covers only the default namespace, so it does not establish completion across all workloads.
4. Where managed identities are involved, review update and sign-in activities using the referenced Managed Identity activity guidance.

Follow AKS release notes for announcements and updates. The retirement announcement also points to the AKS public roadmap, but its supplied content contains no usable retirement details or resource-level completion tracker.

For questions, use Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and need technical help, create a support request.
